# Agent trace states

An agent's reply has two parts: the answer, and the work behind it. Most UIs get the second one wrong in one of two directions: a wall of raw tool JSON, or a spinner that says nothing until it stops. AI Elements, now 21 copy-in patterns inside shadcn/ui, settles it with one primitive, **Trace**: a list of lines, each an icon, a title, an optional description and a status, that can expand, link out or open a sheet, and can nest (a subagent's own steps). [[states-are-the-work]] applies: each of these states is designed, not left to the default.

## Map the real state, every time

For an AI SDK tool part (`tool-<name>`, keyed by `toolCallId`):

| Tool state | Line | Title |
|---|---|---|
| `input-streaming`, `input-available` | running while the chat streams; **error** once it has stopped | "Running …" / "Failed to run …" |
| `approval-requested` | not a line: a question outside the trace, Deny (outline) and Approve (primary) | — |
| `approval-responded` | running if approved | "Running …" / "Denied …" |
| `output-available` | done | "Ran …" |
| `output-error` | error, with the error text | "Failed to run …" |
| `output-denied` | done | "Denied …" |

The exception: a client-side tool waits in `input-available` until the app supplies its output. That is **waiting**, not failed.

## The rest of the work

- **Reasoning** opens while it streams and closes when it ends, unless the person toggled it, whose choice wins (`open = userChoice ?? running`). Show the disclosure only once text exists. Its duration is measured on the server; the SDK does not time it.
- **Several steps of one run** are lines in one trace, not a stack of bespoke collapsibles.
- **Plans, tasks and todo queues** update in place: a data part with a stable id replaces the last one, so the list ticks rather than grows.
- **Sources** dedupe by URL and fall back to the hostname when there is no title; they come last, after the answer.
- **Context used** is (input + output tokens) ÷ the model's window, which the app supplies.
- **Message actions** are quiet icon buttons with tooltips under the reply: Copy swaps to a check for about 2 s, thumbs up and down are toggles with `aria-pressed`, Edit puts the text back in the field.
- **Running** shimmers the line's title; under reduced motion it holds still and the word carries it ([[reduced-motion-by-pointer]]).

## Questions to ask in review

Astryx's agentic-states record leaves these open on purpose; ask each of a new agent UI: does thinking need a state distinct from ordinary processing? Is user-visible rationale marked as authored content, without implying access to hidden reasoning? Does streaming text look unfinished without pulling the eye from finished text? Which tool details are useful, and do the rest stay collapsed? Does a required human answer outrank passive progress? Are syncing and synced distinct from processing and success? Does partially rendered generated UI hide its churn?

## Gotcha

Inferring "done" from the spinner stopping marks every interrupted tool call as a success. Map from the part's state, and treat *still running after the stream ended* as the failure it is.

Design card interiors intentionally — whitespace, hover-only actions, subtle icons. tags: [components, cards] --- # Cards design Cards are easy to over-use and easier to over-nest. A well-designed card is a self-contained unit of content with intentional interior structure. Nested cards are usually a sign the design has lost its way. ## The no-nesting rule ``` Bad: card > card > card (three borders, three shadows, three radii) Good: card > content with internal hierarchy (one border, one shadow) ``` If you find yourself reaching for a card-inside-a-card, the inner card is probably: - A list item (use a `
  • ` with hover state, not a card). - A heading + content block (use typography hierarchy, not a wrapped container). - A status indicator (use a badge or chip inline, not a card). The exception: a *single* call-out card inside a parent card (e.g., a pinned highlight) can work. Beyond that, you're overusing the pattern. ## Designing card interiors A card is a small layout problem. Its interior deserves the same care as a screen: - **Whitespace beats borders for separating sections.** A 24px gap between header and body reads cleaner than a 1px divider. - **Hover-only actions** for editing, deleting, more options. Show them on `:hover` (or always on touch). - **Subtle icons** to anchor information types — but don't add an icon to every line. One per card maximum, usually. - **Variable density inside.** A list of recent activity inside the card can be tighter than the card's outer padding. Example card structure: ```tsx Project Atlas {/* Edit, Archive, Share */} 12 files · Updated 2h ago

    Brief description that fits on 2–3 lines max.

     Active     ``` ## Card hover states Most cards in a grid should have a hover state. See [[hover-states-subtle]] — the right answer is usually: - 1px lift (`transform: translateY(-1px)`). - Slight background-color shift on the card body. - Hover-only action buttons fade in. NOT a 4px lift, NOT a large shadow change. Those are the [[ai-default-tells]]. ## Cards as the wrong choice Cards aren't always the right container. Alternatives: | Content | Better than card | |---|---| | A list of items the user reads top-to-bottom | Use a list with hover rows | | A single highlighted piece of content | Use typography hierarchy + whitespace | | Status that updates frequently | Inline badge or pill | | Tabular comparison data | Use a real table ([[data-is-content]]) | | Long-form content | Use sections with headers, not cards | If your screen is *all* cards, it probably has no hierarchy. Some content earns a card; most doesn't. ## When to apply - Grid of equally-weighted items (projects, products, users). - Bento layouts on landing pages. - Dashboards with discrete widgets. - Anywhere the content is self-contained and benefits from a clear boundary. ## When NOT to apply - Long-form reading. - Single-focus screens (each card competes with the focus). - Lists where every row is just text + metadata (use rows, not cards). - Inside an already-cardified container. ## Reference ```css .card { --pad: 16px; /* 12 small, 20 large: one value on every side */ --inner: max(4px, calc(var(--radius) - var(--pad))); /* radius for a group inside */ display: grid; gap: 12px; padding: var(--pad); box-shadow: inset 0 0 0 1px var(--line), 0 1px 2px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.04); /* ring drawn inside */ } ``` - **Bad → good:** `padding: 20px 16px 12px` plus a title `margin-bottom: 18px` → one padding value, spacing from `gap`, and the ring inset so it never adds to the padding; measure the inset to the avatar's and button's edges, not their words. - **Gold example:** `stageshow/examples/cards/`: a comment card, a flush card split by edge-to-edge rules, and a group inside it drawn as a sunken tone with no shadow and its radius taken from the card's. Benji's call differs on separation: his `Card` spaces children 12px apart and divides sections with 1px rules (`data-flush`), where this node prefers a 24px gap over a divider. - **Check:** screenshot at 2x and measure the four insets (equal) and the inner radius (outer minus padding, never under 4px); a card whose bottom inset differs from its top is the fix. ## Gotcha The nested-radius rule from [[border-radius]] applies: if a card has `border-radius: 12px` and contains a media (image, video) that fills the top, the media needs `border-radius: 12px 12px 0 0` to match. # Component confusables

Some components look alike and get used interchangeably. The cost is silent: the wrong one breaks an expectation the user already has. Pick by *behaviour*, not by appearance. This is [[articulate-precisely]] applied to the component layer — naming the difference is choosing the right one.

## Tooltip vs popover

The line is interactivity:

- **Tooltip** — a hover/focus label that explains an element. It *cannot* hold interactive content. No links, no buttons — the pointer can't move into it without dismissing it.
- **Popover** — a click-anchored overlay that *can* hold interactive content: links, buttons, a small form. It stays open until dismissed.

If you need a link inside the floating thing, it is a popover, not a tooltip. A button living in a tooltip is the tell that the wrong primitive was chosen. Both still need [[accessibility-baseline]] focus handling.

## Badge vs tag

The line is ownership and interactivity:

- **Badge** — attached to another element and read-only. Numeric badges imply a count (the "3" on an inbox); word badges ("New", a status) are informational.
- **Tag** — standalone and interactive: selectable, removable, used to categorise or filter. A chip the user can pick up or discard.

A badge is pinned on; a tag is handled. Styling one as the other collapses a real behavioural difference and trains the user to expect the wrong affordance.

## Sheet vs drawer vs dialog

All three are overlays; the difference is origin and intent — and all three share the same focus-and-dismissal rules as a modal (see [[tray-rules]]):

- **Dialog / modal** — interrupts the flow centre-screen to demand a decision. Focus trapped, background inert.
- **Sheet** — slides in from a screen edge; common on mobile for secondary nav or contextual actions.
- **Drawer** — a bottom sheet pulled up from the base; a frequent mobile replacement for a dialog.

Reach for a dialog when the choice must be made now; reach for a sheet or drawer when the surface is secondary and dismissible.

## Reference

| Kit part | Behaviour | Motion |
|---|---|---|
| `Tooltip` | Names the icon under a resting cursor; hides on the click; never carries the story | In 0.15s, out 0.1s, 2px of travel |
| `Popover` | Measured from its trigger (right edge on the button's, top 8px below); holds a field, a menu, actions | Surface from scale 0.96 at its origin over 0.24s `cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)`; closes as one object |
| `Badge` | A read-only status pill, with a dot or a glyph beside the label | None; it changes with its status |
| `Chip` | A filter chip with a remove x | Opens and closes its own width over 0.4s `cubic-bezier(0.25, 0.8, 0.25, 1)`, so the chips after it slide |

- **Gold example:** `stageshow/examples/share/` (the popover holds an email field, a role menu and Invite) and `stageshow/examples/gmail/` (the tooltip says "Archive" over the icon and goes on the click).
- **Check:** hover each floating thing, then try to click or Tab into it: anything that takes a click is a popover, a tooltip still showing after its click is a bug, and a badge with an x is really a tag.

## Gotcha

The trap is choosing by how it looks in the design file ("a little floating box") instead of how it behaves. Ask three questions: does the user need to *interact inside* it (popover, not tooltip)? Can they *act on* it (tag, not badge)? Must they decide *now* (dialog, not sheet)? Behaviour picks the component.

## Sources

- *Index — Say Precisely What You Mean*, Emil Kowalski & Glenn Carstens-Peters — [index.how/to/articulate](https://index.how/to/articulate). The components vocabulary these distinctions sharpen; see also [[design-vocabulary]].
- [[tray-rules]] — Benji Taylor's overlay/sheet rules. [[accessibility-baseline]] — the focus and dismissal floor.
- Benji Taylor, Stageshow 1.1.1 (MIT, github.com/benjitaylor/skills, HEAD `299140f`, read 2026-11-07): `stageshow/kit/parts/Tooltip.tsx`, `stageshow/kit/parts/Tooltip.css`, `stageshow/kit/motion/Popover.css`, `stageshow/kit/controls/Badge.tsx`, `stageshow/kit/parts/Chip.tsx`, `stageshow/kit/parts/Chip.css`, `stageshow/examples/share/index.tsx`, `stageshow/examples/gmail/index.tsx`.

# Copy and voice

Microcopy is design. The button label, the empty state, the error message — they ship every day, and the wrong word in any of them quietly ages the product.

This node is the universal rules. For broader content authenticity (real data vs lorem, specific numbers, real photos), see [[content-authenticity]].

## Universal rules

### Voice

- **Active voice.** "Saved your changes" beats "Your changes have been saved."
- **2nd person, addressing the user.** "You can…" beats "Users can…"
- **Be specific.** "Couldn't connect to the server" beats "Something went wrong."
- **Be positive.** "Add another" beats "You can't add fewer than one."
- **Drop the throat-clearing.** "Saved." beats "Awesome, your changes were saved!"

### Capitalization

- **Title Case for headings and buttons.** "Create Project" not "Create project" or "CREATE PROJECT" (uppercase is harder to read — see [[line-length-tracking]]).
- **Sentence case for body and tooltips.** "Click here to learn more" not "Click Here to Learn More."
- **Consistent within a surface.** Don't mix Title Case buttons with sentence-case buttons.

### Numerals + units

- **Numerals for counts.** "3 projects" not "three projects". Even small numbers.
- **Non-breaking space between number and unit.** `3 MB` (3 + nbsp + MB) so it doesn't line-break.
- **Consistent currency decimals.** $5.00 not $5 (in financial / commerce contexts where 2 decimals are the norm).
- **Singular/plural matters.** "1 item" not "1 items".

### Punctuation

- **Typographic quotes.** Use `"` and `'`, not `"` and `'`. Most editors auto-correct.
- **Ellipsis character `…`**, not three dots `...`. Single character; better-rendered.
- **Em-dash `—` for parentheticals.** En-dash `–` for ranges (5–10 items).
- **"&" only where it's part of brand or label**, never in body prose. "Q&A" yes; "Save & Continue" — usually no, just "Save and Continue" or split into two buttons.

## Error messages

A good error message answers three questions:
1. **What went wrong** (specific, not generic).
2. **Why** (if helpful).
3. **What the user can do next** (actionable).

```text
Bad:   Something went wrong.
Bad:   Error: 500 Internal Server Error
OK:    Couldn't save. Network connection lost.
Good:  Couldn't save. Network connection lost. Try again, or check your
       internet connection.
```

Errors should never just announce. They should guide.

## Empty states

A good empty state has:
- **A title** stating what the user is looking at (or *not* looking at).
- **Why it's empty.** "No projects yet" not "Empty."
- **The next action.** "Create your first project →" with the actual link.

See [[empty-loading-states]] for full empty-state design.

## Async status

- **"Saving…"** (with ellipsis) — operation in progress.
- **"Saved"** — complete.
- **"Couldn't save"** — failed.
- **Say it where it happened.** The button that saved says so on itself, and an edited cell is its own confirmation; a toast that repeats it says it twice. A toast earns its place when it carries an action, like Undo (Benji Taylor, Stageshow `examples/form-error`, `examples/table-edit`, `examples/gmail`).
- **`aria-live="polite"`** on the status element so screen readers announce changes. See [[accessibility-baseline]].

## When to apply

Every label, every error, every empty state, every tooltip. Microcopy is the highest leverage / lowest cost design intervention available.

## Reference

```text
Bad:   Invalid email address.                     Good:  Add the domain, like name@company.com
Bad:   [Submit], spinner, toast "Success!"        Good:  Create account → Creating account → Account created, on one button
Bad:   The conversation was successfully moved.   Good:  Conversation archived.  Undo
```

- **Gold example:** `stageshow/examples/form-error/`: the hint ("We'll send a link to confirm it") and the error swap in one lane under the field, and the button's words crossfade in place while its check holds still. `stageshow/examples/gmail/` has the toast.
- Benji's call differs on case: sentence case on titles, labels and buttons ("Create your account", "Create account") unless the real product capitalizes (`stageshow/references/craft.md`, `stageshow/teaching/style.tsx` style-caps), where this node sets Title Case for headings and buttons. Pick one per product and hold it.
- **Check:** render every string at its real width and at 390px: no truncated chip, no wrapped name, no button label that changes the button's height (`stageshow/teaching/details.tsx`, detail-copy); then count the strings that say the same thing and cut all but one.

## Gotcha

Don't be cute in error messages. "Oops! Something tripped on the wires!" is funny once and annoying forever. Error messages get re-read every time the user hits the error — write them for the 10th encounter, not the 1st.

Also: don't put microcopy decisions in code reviews. Microcopy lives in design files and content systems. If you're approving "Save" vs "Save Changes" in a PR, the team is missing a design step.

## Sources

- Vercel Web Interface Guidelines — Copywriting and Content sections.
- Erika Hall — *Conversational Design* on tone, voice, error messages.
- Material Design — writing guidelines.
- Benji Taylor, Stageshow 1.1.1 (MIT, github.com/benjitaylor/skills, HEAD `299140f`, read 2026-11-07): `stageshow/examples/form-error/index.tsx`, `stageshow/examples/gmail/index.tsx`, `stageshow/examples/table-edit/index.tsx`, `stageshow/teaching/details.tsx` (detail-copy), `stageshow/teaching/style.tsx` (style-caps), `stageshow/references/craft.md` (Type: sentence case; Restraint: say it once).

title: dashboard-tells
summary: An app screen is not a landing page. Headline numbers without icon circles or sparklines, at 16–40 px; deltas coloured by good or bad rather than up or down; zero change in grey; numbers right-aligned in tabular figures; one grotesk, 4–9 sizes.
tags: [components, dashboard, kpi, data, tables, app-screens, measured]
---

# Dashboard tells

The generated dashboard is a landing page with numbers on it: four tinted tiles, an icon in a coloured circle on each, a 48 px figure, a green "+100 %" pill and a sparkline nobody reads. taste-skill measured 23 real product screens (17 products, 1440–1512 px) and they share none of it. The data is the content ([[data-is-content]]), and on a real screen the chrome gets out of its way.

## Headline numbers

- **No icon circles, no sparklines** on KPIs: 0 of 23 screens use either. An info icon beside the label is fine.
- **Often no tile at all.** 11 of the 20 screens with headline numbers give a KPI no tile of its own: bare text, or one container split by 1 px dividers. 7 put each number inside the card that explains it, which is often better.
- **Size.** Values 16–40 px, median 26; nothing at 48 px or over. Labels 12–16 px, label above the value, sentence case, in grey. When one figure *is* the screen's answer (a balance, net worth), it runs 30–36 px and at least 1.3× its siblings, and no other number on the screen is larger.
- **1–6 per row**, median 3–4, matching the grid's columns.

## Deltas

- Optional: 9 of the 20 show one. 10–15 px, never larger than the label, with the window in words ("vs prior 30 days").
- **Colour says good or bad, not up or down.** Latency, error rate, cost and churn are better when they fall. A rise in errors in the same green as a rise in visits hides the screen's only bad news.
- **Zero or undefined change is grey.** The commonest failure in the study is a change grown from zero shown as a signal: green "up 100 %" pills, ">999 %", a bold red "0.00 %". Write "+4 (new)" when the prior period was zero, and a grey dash when there is nothing to compare.

## Tables and figures

Numbers right-aligned in tabular figures, with `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` checked to actually change the digit widths. Fixed decimals per metric (money 2, counts 0), a sign on every change, and the sign in the text rather than red on every negative. Only the identity and the key number get the primary ink; the rest is grey. A missing value is a grey dash, a real zero is printed. No zebra rows, no uppercase headers. 17 of 23 put no shadow on resting cards ([[depth-and-nesting]]).

## Type

All 23 use one neo-grotesk, 14 of them alone; a second face has one job (monospace for numbers or IDs). 4–9 sizes per screen, median 6, as a scale like 12/14/16/24. The page title runs 18–32 px. A 50 px title and a 76 px balance make a budgeting screen read as a landing page ([[marketing-vs-product-ui]]).

## Reference

```css
.kpi { font-size: 26px; font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; white-space: nowrap; } /* the unit stays on the figure's line */
td.num { text-align: right; font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; }
.delta[data-tone="bad"] { color: var(--danger); }
.delta[data-tone="none"] { color: var(--text-faint); } /* zero, or nothing to compare */
```

- **Bad → good:** on refresh "1,284" fades out and "1,291" fades in → only the changed digits roll, last digit first, the rest still (Stageshow's `Count`: 700ms, 45ms stagger, tabular figures, the unit in its own box a hair off the last digit); a total that depends on an edited row changes a beat after the commit, not with each key.
- **Gold example:** `stageshow/examples/linear/` (grayscale chrome, colour only on the product's own content marks: status circles, label dots, avatars) and `stageshow/examples/table-edit/` (right-aligned tabular amounts, no toast: the table is the confirmation). Benji's "one number gets to be big; the rest are lines" (`stageshow/references/craft.md`) is this node's single-answer rule.
- **Check:** film a refresh and step it at 40 to 80ms: no column changes width as digits change, no unit wraps onto its own line at 390px, and every coloured delta means good or bad, not up or down.

## Gotcha

These numbers come from 23 screens the skill's owner chose, and the screenshots are private, so the medians cannot be checked and the sample has a taste. The two delta rules don't need the sample: they are logic, and they are the ones to enforce first.

## Sources

title: destructive-actions
summary: Undo beats confirmation for frequent, reversible actions; confirm only what cannot be reversed, affects other people or destroys many items. A confirmation names the action and object in its title, the loss in its body, verb-plus-object on its buttons, focuses the safe button, and asks for the name when an account, workspace or repository is at stake.
tags: [components, destructive, confirmation, undo, copy]
---

# Destructive actions

A confirmation dialog on every delete trains people to click through it, so the one that matters gets clicked through too. Decide **undo or confirm** first; then make whichever you chose impossible to misread.

## Undo or confirm

| The action | Pattern |
|---|---|
| Reversible and frequent — archive, move, delete into a trash | Act at once; offer undo in the result: "Project archived. Undo" |
| Irreversible, one item | Confirm |
| Irreversible, many items | Confirm, with the count |
| Affects other people | Confirm, and name who: "The 8 members of Design lose access." |
| An account, a workspace or a repository | Confirm by typing its name: "Type 'acme-web' to confirm"; the button stays disabled until it matches |

Undo is cheaper for the user and more honest about what happened. It is also the optimistic pattern — the server call can run behind it ([[optimistic-updates]]).

## A confirmation answerable without the body

- **Title** names the action and the object: "Delete 'Q3 report'?" — never "Are you sure?".
- **Body** says what is lost and what cannot come back, with counts: "This permanently deletes the report and its 4 comments."
- **Buttons** are verb plus object: `Delete report` and `Cancel` — never `Yes` and `No`.
- **Focus** lands on the least destructive action, so a reflexive Enter cancels ([[keyboard-patterns]]).
- **The destructive button looks destructive** and nothing else does: the danger hue only on destruction, and a danger hue at least 15° of OKLCH hue from the accent. A red brand gives destruction a distinct treatment instead — outlined, with an icon — or it reads as the primary action ([[palette-step-roles]]).

## The undo toast is not a normal toast

It carries an action, so it stays until dismissed or gets at least 5 s and pauses while hovered or focused ([[wcag-thresholds]]). It is announced with `role="status"`, and focus never jumps to it ([[screen-reader-announcements]]). A toast whose only undo link vanishes on a timer turns a reversible action into an irreversible one.

## Reference

```text
Bad:   Archive → "Are you sure?" [Yes] [No] → the row vanishes in one frame
Good:  Archive → the row folds away and the rows below close the gap, the count drops 12 → 11,
       "Conversation archived." rises 320ms later with Undo → Undo folds the row back in and the count returns
```

- **Danger fill:** `background: var(--danger); color: #fff`, hovered one step of its own colour (`color-mix(in srgb, var(--danger), #000 10%)`), never a gray swap; it is the only button in the set with that fill.
- **Gold example:** `stageshow/examples/gmail/` (the product's own Material Symbols, a tooltip naming Archive, a reset whose seen cause is Undo) and the `danger` variant in `stageshow/kit/controls/Button.css`.
- **Check:** film archive then undo and step it: the row leaves and comes back as one object with the rows below moving with it, nothing pops, and the toast never covers the row it is about.

## Gotcha

"Delete" in a menu next to "Duplicate" and "Rename" with no separation is the most common destructive path that has neither undo nor confirmation. If undo is impossible and a dialog is too heavy, the third option is a distinct treatment — a separated group, the danger colour, a two-step press. One of the three must exist: an unguarded destructive action is a top-severity finding.

## Sources

- Jakub Krehel, interfaces skills (MIT, github.com/jakubkrehel/skills, HEAD `592aedc`, read 2026-10-25): `skills/better-writing/SKILL.md` (**Undo beats confirmation**), `patterns.md` (destructive flows), `better-accessibility/focus-and-keyboard.md` (focus the least destructive action), `better-colors/palette-structure.md` (the 15° status rule), `better-interface/SKILL.md` (the escalation trigger).
- Benji Taylor, Stageshow 1.1.1 (MIT, github.com/benjitaylor/skills, HEAD `299140f`, read 2026-11-07): `stageshow/examples/gmail/index.tsx`, `stageshow/kit/controls/Button.css`, `stageshow/kit/controls/Button.tsx` (the `danger` variant), `stageshow/references/motion.md` (Loops: every reset has a cause).

title: drawing-toolbar
summary: A drawing or markup tool inside a product — a toolbar that changes shape instead of swapping panels, pens in a tray rather than a row of icons, strokes whose width answers speed or direction, an eraser that removes area, export that matches the screen exactly, defaults that are the shipping version, and a bar that stands up on the side of a phone. From Benji Taylor's Drawesome.
tags: [components, toolbar, drawing, annotation, morph, canvas]
---

# Drawing toolbar

Annotating a screenshot, marking up a frame, circling the bit that is wrong: many creative tools need a little drawing, and most bolt on a row of icons over a canvas. Drawesome is the version worth copying.

## The bar morphs, it does not swap

One bar, many shapes. Pick a colour and the row of pens becomes the palette; open size and it becomes two sliders; minimise it and it rolls into a disc that still shows the tool in hand. Each state morphs into the next as one object ([[fly-not-teleport]], [[shared-letter-morph]]); no panel pops open beside it. The minimised disc keeps the current tool visible, so collapsing it loses no context.

## Tools behave like the thing they are named after

- **Pens in a tray beat a row of icons:** drawn as objects with light on them (Apple's markup tools are the reference), so the tool in hand is obvious at a glance.
- **Width answers the hand.** Pencil, pen and brush thin as the stroke speeds up; fineliner and highlighter keep a constant width; a fountain pen answers direction, thick one way and a hairline the other.
- **The eraser removes area, not whole strokes**, so part of a line can go and the rest stay.
- **Shift locks a stroke to the nearest of eight directions.** Each pen has a single-key shortcut shown in its tooltip; `E` erases, `[` and `]` resize, ⌘Z and ⇧⌘Z undo and redo. Single-key shortcuts switch off where the page has its own.
- **The picked tool eases in.** Its fill and colour fade in over about 150ms and back out the same, never switching on in one frame (Benji Taylor, Stageshow `references/motion.md`).

## Defaults are the shipping version

Opinionated defaults that feel right untouched; every prop exists to turn something off or move it, not to make it good. The canvas can be transparent so the page's own paper shows through, and export (`toSvg`, `toPng` at 2–3× for print) returns exactly what is on screen, erasing included. Strokes are plain data, saved as they are and restored as they were.

## Narrow screens

The bar is as wide as its tools, so on a phone it runs off both sides. Under about 680px stand it up as a rail on the left edge and trim the toolset; drop the controls that would stack taller than the canvas (keep size, drop opacity). A control whose contents are all switched off removes its button too ([[viewport-custom-design]]).

## When to apply

Adding drawing, markup or annotation to a product. To assemble a full whiteboard, a canvas SDK suits better ([[tldraw-canvas]]); for annotating a UI for an agent, see [[agentation-workflow]].

## Reference

Bad: the pen tray pops open as a second panel beside the bar in one frame, and the picked pen turns blue instantly.
Good: a 36px disc widens into a 200px bar over 0.4s; its glyph fades out in 0.12s and the 28px tools fade in 0.16s after a 0.22s wait, so the bar is one object changing shape.

```css
.bar { width: 36px; border-radius: 18px; overflow: hidden;
  transition: width .4s cubic-bezier(0.19, 1, 0.22, 1), border-radius .4s cubic-bezier(0.19, 1, 0.22, 1); }
.bar[data-open] { width: 200px; border-radius: 20px; padding: 0 6px; }
.bar__glyph { transition: opacity .16s ease .22s; }
.bar[data-open] .bar__glyph { opacity: 0; transition: opacity .12s ease; }
.bar__tools { opacity: 0; transition: opacity .12s ease; }
.bar[data-open] .bar__tools { opacity: 1; transition: opacity .16s ease .22s; }
```

Gold example: `stageshow/examples/hero-demo/hero.css` (the annotation toolbar's disc-to-bar morph, round 28px tools 3px apart, a 1px by 12px divider); `stageshow/examples/figma/index.tsx` for a docked tool row (26px tools, 14px icons at one stroke).
Check: film the open and the close at 40 to 80ms steps: no frame shows the disc glyph and the tools both at full opacity, and over the canvas the pointer is already a crosshair as it crosses the edge, not after it lands.

## Gotcha

A drawn stroke at constant width with a hard round cap reads as a vector tool, not a pen. If the tool is called a pen, the width must answer speed; if it must not, call it a fineliner.

## Sources

- Benji Taylor, *Drawesome*, [benji.org/drawesome](https://benji.org/drawesome) and the `drawesome` npm package (read 2026-11-01). Paraphrased.
- Benji Taylor, Stageshow 1.1.1 (MIT, github.com/benjitaylor/skills, HEAD `299140f`, read 2026-11-07): `stageshow/examples/hero-demo/hero.css`, `stageshow/examples/hero-demo/HeroDemo.tsx` (crosshair while the toolbar is on), `stageshow/examples/figma/index.tsx`, `stageshow/examples/figma/figma.css`, `stageshow/references/motion.md` (the cursor's kind; a state the click sets).
- Related: [[morphing-icons]], [[tray-rules]], [[keyboard-patterns]].

title: forms-behavior
summary: The semantics the platform gives you, then the details — label wiring, right input type and keyboard hints, 16px, focus-visible, autocomplete where it helps, decorations over the input, autofocus only on desktop modals, a real form so Enter submits, buttons that disable while submitting and re-enable in finally, failed submits that keep every value, no dead zones, confirmed destruction, prefilled everything, drafts that survive a refresh.
tags: [components, forms, inputs, buttons, keyboard]
---

# Forms — behavior

Forms are where users do real work, and they notice every rough edge: the label that doesn't focus the input, the page that zooms on iOS, the button that fires twice, the Enter key that does nothing. None of it is hard; it is easy to forget. [[forms-validation]] owns *when* to validate and how errors look; this node owns everything else a form has to do.

## Wire the platform first

- **Every input gets an associated label** — `for`/`id` or wrapping — so clicking the label focuses the field.
- **Right `type`** (`email`, `tel`, `url`, `number`, `search`, `password`): the correct mobile keyboard, native validation, and autofill come free.
- **Inputs, textareas, and selects at ≥ 16px** on touch viewports (see [[line-behavior]] for why not `maximum-scale`).
- **`:focus-visible`, never bare `outline: none`.** Keyboard users get the ring; mouse users don't see it on every click. Keep the ring neutral (grey, black, white) unless a focus token exists.
- **Real `<button>` elements.** A `<div onClick>` is invisible to keyboards and screen readers. Default `type="button"`.

## Browser behaviors, curated

Keep `autocomplete` **on** for identity, address, and payment fields — there it helps. Turn `spellcheck` and `autocomplete` **off** for usernames, search, codes, and slugs, and suppress password-manager overlays (`data-1p-ignore`, `data-lpignore`) where they don't belong. Ask for the keyboard you need: `inputmode="numeric"` for codes, `"decimal"` for amounts, `autocomplete="one-time-code"` on verification fields, and `enterkeyhint` (`search`, `send`, `done`) so the return key says what it does. Usernames, handles and codes also take `autocapitalize="none"` and `autocorrect="off"`, or iOS capitalises the first letter and swaps in a dictionary word. Login passwords take `current-password`, signup and change-password take `new-password`.

## Decorations, focus, submission

- **Prefix/suffix icons overlay the input** (absolutely positioned, padding reserving room), never siblings. A sibling icon does nothing when clicked and the border lies about the hit area. Clickable decorations (clear, search) refocus the input.
- **Autofocus the first input when a desktop modal opens; never on touch** — it shoves the keyboard into the user's face. Gate it on `matchMedia("(pointer: coarse)")`, not on screen width.
- **Wrap inputs in a `<form>`** so Enter submits. Textareas submit on Cmd/Ctrl+Enter.
- **Disable the submit control while the request is in flight** and change its label to say what's happening; that is the double-submit fix. Keep its width fixed so "Saving…" doesn't shove neighbours, and re-enable it in `finally`, or one failed request locks the form for good.
- **The pressed button answers on itself.** Its new label goes in the same button; never swap in a second button or a banner for the new state (Benji Taylor, Stageshow `references/motion.md`).
- **A failed submit says so and keeps every value.** `fetch` does not throw on a 500, so check `ok`; a `catch` that only logs is a silent failure; calling `reset()` before the response is checked wipes the user's work. Put the message beside the form and the field-level server errors beside their fields ([[forms-validation]]).
- **Press feedback** `scale(0.97)` on `:active` through a ~150ms transition — see [[responsive-feedback]].
- **Surface the shortcut** in the button's tooltip ("Save (⌘S)"), bound to Cmd on macOS and Ctrl elsewhere.

## Rows, danger, prefill

- **No dead zones.** The control, the label, and the gap between them are all clickable — wrap the row in one `<label>` or make the label `flex: 1`.
- **Destructive actions are confirmed** and spatially separated from the primary action, through the project's dialog primitive with a button that names the outcome ("Delete project"), never `window.confirm()` and never "OK". Prefer easy undo everywhere the action is reversible ([[destructive-actions]]).
- **Prefill everything you can** from the logged-in user and the link context: a "change username" link lands on a form already carrying the current value, and a signup reached from an invite reads the `?email=` it carries.
- **Long forms survive an accident.** An editor, a multi-step flow or a settings page warns on `beforeunload` while dirty, or keeps its draft in `sessionStorage`, so a stray back-swipe or refresh costs nothing.
- **Build on accessible primitives** (Base UI, Radix, React Aria) rather than hand-rolling focus management. The bar — focus, ARIA, keyboard — is non-negotiable whichever library you pick.

## When to apply

Any form, input, search field, login/signup, settings page, checkout, or submit handler — building or reviewing.

## Reference

Bad: "Create account" is replaced by a spinner and "Creating…" centred as one group, so icon and words slide as the group's width changes, then the button vanishes for a success banner.
Good: the idle label and the busy group are two layers in one grid cell that crossfade; inside the group a 14px check holds still while "Creating account" crossfades to "Account created", and the 38px full-width button turns success green on itself.

```css
.submit { display: grid; grid-template-areas: 'stack'; place-items: center; height: 38px; }
.submit__layer { grid-area: stack; display: inline-flex; align-items: center; gap: 8px;
  opacity: 0; transition: opacity .25s ease; text-box: trim-both cap alphabetic; }
.submit__layer[data-on] { opacity: 1; transition-delay: .08s; }
```

Gold example: `stageshow/examples/form-error/` (`index.tsx` and `form.css`).
Benji's call differs: a kit `Button` that is not full width crossfades its label and eases its width so neighbours move with it, where this node fixes the width; in a full-width submit both rules hold.
Check: film the submit at 40 to 80ms steps: the check never moves sideways, no frame shows both labels at full strength, and a forced 500 brings the idle label back with every value still in its field.

## Gotcha

Auto-advancing verification-code inputs feel clever until someone needs to correct a digit. Waiting for Tab is safer; if you auto-advance, Backspace must move back and select.

title: forms-validation
summary: Validate at input, not on submit. Inline errors beat error summaries. Soft validation while typing, hard validation on blur.
tags: [components, forms, validation]
---

# Forms — inline validation

The on-submit error summary is dead. Modern forms validate at the field level, inline, as the user moves through them.

## The validation cadence

1. **While typing — soft signals only.** Don't fire red borders or error text on keystroke. The user is still composing. The only allowed feedback while typing is *positive* — a green check appearing when the field becomes valid.
2. **On blur — hard validation.** When the user leaves the field, validate. Fire the error if it fails. This matches user intent: "I'm done with this field; tell me if it's wrong."
2a. **After an error has shown, re-validate on change.** Once a field is in error, check it on every keystroke so the message clears the moment the value is fixed. Making the user blur again to see that they fixed it reads as the form still being cross.
3. **On submit — final pass.** Catch anything blur-validation missed (cross-field rules, server-side checks). If errors exist, scroll to the *first* invalid field and focus it.

The cardinal sin: validating on every keystroke and showing errors mid-typing. This punishes the user for an in-progress action and reads as nagging.

## Error display

Each errored field has:

- **Border color** — `var(--danger)` outline (1px, slightly stronger than default).
- **Background tint** (optional) — very subtle, `rgba(danger, 0.04)`.
- **Inline error message** — below the field, in danger color, 13px–14px. Don't bury it in a sidebar.
- **A reserved lane** — the hint and the error swap in one fixed-height line under the field, there from the first frame, so an error never moves the form (Benji Taylor, Stageshow `examples/form-error`).
- **Optional: shake animation on the error fire.** See [[multi-segment-shake]]. Use only on submit, not on blur (too aggressive otherwise).

```tsx
<FormField>
  <Label>Email</Label>
  <Input
    value={email}
    onBlur={validateEmail}
    aria-invalid={hasError}
    aria-describedby="email-error"
  />
  {hasError && (
    <ErrorMessage id="email-error">
      Email looks invalid. Try the format name@example.com.
    </ErrorMessage>
  )}
</FormField>
```

## Error copy

Bad error copy:
> "Invalid input."
> "Email is invalid."
> "Please enter a valid email."

Good error copy:
> "Email looks invalid. Try the format name@example.com."

Rules:
- Tell the user *what* is wrong.
- Tell them *how to fix it*.
- Skip "Please."
- Don't say "Invalid" — say what was expected.
- Sound like a person, not a 1990s database.

## Success states

Valid fields can show a subtle green check inside the input on blur. This is optional but rewards the user for getting a field right. Don't overdo it — checks on every field becomes noise. Use for fields where validity is non-obvious (email format, password strength) and skip for trivially-valid ones (first name).

## Multi-field validation

For rules that involve multiple fields (password confirmation, date range start ≤ end), validate when the *second* field blurs, not the first. The first field can't be wrong in isolation; only the relationship is wrong.

```tsx
function PasswordFields({ password, confirm, setConfirmError }) {
  return (
    <>
      <Input name="password" />
      <Input
        name="confirm"
        onBlur={() => setConfirmError(confirm !== password ? "Doesn't match." : null)}
      />
    </>
  );
}
```

## Server-side validation

Server errors (email already in use, network error) come back after submit. Handle them by:

- Scrolling to the relevant field.
- Replacing the inline error message with the server message.
- NOT clearing what the user typed. Never make the user retype.

## When to apply

Every form: signup, login, settings, payment, anything.

## When NOT to apply

- Single-input search boxes — don't validate, just search.
- Free-form comments / chat messages — no "wrong" answer to validate.
- Inline edits of single fields (rename, status change) — validate on Enter or commit, not on blur (the user might be navigating elsewhere with the value intact).

## Reference

Bad: "Email is invalid." appears under the field on blur and pushes Password and the button down a line.
Good: the field owns an 18px lane from the start; its hint ("We'll send a link to confirm it") gives way to "Add the domain, like name@company.com", said by the danger ring and the line together, and the moment the ending is typed the ring turns calm, a check appears and the hint comes back.

```css
.lane { height: 18px; } /* always there, so the error never moves the form */
.box { transition: box-shadow .2s ease; }
.field[data-focused] .box { box-shadow: inset 0 0 0 1px var(--accent), 0 0 0 3px var(--accent-soft); }
.field[data-status="error"] .box { box-shadow: inset 0 0 0 1px var(--danger), 0 0 0 3px var(--danger-soft); }
```

Gold example: `stageshow/examples/form-error/` (type, error, fix, send) with the ring states in `stageshow/kit/controls/Field.css`.
Check: screenshot the form clean and in error at phone width and diff them: only the ring and the lane's words differ; no label, field or button has moved, and the error copy names the fix, not the fault.

## Gotcha

`required` on every field is lazy. Mark *only* the fields that genuinely require user input as required. Optional fields should clearly indicate "Optional" — don't leave the user guessing whether a missing value will fail submit.

Also: don't disable the submit button until the form is valid. It tells the user *nothing* about why. Better to let the click happen, run validation, and surface the errors clearly.

## Sources

- guidelines.sh — "Validate forms inline at input."
- Material Design — form patterns.
- Stripe — best-in-class form copy.
- Benji Taylor, Stageshow 1.1.1 (MIT, github.com/benjitaylor/skills, HEAD `299140f`, read 2026-11-07): `stageshow/examples/form-error/index.tsx`, `stageshow/examples/form-error/form.css`, `stageshow/kit/controls/Field.css`.
- Related: [[multi-segment-shake]], [[states-are-the-work]], [[empty-loading-states]], [[screen-reader-announcements]] (how the error is heard), [[interfaces-reconciliation]] (blur vs submit timing).

title: icon-systems
summary: Never mix icon packs. 10-32px range. Match stroke to font weight. Lucide is overused.
tags: [components, icons]
---

# Icon systems

Icons are the most replicated UI element in a product. They are also the easiest to get wrong via mismatch — three icons from three different packs at three different stroke widths in the same UI.

## Pick one icon pack

The single most important rule: **never mix icon packs**. The eye notices instantly, even if the user can't articulate why the UI feels off.

If you started with Material Icons and now want a feature that needs a custom icon, draw the custom icon to match Material's style (rounded, filled, 24px viewbox). Don't reach for Heroicons "just for this one."

To fetch icons, `better-icons` searches Iconify's sets from the CLI or an MCP server. Always pass `--prefix <your pack>`: its similar-icon tool and usage ranking pull from other packs, which this rule forbids. It never shows a set's license, so check the license yourself. Then run the [[svg-creation]] cleanup.

## Packs worth considering

| Pack | Style | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| **Lucide** | Outline, 24×24 | Solid default but overused — pick Phosphor or Hugeicons if you want differentiation |
| **Phosphor** | Multi-weight outline | More personality than Lucide, same coverage |
| **Hugeicons** | Wide library | Less common, distinctive |
| **Tabler** | Outline, 1.5px stroke | Cleaner than Lucide at small sizes |
| **Iconoir** | Outline, hand-drawn feel | Editorial / blog energy |
| **Heroicons** | Outline + solid pairs | Tailwind ecosystem |
| **Material Symbols** | Filled, variable | Apps that already use Material |

## Sizing

| Use | Size |
|---|---|
| Inline with body text | 16px |
| Toolbar buttons | 20px |
| Primary navigation | 20–24px |
| Hero / empty state | 32–48px |
| Marketing | 24–96px |

Below 14px, most icon packs lose detail. Above 32px, hand-drawn or larger-viewBox icons fare better than 24px-viewBox stretched up.

## Match stroke weight to font weight

If your font is **500 (Medium)**, your outline icons should have a **1.75–2px stroke** at 24px.
If your font is **400 (Regular)**, your icons should have a **1.5px stroke**.

Phosphor's "regular" weight is 1.5px; "bold" is 2.5px. Pick the one that matches your type.

## Icon transformations, not crossfades

When toggling an icon (e.g., chevron expand/collapse, play/pause, sun/moon), **rotate or transform** rather than crossfade between two icons. See [[fly-not-teleport]].

- Chevron up/down: rotate 180°.
- Play/pause: replace via opacity *but* if you have the bandwidth, draw a single morphing path.
- Sun/moon: morph via shared geometry (lucide-animated.com has examples).

See [[animations-dev-curriculum]] for the canonical resource on icon animation.

## Drawing and meaning

- Below ~12px, swap outline icons for the filled variant; 1px strokes vanish. Snap coordinates to whole pixels so 1× screens don't blur.
- Round caps by default; square caps read unfinished. Union multipath icons into one path with one fill.
- Don't upscale: a 16px icon at 48px keeps its spindly stroke. Redraw it heavier. Favicons get a simplified mark hinted for 16px ([[svg-creation]]).
- One icon, one meaning: a chevron can't mean both "expand" and "next page"; a star can't mean both favourite and rating (heart for favourite).
- Pairs that differ only by a 180° turn (upload/download) need a second cue, such as a label or a baseline bar.
- 6–8px between an icon and its label; ambiguous metaphors (the floppy disk) get the text label.
- Each icon is one opaque colour. A translucent ink paints darker wherever strokes cross (onion skin); for a lighter icon pick a lighter opaque gray (Benji Taylor, Stageshow `teaching/style.tsx`).

## Illustration cohesion

Illustrations obey the icon system: same stroke weight, about three colours recoloured to the UI's tokens, light falling from the same side as the UI's shadows, one perspective per scene, negative space drawn in rather than padded on afterwards. Complexity matches the spot (a tooltip gets a small mark, not a scene), and they get redrawn, not scaled, for larger slots. Generic blob-and-character packs read as no budget; a typographic treatment or nothing beats them.

## When to apply

- Setting up a new design system: pick the pack, document it, lock it.
- Reviewing a PR that introduces a new icon: check the pack source.
- Auditing an existing UI: grep for `<svg>` elements from different packs.

## Reference

Bad: deploy-status glyphs drawn for the screen, each in a different-hued squircle, one filled beside two outlined.
Good: three icons from one pack at 16px and `strokeWidth={1.75}`, all in the one icon ink (`#707074` in Stageshow's light tokens); only the status itself carries colour; icon buttons are `flex: none`, even glyphs in even boxes.

| Context | Pack |
|---|---|
| The product ships its own set | that set (Gmail: Material Symbols paths) |
| Apple chrome | SF-style glyphs |
| Anything else | one chosen on purpose: Phosphor, Iconoir, Radix, Tabler, Heroicons; Lucide deliberately |

Gold example: `stageshow/teaching/style.tsx`, pairs `style-icons` and `style-onion`; `stageshow/examples/gmail/index.tsx` for a product's own family used throughout.
Benji's call differs: filled glyphs start at 14px and under (and in tinted tiles), where this node switches at about 12px.
Check: contact-sheet every toolbar, nav and list at the shown size: no filled glyph sits beside outlined ones (Stageshow's film names it `mixed icons`), none lands on a half pixel once motion ends, and a grep finds one icon package.

## Gotcha

Icon stroke is `stroke-width`, not `border-width`. Setting `stroke-width: 2` on a 16px icon yields a different visual weight than 2px on a 24px icon (the smaller icon looks heavier). Either scale stroke proportionally or use a variable-weight icon pack like Phosphor.

## Sources

- guidelines.sh — "Never mix icon packs; match stroke to font weight; Lucide is overused."
- lucide-animated.com — icon animation patterns.
- Phosphor Icons — weight system documentation.
- Emil Kowalski's design-engineering practice, distilled by AgentsORG — the drawing, meaning and illustration rules.

title: interaction-personality
summary: Unique microinteractions, easter eggs, contextual feedback, sound. Personality lives in how the product responds, not how it looks.
tags: [components, interaction, personality, easter-eggs, sound]
---

# Interaction personality

Two products with identical visual design can feel completely different based on how they *respond* to the user. Personality lives in interactions, not in static screens.

## What "interaction personality" means

- A hover state that does something specific to this product, not a generic 1px shift.
- A success state that *celebrates*, even briefly, not a silent "Saved.".
- An error state that explains in a voice (see [[forms-validation]] copy).
- A button that has a tiny physical response (slight squish, subtle haptic on touch).
- A loading state that informs ("Fetching your last 30 days…") instead of spinning anonymously.
- An empty state that suggests a next step in the product's voice, not "No data."
- Easter eggs — hidden, never-prompted small delights for users who explore.

The total is what users mean when they say "the product feels alive."

## Easter eggs — when they're earned

Easter eggs work when they:
- Reward exploration without depending on it (no user must find them).
- Match the product's tone (a financial app's easter egg should still be on-brand).
- Are cheap to maintain (don't ship a complex hidden feature that breaks silently).
- Appear at moments of natural curiosity (404 page, settings deep-dive, long-press, secret keyboard combo).

Classic spots:
- **404 page** — the most-explored "broken" page in any product. Most companies put a generic robot there. Put something specific.
- **Long-press on logo** — credits, a thank-you, a small animation.
- **Settings → About** — version number that flips on click, a hidden joke, a contributors list.
- **Konami-code-style sequences** — for the truly curious.
- **First-of-its-kind moments** — first project created, first 100th visit, etc.

What easter eggs are NOT for:
- Surprising users in the middle of a critical flow (signup, payment).
- Adding personality the product otherwise lacks (you can't easter-egg your way out of bad core UX).

## Imperfect timing — varied micro-delays

Generic animation has uniform timing — every button responds the same way, every hover state has the same duration. Products with personality often vary timing slightly:

- Hover delays of 80ms on one component, 120ms on another, deliberately.
- A "Save" button that responds at 100ms; a "Delete" button that responds at 200ms (the 100ms extra reads as deliberation, which is right for destructive actions).
- A "Done" success state that holds for 800ms before fading; a "Continue" state that exits at 200ms.

This is the opposite of design-tokens-make-everything-consistent. Tokens are right for *visual* properties. Timing has more room for narrative pacing.

## Contextual feedback

Error messages, success states, and confirmations should reflect the user's specific action.

| Generic | Contextual |
|---|---|
| "Saved." | "Saved your 3 changes." |
| "Item deleted." | "Deleted project Atlas." |
| "Network error." | "Couldn't reach our server. Trying again in 4s…" |
| "Success!" | "Sent to 47 recipients." |

Specificity costs you almost nothing and signals attention. The agent doing the action knows what was done — surface it.

- **The answer lands on the thing that was pressed.** A button whose label changes changes on itself; a draft becomes the posted comment in place (Benji Taylor, Stageshow `references/motion.md`).

## Sound design (use sparingly)

Sound is a personality lever most products skip entirely. When done well:

- Tied to *specific* interactions, not generic events. A send-message ping is fine; a beep on every button click is grating.
- Designed by someone, not pulled from a stock library. Stock UI sounds are tells.
- Off by default with a clear toggle. Most users will keep it off, but the ones who keep it on become attached.
- Synced precisely to the visual animation. The sound and the motion are one event.

Examples done well: Linear's command palette open sound, Apple's "swoosh" on Mail send (in earlier versions), Honk's [bespoke sound design tied to each interaction](https://benji.org/honkish).

Examples done poorly: Microsoft Office's pre-2007 default sounds. Discord's default ping (lovable, but obviously stock).

The sound cluster goes deeper: [[sound-decision-framework]] for whether, [[sound-palette]] for the family, [[sound-motion-sync]] for timing.

## When to apply

- Consumer products where personality is a competitive advantage.
- Brand-led products (financial apps with attitude, music apps, social apps).
- Products with a strong founding voice that the team wants to preserve at scale.
- Onboarding flows specifically — every first impression is a personality opportunity.

## When NOT to apply

- B2B power-user productivity tools where consistency and predictability win. Adding personality to an analyst's dashboard slows them down.
- Healthcare, finance, or other contexts where users want the product to be *calm* and reliable, not playful.
- Anywhere the personality would conflict with the brand's primary value (a "professional" service shouldn't easter-egg about pizza).

## Reference

Bad: Resolve is pressed, nothing on it changes, and a generic "Success!" toast drops in at the corner 400ms later.
Good: the press scales the button to 0.97 at once; its label crossfades to "Resolved" in the same button while its width eases over 0.5s `cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)` so neighbours make room; a reply typed in its `Draft` settles into the posted comment, and "Just now" fades in on the name's line.

| Job | Timing |
|---|---|
| Direct feedback (press, hover, toggle) | starts on the input, as fast as the real product |
| A state the click sets | fades in over about 150ms |
| Storytelling (a result arriving, a number counting up) | may take longer than the action that caused it |

Gold example: `stageshow/kit/controls/Draft.tsx` and `stageshow/examples/form-error/` ("Creating account" to "Account created" on one button).
Benji's call differs: vary timing by job, not for flavour; direct feedback never waits, so a deliberate 200ms on Delete belongs in a confirmation step, not in the button's response.
Check: film one press at 40 to 80ms steps: the response starts in the frame after the input and lands on the pressed thing, and covering the toast loses nothing the button didn't already say.

## Gotcha

Personality lives in restraint. A product with one well-placed easter egg and one specific success message feels alive. A product with ten easter eggs and animated success states everywhere feels exhausting.

The Benji rule: *"A lifeless product feels like a dead product, and a dead product feels uncared for."* Add personality where it matters most, not everywhere.

## Sources

- Benji Taylor — *Honkish*, [benji.org/honkish](https://benji.org/honkish).
- Benji Taylor, Stageshow 1.1.1 (MIT, github.com/benjitaylor/skills, HEAD `299140f`, read 2026-11-07): `stageshow/references/motion.md` (Story; Pace and easing; a state the click sets), `stageshow/references/choreography.md` (Timing has different jobs), `stageshow/kit/controls/Button.tsx`, `stageshow/kit/controls/Button.css`, `stageshow/kit/motion/Roll.css`, `stageshow/kit/controls/Draft.tsx`, `stageshow/examples/form-error/index.tsx`.

title: keyboard-patterns
summary: The key maps a custom widget owes (ARIA APG): tabindex only 0 or -1, roving tabindex for composite widgets, aria-activedescendant for a combobox, showModal() or inert for dialogs, Escape closes the last thing opened, destructive confirms focus the safe button, and a client-side route change moves focus and retitles the page.
tags: [components, accessibility, keyboard, focus, aria, apg]
---

# Keyboard patterns

Native elements ship their keyboard behaviour; a custom widget has to rebuild it, and the rebuild is where it fails. Before writing one, check that a native element or a headless library (Radix, React Aria) can't do it ([[accessibility-baseline]]). If you do write one, it owes these key maps — the ARIA Authoring Practices patterns — exactly.

## tabindex has two legal values

- `tabindex="0"` joins the natural tab order. Only for a custom control that is not natively focusable.
- `tabindex="-1"` is focusable from script only: a heading you move focus to, a dialog container, a roving-tabindex member.
- A positive `tabindex` hijacks the order of the whole page. Fix the DOM order instead.

## One tab stop per composite widget

Tabs, menus, toolbars, radio groups and listboxes take **one** Tab stop. With **roving tabindex** the active item is `0`, every other `-1`, and the arrow keys move both focus and the `0`. A combobox keeps DOM focus in its input instead: `aria-activedescendant` on the input points at the highlighted option's `id` and moves with the arrows.

| Widget | Keys |
|---|---|
| Dialog | Tab / Shift+Tab cycle inside and wrap; Escape closes |
| Tabs | Arrows move (wrapping); Home / End jump; Tab leaves to the panel. Automatic activation when panels render instantly, manual (Enter / Space) when switching is expensive |
| Menu button | Enter, Space or ↓ opens on the first item; ↑ opens on the last; Escape closes and refocuses the button |
| Disclosure, accordion | The header is a `<button aria-expanded>`; Enter and Space toggle |
| Combobox | ↓ opens or moves in; Enter accepts; Escape closes back to the input; typing filters |
| Listbox, radio group | Arrows move the selection; one Tab stop for the group |

Escape dismisses whatever opened **last** — tooltip, then menu, then dialog. Enter in a single-line input submits natively; in a `<textarea>` it is a newline, and ⌘ / Ctrl+Enter submits only because you wired it ([[forms-behavior]]).

## Dialogs: trap, then give back

Prefer `<dialog>` opened with `showModal()`: the background goes inert and Escape closes, for free. A custom overlay needs `role="dialog"`, `aria-modal="true"`, a name through `aria-labelledby`, and `inert` on everything behind it — one property that removes the background from both the tab order and the accessibility tree.

On open, focus the first focusable element; **in a destructive confirmation, focus the least destructive action** so a reflexive Enter cancels ([[destructive-actions]]). On close, return focus to the trigger, or the nearest logical container if the trigger is gone ([[touch-and-focus]] rule 7).

## Client-side navigation announces nothing

A router swap resets neither focus nor the title. On every route change: set `document.title` for the new view, then focus its `<h1>` (given `tabindex="-1"`) or `<main>`. Restore the scroll position on back and forward; scroll to the top on a new navigation ([[url-as-state]]).

## Focus that stays visible

`:focus-visible`, never bare `:focus`. Prefer the browser's own ring — adding only `outline-offset: 2px` keeps it, and it already adapts to platform and forced colours. A custom ring is allowed when it is a verified token that clears 3:1 against **every** colour it crosses, and the focused element is never fully hidden under sticky chrome (`scroll-padding-block-start`, [[growth-and-overflow]]). The numbers are in [[wcag-thresholds]].

- **A ring means focus.** Never ring a card to point at it, and never walk a ring between controls as a stand-in for a pointer (Benji Taylor, Stageshow `references/craft.md`, `references/motion.md`).

## Reference

```tsx
// Roving tabindex for a toolbar or tablist: the part most custom widgets skip
function onKeyDown(e: React.KeyboardEvent, i: number) {
  const last = items.length - 1
  const keys: Record<string, number> = { ArrowRight: i === last ? 0 : i + 1, ArrowLeft: i === 0 ? last : i - 1, Home: 0, End: last }
  const next = keys[e.key]; if (next === undefined) return
  e.preventDefault()
  setActive(next) // active item renders tabIndex={0}, every other tabIndex={-1}
  refs.current[next]?.focus()
}
```

Print the shortcut as the product does: one keycap per key, 18px tall, 11px at weight 500, 4px radius, 3px apart, tabular digits (`⌘` `K`), or flat gray `⌘K` beside a menu item.
Gold example: `stageshow/examples/raycast/index.tsx`, a keyboard-only loop (type "clip", Enter pushes the command, ↓ moves the selection, Esc pops back to root search); keycaps from `stageshow/kit/parts/Kbd.css`.
Check: put the mouse away and run the widget: Tab enters it once, the arrows wrap end to start, Home and End jump, Escape hands focus back to the trigger, and every recorded frame shows exactly one ring.

## Gotcha

`role="tab"` with no `onKeyDown` is a tab the mouse can use and the keyboard cannot: it looks finished in every screenshot. Grep for `role="button"`, `role="tab"`, `role="menuitem"` and check each has the key map above, or swap it for the native element.

title: measured-skeletons
summary: Draw a skeleton from the content itself, not by hand. Lay a sample render out unseen, measure it, and paint one bar per line of text between the font's own ascender and descender lines, one block per image or control. The shape comes from the best source on hand, the reveal is decided when the data lands, and every skeleton shimmers on one page clock. From Lochie Axon's skullet.

---

# Measured skeletons

A hand-drawn skeleton is a second layout that drifts from the real one: a bar 20px too short, a list of three when five arrive, and the page jumps when data lands. Skullet takes the opposite route. It renders the content from sample data where no one can see it, measures every element, and paints a skeleton in exactly that shape. The skeleton and the content then hold the same space by construction, which is the rule [[empty-loading-states]] can only ask for.

## What gets drawn

- **Text: one bar per rendered line**, however many lines a string wraps to. The bar runs between two of the typeface's own lines, read from the font with canvas `measureText`: a top of ascender, cap height or x-height, and a bottom of baseline or descender. The default, ascender to descender, covers the tails of g, p and y. A bar centred in the line box looks too fat on loose leading and too thin on tight.
- **Media and controls: one block at their box.** `img`, `video`, `svg`, `canvas`, `input`, `select`, `textarea`, `iframe`.
- **A painted box around one label** (a button, a chip) fills as a block; a card keeps its own surface and gets bars inside it. Media clipped by a rounded parent of the same size, like an avatar, takes the parent's corners.
- **Visually hidden text draws nothing**, and a box that clips its children clips their bars too.
- Escape hatches: mark an element to draw it as one block, or to draw nothing; a component can ship its own static skeleton.

## Where the shape comes from, best first

1. The data already on screen, when a refetch forces loading over it.
2. The data last shown under the same id, so a reload is exact.
3. A shape remembered from a previous visit.
4. The `sample` the author passed.
5. The children rendered without their data.
6. A few generic lines, with a development warning.

Remembered shapes keep layout and never content: text becomes filler, media sources and form values are dropped, and the store is cleared on sign-out. In development the library warns when a skeleton and its content differ in size, and logs a ready-to-paste `sample` with the data's keys and string lengths and every value replaced.

## The reveal is decided when the data lands

| Situation | Reveal |
|---|---|
| Loaded in under 150ms, or the user scrolled, swiped or typed in the last 400ms | At once. The skeleton was held back 150ms, so a fast load never shows one |
| A refetch over data already on screen | A quick 120ms crossfade |
| Small: under 72px tall, or 3 pieces or fewer | One crossfade for the whole thing |
| Anything larger | By row: each row or card arrives whole, in screen order across a 320ms spread, smaller text 60ms behind the text above it, off-screen rows at once |

A "row" is the nearest ancestor with at least three siblings of the same tag and class. Reveals landing within 150ms of each other share one top-to-bottom order, so three widgets loading together read as one page. A custom entrance may set only filter, transform and clip-path on top of the fade, never layout, so no reveal moves the page; a skeleton that guessed the height wrong eases to the real height over 280ms.

## Motion and the page clock

Every skeleton on the page shimmers in one stream, timed off the document clock, so one mounting late joins the sweep already running instead of starting its own. The highlight is a 20° diagonal at most 320px wide, and the loop time is set per 1280px of screen (4s slow, 2s fast), so a wide monitor doesn't make it race. Pulse loops at 2.4s or 1.2s down to 45% opacity. Both stop under `prefers-reduced-motion`.

## Images and accessibility

An image never holds the rest back: each one still loading keeps its own block until it has loaded and decoded, then crossfades, with a 10s ceiling. Give images a size, or they move once they arrive. A loading region is `aria-busy`, its skeleton is `inert` and hidden from assistive tech, and an optional label is read in its place ("Loading profile"). Server-rendered skeletons are measured by a small inline script before first paint, so hydration changes nothing.

## Gotcha

Tests run in jsdom or happy-dom have no layout, so every reveal there is instant and the sample's text sits inside an `aria-hidden` skeleton. Query by role, which skips it; a query by text finds the sample. And the measured shape is only as good as the sample: a sample name of "A" draws a one-letter bar where "Alexandra Whitfield" will land.

## Sources

# Presence signals

Most real-time products show presence as one green dot and a "typing…" line. Honk made presence the axis every feature was designed around, and the patterns transfer to any shared surface: chat, docs, canvases, live games.

## States, each with its own signal

| State | Signal | Honk's version |
|---|---|---|
| Arriving | A transition with a moment to it, not a dot switching colour | A ring around the friend's avatar fills, with a sound ([[sound-motion-sync]]) |
| Fully here | Live activity, not a label | Every character appears on the other screen as it is typed, typos and edits included |
| Half here | A weaker version of "here", not "away" | The avatar becomes a dashed outline while the friend looks elsewhere in the app |
| Leaving | A short goodbye beat, then gone | A brief burst of waving emoji (in the user's skin tone) with a sound |

Three states read better than two. "Here but looking elsewhere" is the one most products drop, and it is the one that explains a slow reply.

## Rules

- **Activity resizes its container live.** The typing bubble grows as you type and shrinks back when you pause; when both people type at once the screen splits 50/50. The layout tells the conversation's rhythm.
- **A reaction is pinned to what it reacts to.** A double tap drops the heart exactly where the finger landed, with a faint ring and a haptic both people feel. Store the position in relative coordinates (10% x, 20% y), so it lands on the same spot across screen sizes.
- **Shared activities need everyone present.** A real-time game pauses when one player leaves; it does not play on against an empty seat.
- **A notification shows its own lifetime.** An in-app banner whose border counts down how long it will stay tells the user how urgent it is and when it will go.
- **The name rides the cursor**, just below and right of its tip, and the person's work shows in the document's own marks (a highlight, words at a caret), not bubbles or badges; a bare coloured arrow reads as a second pointer (Benji Taylor, Stageshow `examples/presence`).
- **One colour per person, everywhere:** cursor, selection, avatar ring, name label. A collaborator recoloured between surfaces reads as two people.
- **Colour carries meaning outside the content too.** Honk turned a tray's background red for destructive actions such as deleting an account ([[destructive-actions]]).
- **Real-time products earn their pauses.** Outside the live chat, Honk added friction on purpose: a slot-machine reveal for finding people, a signature before chatting with strangers that measurably reduced bad behaviour. Immediacy reads as immediacy only next to something slower.

## Accessibility

Every presence change that matters (someone joined, someone left, a reaction landed) is also announced in a live region ([[screen-reader-announcements]]); a ring filling is invisible to a screen reader. Dashed versus solid needs a second cue (a label or tooltip) for anyone who cannot tell them apart.

## When to apply

Designing chat, multiplayer docs and canvases, live cursors, shared games, or any surface where two people are in it at once. In a faux-UI demo of collaboration, each person keeps one colour and their name rides their cursor ([[MOC-faux-ui]]).

## Reference

| Mark | Maya | Jon |
|---|---|---|
| Face in the pile, cursor, name flag, selection or caret | `#d1478a` | `#2f9e8f` |

- Bad: two grey arrows, a "Maya is editing" chip over the page, her selection in the doc's blue accent. Good: each arrow carries its name just below and right of the tip; Maya's highlight sweeps across the sentence on the same duration and curve as her cursor, so its edge stays at the tip; Jon's words arrive at a caret in his colour; neither colour is the accent.
- The two cursors move like hands, eased over most of a second and never in step; a deselect is instant, as in the app; the viewer has no cursor of their own on stage.
- Gold example: `stageshow/examples/presence/` (doc with a three-face pile, two named cursors, selection and typing).
- Check: pick any frame and confirm each person's face in the pile, cursor, flag and mark share one hex value that is not the accent; at 358 wide the name flag still stays inside the doc (the example clamps it about 64px from the right edge).

## Gotcha

Presence animation is frequent. An arrival ring with sound is a delight once an hour and noise in a busy channel; scale the signal down as frequency goes up ([[delight-impact-curve]]), and never fire it for your own presence.

## Sources

- Benji Taylor, *Honkish*, [benji.org/honkish](https://benji.org/honkish) (read 2026-11-01): presence, reactions, mini games, in-app notifications, tray colours, friction moments. Paraphrased.

# Press and pending states

Press feedback answers one question: *is the thing under my finger responding?* Astryx (Meta's open-source design system, 150+ components) pins that down per component instead of leaving it to each author, and the result is a short set of rules that most hand-built controls break. They sit under [[responsive-feedback]], which owns the *motion* of a press (scale, timing); this node owns *which surface paints and when*.

## Where the press paints

Paint one pressed-overlay token (Astryx: `--color-overlay-pressed`) over the existing fill of the **part the hand is moving**, not the whole row:

| Control | Paints | Never paints |
|---|---|---|
| Checkbox, radio | the indicator | the label row |
| Switch | track and thumb together | — |
| Slider | only the thumb being dragged, even when the drag began on the track | the track |
| Tab, link, collapsible trigger | its own surface | siblings |
| Segmented control | an unselected item | the selected item, which keeps its raised surface |

The overlay is transient: it clears on release or cancel, and the control returns to the **same** pixels it would have had without the press. A press is never a state that persists.

## The rules around it

- **Disabled means no response.** A disabled control gains no pressed paint and does nothing on release. Keeping it focusable (to explain why it is unavailable) does not make it operable.
- **Persistent selection wins.** Pressing what is already selected leaves its selected treatment untouched.
- **Pending keeps purpose and geometry.** While an action runs, set `aria-busy`, keep width and height fixed and show a spinner inside; the accessible name does not change. Pending styling and disabled styling stay visibly different ([[empty-loading-states]]).
- **Elevation belongs to the painted surface.** A standalone button owns its resting shadow; a connected group that paints one surface owns one shadow and its members none; a layout wrapper that paints nothing never gains a shadow because it holds buttons. Hover, press, focus, loading and disabled change the paint, **never the elevation tier** ([[depth-and-nesting]]).

## Slide to choose (touch action groups)

Under a touch presentation, a press in a toolbar, segmented control or menu that slides across siblings acts on the action **it lifts on**, through that action's own activation; at most one action fires per gesture. While held, the highlight follows the finger, one action at a time, and nothing is highlighted over a disabled action, a gap or outside the group. Lifting outside the group, a second finger, lost focus or a cancelled pointer acts on nothing. A mouse keeps the platform rule (press and release on the same target).

## Gotcha

Darkening the whole list row while its checkbox is pressed reads as "the row is selected." Paint the indicator, and let [[hover-states-subtle]] own the row.

## Sources

- Meta, Astryx (MIT, github.com/meta/astryx, HEAD `9f55320`, read 2026-11-09): `docs/design/user-states.md` (current), `docs/families/buttons.md` FR3, FR4, FR8, FR9, FR12 and `docs/families/action-groups.md` FR1–FR3 (current). Paraphrased.
- Related: [[touch-and-focus]], [[astryx-reconciliation]].

# Reorder with an insertion cue

The common sortable list lifts the dragged row into a shadowed card and reshuffles its neighbours on every pixel of travel. The list never holds still long enough to read, and the "lift" implies the row became a different kind of object. Astryx's current reorder spec does the opposite: **show where it will land, change nothing until it lands.**

## Anatomy

| Part | Treatment |
|---|---|
| Reorder handle | A dedicated grip, discoverable at rest without overpowering the row. Starting a drag anywhere else on the row stays free for the row's own actions |
| Source row | Stays in place during the drag, in a temporary reduced-emphasis treatment |
| Moving preview | Follows the pointer on both axes in the **same** quiet treatment as the source; no raised-card shadow |
| Insertion cue | An accent line between rows on the list's ordering axis; length and inset follow the row geometry |
| Neighbours | Do not move until commit |

## The sequence

1. **Start** from the handle only.
2. **Drag:** the preview moves freely, but the candidate position is computed on the ordering axis alone (vertical list → pointer y).
3. **Drop:** the list adopts the new order **once**, then rows settle with the system's fast movement; all drag styling clears immediately.
4. **Cancel** (Escape, pointer cancel): original order and full contrast come back at once, even when motion is enabled.
5. **Reduced motion:** the order updates with no travel ([[reduced-motion-by-pointer]]).

## Keyboard parity

Keyboard reordering moves the **same** insertion line one position at a time; focus stays on the handle throughout; position, cancel and completion are announced in words ("Moved to position 3 of 7") through a polite live region ([[screen-reader-announcements]]). The quiet drag treatment is allowed only while the reorder is active, never as resting styling.

## Gotcha

Live reshuffling feels responsive in a demo with five rows and breaks in a long list: every crossed row shifts, the target moves out from under the pointer, and the drop lands one row off. Freeze the neighbours and draw the line.

## Sources

- Meta, Astryx (MIT, github.com/meta/astryx, HEAD `9f55320`, read 2026-11-09): `docs/design/ordered-collection-reordering.md` DR1–DR8 (current). Paraphrased.
- Related: [[gesture-phases]], [[keyboard-patterns]], [[astryx-reconciliation]].
