Choose the mechanism by what the change is tied to, and pick the quietest one that works. [[accessibility-baseline]] states the floor ("polite for async"); this node is how to make that floor actually speak. ## The ladder — stop at the first match 1. **Focus moves there anyway** — an opened dialog, the first invalid field after submit. The focus move is the announcement; add nothing. 2. **Tied to one control** — a field error, a character count: `aria-describedby` on the control, read with the field. 3. **Not urgent, not tied to a control** — a toast, "Saved", a result count, a loading state: a polite region, `role="status"`. 4. **Urgent, not tied to a control** — a form-level failure, session expiry: `role="alert"`, and nothing else gets it. `role="status"` is `aria-live="polite"` plus `aria-atomic="true"`; `role="alert"` is the assertive twin. Default to polite — assertive interrupts whatever the user was reading. ## Rules that make it reliable - **Render the region empty first, then change its text.** `{msg &&
{msg}
}` mounts the region with its content, which screen readers announce inconsistently. Keep `
{msg}
` in the DOM from the start. - **Short, self-contained messages.** `aria-atomic` re-reads the whole region on every change. - **Never move focus to a toast.** Announce it and leave focus where the user is working — the toast's own timing rules are in [[wcag-thresholds]]. - **Loads:** `aria-busy="true"` on the updating region, "Loading…" politely, then the outcome: "Loaded, 12 results". The copy pattern is in [[strings-and-locale]]. - **Inserted alerts vary by reader.** Test the browser and screen-reader pairs you support before relying on one. ## Hiding, two opposite ways - **Visually hidden, still read** — `.sr-only` / Tailwind `sr-only`: `position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; margin: -1px; overflow: hidden; clip-path: inset(50%); white-space: nowrap`. One pixel, not zero: some readers skip zero-sized boxes. `nowrap` stops words being read as one run-together string. - **Read-hidden, still visible** — `aria-hidden="true"` removes the subtree from assistive tech. Use it on decorative icons and visual duplicates; never on or above a button, link or input, or Tab lands on a stop the reader says does not exist. Hiding something interactive means `inert` ([[touch-and-focus]]). ## Alt text by purpose | Purpose | `alt` | |---|---| | Decorative, or repeats adjacent text | `alt=""` — present and empty | | Informative | The meaning it adds: "Ticket QR code" | | Functional (the image is the link or button) | The action: "Search", never "magnifying glass" | | Image of text | The exact text — better, real text | | Chart or diagram | A one-line summary; the data as a table nearby | A missing `alt` is worse than an empty one: readers fall back to the file name. {announce}

Saved successfully!
}`, mounted with its text and interrupting. [[sonner-principles]] covers why the library is built this way; this node covers how to use it. ## Setup - **One Toaster, at the root** (in Next.js, the root `layout.tsx`). Rendering it per page or conditionally duplicates or drops toasts. - **`toast()` is a plain client-side function.** It does nothing on the server; a server action returns its result and the client calls `toast()`. ## Picking the call | Need | Call | |---|---| | Plain message, optional second line | `toast('Saved', { description })` | | Typed icon | `toast.success` / `.error` / `.info` / `.warning` | | Loading tied to a promise | `toast.promise(p, { loading, success, error })`; `success` and `error` can be functions of the result or the error | | Loading you manage yourself | `const id = toast.loading(…)`, then `toast.success('Done', { id })` | | A button | `action: { label, onClick }`; `event.preventDefault()` keeps it open | | Your own JSX, no default styles | `toast.custom((t) => …)` | Calling `toast()` again with the same `id` updates that toast. `duration: Infinity` persists it. `onDismiss` (close button or swipe) and `onAutoClose` (timeout) are separate callbacks. Conversation archived.
) */ .toast { display: inline-flex; align-items: center; gap: 8px; padding: 8px 12px; border-radius: 10px; background: #1c1c1f; color: #fff; font-size: 12px; } .toast button { margin-left: 6px; color: rgb(255 255 255 / 0.6); font-weight: 500; } .dark .toast { background: #26262a; } /* raised surface on dark, never near-black on near-black */ ``` - Bad: a grey default pill reading "Success!" with a green check. title: streaming-chat-scroll
summary: A streaming chat never moves the reader against their intent. Follow the reply only while the reader sits at the live edge; any scroll, selection, keypress, link or search stops the follow; a new turn anchors near the top with part of the last one still visible; off-screen activity gets a Jump to latest; saved threads reopen at the last meaningful turn; the log is announced as additions, busy while streaming. From shadcn/ui's Message Scroller.
tags: [components, ai, chat, streaming, scroll, accessibility, shadcn]

# Streaming chat scroll

The defining bug of AI chat UIs is the hand-rolled stick-to-bottom hook: the reply streams, the page drags the reader down while they are reading the paragraph above, and selecting text to copy is a fight. shadcn/ui rebuilt its chat layer around one rule, **never move the reader against their intent**, and published the fifteen behaviours it implies with its Message Scroller primitive. They hold for any chat, built with shadcn or not.

## The rules

| Situation | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| A reply is streaming and the reader is at the bottom | Follow it. Auto-scroll is never the default otherwise |
| The reader scrolls, selects text, presses a key, opens a link or searches | Stop following at once. Interaction always wins over the stream |
| The person sends a message | Anchor **their** turn near the top of the viewport and let the reply grow below it; keep a sliver of the previous turn visible for context |
| New content arrives off-screen | Show it: a "Jump to latest" button, which also re-engages following |
| A saved thread reopens | At the last meaningful turn (often the person's last message), not the bottom of a long answer |
| History loads above, layout shifts, stop, retry, branch, an error | Keep the reader's position: the line they were reading stays put ([[scroll-anchoring]]) |

## Accessibility

- The scroll viewport is `role="region"` with `aria-label="Messages"` and `tabIndex={0}`, so a keyboard can scroll it.
- The message list is `role="log"` with `aria-relevant="additions"`: a screen reader hears new turns, not every token ([[screen-reader-announcements]]).
- `aria-busy` on the list while a turn streams; the scroll button is `inert` when there is nothing to jump to.

## Text that streams

Render the reply with an append-stable markdown renderer (shadcn uses Streamdown) and append-stable type: no `:last-child`, `:has()` or `:empty` in layout rules, spacing only from `margin-block-start`, so each new token never re-lays out the paragraphs above it. Fenced code goes to a code block whose Copy stays disabled until the closing fence arrives; inline code stays inline.

## In a shadcn project

Build from `message-scroller`, `message`, `bubble` and `input-group` (`npx shadcn@latest add message-scroller message bubble input-group`), wrap every row in its scroller item, and never add `use-stick-to-bottom` or a raw `ScrollArea` for the thread ([[shadcn-reconciliation]]). The step list inside a reply is [[agent-trace-states]].

## Gotcha

Scrolling to the bottom on every token "works" in a demo with short answers. Test with a reply three screens long while selecting a sentence in its first paragraph: if the selection is dragged away, the follow rule is missing.

## Sources

- shadcn/ui (MIT, github.com/shadcn-ui/ui, HEAD `8ab2771`, read 2026-11-09): `apps/v4/content/docs/components/base/message-scroller.mdx` ("What Makes a Great Streaming Chat Experience"), `code-block.mdx#markdown`, `(root)/typeset.mdx`, `skills/shadcn/rules/chat.md`. Paraphrased.

# Strings and locale

Copy breaks two ways: it contradicts the product's own vocabulary, or it is assembled so it cannot be translated. Both are visible in the code before anyone reads the screen. [[copy-voice]] sets the voice; this node is how the strings are found, built and formatted.

## Inventory before writing

Find where the copy lives first: the translation call (`t(`, `i18n.`, `<FormattedMessage`, `$t(`) and its catalogues (`locales/**/*.json`, `messages/*.json`, `*.po`, `*.strings`), or a CMS or API. List the noun used for each object and the verb for each action — "project" or "workspace", "Delete" or "Remove" — and the case used per element type. New copy uses those words. A synonym is a finding only where one thing is now named two ways: if it is "Archive" in the menu it is not "Move to storage" in the toast.

A multi-step flow uses one vocabulary end to end: "Get started" to enter, "Continue" *or* "Next" to advance, "Done" to finish.

## Build strings whole

Never assemble a sentence around a variable — `"You have " + n + " new messages"` — because word order changes per language. Write one message with placeholders, and never `n === 1 ? "" : "s"`: many languages have more than two plural forms.

```text
inbox.count = {count, plural,
  =0 {No new messages}
  one {# new message}
  other {# new messages}
}
```

`=0` matches zero exactly; `one` and `other` are categories, and a translator adds `few` or `many` where the language needs them. Without a library, `new Intl.PluralRules(locale).select(count)` picks the category.

## Format through Intl, with the user's locale

| Value | Call |
|---|---|
| Currency | `Intl.NumberFormat(locale, { style: "currency", currency })` |
| Unit | `Intl.NumberFormat(locale, { style: "unit", unit: "megabyte" })` |
| Date | `Intl.DateTimeFormat(locale, { dateStyle: "medium" })` |
| Relative time | `Intl.RelativeTimeFormat(locale, { numeric: "auto" })` → "yesterday" |
| List | `Intl.ListFormat(locale, { type: "conjunction" })` — never join with `", "` and `" and "` |

`toLocaleDateString()` with no locale, or a date built from `getMonth()`, is the finding. Translated strings grow — a one-word button grows most — so the container rules are in [[growth-and-overflow]].

## Labels that do their job

- **Buttons start with a verb** naming the action: "Send", "Save draft", "Delete project" — never "OK" or "Let's go!". An icon button's accessible name follows the same rule: "Delete project", never "Trash icon" ([[screen-reader-announcements]]).
- **Links name their destination** out of context: "Read the billing docs", not "Click here". Two bare "Learn more" on one page each get a suffix: "Learn more about exports".
- **Toggles describe the ON state.** "Send read receipts", never "Don't send read receipts", which makes the switch a double negative. Link straight to a referenced setting instead of narrating its path.
- **Address the reader as "you"**; in errors, "we" reads as deflection. Possessives sparingly — "Favorites" beats "Your favorites" — and never "My account" beside "Your settings".
- **Match the device:** "tap" on touch, "click" with a pointer, "select" when both.

## Status copy stays parallel

| State | Pattern |
|---|---|
| In progress | `-ing` verb + object: "Saving changes…" |
| Done | object + past tense, no "successfully": "Changes saved" |
| Failed | what did not happen, then the next step: "Changes not saved. Check your connection and try again." |
| Unavailable | why, beside the control: "Add a payment method to publish" |
| Partial | both counts: "9 of 12 files uploaded. Retry 3 failed files" |

"Saving changes…" resolves to "Changes saved" — same object, same order. Cut "Please" from routine instructions.

## Reference

| Slot | String |
|---|---|
| Button, idle | Create account |
| Button, in progress | Creating account |
| Button, done | Account created |
| Lane under the field, hint | We'll send a link to confirm it |

- One object, one order through the lifecycle; the labels crossfade on the same button and the hint and error swap in one lane, so no string moves the layout.
- Sample strings are picked to fit: a short real name and an email that fits its chip, never a truncated email or a wrapping name.
- Benji's call differs on money in a demo: `table-edit` writes `$` plus `toLocaleString('en-US', { minimumFractionDigits: 2 })`, with the locale named, and `craft.md` hangs a centred amount's sign outside its digits. In a product keep `style: "currency"` and use `formatToParts` when the sign must be split off.
- Gold example: `stageshow/examples/form-error/` (status labels and the message lane) and `stageshow/teaching/details.tsx` (`detail-copy`).
- Check: count the real strings on the screen, find each in the catalogue, confirm every in-progress and done pair shares its object, and at 390 wide nothing truncates or wraps.

## Gotcha

A placeholder is an example in the accepted format — `name@example.com`, `DD/MM/YYYY` — never an instruction and never the label ([[forms-behavior]]). And a deliberate brand voice is not a defect: reword only where copy is inconsistent, ambiguous, untranslatable or wrong for the stakes.

## Sources

- Jakub Krehel, interfaces skills (MIT, github.com/jakubkrehel/skills, HEAD `592aedc`, read 2026-10-25): `skills/better-writing/SKILL.md` (**Inventory the existing strings first**, **Build strings whole**, **Verb-first buttons**, **Links describe their destination**, **Settings describe the ON state**), `patterns.md` (status copy, plurals, locale formatting).
- Unicode ICU MessageFormat; ECMA-402 `Intl`.

title: touch-and-focus
summary: Hover enhances, never enables. 44px hit areas by pseudo-element, touch-action set on purpose, muted + playsinline, aria-label on icon buttons, hidden content out of the tab order, focus moved in and restored, timers paused when hidden, tooltip warm state, submenu safe area — plus the mobile-native fixes table.

# Touch and focus

A large share of users experience the interface through a thumb, a keyboard, or a screen reader — never a mouse. UI that only works with a fine pointer and perfect vision is broken UI however polished it looks. [[accessibility-baseline]] states the floor; this node is the implementation.

## The rules

1. **Gate hover behind capability**: `@media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)`. Touch fires `:hover` on tap and leaves it stuck. Nothing core is reachable only by hover.
2. **Tap targets ≥ 44px** (40px desktop). Keep the visual small and grow the hit area with a pseudo-element (`inset: -10px` on a 24px icon = 44px). Hit areas never overlap; shrink to the largest non-colliding size.
3. **`touch-action: manipulation`** on buttons, links, inputs (kills the double-tap-zoom delay); **`touch-action: none`** on surfaces that implement their own pan or drag so native gestures don't fight yours.
4. **Autoplaying video needs `muted` and `playsinline`**, or iOS refuses or goes fullscreen. Under `prefers-reduced-motion`, swap autoplay for a poster and a play button.
5. **Every icon-only button has an `aria-label`** that names the action ("Close dialog", never "icon"). Code-built illustrations get `role="img"` + `aria-label`, or `aria-hidden` when decorative.
6. **Hidden content leaves the tab order**: `visibility: hidden`, `display: none`, or `inert` — never `opacity: 0` or an off-screen transform. To keep an exit animation, delay the flip: `transition: visibility 0s 200ms` on close. Focus must never land off-screen; scroll focused elements into view (`scrollIntoView({ block: "nearest" })`).
7. **Overlays move focus in and give it back.** Open: focus the first control or the dialog. Close: return focus to the trigger. Never strand focus on a removed node: deleting the focused row moves focus to the next row, else the previous one, else the list heading.
8. **Timers pause when the tab is hidden** (`visibilitychange`), resuming with the remaining time. Toasts and undo windows also pause on hover and focus, and their duration scales with the text (read at roughly 200–250 words a minute), never a flat 2s.
9. **Shortcuts show the user's OS**: Cmd on macOS, Ctrl elsewhere, bound to match.
10. **Feedback is on the page.** Errors, confirmations, and status never live only behind hover or inside a modal the user has to find.
11. **In a touch-scrolled list, select on release.** The press that starts a scroll ends in `pointercancel`, so selecting on press fires on every scroll; a release over the list, when the press started there too, never does ([[animated-hit-testing]]).

## Tooltips and menus

A tooltip waits ~200ms so it doesn't fire on incidental travel; once one is open, siblings open **instantly** with no delay and no entrance (the warm state), clearing ~300ms after the last closes — see [[responsive-feedback]]. Submenus get a triangular **safe area** (`clip-path` on a pseudo-element) so a diagonal cursor path toward the submenu doesn't close it mid-flight.

## Mobile-native fixes

| Problem | Fix |
|---|---|
| Hover state stuck after tap | `@media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)` |
| Gray or blue flash on tap | `-webkit-tap-highlight-color: transparent` |
| Layout has the wrong height | `100dvh` (app) or `100svh` (hero), never `100vh` |
| Page zooms into an input | Input font-size ≥ 16px |
| Tap feels laggy | Feedback on pointer-down + `touch-action: manipulation` |
| Pull-to-refresh hijacks scroll | `overscroll-behavior: none` on `html, body` |
| Content stops at the notch | `viewport-fit=cover` + `env(safe-area-inset-*)` |
| Long-press selects button text | `user-select: none` and `-webkit-touch-callout: none` on controls, never on `body` |
| Keyboard covers the composer (Android) | `interactive-widget=resizes-content` in the viewport tag ([[production-baseline]]) |
| Whole page pans sideways | Fix the element that overflows (`overflow-wrap`, a scroll wrapper on tables and `pre`, no `100vw`); `overflow-x: hidden` on `body` hides it and breaks sticky |
| Carousel scrolls vertically | `touch-action: pan-y` on the gesture surface |
| Status bar color doesn't match | `theme-color` meta per color scheme |
| Right in Chrome, wrong on the phone | Real hardware: dev server on `0.0.0.0`, open by LAN IP, Safari Web Inspector or `chrome://inspect`, a phone a few years old |

Before a carousel gets a JS drag and `touch-action: pan-y`, check whether native scroll does the job: `scroll-snap-type: x mandatory` on the track and `scroll-snap-align: start` on each slide keep the platform's momentum and need no `touch-action` ([[sticky-and-scroll-tells]]). When you do set it, the value names what the browser keeps: `pan-y` leaves vertical panning to the browser and horizontal to your code.

## When to apply

Any interactive UI — buttons, modals, tooltips, menus, video, timers — and every mobile bug report. Run it even when the screen already looks finished: a failure here ships broken for someone.

## Reference

```css
.icon-btn { position: relative; flex: none; width: 24px; height: 24px; touch-action: manipulation; }
.icon-btn::after { content: ""; position: absolute; inset: -10px; } /* 44px hit, 24px visual */
@media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine) { .icon-btn:hover { background: var(--ink-2); } }
.trigger[data-open] { background: var(--ink-2); } /* keeps its pressed look while its popover is open */
```

- Bad: an icon button squeezed to 18px by its flex row, a hover fill as the only sign it is a control, the trigger going flat while its menu is still open. Good: `flex: none`, a surface visible at rest, the pressed look held through `data-open`.
- Gold example: `stageshow/examples/buttons/` and `stageshow/kit/controls/Button.css` (sizes 24, 28 and 32px, hover one step of its own colour, press `scale(0.97)`).
- Check: Benji's own caveat applies, a narrow viewport changes width but not touch. On a real phone or with touch emulation, tap every icon button at its outer edge, then Tab through with every drawer closed and confirm no stop lands on something hidden.

## Gotcha

Tabbing into a closed drawer is the classic miss. It was hidden with `opacity: 0` or `translateX(100%)`, which keeps every control focusable; the keyboard user lands inside a thing they cannot see.

## Sources

- Emil Kowalski's design-engineering practice on touch and accessibility, distilled by AgentsORG.
- Emil Kowalski, skills (MIT, github.com/emilkowalski/skills, HEAD `715c180`, read 2026-11-09): skills/mobile-native/SKILL.md §9 (native snap over a JS carousel, reading `touch-action` values).
- Benji Taylor, Stageshow 1.1.1 (MIT, github.com/benjitaylor/skills, HEAD `299140f`, read 2026-11-07): `stageshow/kit/controls/Button.css`, `stageshow/references/craft.md` (`flex: none`, links and controls at rest, `data-open`), `stageshow/references/rehearse.md` (width is not touch).
- Related: [[accessibility-baseline]], [[hover-states-subtle]], [[prefers-reduced-motion]], [[forms-behavior]].

title: ui-polish-pass
summary: The invisible finish, as a pass — antialiasing, constant weight on interaction, tabular numbers, no layout shift, real characters, states that stay put, a z-index scale, hit areas, optical alignment, native page scrollbars, designed empty states, inert decoration, no flash on refresh.

# The UI polish pass

A finished interface is mostly invisible work: text that renders crisply, numbers that don't jiggle, hover states that don't shift layout, focus rings that don't clash, hit areas you never miss. No single item is noticeable on its own; their absence is. Run this as a pass over every component *after it works* and *before* [[review-checklist]] gates it. If the pass finds the structure itself is wrong, escalate to [[feeling-right]].

## The pass

1. **Antialiased smoothing once at the root**; fonts subsetted.
2. **Never change font weight on hover, active, or selected.** Weight reflows the text. Hold weight; signal with color.
3. **`tabular-nums` on anything that changes** — counters, prices, timers.
4. **No layout shift from dynamic content.** Skeletons, placeholders, and images carry the dimensions (or `aspect-ratio`) of the loaded state.
5. **Real typographic characters** and `text-wrap: balance` on headings — see [[line-behavior]].
6. **Interaction states that stay put.** Hover transitions only the properties that change, ~150ms ease-out. Press is `scale(0.96)`, never below 0.95. Focus rings stay neutral (grey, black, white) and never disappear. `::selection`, if styled, stays a legible tint. `will-change` only for transform/opacity/filter, only after observing a first-frame hitch.
7. **A fixed z-index scale** (`--z-dropdown: 100`, `--z-modal: 200`, `--z-tooltip: 300`, `--z-toast: 400`) — or avoid it with `isolation: isolate` so children can't leak above unrelated UI. DOM order first, then one global file of sequential layers ([[z-index-strategy]]).
8. **Hit areas ≥ 44×44 touch / 40×40 desktop**, extended with a pseudo-element, never overlapping — see [[touch-and-focus]].
9. **Align by eye.** Trailing-icon padding = text-side padding − 2px; play triangles nudge 1–2px toward the point; asymmetric SVGs are fixed in the viewBox.
10. **Native scrollbar on the page.** Customize only inside small scrollers (code blocks): 8px, translucent rounded thumb.
11. **Empty states teach**: headline, one line, primary action — sized to the filled state so completing the action doesn't shift the layout. See [[empty-loading-states]].
12. **Decorative elements are inert**: `pointer-events: none`, `user-select: none`.
13. **No flash on refresh.** Persisted interactive state is set before first paint, never default-then-correct.
14. **Anchors clear the sticky header** (`scroll-margin-top`); fixed bottom chrome pads `env(safe-area-inset-bottom)`.

## Frequent offenders

| Problem | Remedy |
|---|---|
| Bold-on-hover tabs shift layout | Constant weight, color signals state |
| Digits jiggle | `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` |
| Content jumps as images load | Explicit dimensions or `aspect-ratio` |
| `scale(0.9)` on press | `scale(0.96)` |
| Brand-colored focus ring | Neutral ring |
| `z-index: 9999` | Scale, or `isolation: isolate` |
| 20px icon with a 20px hit area | Pseudo-element to 44px |
| Custom page scrollbar | Native; customize only small scrollers |
| Blank div for an empty list | Headline + line + action, sized like the filled state |
| Theme flashes on refresh | Persist + set before render |

## When to apply

The build works and now needs the last ten percent; "feels unfinished" with no single dimension obviously wrong; before any review. [[disambiguation]] routes *looks right* to [[feeling-right]], *feels finished* here, *should ship* to [[review-checklist]].

## Reference

| Detail | Value |
|---|---|
| Label beside an icon, in a pill or disc | `text-box: trim-both cap alphabetic` |
| Words to any container edge | 12px; under 8px is a finding |
| Text to its neighbour | A fixed gap of 8 to 12px, never leftover `space-between` |
| Edges 1 to 3px apart | Align exactly, or part by 8px or more |
| Filled button hover | One step of its own colour: `color-mix(in srgb, var(--accent), #000 10%)` |
| Unread dot | Hangs 7px left of the lead in the margin; the row never moves |

- Benji's call differs on press depth: the Stageshow `Button` presses to `scale(0.97)`, a hair shallower than this pass's 0.96; both clear the 0.95 floor.
- Gold example: `stageshow/teaching/composition.tsx` (`edge-separation`, `control-alignment`, `unread-gutter`) and `stageshow/examples/buttons/`.
- Check: screenshot at 1:1 and measure every word to its container (12px or more) and every pair of near edges (0 or 8px or more), the checks Stageshow's film gate runs as `tight inset` and near-tangent.

## Gotcha

Polish applied to the wrong structure is thrown away with the structure. If hierarchy or spacing is wrong, this pass is premature; fix the layout, then polish.

## Sources

- Emil Kowalski's design-engineering practice on polish, distilled by AgentsORG.
- Benji Taylor, Stageshow 1.1.1 (MIT, github.com/benjitaylor/skills, HEAD `299140f`, read 2026-11-07): `stageshow/references/craft.md` (Spacing and alignment), `stageshow/kit/controls/Button.css`, `stageshow/kit/parts/Row.css`, `stageshow/scripts/film-checks.mjs` (`nearTangent`, `tight inset`), `stageshow/teaching/composition.tsx`.
- Related: [[review-checklist]], [[responsive-feedback]], [[touch-and-focus]], [[line-behavior]], [[depth-and-nesting]].

title: wcag-thresholds

A finding cites one of these or a task an assistive-tech user cannot finish; 44px targets and heading outlines are recommendations.

# WCAG 2.2 thresholds

A review blocks on evidence, not taste. In accessibility the evidence is a WCAG 2.2 Level A or AA criterion by number, or a concrete task an assistive-technology user cannot complete. Everything else — AAA, APG conventions, one `<h1>` per page, no skipped heading levels, 44px touch targets — is a **recommendation** and never the top severity in a [[review-format]] table.

## The numbers

| Criterion | Rule |
|---|---|
| 1.4.3 Contrast | Text 4.5:1; large text (≥ 24px, or ≥ 18.67px bold) 3:1 |
| 1.4.11 Non-text contrast | Component boundaries, states and meaningful graphics 3:1 — includes input borders and custom focus rings against **every** adjacent colour |
| 1.4.1 Use of colour | Status never by colour alone: add an icon, text or underline |
| 2.5.8 Target size | 24×24 CSS px, or a smaller target spaced so a 24px circle centred on it touches no other target (links inside a sentence are exempt) |
| 2.5.7 Dragging | Every drag has a single-pointer alternative — buttons or a menu that reach the same result |
| 2.4.7 / 2.4.11 Focus | A visible indicator, and the focused element never **fully** hidden behind a sticky header, footer or banner |
| 1.4.4 Resize text | Everything survives 200% text |
| 1.4.10 Reflow | Works at 320px wide (400% zoom on 1280px) with vertical scroll only; tables, maps and code scroll in their own box |
| 2.2.2 Pause, stop, hide | Anything that moves, blinks or updates itself for more than 5 s has a visible pause |
| 1.4.2 Audio control | Nothing autoplays with sound |

Inactive controls and logos are exempt from contrast. Measuring a pair is a colour job ([[contrast-and-color-scheme]], [[color-scales-oklch]]): measure the foreground against what it **actually renders on**, report the pair, the value and the threshold missed, and leave the colours alone unless asked.

## The fixes the numbers imply

- **Targets** — keep the visual small and grow the hit area with a pseudo-element; hit areas never overlap; decorative layers get `pointer-events: none` so a glow never swallows the click beneath it. Aim for 44px touch and 40px desktop where density allows ([[touch-and-focus]]), but keep an established, usable dense tool dense.
- **Focus under sticky chrome** — `scroll-padding-block-start` on the scroller equal to the header's height; `-block-end` for a sticky footer or cookie bar ([[growth-and-overflow]]).
- **Zoom** — never `maximum-scale=1` or `user-scalable=no`; the iOS input-zoom fix is a 16px input, not a locked viewport ([[forms-behavior]]). Text boxes take `min-height`, never `height`. Write media queries in `rem` so a larger browser font size reaches the narrow layout.
- **Forced colours** — Windows High Contrast drops every `box-shadow`. A shadow ring keeps `border: 1px solid transparent` under it so an edge still draws; never `forced-color-adjust: none` without checking the control stays visible.
- **Timed UI** — auto-dismiss only low-stakes confirmations. A toast carrying an action, an error or something the user may need stays until dismissed; one that must time out gets ≥ 5 s and pauses while hovered or focused. An undo link that vanishes on a timer is data loss on a schedule.

## Reference

| Pair (Stageshow light tokens) | Ratio | 1.4.3 / 1.4.11 |
|---|---|---|
| text-strong `#262628` on `#fff` | 15.1:1 | Pass |
| text `#7a7a7d` on `#fff` | 4.28:1 | Fails body text |
| text `#7a7a7d` on canvas `#f6f5f4` | 3.93:1 | Fails body text |
| text-faint `#9a9a9d` on `#fff` | 2.81:1 | Fails even 3:1 |
| danger `#ef4444` on `#fff` | 3.76:1 | Ring passes 3:1, fails as text |
| danger-text `#b91c1c` on `#fff` | 6.47:1 | Pass |

- Benji's call differs on purpose: these tokens are tuned for product pictures, and his own floor there is nothing under 10px at phone width. In a shipped product lift secondary ink to `#767676` or darker on white (4.54:1).
- Copy the split: one danger hue for rings and a darker danger text token for words, as `form-error` colours its error line.
- Gold example: `stageshow/kit/stage.css` (tokens) and `stageshow/examples/form-error/form.css`.
- Check: measure every text token against every surface it renders on and report pair, value and threshold; with reduced motion on, anything that moves over 5s shows one complete still.

## Gotcha

This graph reaches for APCA when *designing* contrast ([[contrast-and-color-scheme]]). A *finding* still cites the WCAG 2 ratio, because that is the criterion a product is held to. Pass both; report the one with a number on it. The split is settled in [[interfaces-reconciliation]].

# MOC — Diagrams

A diagram is the costliest way to say something, so the first decision is whether to draw at all. The second is which surface the picture lives on: a finished figure for readers, an editable canvas the team keeps working in, or docs-as-code beside the text. Two companions do the drawing. Cathryn Lavery's `diagram-design` draws editorial figures (44 visual types) as one self-contained HTML file with inline SVG. tldraw's agent surfaces edit live canvases: tldraw Desktop's `tldraw-offline` skill and the tldraw MCP app. This cluster decides; the companions draw.

## The decision flow

1. [[diagram-decision]] — prose, a table, or a picture; then the surface, chosen by who touches it next; the budget (9 nodes, 12 connectors, 2 accents) that says split it.
2. [[diagram-craft]] — the figure's rules for drawing without diagram-design or reviewing one made with it: delete first, focal accents, treatments, the six connector rules, the 4px grid, the bottom legend, an accessible SVG.
3. [[diagram-design-reconciliation]] — inside a diagram-design file: how a `.design` contract reaches its color roles and families, and which value wins on paper, small type, the motion clock, export and pov.
4. [[tldraw-canvas]] — an editable board: which tldraw surface, bound arrows, Mermaid for structure, one shape per card, lints before done, anchored comments, scripts and their trust.

## Who draws it

- **diagram-design** (MIT): `npx skills add cathrynlavery/diagram-design`, or its Claude Code / Codex / Copilot / Droid marketplaces, which also bring its export, import, profile and doctor commands. Its `self_check.py` checks accessibility and motion in any install; its geometry verifier runs from a repo checkout. Export is manual only.
- **tldraw Desktop**: the app's agent setup installs the `tldraw-offline` skill and subagent; the canvas runs locally. **tldraw MCP app**: one URL in any client that supports MCP apps. **tldraw SDK**: `tldraw-migrate` handles version upgrades. Routing lives in [[skill-router]].

## Cross-cluster

- [[svg-creation]] owns the markup under an exported figure: `viewBox`, prefixed ids, SVGO flags, `<title>` and `<desc>`.
- [[animation-decision-framework]] decides whether a figure moves; diagram-design's clock decides how ([[diagram-design-reconciliation]]).
- [[data-is-content]] and [[empty-loading-states]] own charts inside a live product, which are components, not figures.
- [[ai-default-tells]] lists the generated-diagram look [[diagram-craft]] removes.
- [[pointing-beats-describing]] and [[agentation-workflow]] are the review loop a canvas's anchored comments repeat.

# Diagram craft

A designed diagram is mostly deletion. Every node is a distinct idea, every line carries information the layout doesn't already show, and the accent marks the one or two things the reader must see first. The figure is done when nothing can be removed. When `diagram-design` is installed it owns these rules and checks the geometry with its own scripts. Without it, draw from this node; with or without it, review against this node.

## Remove before you add

Run four tests before drawing. Can a node go? Can two nodes merge, because they always travel together? Can an arrow go, because the layout already implies it? Can a label go, because shape or color already says it? Then hold the budget from [[diagram-decision]]: 9 nodes, 12 connectors, 2 accents, 2 callouts.

## Signal

- **One accent, on one or two elements.** An accent on five nodes is no accent ([[color-monochromatic]]). Everything else is ink, muted or soft.
- **Hierarchy by treatment, not by size alone.** Focal: accent tint fill, accent stroke. Service: white fill, ink stroke. Store: ink at 5 %. External: ink at 3 % with a 30 % stroke. Optional: dashed `4,3`. Trust boundary: dashed accent at 50 %. Identical boxes for every node erase the hierarchy.
- **Borders, not shadows.** Nodes at radius 6, type tags at 2, never a pill or a soft 16px card. A figure is print, so [[shadows-whisper]] does not apply here.

## Connectors: the six rules a figure fails on

1. Orthogonal only. Off-axis links are right-angle elbows rounded at r=8 (r=6 in tight layouts); a straight line only when both ends share an x or a y.
2. Every arrow label sits on an opaque paper mask, 6–10px clear of its stroke, beside a vertical segment, never on the line. 14 characters at most.
3. No shared or stacked strokes. Offset parallel routes by 12px or more; hop at a single crossing.
4. Connectors on one edge each get their own attach point at `L·k/(N+1)`, at least 12px apart.
5. No line passes behind a box it doesn't end at. Reroute it.
6. No label mask overlaps a node drawn after it. Draw arrows before boxes, so lines sit behind nodes.

Strokes are muted by default, accent on the headline path, a link color on HTTP and external calls, and dashed `5,4` for async or return paths.

- **A fan-out draws its shared trunk once**, then branches from a junction; copies of one path laid over each other darken and knot (Benji Taylor, Stageshow `references/annotations.md`).
- **A reply is its own line from the recipient.** A two-headed line can't say who asked; a solid request and a dashed return can.

## Grid, type, legend

Node origins, sizes, gaps and padding divide by 4. Names go in a sans at 600; technical sublabels (ports, commands, URLs, field types) go in mono. Never use mono as a blanket "dev" font ([[typography-humanity]]). The legend is a horizontal strip under the figure, never floating among the nodes; widen the `viewBox` by about 60px to hold it. On a phone, keep the SVG's `min-width` at its viewBox width inside a local `overflow-x: auto` wrapper, so the figure scrolls and the page doesn't.

## Accessible SVG

`role="img"` with `aria-labelledby` naming a `<title>` and a `<desc>`. `<title>` is the first child, before `<defs>`. Prefix both ids with the figure's slug, never bare `title`, because figures get inlined side by side. `<desc>` is one sentence about the content, not the geometry. The general markup rules are [[svg-creation]]'s.

## Reference

Bad: three usage sources each run a full line into the invoice box, `POST` sits on its stroke, and client and API share one two-headed arrow.
Good: the three routes meet at one junction and a single delivery leaves it; the request is solid, the reply dashed and starting at the API; `POST` and `200 OK` sit on paper masks 8px clear of their strokes.

```svg
<path d="M96 64 H216" class="edge accent" marker-end="url(#fig-arrow)"/>
<path d="M216 88 H96" class="edge muted" stroke-dasharray="5 4" marker-end="url(#fig-arrow)"/>
<circle cx="272" cy="160" r="3" fill="var(--accent)" stroke="var(--paper)" stroke-width="2"/>
```

Gold example: `stageshow/examples/annotations/index.tsx`, the "A request and its reply" and "A shared processing graph" studies (trunk, junction, branches); node treatments from diagram-design's `references/style-guide.md`. The junction dot copies Stageshow's `Connector` endpoint (3px radius per `references/kit.md`, 2px white rim in `kit/motion/Connector.css`).
Benji's call differs: Stageshow's `Connector` offers `route="curve"`, one soft S, for a looser diagram; in an editorial figure the orthogonal rule above stands.
Check: cover each connector in turn and ask what the reader loses; a line that loses nothing goes. Then zoom to 400%: every end has its own attach point and no two strokes share a pixel at a node's edge.

## Gotcha

AI-default diagrams have a look: dark mode with a cyan or purple glow, identical rounded boxes, a legend floating among the nodes, labels sitting on their lines, diagonal connectors, and Mermaid's auto-layout passed off as a design ([[ai-default-tells]]). A redraw keeps the content (components, relationships, grouping, direction) and throws away the source's coordinates, colors and fonts.

# Should this be a diagram, and where does it live?

Draw only when a reader learns more from the picture than from a paragraph or a table. A diagram is the most expensive way to say something: it costs layout, labels, a legend and a review, and a wrong one teaches the wrong structure faster than prose would. Ask that question before choosing a diagram type, then choose the surface by who will touch the picture next.

## Picture, table, or sentence

| The content is… | Use |
|---|---|
| A list of things, or attributes compared side by side | a table or bullets |
| One relationship ("the API calls the queue") | the sentence |
| A before / after that changes attributes only | a table; a change of topology is a diagram (an architecture delta) |
| Flow, containment, order in time, dependency, position on two axes | a diagram |
| Live numbers inside a product | a chart component with states, not a figure ([[data-is-content]]) |

If a three-column table carries the same meaning, the table wins.

## Who touches it next decides the surface

| Next touch | Surface | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| Readers of a doc, post, README, deck or PR | a finished editorial figure: one self-contained HTML file with inline SVG; PNG or SVG only on request | `diagram-design`; [[diagram-craft]] when it is not installed; [[diagram-design-reconciliation]] when the project ships a contract |
| A team that keeps moving boxes: whiteboarding, planning, review in comments | an editable tldraw canvas | tldraw's agent surfaces ([[tldraw-canvas]]) |
| The code: versioned beside the text it explains | a Mermaid block in Markdown | the docs renderer; redraw it in diagram-design when it ships to readers |
| A team that lives in Figma | FigJam | Figma's `figma-generate-diagram` |

One picture, one surface. When a canvas becomes a published figure, redraw it: diagram-design imports Mermaid, draw.io and Excalidraw sources and lays them out again. From a tldraw board, take the structure from its shapes and bindings, not from a screenshot. Never screenshot a canvas into a doc and call it the figure.

## The budget

A figure holds about 9 nodes, 12 connectors and 2 accents. Past that it is two diagrams, an overview and a detail. diagram-design aims at a density of 4/10: complete enough to be correct, sparse enough to need no guide. An import set to `faithful` may run to 24 nodes in zones, and splits above that. A canvas has no hard budget. If a board needs a legend to get around, it needs frames instead ([[tldraw-canvas]]).

## When to apply

Before drawing any architecture, flow, sequence, state, ER, timeline, org, journey or chart figure. Also before opening a canvas, and whenever someone asks "can you diagram this?".

## Reference

| Request | Ship |
|---|---|
| "Diagram how the API, queue and worker connect" | the sentence: "The API writes jobs to the queue; the worker drains it." Three boxes in a row add nothing. |
| "Diagram our 14 services" | two figures: an overview of five zones, then the checkout path in detail at 8 nodes |
| "Sketch the launch plan with me" | a tldraw board, one frame per phase ([[tldraw-canvas]]) |
| "Show which payout this settlement belongs to", on a product shot | one leader inside the shot ([[product-shot-framing]]), not a figure beside it |

Benji Taylor makes this rule for annotated product shots, and it holds for figures too: a line earns its place by removing ambiguity, and when the layout already shows a relationship, leave the line out.
Gold example: diagram-design's SKILL.md §2 (when not to draw); for the product-shot row, `stageshow/references/annotations.md` ("Choose a line for a relationship").
Check: write the paragraph first. If someone could redraw the picture from it and lose nothing, ship the paragraph; otherwise count nodes, connectors and accents against 9, 12 and 2, and split before drawing past them.

## Gotcha

"Make a diagram" from someone who will edit it tomorrow is a canvas job, not a figure job. A diagram-design file is finished output, and changing it means running the skill again. When the request doesn't say who touches it next, ask. And a chart inside a live product is a component with loading, empty and error states ([[empty-loading-states]]), not a figure exported once.

# diagram-design reconciliation

Inside a diagram-design file, diagram-design's geometry, connector rules, type ramp and motion controller win, because its scripts check them and its linter rejects edits to the controller. The project's design contract supplies the skin: the color roles and the type families. This graph owns three things: whether to draw at all ([[diagram-decision]]), whether the figure moves ([[animation-decision-framework]]), and the review ([[diagram-craft]]). Where two of these give different values, the table names the one to use.

## Precedence

User prompt → nearest `.design` (or DESIGN.md) for the skin → the project's `.diagram-design` profile → diagram-design's rules for geometry, type ramp and motion → this graph → model defaults. A `.design` outranks every generic taste skill ([[using-design-file]]), and diagram-design's shipped style guide is one: its defaults are taste, not the project's brand.

## The handoff

diagram-design's first-run gate asks where the skin comes from. Its own discovery reads CSS, token JSON, Markdown and HTML `<style>` blocks. A `.design` file is YAML, and none of its patterns match it. So read the contract here ([[using-design-file]], or spawn [[design-md-consumer]]), map it onto the roles `paper`, `paper-2`, `ink`, `muted`, `soft`, `rule`, `accent`, `accent-tint` and `link`, and answer the gate with option (d), pasted tokens. Then offer to save a named profile. Write the `.diagram-design` marker (`profile: <slug>`) only with consent, as diagram-design's own rules require.

## The table

| Topic | diagram-design | Contract or this graph | Use inside a diagram-design file |
|---|---|---|---|
| Paper | warm-neutral, never pure white; URL onboarding swaps `#ffffff` for `#fafaf7` and asks | the contract's surface token | the contract's surface, white included; the contract is the confirmation it asks for |
| Families | Instrument Serif for title and callouts, Geist 600 names, Geist Mono technical text; keep the serif even when the brand is all-sans; never JetBrains Mono | the contract's typography | the contract's families in those role slots; the serif only if the contract has one or says nothing; mono stays for technical text, in the contract's mono |
| Accent | one accent, on 1–2 elements | the contract's signature color | the contract's accent in the `accent` role; the 1–2 limit still holds |
| Component tokens (radius, elevation, padding) | node `rx` 6, no shadows | bind to the components that list them | not mapped: a figure node is not a contract component; no shadows |
| Small type | names 12, sublabels 9, arrow labels 8 on doc presets; 16 / 12 / 12 on slides | below 12px needs an excuse ([[line-behavior]]) | diagram-design's ramp, in SVG units held at the viewBox width; a figure scaled below that width is a finding, and so is the doc ramp on a projected slide |
| Motion | static by default; `reveal` runs once, `step` waits for the reader; clock 160 / 480 / 720 ms, ease `cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1)`, ≤8 steps, ≤24px travel; the controller copied verbatim | UI under 300 ms ([[duration-table]]) | diagram-design's clock: a 480 ms step is reading pace, not UI feedback, so don't flag it against the duration table; this graph still decides whether to animate |
| Reduced motion | the complete static frame, controls hidden | [[prefers-reduced-motion]] | the same; no conflict |
| Export | manual only; `export_svg.py` carries class CSS and namespaces `<defs>` ids | [[svg-creation]]'s SVGO pass | export with `export_svg.py` only when asked; SVGO afterwards keeping `viewBox`, `<title>` and `<desc>` |
| [[pov]] | none | the product-UI sections govern product UI | a figure follows contract → profile → diagram-design; pov's "Diagrams (AgentsORG)" sets the defaults where all three are silent |

## When to apply

Any diagram-design figure in a project that ships a `.design`, a DESIGN.md or a `.diagram-design` marker, and any review of such a figure by [[ui-reviewer]] or [[motion-auditor]].

## Reference

A figure for a page built on Stageshow's default light tokens (`kit/stage.css`) answers the gate with option (d) like this:

| Role | Pasted token |
|---|---|
| `paper`, `paper-2` | `#fff` (surface), `#f6f5f4` (canvas) |
| `ink`, `muted`, `soft` | `#262628`, `#7a7a7d`, `#9a9a9d` |
| `rule` | `rgba(0,0,0,0.06)` (line) |
| `accent`, `accent-tint`, `link` | `#3b82f6`, `rgba(59,130,246,0.12)`, `color-mix(in srgb, #3b82f6 82%, #000)` |
| families | `system-ui` for title and names (no serif: the contract has one family), `"SF Mono", ui-monospace` for technical text |

Not mapped: Stageshow's radii (6, 8, 10) and shadow tokens; nodes stay `rx` 6 with no shadow.
Gold example: diagram-design's `onboarding.md` (option d) and `references/style-guide.md` (the role list).
Check: grep the exported file for `#f5f5f5`, `#2d3142` and `#eb6c36`; any hit means the shipped palette leaked. Then set the figure on the page it lives on: its paper and the page surface match exactly, and the accent sits on no more than two elements.

## Gotcha

Don't let diagram-design's defaults pose as the brand. Its shipped tokens (paper `#f5f5f5`, ink `#2d3142`, accent `#eb6c36`) trigger the first-run gate for a reason, and skipping the gate in a branded project ships someone else's palette. The reverse also happens: re-skinning the connector rules or the type ramp "to match the brand" breaks the checks diagram-design runs on them. The brand reaches the color roles and the families, and nothing else. diagram-design moves fast (plugin 2.6.68 on 2026-10-08), so re-read the named file before relying on a row.

# tldraw canvases

A canvas is for pictures people keep editing. Its quality is measured by what survives the next person's drag: arrows that stay attached, cards that carry their own words, groups that move as one. So build boards out of real relationships (bindings, frames, parents), not coordinates that only look right. tldraw ships three agent surfaces. This node routes between them and holds the canvas rules; the surface's own skill holds the API.

## Which surface

| Situation | Surface | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| The user has tldraw Desktop open (`.tldraw` files, or legacy `.tldr`) | the `tldraw-offline` skill and subagent, installed by the app's agent setup | a local HTTP server: `/api/search` to read, `/api/doc/:id/exec` to edit, a script workspace for durable behavior; a per-launch bearer token |
| A hosted client with no local app (Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor) | the tldraw MCP app, `https://tldraw-mcp-app.tldraw.workers.dev/mcp` | tools `search` (the Editor API) and `exec` (code against the live canvas in the client) |
| Building a canvas product | the tldraw SDK; `tldraw-migrate` for version upgrades | product engineering: this graph owns only the UI's craft |

Delegate long Desktop jobs to its subagent.

## Canvas rules

- **Bind every meaningful connection** with `helpers.createArrowBetweenShapes`. A raw arrow that only looks attached detaches on the next drag. Unbound arrows are for decoration only.
- **Generate structure; don't place it.** A flowchart, sequence, state machine or mind map comes from `helpers.mermaid(source)`, which creates bound shapes. Two diagrams to compare are subgraphs of one source. On a canvas Mermaid is the right start, because people rearrange the result; in a finished figure Mermaid's layout is a tell ([[diagram-craft]]).
- **A card and its words are one shape.** Put the label in the geo shape's `richText`; a long label needs a bigger card. Use `text` shapes only for words that stand alone, like a heading over a group.
- **Arrange with the editor, not with arithmetic.** Use `alignShapes`, `stackShapes` and `distributeShapes`, and draw containers with `helpers.boxShapes`. Shapes inside a frame take coordinates relative to the frame, and text never crosses a frame's edge.
- **Lint before you call it done.** Run `helpers.getLints()` and fix every lint your edit introduced, on the shape you edited. Don't move a neighbour you weren't asked to touch.
- **One accent here too.** Canvas styles are named colors (`black`, `grey`, `blue`, `orange`…), not hex, so a contract's palette can't reach a stock board. Pick one named color for the focal shapes and keep the rest neutral ([[color-monochromatic]]).

## People share the board

- **Comments are anchored instructions.** Read the threads first and use each anchor to find the shapes it means. Reply in the thread you acted on, and resolve it. A thread addressed to someone else is not yours. This is [[pointing-beats-describing]] on a canvas, the same loop as [[agentation-workflow]].
- **Ambiguity stops the edit.** "Make the important one stand out" over six identical cards is a question, and an unanswered question is not permission to pick one.
- **Static edits go through `/exec`; behavior goes in the script workspace.** A board script runs whenever the file opens, so treat a `.tldraw` file from someone else as code. Ask before writing to a board whose scripts you did not start.

## When to apply

Whiteboarding, planning boards, editable architecture sketches, design review on a canvas, and any task that names tldraw, a `.tldraw` or `.tldr` file, or a board. For a figure readers will only read, use [[diagram-decision]].

## Reference

| Part | Bad | Good |
|---|---|---|
| Connection | a raw arrow whose ends sit at `x: 320` because the card did | `helpers.createArrowBetweenShapes` from "Queue" to "Worker"; drag either card and the arrow follows |
| Label | a `text` shape floating over the card | the card's `richText`, three to six words: "Billing worker" |
| Groups | a grey rectangle drawn behind four cards | one frame per stage, named the way the team says it: "Intake", "Review" |
| Color | blue, orange, green and violet across eight cards | `blue` on the one focal path, `grey` and `black` everywhere else |
| Reply | "Done, fixed it" | "Moved 'Billing worker' into Review and bound its arrow to 'Queue'." Then resolve the thread |

The reply row is Benji Taylor's pointing-beats-describing applied to a board: name the shape by what identifies it, so the next reader finds it without asking.
Gold example: the `tldraw-offline` skill's own docs, read through `/api/search` before writing code.
Check: on a copy of the board, drag every card you touched 200px and undo; no arrow detaches, no word stays behind. Then `helpers.getLints()` reports nothing your edit introduced.

## Gotcha

The surfaces speak different shape formats. Desktop takes raw tldraw SDK records; the MCP app's `exec` goes through a focused proxy with simple string ids and flat `_type` shapes. Read the surface's own `search` before writing code, and never paste a snippet from one into the other. On Desktop, never edit a `.tldraw` archive while it is open. Save a local document yourself with `helpers.saveDoc()` instead of asking the user to.

summary: Faux product UI — the still or short animated product shot on a landing page, feature card, docs hero or bento tile. # MOC — Faux UI

A product shot is not the product. It is an illustration of one moment in it: a window cropped to the panel where the story happens, a cursor that does one satisfying thing, a payoff that holds. Agents can build the parts; what they get wrong is the hundred small decisions around them, and the result reads as generated. This cluster writes those decisions down.

The one sentence the cluster hangs on: **it reads as a real product, simplified to what the viewer needs, framed with intent, and every motion has a cause.**

Five ways it fails, each owned by a node:

| Failure | Looks like | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| Too much | Real text in every row, numbers everywhere | [[faux-ui-restraint]] |
| Wireframe | Two grey blobs and a button | [[faux-ui-restraint]] |
| Boxed | A whole window shrunk into a card with even margins | [[product-shot-framing]] |
| Flat | Every object the same weight in the same bordered card | [[product-shot-framing]], [[bento-grids]] |
| Bland | A grey window and a cursor, whatever the brief's style was | [[faux-ui-restraint]] (character is real too) |

## Order of work

Most of the quality is decided before code. Run `/design-engineering stage` ([[cmd-stage]]) or follow this order by hand:

1. [[product-shot-framing]] — medium, size, layout and crop, decided first.
2. [[faux-ui-restraint]] — the word budget, fidelity, type, spacing, icons and chrome of the still.
3. [[demo-story-and-loops]] — story shape, beats, poster, loop and reset, the timing of things that change.
4. [[demo-cursor-and-touch]] — the cursor, drags, selection, scroll, camera, phones.
5. [[demo-rehearsal]] — film it, read every frame, a fresh-eye review, the handover note.

A grid of tiles is one picture planned as a set: [[bento-grids]]. With Stageshow installed (1.1.1) it owns the build, every button, card, draft and shortcut comes from its kit part, and nothing ships until `--gate` ends `rehearsal passed`: [[stageshow-reconciliation]].

Each node ends on a **Reference**: a before/after to copy, the closest Stageshow gold example to open, and one check to run on your own output.

## Cross-cluster

- A product demo inside a rendered launch film is [[launch-video-ui-demo]]: a different medium with bigger cursors and no replay. [[stageshow-reconciliation]] says which owns which.
- Page-level motion rules ([[marketing-surface-rules]]) still bind the page around the demo; a looping demo needs the pause [[wcag-thresholds]] asks for.
- Fake content tells ([[content-authenticity]], [[ai-default-tells]]) apply to the words a demo shows; filler bars at its edges are not lorem ipsum.
- Collaborators shown live in a demo follow [[presence-signals]].

# Bento grids

A grid where every tile is a cropped window reads as generated however well each window is made: the same signal four times. Most of the quality is decided in the tile list, before anything is drawn ([[unslop-pass]] names the three-cards-with-better-kerning failure; this node is the cure).

## The rules

1. **Not every tile is UI.** About a third to a half show product UI; the rest are other kinds (below).
2. **One hero:** two columns or two rows, the richest picture or the main idea. Equal tiles need a clear difference in content and weight.
3. **A UI tile shows one thing, not a window:** crop to the single component (the button, the stepper, the fee picker) at real size or larger. Window chrome appears at most once in a grid, on the hero.
4. **Neighbours contrast,** across and down like a checkerboard: a picture beside a number, dense beside calm. Two window crops never sit side by side.
5. **A stat tile is one real number at display size** (48–72px as shown), a short lead ("Up to"), a one-line label, at most one coloured glyph. The number and its unit sit on one line (`white-space: nowrap`, or move the unit into the lead). Real figures, never "10x".
6. **Copy is short and outside the picture:** one to four words or one sentence, at page size (17–24px), never the 12px of the UI inside. A run-in works: a bold lead and a grey continuation at the same size.
7. **One frame, varied contents:** shared radius, gap, padding and copy position; the gap equals the tiles' inner padding or a clear fraction of it. Pick one family — rounded tiles on a gap, or a ruled grid with 1px lines and no gap.
8. **Say each thing once across the set.** No real string, avatar, colour mark or chrome repeats from tile to tile.
9. **Compose the grounds together:** a quiet grid shares one surface with one photo, accent or inverted tile as punctuation; an expressive one may use several grounds if their lightness, temperature and saturation make a rhythm.
10. **Motion has one place to lead.** A supporting tile does one small thing once as the grid scrolls in (staggered 80–120ms in reading order) or on hover; at most the hero tells a short cursor story. Several competing loops leave the eye nowhere to land.
11. **One Stage per tile at 1:1,** copy as page HTML beside it. One Stage around the whole grid scales every tile's type with it: a 1000px grid in a 630px column draws 15px titles at 9.5px.
12. **The tile edge owns the bleed.** An inner fixed-width picture must not slice a window halfway across a wider tile and leave a blank strip; match the picture slot's width at every breakpoint.
13. **Every width is its own design.** Two columns only while each tile stays readable (an article column around 550px may hold two); a phone column stacks, hero first. Important text stays at least 10px at a 320px host.

## Kinds of tile

| Kind | Holds |
|---|---|
| One component | A single control or panel at real size or larger, cropped by the tile |
| Hero UI | The one tile with a real screen, framed by [[product-shot-framing]] |
| Stat | One big number, a lead, a label, maybe one coloured glyph |
| Statement | One sentence in large type |
| Object | A card, chip, keycap or device, one light source, a real material |
| Diagram | A grid, heatmap or nodes and lines in one stroke weight, holding still |
| Collection | Logos, app icons, file tiles, bleeding off an edge |
| Photo | A licensed photograph; never a scene drawn in CSS or SVG passed off as one |

A grid of five usually wants one hero UI, one or two components, one stat or statement, and one object, diagram or collection. Layouts: hero and strip (2/3 + 1/3, then three), staggered pair, big square (a 2×2 hero in four columns), ruled (one container, 1px rules) for technical pages; an even 3×2 only when every neighbour is a different kind.

## Plan it as a table

| Tile | Span | Kind | The one thing | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Inbox | 2×1 | Hero UI | One conversation arriving, selected | "Shared inbox" + a sentence |
| SLAs | 1×1 | Stat | "14m" left, in the warning colour | "Never miss a reply." |
| Assign | 1×1 | Component | The assignee menu, one person checked | "Assignments" |

Then check the plan against rules 1–4 and 8 before building: how many tiles are UI, which is the hero, does any tile touch the same kind, does any string repeat.

## Objects

A drawn object gets one light source and the shadow of the tiles around it. A payment card keeps its real anatomy at any size: the chip about an eighth of the card's width, a third of the way down, contactless arcs beside it at half the chip's height, name and number along the bottom, the network mark bottom-right. A chip the size of an icon on a tile-sized card is the giveaway.

## When to apply

Any feature grid, bento section or set of feature cards on one page. [[viewport-custom-design]] owns the page grid around it; [[cards-design]] owns product cards.

## Reference

A five-tile plan, generated and then fixed by the rules above:

| Before | After |
|---|---|
| Five 1×1 tiles, each a cropped window with traffic lights | Hero UI 2×1 holding the only chrome; one component; one stat; one object; one statement |
| "10x faster" at 32px, "faster" wrapping under the number | "14m" at 56px on one line (`white-space: nowrap`), lead "Under", label "median first reply" |
| One `<Stage width={1000}>` around the grid in a 630px column | One `Stage` per tile at its slot width; copy at 17–24px as page HTML beside it |

Gold example: `stageshow/examples/bento/` (Kite's features grid, hero and strip, its tile list written in the file before any tile was built); `stageshow/examples/hero-grid/` for an image-led grid where only one tile moves.
Check: before building, count the UI tiles in the plan (a third to a half) and scan it for a repeated string or two same-kind neighbours; after, film the grid at a 320px host and confirm no important text renders under 10px.

## Gotcha

One conversation threaded through five tiles ("Refund for order #4821" three times) feels like a story to its builder and reads as one signal repeated. Each tile gets its own specific moment.

title: demo-cursor-and-touch
summary: Driving a product demo like a hand — cursor kinds set by the elements it crosses, travel timed by distance on a shallow arc, a visible press, never over the label it clicks, rests on empty surface; drags as one motion with a fixed grab offset; selections that stay under the I-beam; one camera push-in; phones driven by touch with flicks and UIKit-quick responses.
tags: [faux-ui, cursor, drag, touch, phone, camera, demo]

# Demo cursor and touch

A cursor in a demo is a character: it moves like a hand, presses visibly, and every move goes somewhere for a reason. No cursor is also a choice — the states and timing carry a system story, and nothing walks a focus ring or spotlight between controls as a stand-in.

## The pointer

- **Travel is timed by distance on a shallow arc:** `clamp(260 + 0.9 × distance, 300, 650)` ms on an ease-in-out, bowing sideways by `min(0.08 × distance, 24)` px. Short hops are quick; long trips don't drag.
- **A press reads:** a 120ms dwell on arrival, the pointer dips to 0.9 over 80ms, holds 100ms, and releases over 260ms on `(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)`. The pressed control shows its own product press ([[responsive-feedback]]), and the state changes after the click completes.
- **The kind comes from the element** (I-beam over text, hand on a link, open hand over something draggable, crosshair on a canvas, resize arrows on edges and corners), switching mid-path as it crosses the edge, never after arriving, and morphing between shapes rather than popping. Native app buttons keep the arrow.
- **It never covers the words it clicks:** aim inside the target, off its text (about 85% across, 60% down). It rests on empty surface near its next move, never on an unused control, and fades after about 4 s at rest.
- **It stays where the press happened** while the result changes size.
- **A state the click sets fades in, quickly:** a picked tool, a selected row, an active filter eases its fill in over about 150ms and back out the same, never on in one frame. A choice that moves between options is a segmented control or tabs whose highlight slides.
- **One cursor style per site,** so every demo on a page points the same way. On a dark stage the I-beam turns white with a dark edge.
- **Keyboard stories show the keys** as keycaps, placed clear of anything open.

## Drags and selection

- **A mouse drag is one motion:** the thing follows the pointer the whole way and leaves on release. Drag time `clamp(360 + 1.1 × distance, 450, 900)` ms.
- **Pickup belongs to the press**; a drag starts where the thing is, and the grab offset is where the hand took hold, kept through travel and release. A file from outside enters already held.
- **A carried card is held, not slid:** scale 1.03, a deeper shadow, a degree or two of tilt with its words tilting too, flat on drop, no selection outline in the air.
- **Drop targets never travel:** the slot jumps cell to cell instead of chasing the card. Moving a card between lists closes the source slot on lift and opens the destination in flight.
- **A text selection reads left to right from a word boundary and stays under the I-beam on every frame**, driven from the pointer's position, not grown by time.

## Scroll and camera

- **Nothing scrolls unless the pointer is on it.** Start with whole rows; fade only the edges hiding content once scrolled. Scroll time `clamp(420 + 1.2 × distance, 500, 1400)` ms, and scroll back before the loop ends, never at the seam.
- **The camera needs a reason:** push in only when the payoff would be too small to read at shown size. Frame the wide shot as a good still first; one push-in per story, in and back out, the cursor still while the view moves.

## Phones

- **Touch, never the macOS arrow:** a dot only where the finger taps or drags. It shows 140ms before a tap and lingers 240ms after the lift.
- **In-app responses are UIKit-quick:** `cubic-bezier(0.3, 0.75, 0.1, 1)` over 0.5 s; a card opens into its screen as one object.
- **A swipe is a flick:** a third of the screen in about a quarter second (`clamp(180 + 0.5 × distance, 240, 300)` ms), lifting while still moving; what it threw carries on at that speed, thrown over 0.5 s on `(0.25, 1, 0.5, 1)`. A swiped row's action is its own back, edge to edge, revealed as the row slides off it.
- **Act where people do:** a notification is tapped to open its app; the reply happens in the app, not through long-press actions few people use.
- **Dynamic Island:** animate the black shape's box and radius together, content on its own layer; about 500ms growth, 380ms shrink after a 120ms delay, a 0.965 press squeeze.

## Typing

Stageshow types at 35ms a character (about 28 a second), which suits a short string the viewer only needs to recognise. A prompt that carries the argument types at read speed, about 15 a second ([[launch-video-ui-demo]]).

## When to apply

Any faux UI with a pointer, a drag, a selection, a scroll, a camera move or a phone gesture.

## Reference

The same click, aimed two ways (the script in Stageshow's `examples/buttons`):

| Before | After |
|---|---|
| `a.click('resolve')`: the centre of the button, the arrow over "Resolve" | `a.click({ at: 'resolve', x: 0.84, y: 0.7 })`: inside the box, off the word |
| Arrive and swap the label in the same frame, glyph still on it | 120ms dwell, dip to 0.9, release 260ms; then `a.set({ resolve: 'Resolved' })`, and `a.move('rest')` to an empty point before the loop resets |
| A 700px trip in 300ms on a straight line | `clamp(260 + 0.9 × 700, 300, 650)` = 650ms, bowed 24px |

Gold example: `stageshow/examples/buttons/index.tsx` (presses beside the word, rests on an empty `rest` target); `stageshow/examples/cursor-morph/` for kinds that change mid-path.
Check: film each press with `--slow 6 --every 40`. In no frame may the cursor cover the label it pressed or is about to change, and every move must end at the next action or at rest.

## Gotcha

A cursor resting on the button it just pressed, or parked on the label it is about to change, hides the one thing the beat is about. Move it off as soon as the press lands.

## Sources

Paraphrased; the numbers are from his code, re-verified at `299140f`.

# Demo rehearsal

Agents check their work by reading the code back or taking one screenshot once it has settled. Neither shows the frames in between, which is where demo bugs live. A dress rehearsal runs the whole demo at real speed, films it, and reads every frame.

## Order

1. **Prove the still before choreography.** Render the opening and the payoff at both shipping widths beside the closest reference at shown size. Can the viewer find the focal object and what changes before any branding? Clear every framing fault before touching motion.
2. **Set the poster first** ([[demo-story-and-loops]]), then film the loop.
3. **Film the whole loop plus the start of the next** as one contact sheet at a fixed interval, at true size: once at the shown width, once at 390, once per look shipped (light and dark are separate passes). With Stageshow, always film with `--gate`: the same contact sheet plus a verdict, so it costs nothing extra.
4. **Step through every beat at 40–80ms:** presses, menus, morphs, hand-offs, exits, the seam. A contact sheet sampled every second cannot show a pop; mark beats by name in the script and film them, never guess delays.
5. **Fix the largest visible fault first** — framing, then hierarchy, then motion, then polish — and re-film from the top.
6. **Hold it beside the closest reference** and ask: what does the eye land on first, and is it the result? Is one window, tile or device clearly leading?

Stageshow automates this with `scripts/film.mjs` (headless Chrome, contact sheets, a JSON report, `--gate` that ends `rehearsal passed` or exits 1 on any never-intentional line), `jumps.mjs` (one-frame snaps between samples) and `layout.mjs` (text and controls fitting their boxes). Don't hand over until the loop's gate passes: every line it prints is a fault a viewer will see, even when the contact sheet looks smooth. Short on time, fixing its lines comes before more stills, the review and the notes. Without it, a Playwright loop that screenshots the stage every N ms and records element rects every animation frame does the same job.

## Faults that are never intentional

Fix the cause and re-film; clearing one by hiding, removing or opting out the thing it points at is itself a bug.

| Fault | What it means |
|---|---|
| Cut by the crop | An action, chip, button or shadow sliced by the stage edge |
| Framing | A floating whole window, a gutter crossed by a few px, a popover against an edge |
| Tight inset / tight control / tight mark | Words under 8px from an edge; a button under 8px below a field; a dot within 5px of its avatar or text |
| Tight or loose stack | A title and subtitle under 3px or over 10px of ink apart |
| Empty pane, loose list, fat row | A void under content; rows spread to fill a pane; a one-line row three times its words' height |
| Onion skin | See-through fills overlapping at rest |
| Unit wrapped | A stat's unit on its own line |
| Unsized text | Text in a window left at the stage's 16px baseline because nothing sized it; app text is about 12–14px |
| Spills its slot | Content running past the width it was laid out in; a ring drawn as its own layer running into a neighbour's words or past its card |
| Mixed icons, emoji icon, invented mark | Filled beside outline; an emoji as an icon; a letter tile beside a real company's name |
| Anchor drift | An open popover moving as its list changes height |
| Selection drift | A text highlight not under the I-beam |
| Kit override | Your CSS reshaping a frame or part's geometry |

Other findings are candidates to judge — an element that appears and then moves, a landing that snaps a few px after motion ends, text that steps inside its box as a layer drops, near-empty frames — fix the real ones and say why the rest stand.

## What the tools can't sign off

A clean report is necessary, not sufficient: it catches mistakes, not a dull idea, a wrong path or an implausible gesture. Still watch playback at speed, slowed transitions, an interruption, reduced motion (the poster, whole and complete), a return from offscreen, pause and replay — and after the final edit. A virtual clock proves geometry, not frame rate. Phone width in a desktop browser is not touch.

## The fresh eye

Give a reviewer the frames, the URL, the checklist and the reference stills — never the builder's plan, reasons or notes. First question: does this composition answer *this* product and page, or could it be any product in its category? Then a ranked list, framing first: what to screenshot, which frame shows it, the fix in one line. A predicted failure is not a finding, and neither is a predicted pass. Platform conventions (Messages' blue, macOS lights, a true-size iOS banner) are never sent back.

## Hand over

A `REHEARSAL.md` beside the component:

```md
# Rehearsal: <demo>
Gold: <example> (kept, changed)
Beats: 1 … 2 … 3 … payoff, loop <n>s
Captured: widths, looks, states, reduced motion
Gate: <the last line of the gated loop film, pasted>
Film: <each fault> → <frame> → <fix or why it stands>
Review: <reviewer's list> → <response>
Not checked:
```

## When to apply

Before handing over any animated faux UI, and after every edit that moves something.

## Reference

The runs behind a handover that holds, then the line that goes in the note:

```sh
node scripts/film.mjs "<url>/?capture=resolve" --out shots/wide.png --every 1000 --count 18 --gate
node scripts/film.mjs "<url>/?capture=resolve" --out shots/phone.png --width 390 --every 1000 --count 18 --gate
node scripts/film.mjs "<url>/?capture=resolve" --out shots/seam.png --at seam --every 60 --count 24
```

Before: `Gate: contact sheet looked clean`. After: `Gate: rehearsal passed (necessary, not sufficient: …)`, pasted from the wide and the 390 run.
Gold example: `stageshow/references/verify.md` (Hand over, the template with its Gate line) and `stageshow/scripts/film-checks.mjs` (what each gate line measures).
Check: the exit code after each gated run is 0, and `Not checked:` names at least one case the films can't cover (real touch, frame rate, a slow device).

## Gotcha

Ten film runs, gate green, frame unchanged: stop iterating and get the fresh eye. The loop has converged on the builder's blind spot.

## Sources
