# Demo story and loops

An animated product demo is a short film the viewer did not ask for, so every move needs a reason and the loop has to survive being watched twice.

## Pick the shape from what the product is valued for

- **How it feels to use:** the gesture is the story. A cursor does one satisfying thing and the result appears under its hand.
- **A flow in an app:** a few screens told as one continuous object, payoff on the last; no bolted-on second device.
- **What the system does:** the consequence lands somewhere else, and the link is drawn (a value on a connector, a card flying into a list). Usually no cursor.

**Beauty decides.** Between a richer story and a calmer, better-framed one, choose the frame.

## Beats

- **10–16 s per loop, 3–5 beats** building to a payoff; one gesture and a response can be enough. A second scene earns its length only with a new outcome or surface, never the same beat twice.
- **Open on a finished screen that works as a still**; the first real content is there before the first beat.
- **The payoff is visible at shown size** (a panel, a window coming forward, a clear state change) and **arrives full** — never a blank surface for a quarter second.
- **A satellite arrives at the beat it pays off**, carrying its payload, or is present from frame one in a reserved column.
- **The poster is the frame most people see** (a thumbnail, reduced motion, a screenshot). Set it to the beat that tells the story on its own, with the result left on screen. Never a frame caught mid-change: a digit mid-roll held still reads as a glitch.
- **Motion without hierarchy is cut.** Cover each moving element in turn; if the story is clearer without it, it goes.

## Loops

- **The payoff holds 2 s; nothing on screen sits still for more than 3 s.** Within about a second of the exit ending, the next action has begun.
- **Every reset has a cause or is invisible**, in that order: a seen cause (undo with its keycaps, Clear, close), an exit around an anchor, a snap while hidden.
- **Data never rewinds in view.** Snap it back off camera or under a closed panel, or bring the next loop's data in as new.
- **A loop never plays a navigation backwards** — no product shrinks an app back into its notification. Undo the state in place instead, in a quick reverse stagger (the last change first, about 70ms apart), or cut while something covers it. Locking the phone or going home resets only a lock-screen story; inside one app, a black screen on a white page reads as the demo ending.
- **Exit around an anchor:** what the story added leaves in one reverse stagger, 40–80ms apart, all moving within half a second, while product content stays. A growing story runs as a conveyor: exit the batch, bring fresh rows in from the crop.

## Pace

- **Storytelling motion is unhurried, on two curves:** travel `cubic-bezier(0.45, 0, 0.1, 1)`; arrival from nowhere `cubic-bezier(0.25, 0.8, 0.25, 1)` over 0.8–1 s.
- **UI feedback stays as quick as the real product** ([[duration-table]]); only the story slows. Feedback starts on the input.
- **Related responses overlap:** a changed setting leads its label, then its dependents; the result still follows its cause. Stagger in reading order 40–80ms within a scene, 80–120ms between tiles of a grid ([[stagger-choreography]]).
- **Colour changes between distant hues take about 200ms**; they pass through mud however they are done.

## Things that change, arrive and leave

- **Change only what changed:** roll the changed span and carry what follows by its measured width. Button states share one slot sized to the largest. Numbers roll digit by digit, last digit first, unchanged digits still.
- **A control changes on itself:** a button whose label or icon changes stays the same button (Resolve to Resolved crossfades and eases its width, neighbours moving with it), and a typed draft becomes the posted comment in place, holding the finished comment's height from the first keystroke. Never swap in a second element.
- **Status words roll** (Queued, Running, Passed), never two spans crossfading in place; rows changing together cascade about 60ms apart, since a column rolling in unison reads as flicker.
- **Nothing pops; no blank frames.** What replaces something arrives as it leaves. A new row carries the rows below it. A resizing surface moves size, position and content as one transition, never stretching its text.
- **Solid things do not fade through:** windows, phones and cards arrive by moving, opaque. Cards, toasts and reactions arrive whole from just above, never uncovered by a hard edge.
- **One object, one trip** ([[fly-not-teleport]]): open the room, measure the landing element itself (not its padded wrapper), fly; the flyer takes its resting look in the last third; landings decelerate with no bounce.
- **An open popover holds the edge it opened from**; reserve the height of its longest list.

## Measured kit values

The timings Stageshow's kit ships, worth copying when building by hand:

| Motion | Value |
|---|---|
| Flight (`Fly`) | 750ms; x on `(0.35, 0, 0.2, 1)`, y on `(0.3, 0.6, 0.15, 1)` — separate axes make the arc; a 1.12 lift at 30% gone by 85% |
| Row opening (`Collapse`) | opening: height 0.46 s `(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1)`, content fading in over 0.24 s after 150ms; closing: height 0.42 s after 50ms, content dimming fast and dissolving as the edge passes, holding its open state until the height settles |
| Rolling text (`Roll`) | old and new travel together on one curve, 0.42 s `(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1)`, under a 0.5em feathered mask, no blur; width 0.5 s `(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)`; a control label (`fade`) crossfades, new in 0.35 s after 120ms, old out 0.16 s, width 0.4 s |
| Button (`Button`) | label through `Roll` fade; an added icon's slot opens over 220ms `(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)`; press 0.97 over 180ms `(0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1)` |
| Popover | scale 0.24 s `(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)` from the side nearest its trigger, contents fading |
| Connector | draws over 1 s `(0.65, 0, 0.35, 1)` after both ends are placed, ends on a dot |
| Rolling digits (`Count`) | `(0.3, 0.75, 0.1, 1)` |

## When to apply

Scripting any animated faux UI: a hero loop, a hover-played feature card, a play-once docs demo.

## Reference

Three loop endings and status changes, before and after Stageshow 1.1:

| Before | After |
|---|---|
| Loop end: the phone locks, the app goes home, 600ms of black, reopen | Undo in place: the last change first, each step 70ms after the one before, all moving within 0.5 s |
| Status cell: `Running` fades out while `Passed` fades in over it | `<Roll delay={row * 60}>{status}</Roll>`: one 0.42 s drum, rows cascading |
| A `Resolve` button replaced by a separate `Resolved` button | `<Button icon={done ? <Check /> : undefined}>{done ? 'Resolved' : 'Resolve'}</Button>` |

Gold example: `stageshow/examples/subscriptions/` (a second scene is the reset) and `stageshow/examples/buttons/` (labels and an icon changing on the same button).
Check: mark the seam (`act.mark('seam')`) and film it with `--at seam --every 60`. No frame may be empty or black, no data may run backwards in view, and every reset step must have a cause you can point to.

## Gotcha

Matching endpoint screenshots prove nothing about the frames between. The bugs live in transit — a pill that hops 4px on its way in, one frame where everything has faded out — so the loop is filmed, not screenshotted ([[demo-rehearsal]]).

# Faux-UI restraint

Left alone, an agent fills every row: it knows what a support inbox contains. The more readable detail, the more generated the picture looks. The fix is a full, structured screen in quiet greys, real words only where the story is, placeholder lines for the rest, and room to breathe. **Simplify the words, not the context.**

## The word budget

- **Count the real strings:** the title, the thing acted on, what is typed, the result. Usually 3 to 7. Everything else is a placeholder bar.
- **A word budget is not an element budget.** A calendar still needs a populated week; a search still needs a collection to search.
- **Bars belong at the edges; words go where the eye lands.** Grey bars on the subject read unfinished. Where the story touches a list: two or three real rows and at most as many bars.
- **In a small surface a row is one line** (avatar, name, value), never a grey bar under a real name.
- **Label and value match:** both words or both bars. A blank pill beside a real control is dead; drop it.
- **Keep the domain's signature content** — album art, thumbnails, avatars. Swapped for the feature's signal, a music app becomes a generic list.
- **One number gets to be big.** **Say it once:** one clear sign of the feature, not its signal in header, satellite and every row.
- **Placeholder widths vary** row to row (60, 45, 70, 52), and a bar sits in the line box of the text it replaces, so a skeleton row keeps the real row's pitch.
- **No masthead for a fictional product.** Its name appears only where the real product would show it (a notification's app name, a title bar), and only when the brief leans on it.

## Fidelity is a dial

`minimal` is all bars; `standard` is words where they carry meaning and bars elsewhere (the default); `realistic` is plausible content everywhere, still with air — the right call at hero scale, for a named real product, or for a still whose subject *is* the list. Write filler once, as text that becomes a bar below realistic, so the dial decides. Realism is the developer's call; so is character: a brief with a style (kawaii, blueprint, paper, glass over colour) gets that style in full, still built to these rules.

## Type and spacing

- UI text at real sizes, 11–15px, scaled by the stage; nothing under 10px as rendered on a phone. One family; monospace only for code, identifiers and aligned numbers. Sentence case unless the product capitalises.
- **No real headings:** a faux app's title is a `div`, never `h1`–`h6`; the demo lives inside someone else's page outline.
- Words keep a 12px inset from any window, card, panel or hovered row edge (under 8px is a fault). Row padding 12px, 8px dense; a one-line row three times taller than its words is a fat row.
- A button sits 8–12px from the field or line above it: closer reads as touching, much further and it drifts off from the field it belongs to. A floating card (a comment popup, a toast) pads the same all round, measured to the avatar's and button's edges, not their words. A title over its subtitle has 4–6px of ink between them; the air comes from the row's padding.
- Buttons, cards, fields, toasts and shortcuts come from a component, never a lookalike class per screen: a hand-built one is where uneven padding, squeezed labels and unsized text come from.
- A progress ring is one track and one arc with round caps, never dashed segments; its number centres on its digits (proportional figures, trimmed to cap height).
- A status dot, badge or ring is not a column: 6px clear of the avatar or text, inside the row's inset.
- No near-tangents: edges 1–3px apart look accidental. Align them exactly, or part them by the gutter and never under 8px.
- Centre a label on its letters (`text-box: trim-both cap alphabetic`), not its line box. A centred amount centres its digits; the currency sign hangs at `right: 100%`.
- Nested shapes pad evenly, and the outer radius is the inner radius plus that padding.

## Icons, marks and colour

- **Icons come from a set, never from your hand** — the product's own pack first, else one chosen on purpose, one size (14–16px) and one stroke throughout; filled at 14px and under ([[icon-systems]]). One opaque colour; fade with `opacity` on the whole SVG, never translucent ink that darkens where strokes cross.
- **Emoji are content, never icons.**
- **A real company carries its real mark** in its own proportions and colours, or a plain text wordmark. A letter in a coloured square beside a real name is an invented logo.
- **No sparkle, wand or purple as the colour of AI.** Show what the AI does. The product's own sparkle icon is fine; a generic one is decoration ([[ai-default-tells]]).
- One neutral family, five inks and one accent to start; status colours mean status. Nothing translucent overlaps. On dark, depth comes from a lighter surface, not a shadow ([[dark-mode]]). The hero is never outlined with an accent ring to point at it: lift it as the product would.

## Chrome and devices

- Chrome for the task: browser chrome only when the browser is part of the picture; a desktop app gets its real chrome; never platform chrome drawn from memory — open the real app or a screenshot.
- The phone draws its own status bar and home indicator; never hand-drawn. Nothing sits under the Dynamic Island. A phone is lit from its first frame.
- An iPhone messaging app keeps Messages' conventions (blue sent, grey received, plus and mic in the composer) unless the brief gives it a look. Platform conventions are the product's chrome, not placeholders.

## When to apply

Building or reviewing the still frame of any faux UI, and the poster frame of an animated one.

## Reference

A comment card at 13px, hand-built and then built on the kit's `Card` (Stageshow `examples/cards`):

| Before | After |
|---|---|
| `padding: 20px 14px`, Resolve 4px under the body, inner quote `border-radius: 12px` | `<Card>`: 16px on every side, `gap` 12, the quote's radius `var(--ss-card-inner)` (the card's radius less its padding) |
| Name, time, body, quote, two rows of metadata, three buttons, all real words | Mara Lind, "2m", one sentence, Reply, Resolve: five real strings; the quote is two bars at 80% and 56% |
| Body left at the 16px page default | Body 13px at a 1.45 line height |

Gold example: `stageshow/examples/cards/index.tsx` for the card; `stageshow/examples/static-card/` for a whole still on the word budget.
Check: count the real strings in the poster (3–7), then measure the card's four paddings to the avatar and button edges; they should match to the pixel.

## Gotcha

Stripping the screen to two blobs is the opposite failure. If it looks emptier, flatter or smaller than the closest reference shot, enlarge the content and add structure before adding words ([[screenshot-critique]] makes the same point for pages).

Paraphrased.

# Product-shot framing

Framing decides whether the picture reads as a product shot or a screenshot pasted into a box. Decide it before building anything: a crop needs nothing past the crop, and it sets how big the type must be.

## Size first

Design at the size it will be seen and show it at 1:1. About 720 × 340 for a hero beside copy, 900–1100 wide for a full-width hero, 400 × 300 for a feature card; never under about 320 wide for a demo (a bento tile or satellite card may be smaller). A lone card in a 680px column wants 500–560 wide so its text reads at 15–20px. Small formats crop harder: a 400px card holds a third of a dashboard at full size, not all of it at a third.

## The rules

1. **One hero, at most one or two satellites** (a receipt, a phone, a detail card) that carry the point. Two satellites are two kinds and two sizes — a card and a small system object — never two equal cards on one edge, which read as a pile.
2. **Keep what identifies the product:** a title, the real chrome, the rows that give the action a reason. Logo and nav are optional.
3. **Crop 10–40% of the hero off stage.** The window or phone fills at least two thirds of the stage width and runs off an edge. Shapes that read when cut (a card, a slider track, a row of avatars) run off by a third or more.
4. **Crop only filler.** The payoff, the action, what the cursor touches and every real word stay whole; a list or terminal may run one line off a bled bottom. A placeholder button the crop would slice is removed, not sliced. If the story does not fit, change the stage size or the layout.
5. **The stage masks everything** (`overflow: hidden`), one rounded corner per edge. Fades only for sliding tracks, stacks, charts, and one crop: a window fading out at its foot, by mask, over filler.
6. **Satellites straddle the hero's edge about half outside**, over chrome or margin, never content; fully outside, tie them back with a 1px leader ending in a dot. Anchored UI (a popover, menu, toast) is not a satellite: it sits where the product puts it.
7. **One gutter**, measured in the final crop: the hero's inset sets every other edge distance. An edge either sits a full gutter in or runs well past; crossing by under 24px or stopping a few px short reads as a mistake.
8. **A window keeps its device's shape:** whole, 1.25:1 or wider; bled, what shows is at least square. Fix by crop, never by squashing.
9. **What the story opens stays in frame**, a gutter from every edge on every frame; place the trigger so the overlay has room.
10. **No dead corners**, at rest or anywhere in the loop.
11. **Start flat and frontal.** Depth from shadow, z-order, scale and opacity; a tilt has to beat the straight version at final size.

## The page is the ground

"White page" means a transparent stage: no plate (a tinted field the window floats on) behind the device on a white or dark page. A whole, centred window with air on four sides floats; bleed it off two edges or fill the slot. Unframed — whole, centred, margin at least the shadow's depth — only when the developer asks for it. The stage is the shot: a tile is cut to the stage's shape, never a stage boxed inside another ground.

## Layouts

| Layout | Hero | Satellite | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Corner bleed | Inset ~10% top and left, 15–35% past right and bottom | Straddling left or bottom | Hero beside copy |
| Pinned, bottom bleed | Inset 8–12% left, right, top; 15–35% past the bottom | Optional, straddling a side | Feature card, bento tile |
| Stage with gutters | Inset 8–20% each side on a coloured stage, off the bottom | One side | Brand moment |
| Satellite focus | Cropped hard, mostly context | Large, 30–40% of hero width, carries the story | A notification, receipt, diff |
| Wide hero | 900–1100px at 1:1, realistic fidelity, off the bottom | A card on its lower edge | Full-width homepage hero |
| Device pair | Desktop ~75–80% wide, off the bottom | Phone straddling right, a third outside, present from frame one | Cross-device story |
| Close-up | Whole window at 1.3–1.6×, chrome and all | None | A card about one control |
| Many of one | A grid of one small thing off every edge, one in focus by depth | None | Templates, previews, sessions |
| Tilted stack | Three cards at −6°, 4°, −2°, offset 12–20px; only the top one has words | None | Paper: receipts, tickets — the one place tilt earns its keep |
| Corner chip | Window inset top-left | A pill centred on its corner, half outside | One live fact about the whole product |

The layouts are recipes, not a mandate: a whole window with even gutters is valid when its contents read and the brief asks for it.

## Phones

A satellite phone starts at 40% of the window's visible width and at least 220px; let it run off rather than shrink. Notifications stay at true iOS size and native width (the screen minus 18pt a side) — size the phone around the banner, never the banner to the phone. A phone cropped at the top loses its status bar and nav bar together; one whose bottom the stage crops stacks its notifications under the clock (Stageshow's `LockScreen stack="top"`), so no banner sits on the cut. In a 400px host a phone is always cropped: a gutter from one edge, off the other, screen at 1:1.

## Compact is a second design

Every demo that can sit in a phone column ships a second composition at the column's width (358 in a 390 viewport): crop closer, drop or stack the satellite, keep action and payoff whole. A desktop scene scaled down passes an overflow check while its 13px text renders at 8px ([[viewport-custom-design]]).

## When to apply

Before any code for a hero illustration, feature card, docs plate or bento tile; again after anything moves.

## Reference

A 400 × 300 feature card, generated framing against the pinned bottom bleed:

| Before | After |
|---|---|
| Whole window 320 × 220, centred, 40px of air on four sides, on a grey plate | Window inset 10% left, right and top, 25% past the bottom, no plate: the page is the ground |
| Detail card beside the window, fully outside, the same width as the sidebar | Detail card straddling the sidebar edge about half outside, over chrome, not content |
| Window runs 6px past the right edge | A full gutter in, or 15–35% past; never a sliver |

Gold example: `stageshow/examples/static-card/` (pinned, bottom bleed) and `stageshow/examples/hero-demo/` (corner bleed beside copy); `stageshow/teaching/scenes.tsx` holds the crop-to-the-action and crop-filler pairs.
Check: film one still at the shown width and one at 358 beside the gold's still. If the hero's top-left is hidden, a real word is sliced, or the bleed is under 10%, re-crop before any motion.

## Gotcha

Told to "run the window off the edge", agents barely do it — a few px past, which is the worst of both. Copy an example that does it, then check the final crop: is the hero's top-left visible, is the bleed a deliberate fraction and not a sliver?

# Stageshow, reconciled

Stageshow 1.1.1 (`npx skills add benjitaylor/skills --skill stageshow`; Node 20.19+) builds faux product UI: stills, feature cards, cursor demos and bento grids as ordinary React components. It ships a `SKILL.md` with a seven-step workflow, fifteen references, about forty gold examples to copy from, product studies, specimen sheets (`buttons` and `cards` new in 1.1), bad/good teaching pairs, a copy-in React kit (`Stage` with a scripted `Act`, real-geometry `Window` and `Phone`, motion parts such as `Fly`, `Collapse`, `Roll`, `Count`, `Connector`, `Camera`, and small parts it insists on over lookalikes, `Button`, `Draft`, `Card`, `Divider` and `Kbd` new in 1.1), and scripts that film the result (`film.mjs`, whose `--gate` exits 1 on any never-intentional fault, `jumps.mjs`, `layout.mjs`). The craft is distilled in [[MOC-faux-ui]]; this node says who owns what and settles the conflicts.

## Who owns what when it is installed

| Job | Owner | This graph keeps |
|---|---|---|
| A hero demo, feature card, docs plate or bento tile in a React project | Stageshow: start from the closest gold example, build on the kit (every button, card, draft and shortcut from its kit part), film with `--gate` and hand over only on `rehearsal passed` | the contract's tokens ([[using-design-file]]) mapped onto the kit's `--ss-*` tokens; whether it should move ([[animation-decision-framework]]); the page around it ([[marketing-surface-rules]]); the accessibility below |
| The same picture in a non-React project, or a static image | This graph: [[product-shot-framing]], [[faux-ui-restraint]], built in the project's own stack | everything; Stageshow's kit is React-only |
| A product demo inside a rendered launch film | The film's engine ([[MOC-launch-video]], "A film, end to end"), timed by [[launch-video-ui-demo]] | everything; a page demo and a film shot are different media |
| A grid of feature tiles | Stageshow per tile, planned with [[bento-grids]] | the plan, the page grid ([[viewport-custom-design]]) |
| Reviewing someone's demo | [[demo-rehearsal]]'s fresh-eye brief, output in [[review-format]] | the format and the severity order |

Without it installed, build to the faux-UI nodes and say Stageshow would have owned the job.

## Conflicts, settled

| Topic | Stageshow | This graph | Settled |
|---|---|---|---|
| Duration | arrivals 0.8–1 s, flights 750ms, rows 420–460ms | [[duration-table]]: UI under 300ms | Illustration time, not interface time. Inside a demo, storytelling motion takes its values; the product's own feedback (a press, a hover, a menu) keeps the product's real timing, as Stageshow itself says |
| Exit easing | a closing popover accelerates (`(0.4, 0, 1, 1)`); since 1.1 `Roll` moves old and new together on one decelerating curve (`(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1)`), no longer an ease-in out | [[easing-curves]]: never ease-in on UI, exits included | An outgoing layer overlapped by its replacement may accelerate, because the eye is on the incoming one. A lone exit in product UI stays ease-out. The roll no longer needs the exception |
| Press scale | the cursor glyph dips to 0.9; since 1.1 the kit `Button` presses to 0.97 | [[responsive-feedback]]: buttons 0.97; films press the cursor to 0.84 ([[launch-video-ui-demo]]) | Three different objects. Cursor 0.9 in a page demo, 0.84 in a film; the pressed control uses the product's own press, which the kit `Button` now matches at 0.97 by default |
| Typing speed | 35ms a character (~28/s) | [[launch-video-ui-demo]]: ~15/s to be read, ~50 to be recognised | 35ms for a short string the viewer only recognises; a prompt that carries the argument types at ~15/s and holds |
| Autoplay | heroes loop 10–16 s; tiles play once in view | [[marketing-surface-rules]]: motion maps to input | A demo is a figure, not page motion: allowed, one lead per viewport, stopped offscreen (the Stage does this), the poster under reduced motion |
| Pause | no pause control; replay is a keyed remount | [[wcag-thresholds]] 2.2.2: anything moving over 5 s has a visible pause | Every looping demo longer than 5 s gets a visible pause/play button in the host, beside Replay. `play="once"` or hover-played scenes under 5 s are exempt |
| Screen readers | faux titles are `div`s, never headings | [[marketing-surface-rules]]: code-built illustrations get `role="img"` and an `aria-label` | Both. Wrap the stage in `role="img"` with a label that says what the demo shows ("Assigning a conversation to Maya"), `user-select: none`, and keep its fake controls out of the tab order |
| Placeholder content | grey bars for filler | [[content-authenticity]]: real data, never lorem ipsum | Not in conflict: authenticity governs what is read. The 3–7 real strings must be specific and plausible; bars stand for what nobody is meant to read |
| Other companies' marks | a bundled registry of real bank, payment and app logos; product studies of Figma, Slack, Linear and others | [[ai-default-tells]]: no invented logos | Real marks only where the relationship is real (an integration you ship, a payment method you accept); studies of other products are for borrowing an interaction, never for a page that implies endorsement. Its `NOTICE.md` says the same |

## Dependencies

The kit is copied source on React 18+, react-dom and lucide-react, with no animation runtime, so it passes [[dependency-discipline]]. Filming needs `playwright-core` and a locally installed Chrome (or `CHROME_PATH`), dev-only. The playground's `npm install` also pulls Vite and an optional `portless`; tell the user before the first install.

## Reference

The job done with Stageshow installed, before and after this node's settlements:

| Before | After |
|---|---|
| Gold copied, product name changed, filmed once without the gate | The brief's tokens mapped onto `--ss-*`, its own icons, chrome and words; filmed with `--gate` until `rehearsal passed` |
| A bare `Stage` in the page, a 14 s loop, no controls | The stage wrapped in `role="img"` with a label, fake controls out of the tab order, a visible Pause beside Replay in the host |
| A hand-styled `.btn` and `.card` beside the kit's `Field` | The kit `Button` and `Card`, restyled by their props and tokens |

Gold example: the Gold table in `stageshow/SKILL.md` (Examples), copy the closest row; `stageshow/examples/buttons/` and `stageshow/examples/cards/` for the parts.
Check: film your copy beside the gold's still; if someone could name the gold's product from yours, the swap is not done. Then tab to the loop's Pause with the keyboard.

## Gotcha

Copying a gold example and changing only the product name is not done: it still reads as the example's product. Swap in the brief's tokens, icons, chrome and words, then film it beside the gold to prove it.

# MOC — Launch video

A launch film is a run of decisions taken in order, and each has one owner node. Name the register first, because cut rate, stillness and loudness belong to it; then time the beats, set the words, the UI demo and the motion, make the seams and cuts, place the sound, and review the render against its own register. HyperFrames builds the film; this cluster decides it.

Evidence: 29 Skale pieces (28 client films and the 2025 reel), 18 acclaimed films from 2024-2026 (13 in-house, 4 studio, 1 uncredited), HeyGen's hyperframes-launches source (20 project folders, 3,446 tween calls) and 3 of its renders, measured by AgentsORG on 2026-09-28, every film at its native frame rate. Per-film metrics and scripts live in `docs/research/launch-films/` (repo only; `npx skills add` does not install them).

## The decision flow

1. [[launch-video-registers]] — name the register; its row medians set the cut rate (3-31/min), the still share (0.09-0.49) and the loudness (-13 to -33 LUFS).
2. [[launch-video-structure]] — time the beats: a word by 0.2-0.7 s; the name early (≤11 %), where a problem act ends (median 29 %, 6-51 %), or at ~70 % after the demo; an endcard of 4.4-6.3 s that holds ~2 s.
3. [[launch-video-type]] — set the words on screen, stepped about 0.2 s apart.
4. [[launch-video-ui-demo]] — drive the product UI, the cursor, typed prompts (~15 chars/s to be read, ~53 to be recognised) and the agent's wait.
5. [[launch-video-motion]] — motion inside a shot: objects settle with a time constant chosen per move, about 0.1-0.15 s (0.13-0.15 s in two Skale films); two measured counters (0.6-0.8 s) and Raycast's camera crane (~0.43 s, one film) settle slower, and a camera may drift at constant speed and be cut mid-drift.
6. [[launch-video-seams]] — what crosses a scene change (fills and zooms into type or a glyph run ~0.33 s); [[launch-video-cuts]] — hard cuts that read as one move.
7. [[launch-video-sound]] — pick the sound register (-1 dBTP is its only fixed number); [[launch-video-music]] places a track or a voice; [[sound-from-motion]] derives the stem; [[sound-motion-sync]] lands every transient on its contact frame, at most one frame late (0-30 ms), never ahead of it.
8. [[launch-video-review]] — review a render or a reference against its own register. The cut detector agreed with a frame reading in only 9/29 and 5/18 films, so recount by eye, or spawn [[launch-film-analyst]] to measure the file.

Around the film: [[launch-video-formats]] for the loop, the sting and the vertical cuts; [[cinetic-reconciliation]] when cinetic builds it in Remotion; [[scenario-kinetic-reconciliation]] when scenario-kinetic-film builds a beat-cut type teaser as one page; [[film-as-function-of-time]] for any film rendered from code (sub-frame motion blur, the beat grid fitted to the track, the delivery gates).

## A film, end to end

This graph directs the film and HyperFrames builds it. When the sound is derived from the motion and there is no stock bed or voice-over, host the build in HyperFrames' `general-video` with `flow: companion`. `product-launch-video` runs its own capture, voice-over and library-music pipeline, so use it only when the user wants that pipeline.

1. **Contract, then taste.** `frame.md` → `design.md` → `DESIGN.md` ([[using-design-md]]). Then [[pov]], which names the default register for an unspecified launch film.
2. **Decide the film.** Pick the register first ([[launch-video-registers]]), then [[launch-video-structure]], [[launch-video-type]] and [[launch-video-ui-demo]].
3. **Write the plan before the timeline.** Record the motion ([[launch-video-motion]]) and one ledger row per seam ([[launch-video-seams]], [[launch-video-cuts]]) in `STORYBOARD.md` and `ledger.json`. Build and gate it in HyperFrames (`check` must pass); inside the project, [[hyperframes-reconciliation]] settles value conflicts.
4. **Lock the picture, then score it.** Write one cue per contact frame and render the stem with `sound-sheet.mjs` ([[sound-from-motion]], [[launch-video-sound]]); designed effects follow [[designed-sfx-anatomy]], and any recording you use passes [[sound-licensing]].
5. **Measure the render against its register** before anyone calls it done ([[launch-video-review]], or spawn [[launch-film-analyst]]); with earshot installed, read its `timeline` and `sheet` too ([[earshot-reconciliation]]). Loops, stings and vertical cuts follow [[launch-video-formats]].

This repo's own launch film, `docs/demo/hyperframes/`, is the worked example: its `STORYBOARD.md`, `ledger.json` and `assets/sfx/cues.json` follow these five steps.

## What every register keeps

- No dead cut (a settled frame followed by a scene that waits): the outgoing scene is still moving on the cut frame, or the incoming frame acts within ~0.3-0.4 s. Hard cuts are fine (26/29 Skale and 14/18 acclaimed films cut); a crossfade fails only when its midpoint exposes a ground neither scene has (the dip law, [[launch-video-cuts]]); a dip through a shared ground, or a straight mix of the two frames, is fine (11/29 Skale and 6/18 acclaimed films dip or dissolve).
- Nothing decorative moves on a UI object (0/18 acclaimed; neither corpus floats UI), while slow drift, creep or ambient light under holds is common (Skale 15/29, or 10/29 counting camera push or drift alone; acclaimed 10/18).
- Display copy, where a register has any, is built per word or letter, never faded in as a block (27/29 Skale films), and holds 1.15 s after its last word (Skale) or 1.5 s per card (acclaimed).
- The low end arrives or returns on the first reveal: in Skale's music films the first drop lands on the brand or title reveal in 11/18 (on the thesis word in a 12th); in the acclaimed films the low end arrives on the first reveal in 10/18, which is the name only when the name comes early.
- Sound is subtracted to punctuate, a sub pulled or a silence placed: before a reveal in 23/28 Skale films with sound; before a reveal, under the name, on a conversational turn, under a diagram or under a premium tier in 14/18 acclaimed.

## Who builds it

HyperFrames builds and gates the film: for a launch piece, `/hyperframes` routes to `product-launch-video`, `motion-graphics` or `general-video`, and to `music-to-video` when a track's beat grid drives the piece. This cluster decides the register, beats and type cadence, and owns the sound; it also authors seams and cuts, but inside a HyperFrames project the seam stamp's eases, zoom values and exit timings win. The end-to-end steps are above; routing to other engines lives in [[skill-router]], and [[hyperframes-reconciliation]] names the value to use for every other conflict.

## Cross-cluster

- A product state change is not a film seam: [[fly-not-teleport]] and [[cross-blur-transitions]] own transitions inside an interface.
- UI durations and springs ([[duration-table]], [[spring-animations]]) do not transfer to a film: a 60 s film has no 300 ms ceiling (Skale's counters run 1.15 s, its dissolves 0.45 s).
- A film inverts the product defaults, sound included: [[marketing-vs-product-ui]] for the picture, [[sound-decision-framework]] for why a product stays mostly silent while a film does not.

## Gotcha

Opening four nodes before naming the register wastes the flow: every number downstream depends on it. Four cuts a minute is Skale's UI-motion median and under a third of the product-camera rate (14.0).

| the scaffold, `timeline.ts`, starters, render and delivery (`render.sh`, `deliver.sh`) | the register ([[launch-video-registers]]) and the structure's beats ([[launch-video-structure]]) |

| Crossfades | "No film crossfades between scenes" | 11 of 29 Skale and 6 of 18 acclaimed films dissolve or dip |
| Loudness | −14 LUFS for anything with music | a register choice; medians −18.1 and −18.4 |
| End card | 2.2 s (0.9–3.9 s), never over ~2.5 s held | Skale 4.4 s, acclaimed 6.3 s |
| Name on screen | by about a quarter of the runtime | early, or a late mode at ~70 % (6 of 18, mostly known brands) |
| Statement size | 5.5–11 % of frame height, median ~8 % | ~5 % (IQR 4–7 %) |

Inside a cinetic project, a value this graph sets goes into `BRIEF.md` as a brand-supplied exception, and the lines that set it carry `// cinetic:brand-supplied <what>` so its lint and its critics accept them. The register's serif, cream or crossfade is then a decision, not a violation.

## Claims waiting for a measurement

cinetic says its numbers were "measured frame by frame in top-tier launch films", but it never names the films or counts them, and its technique library rates evidence 0–9 with no sources. These are worth testing on the 47-film corpus before any node adopts them:

- **Energy arc:** an early peak at 10–25 %, a 1–4 s lull at ~65 %, the biggest peak at ~82 %; films whose last peak comes before 60 % sag.
- **Speed in px per frame (1080p60):** each shot enters at 20–45, cruises at 1.5–8, and leaves accelerating ×1.14 a frame; text being read moves ≤ 3 px/f.
- **Fragment flow:** 2 words per beat, 56 % of beats continue a sentence, copy on ≤ ~65 % of frames, a text-free stretch of ≥ 1.5 s in every 10 s.
- **Effects census:** ~85 % of hard cuts carry no sound and under 5 % a whoosh; ~5 designed effects per 10 s; ~75 % of on-screen typing is silent.

Until then, quote them as "cinetic reports" with the qualifier, or not at all.

## Reference

One overridden value, written so cinetic's lint and critics accept it (Remotion, 60 fps):

```tsx

// cinetic:brand-supplied crossfade over a shared ground
const out = interpolate(frame, [cut - 36, cut], [1, 0], { extrapolateRight: 'clamp' }) // 36 f = 0.6 s
```

cinetic's evaluations were judged by language models, one run per brief. A neutral judge preferred it in 7 of 23 comparisons; a judge scoring against cinetic's own bans preferred it 4 of 4, which is circular. # A film as a function of time

When a film is code, every frame must be a pure function of `t`: no `Math.random`, no `Date`, no state carried from one frame to the next. A renderer can then seek to any time, out of order, and average several sub-frame samples into motion blur that is real rather than painted. One stray `Math.random` makes the samples of a frame disagree with each other, and the blur turns to noise. Seeded randomness is fine; the rule is the same one [[vibe-to-generator]] sets for generators.

## The shutter

- **Default:** a 180° forward shutter, 4 samples a frame. Grain and bloom are added in the render, after averaging, and the grain is seeded so a re-render matches the last one. Never fake blur, grain or bloom in the page.
- **Fast windows raise the count:** a whip pan stretches the shutter to about 600° with up to 24 samples. The smear is what makes a whip read as one move ([[launch-video-cuts]], "into motion").
- **Never cross a hard cut.** If a cut falls inside the shutter, slide the window back so it ends on the cut. A clipped window renders the fastest frame of a whip sharp, which reads as a stutter on exactly the frame the eye is following.
- **Counters and HUD digits read the output frame time**, not the sample time, or blur smears the numbers.

## The grid comes from the track, not from the brief

Everything is placed in beats (`B(k)` = k × 60 / bpm), so one tempo change retimes the film. A generated track's tempo is a hope until it is measured:

- Give the beat tracker the intended tempo, or it can lock to half or two thirds of it.
- Fit only the stretch the film uses. Generated music drifts, and only that stretch has to be exact.
- Drop alignment: `music.offset = drop_seconds − planned_drop_beat × 60 / bpm`. Check the result against the listed downbeats.
- Prefer a music model whose schema takes a tempo. In the Kaiju Postal build, both takes asked for 172 BPM measured 172.0.

Over a 50 s film, a 0.15 % tempo error puts the last hits about 70 ms late. The sync budget is 0–30 ms, never early ([[sound-motion-sync]]), so a grid that is "nearly right" fails by the end card.

## Delivery gates

Hand over nothing until every file passes all of these:

| Gate | Why |
|---|---|
| Frame count equals the film's | a mux with `-shortest` silently drops the last frames when the audio ends a few ms early |
| H.264 Level ≤ 5.2 at 4K, ≤ 4.2 at 1080p | a slower x264 preset without `-level` writes Level 6.0, which plays in ffmpeg and fails in QuickTime, Safari and on phones |
| Under 1 GB at 4K | a 52 s 4K master with grain is 0.96 GB at CRF 12.4 (preset slower, ~50 dB PSNR); CRF 11 at preset medium reaches 1.37 GB for a 51 dB difference no one can see |
| A full decode on the hardware decoder | what QuickTime and phones use; a software decode passing proves nothing |
| Loudness written for the register, −1 dBTP | [[launch-video-sound]]; the engine's −14 LUFS default is not a standard ([[scenario-kinetic-reconciliation]]) |

Render 1080p until the film passes, then the 4K master once, then run the gates again on the master. Make the 1080p and 9:16 files from the master, and lay the 9:16 one out again per [[launch-video-formats]], not as the film centred on black.

## Reference

```ts
// Bad: wall time and fresh randomness differ between renders and between the samples of one frame
const t = (Date.now() - start) / 1000, jitter = Math.random() * 2
// Good: time from the stepped clock, noise seeded by the output frame
const t = clock.now() / 1000, jitter = hash01(seed, Math.floor(t * fps)) * 2
```

- Stageshow's recorder solves the same problem in the browser: `installVirtualClock()` replaces the page's clocks so time moves only on `step()`, by exactly 1/fps, firing due timers in order, running one animation frame and moving every CSS transition and animation to the new time. Chrome's own virtual time is not enough: it moves timers but runs no animation frames and leaves CSS animations where they are.
- A clock or date drawn in a scene reads a fixed `epoch`, so it shows the same time on every render.
- Gold example: `stageshow/kit/clock.ts` (the virtual clock) and `stageshow/references/kit.md` (Timing: time scripts with `clock.now()`, never `Date.now()`).
- Check: render the same 2 s twice and hash every frame; a mismatch is a stray wall-clock read or an unseeded random. Then log real rAF timestamps on the live page, because a virtual clock proves geometry, not frame rate (`stageshow/references/rehearse.md`).

## Gotcha

Headless Chrome has capture traps of its own, separate from the render traps in [[gotchas]]. A 1920 × 1080 viewport paints only about 990 px, so use a taller viewport and clip. `captureScreenshot` returns CSS pixels unless `clip.scale` equals the device scale factor, so a "4K" render comes back at 1080p. Large 3D layers are captured half-drawn without `--run-all-compositor-stages-before-draw`. Each 4K worker needs about 11 GB of memory; six of them stalled a 36 GB machine.

# HyperFrames reconciliation

Inside any HyperFrames project the seam stamp's values win for seams and seam eases: where the repo-internal doctrine is installed, seam-stamp.mjs writes them and the seam gate verifies them; where it is not (the default after `npx skills add`), write them by hand from the values below. ## Precedence

User prompt → `.design` / `frame.md` → HyperFrames' motion-doctrine (repo-internal) for seams → HyperFrames' distributed skills for build mechanics → this graph for register, structure, type cadence and sound → model defaults. Where HyperFrames' two layers disagree, the internal doctrine is the stricter one, and it declares that it supersedes upstream motion guidance. # Launch-video cuts

A launch film cuts. How often it cuts belongs to its register, not to its quality. A good hard cut is taken on motion, on a visible cause, on a ground that does not change or on the element being read, so the eye takes it as a camera move and not as a new scene. Two cuts fail in every register. One is the **dead cut**: a settled frame followed by a scene that waits, where the outgoing scene is not moving on the cut frame and the incoming frame does not act within ~0.3-0.4 s. The other is a **crossfade whose midpoint shows a ground that differs from both scenes**. When the scene change is a morph, a dock or a fill, [[launch-video-seams]] covers what carries the eye across it.

## Rates

Counted frame by frame, rates run from ~0 in the zero-cut morph chains that [[launch-video-seams]] names, through 4.0 a minute in Skale's UI films [1.5, 5.7] and 12-14 in the acclaimed keynote and product-camera films, to 30.7 in beat-cut sizzles. The 14 acclaimed in-house or uncredited films cut at 15.6; the four studio films cut at 3.1, and two of those credits are unconfirmed. A scale jump inside one composition is not counted as a scene cut. Each register's row, founder and live-action films included, is in [[launch-video-registers]].

2.4.0's "no cuts, no crossfades" holds at HeyGen only in the four heygen-apple-motion templates and the one-shot Codex replica (codex-five-hour-limit-replica). pr-to-video-launch runs eight 0.28-0.35 s power1.inOut crossfades; claude-paper-launch has a 0.6 s crossfade and a hard cut at 6.7 s; the frame.md launch render has 4 hard cuts; k3-promo has a 2-frame inversion flash and a 2-frame black dip.

## Where the eye accepts a cut

1. **On the cause or its result.** Skale 9/29 make the click the seam (Skale's 2025 reel, Aside, Browserbase, Bud, Replit Slides, Replit Canvas, Bevel, Wonder (second film), Bolt). In the hard-cut form the press is visible, and the cut lands 0.3-1.0 s later on the consequence. The fill and circle-wipe forms are in [[launch-video-seams]]. Linear Agent clears the input on Enter at 10.53 s and cuts 0.7 s later to the prompt already posted; the answer lands 0.5 s after the cut.
2. **On a constant ground.** Keep one world, wallpaper or layout and cut freely (8/18 acclaimed). Linear Agent cuts 7 times in 45 s of product, Raycast 9 times in 28 s, Notion 3.0 at least 25 times in 90 s.
3. **On the element being read.** A 1-2 frame scale jump of ~2-3× inside the same composition (Skale 9/29: Browserbase, Bud, Taste Labs, Replit Slides, Replit Parallel Agents, Poke '7', Wonder (second film), Contra Indy, Contra x fal; acclaimed 8/18). Anchor the jump. Either the cursor keeps its row across the cut (Notion Mail 22.43 s, Notion 3.0 60.165 s), or the element lands in its real place (Claude Cowork cuts a huge chat bubble to ~0.35× in its actual chat position at 37.9 s).
   Hide the jump with an incoming defocus that sharpens over 6-8 frames (Poke '7'), or let the zoom run on for 3 frames after the punch-in (Claude Cowork, 44.12 s). The sharp variant is the snap zoom (5/18 acclaimed): Notion Mail's scale steps 1.0 / 1.05 / 1.25 / 1.5 / 2.0 / ~2.4 over 5 frames, then settles in ~0.35 s.
4. **To a still, readable frame or an empty ground, then act.** The action starts 0.3-0.4 s in, about one beat (Arc on Windows, Figma Motion, Raycast, Spline Hana). Skale's Typesafe, Pilot Protocol, Contra Indy and Tembo cut to an empty frame that builds within 1-3 frames. HeyGen's frame.md render twice cuts to empty cream, and the next card enters blurred and rotated ~-4°, sharpening within ~0.2 s.
5. **Into motion.** Cut mid-drift on a constant-velocity camera (Linear Agent; its speeds are in [[launch-video-motion]]). Cut at peak velocity after an acceleration (Raycast trucks from 3 to 8 %W/s over 1.8 s and cuts at the peak). Cut onto elements already travelling (Taste Labs' card sweeps, the cursor Wonder (second film) carries across the cut, Bolt's 1-frame push), or on motion blur (Skale's 2025 reel, Wonder (first film)).
6. **Inside a fill or a luminance flip.** Google Gemini app hides all 4 of its cuts in full-frame glyph fills or in a one-frame ground inversion while the particles keep moving (14.48 s).
7. **On a palette flip alone.** Aside, Agent Arcade and Tembo save their hard cuts for the frame where the ground changes colour.
8. **In an accelerating ladder.** figma-launch cuts 9 times on holds shrinking .8 / .5 / .4 / .3 / .2 / .15 / .12 / .1 s while the zoom only climbs (1.32 → 4.4). Claude Opus 4.6 stamps 24 press crops into 4.125 s, with holds falling from 11 frames to 3, then 2-3. Arc on Windows swaps Start-button eras every 0.38-0.54 s with the cursor held in place.
9. **As an accent, in a digital register.** A 1-frame black blink between shot families (Figma glass, 33 ms), a 2-frame white flash 2 frames before a cut (Spline Hana), or a 2-frame colour inversion as the cut itself (k3-promo).
10. **The rack-focus blur-cut, the one cut meant to be seen.** A defocus spike (peak 8-12 px, at least 6 px on the cut frame) hides a one-frame swap of the same surface, and the outgoing scene stays fully opaque until the cut. Use it at most once per ~8 s, on a narrative beat, never mid-caption (HyperFrames cut-the-curve §5).

Inside a HyperFrames project with its internal doctrine installed, cut-the-curve is the default for every scene boundary and an entry from rest after a cut is on the doctrine's anti-pattern list. There, item 4 does not apply and the other cuts above serve as accents; [[hyperframes-reconciliation]] settles each value.

## The crossfade-dip law

Tween both scenes' opacity at once and whatever lies under them shows through at the midpoint: cloud-render-launch's crossfades flashed its cream page ground, and on a dark film an unpainted #root shows as a white flash. When the scenes share a ground there are two fixes. Hard-cut on a continuous background whose media start equals the scene start, so both sides of the cut show the identical frame (HF-heygen-stripe). Or fade the outgoing content down to a bare surface identical to the incoming first frame, then cut (cloud-render-launch's fix, round 6). Either way keep an opaque ground under everything: timeline-launch sets its body to #f5f5f7, and HyperFrames' seam-craft makes the assembler paint #root, because any seam window where the summed opacity falls below 1 composites over the page's default white. claude-paper-launch's 0.6 s crossfade is seamless because the page and root are painted the same paper as both sections, and the message and composer hold identical positions.

11/29 Skale films dissolve or dip at a scene change (0.45 s median, 0.1-1.0 s, 10 timed), and so do 6/18 acclaimed films (Claude Cowork's lasts 3 frames). On graphics they pass through a shared ground: Adaline dips to paper (~6 frames out, 1-2 blank, ~10 in), Extend dips through its brand colour (0.25 / 0.1 / 0.4 s), and Poke '7' dips once to white as its act break. The live-action and founder films dissolve footage to footage (Poke x Cognition's one ~0.17 s dissolve) or UI to founder (Conduit, at least 7 dissolves). HyperFrames' distributed launch workflow defaults `transition_in` to a crossfade; [[hyperframes-reconciliation]] says which value wins inside a project.

## After the cut

Motion either decays (the cut was taken mid-motion) or rises (the cut went to an empty ground and then built). Measured at 800 ms relative to the first frame after the cut: Skale 0.82 [0.39, 1.50] (n = 24; 7 decay to ≤0.4, 8 rise above 1.0); acclaimed 0.58 (n = 14; 5 decay to ≤0.4, 5 rise above 1.0 by 400 ms). HeyGen's renders rise (frame.md 1.0 → 2.13 → 2.57 at 100 / 200 ms). Both work. The dead cut is the settled frame that then waits.

## Cuts and music

Locking cuts to the track is optional: 7/18 acclaimed films lock stamps, cuts or act seams, and 6 cut at chance. A cut that does lock sits on the onset frame. See [[launch-video-music]] for placement and [[sound-motion-sync]] for the tolerance.

## When to apply

Any film with more than one shot: launch films, feature sizzles, README demos. Never in product UI, where [[fly-not-teleport]] owns state changes and [[cross-blur-transitions]] masks the rare crossfade that cannot be avoided.

## Reference

A cut into motion (item 5) on the two curves Stageshow's kit names for it:

```ts
import { bezier } from './kit/ease'            // Stageshow kit
const through = bezier('through'), settle = bezier('settle')
const outX = (t: number) => lerp(0, -240, through((t - (CUT - 0.45)) / 0.9)) // 0.9 s push cut at 0.45 s, near its speed peak (~46 %)
const inX = (t: number) => lerp(120, 0, settle((t - CUT) / 0.7))           // moving on its first frame, settled by 0.7 s
```

- Bad: the outgoing push on `ease-out` rests 0.2 s before the cut and the incoming shot waits 0.6 s: a dead cut from both sides. Good: the push is near peak speed on the last outgoing frame and the incoming one is already moving.
- Gold example: `stageshow/kit/ease.ts` (`through` accelerates into the cut; `settle` runs 0.6 to 0.8 s after it, 1.6 s for a big pull-out; the ~46 % peak is computed from its control points); Linear Agent and Raycast (item 5) for the rhythm.
- Check: a contact sheet stepped every 2 frames across the seam; the last outgoing and first incoming frames both differ from their neighbours.

## Gotcha

Banning cuts forces every film into a zero-cut morph chain, which only 3/29 Skale and 2/18 acclaimed films chose. 2.4.0's "no cuts" came from four HeyGen templates and one studio reel, yet 26/29 Skale pieces and 14/18 acclaimed films hard-cut. Count cuts by reading frames; the detector's misses and the recount method are in [[launch-video-review]].

# Launch-video formats

A launch film rarely ships alone. Around it go a landing-page loop, a logo sting and vertical cuts for the feeds, and each one breaks a different rule of the 16:9 master. A loop has no beginning or end card. A sting is all end card. A vertical cut is watched on a phone, under someone else's interface. None of the three is the master trimmed.

## Feature loop

- **A cycle, not enter → hold → exit.** A loop that fades out and back in is a slideshow. Return to the start through an action: a conveyor whose last item lands where the first began, a relay that carries the result out one side and a new input in the other, or a state round-trip where B becomes the next A.
- **A whole number of bars, no tail.** Design motion so the unrendered frame `TOTAL` would equal frame 0; a duplicate of frame 0 at the end stutters every cycle. Springs are at rest before the seam, and text is fully resolved or fully gone across it.
- **Seam gate.** The last-to-first frame difference is at most max(0.4, 1.5 × the median of the 8 steps at each end). Render lossless PNG intermediates: with JPEG frames the encoder smooths noise between neighbours but not across the seam, which then measures ~1.7× its neighbours.
- **Frame 0 is the poster.** It is what a paused or not-yet-autoplayed page shows, so it names the product. The product and the action start in the first 2 s, and the loop reads with the sound off.
- **A reset has a seen cause or is invisible.** What the loop added leaves as one thing, in a reverse stagger (last change first, about 70 ms apart); data never rewinds in view; the next action begins within about a second of the exit (Stageshow).
- **10 to 16 s, three to five beats, a payoff that holds 2 s.** Nothing else sits still over 3 s, and a repeat is a short beat, never the whole flow twice (Stageshow).
- **GIF at 25 or 50 fps.** GIF delays are whole hundredths of a second, so 30 fps plays 11 % fast. Ship MP4 and WebM for `<video autoplay muted loop playsinline>` at ≤ 4 MB per 10 s of 1080p; a GIF only when asked, ≤ 960 px wide.

## Logo sting

- **3–8 s, the name plus three words at most.** The resolved lockup spans 28–45 % of the frame's width; smaller, the brand is an object in a void.
- **Assemble the mark from its primitives**: 2–4 pieces accelerate into contact, and one hit tuned to the track's root lands on the contact frame ([[designed-sfx-anatomy]]). A scale-up of a flat logo teaches nothing. Clamp any spring that could push one piece into another.
- **Hold and build.** The lockup cue sits ≥ 1.5 s before the end, and scale changes 3–20 % across the last 1.5 s. Never end on a fade that leaves the full lockup readable for under 1.5 s. The tail decays to digital zero.
- **Loudness.** A sting played at the head of other videos can sit near −16 LUFS; −1 dBTP after the encode, as everywhere ([[launch-video-sound]]). Deliver an alpha version (ProRes 4444, VP9 alpha WebM) for editors.

## Vertical and square

**Re-lay out; never crop.** A centre crop of a 16:9 master cuts the type and pushes the product off frame. Make each aspect its own composition on the same timeline and soundtrack, with line breaks written into the copy, not left to a wrap.

| Aspect | Keep text and key action inside | Type minimums |
|---|---|---|
| 9:16 feed, 1080 × 1920 | top 270, right 120, bottom 420, left 64 px (bottom 672 for long captions and paid posts) | statement 110–140 px, secondary ≥ 60, UI ≥ 32 |
| 1:1, 1080 × 1080 | 64 px on every side | statement ≥ 72, secondary ≥ 44, UI ≥ 28 |
| 4:5, 1080 × 1350 | 64 px at the sides, 96 top and bottom | statement ≥ 80, secondary ≥ 48, UI ≥ 30 |

In 9:16 the content's mass sits on the safe band's centre (y ≈ 885), not the frame's, and the bottom 40 % is never empty: stack the statement above the product or let the product bleed past the sides. Type and UI run 1.3–1.5× their 16:9 sizes. Burn captions into every feed cut, because feeds autoplay muted.

## Reference

A 12 s landing-page loop (6 bars at 120 BPM):

| t (s) | beat |
|---|---|
| 0.0 | a finished screen with the product named; it works as the only frame |
| 0.2-9.0 | three or four beats, each caused by the last |
| 9.0-11.0 | the payoff arrives full and holds 2 s |
| 11.0-12.0 | by 11.5 what the loop added has left in one reverse stagger, last change first, ~70 ms apart; frame 12.0 is frame 0, and the next action starts 0.7 s after the exit ends |

- Benji's call differs: a Stageshow poster is whichever beat tells the story on its own, never one caught mid-change, not necessarily the opening. Where the page sets `<video poster>`, use that beat and keep frame 0 a finished still.
- Gold example: `stageshow/examples/subscriptions/` (a system loop that resets by changing to a second company rather than rewinding) and `stageshow/references/motion.md` (Loops).
- Check: film one loop plus the start of the next at 60 ms a frame and look at the seam (Stageshow's kit warns `loop seam:` when the end state or cursor differs from the start), then run the seam gate above on lossless frames.

## Gotcha

The zones are snapshots of the big feeds' current overlays (header 240–290 px, action rail 120–190 px from about y 840, caption block 380–450 px, up to ~670 with a call-to-action button). They move when the apps redesign. Check the destination's overlay before a paid launch.

# Launch-video motion

Inside a shot, things arrive on an exponential settle whose time constant is chosen per move — about 0.1-0.15 s for an object, ~0.43 s for Raycast's four-frame-height crane and 0.6-0.8 s for the two measured counters — and leave on the mirror curve. Nothing decorative moves on a UI object. Overshoot, velocity blur and camera drift are register choices with measured base rates, and a film reads as lively because of creep, accelerating rhythm and causes that ignite their effects, not because anything bounces. This is the 2.4.0 four-rule motion system, split out of [[launch-video-seams]] and corrected against 29 Skale films, 18 acclaimed films and HeyGen's source.

## Settle exponentially; size tau to the travel

Write the curves once and pass tau as a parameter:

```js
const TAU = 0.131;
const eo = (dur, tau = TAU) => (p) => (1 - Math.exp(-p * dur / tau)) / (1 - Math.exp(-dur / tau));
const ei = (dur, tau = TAU) => (p) => 1 - eo(dur, tau)(1 - p);
```

- **Objects, ~0.1-0.15 s.** HeyGen's 02-bouncy-ui declares tau 0.131 s in its header but never calls that constant: its moves pass their own, 0.04-0.18 s (median ~0.11 s; 0.135 for the flip, 0.168 for a growth). 01-ui-sting's `1 - 2^(-10p)` works out to ~0.146 s at its median 1.01 s tween. Skale's Replit Parallel Agents decays its opening slam word's drift ×0.78 per frame at 29.97 fps (tau 0.134 s), and Poke '7' whip-scrolls at tau 0.13-0.15 s both ways. 03-message-sting runs faster: it writes each move as `1 - 2^(-10t/T)` with settle times T of 0.12-0.53 s, a tau of 0.02-0.08 s.
- **Longer travel settles slower.** Raycast's crane covers ~4 frame heights with a half-life of ~0.3 s (tau ~0.43 s, n = 1), while Apple Liquid Glass's snap pull-back settles at tau ~0.2 s; the counters in Taste Labs and Contra Indy settle at tau 0.6-0.8 s (n = 2).
- **Shipped durations** over 2,064 HeyGen tweens: median 0.35 s (p25 0.20, p75 0.55); by ease, `power2.out` 0.26 s, `power3.out` 0.46, `expo.out` 0.50.
- **Exits by seam type**, not a fixed ratio: HeyGen's run 36-82 % of the entry (zoom exits 0.18-0.22 s against 0.5 s entries; cut-the-curve pairs 69-82 %). A mirrored letter-by-letter un-type can run as long as the entry or longer (Extend: 0.43 s in, 0.5 s out, ~116 %; n = 1). Inside a HyperFrames project, motion-doctrine's exit at ~75 % of the entry and the seam stamp's timings win.

GSAP's `expo.out` differs from `1 - 2^(-10p)` by at most 0.78 % of travel: it matters for exact mirrors and pixel replicas, not for feel.

## Cameras are the exception

A camera may run at constant velocity and be cut mid-drift. Linear Agent drifts 1.2-4 % of the frame per second on each axis, with identical displacement every 0.25 s and no ease at either end; Apple Liquid Glass's shots open mid-drift and accelerate to 1.26× by 400 ms. HeyGen's `none` ease (313 of 2,284 non-set tweens, median 0.85 s) is drifts and progress fills. Drive a camera from one progress channel and derive the rest: claude-design-send sets `scale = 1 + 0.48a` and `x = -(scale - 1) × 118`, pinned on the column the eye tracks, because a push and a pan on two eases read as two movements. A drift continues the entry vector. Never start a new pan or push in a scene's back half; product-launch-video's rule 3 bans even a slow one there, so inside a project keep creep to the entry's continuation. Never put a spring or back ease on a camera: the whole frame sways.

## Overshoot is a register

Visible overshoot appears in 4 of 29 Skale films (Replit Slides' liquid glyph, Replit Parallel Agents' tile tilt, Bevel's check mark, Contra x fal's trophy pill) and 3 of 18 acclaimed (Apple Liquid Glass's toggle swelling mid-travel, Claude Cowork's mark at ~2×, Notion 3.0's face). HyperFrames defaults an entrance to `power3.out` or a critically damped `springEase`, allows 0.80-0.85 damping for an iOS feel (~1-1.5 % overshoot) and 0.60-0.70 only when playful; motion-doctrine forbids bounce and elastic but allows `back.out(1.4-1.7)` on an entry; HeyGen's claude-paper frame law says settle, never bounce. The bouncy-sting register is 02-bouncy-ui: zeta 1/3 on three channels of one body, position 1.45 Hz, shape 1.88 Hz, rotation 2.5 Hz, the lighter channel ringing faster. HyperFrames calls damping under 0.55 cartoon wobble, so inside a project use zeta 1/3 only when the brief names the sting ([[hyperframes-reconciliation]]). As a GSAP ease windowed to end at rest:

```js
const spring = (dur, f = 1.45, z = 1 / 3) => (p) => {
  const u = p * dur, wd = 2 * Math.PI * f * Math.sqrt(1 - z * z);
  return 1 - Math.exp(-2 * Math.PI * z * f * u) * Math.cos(wd * u) * (1 - p);
};
```

01-ui-sting's lockup rides one decaying sine, `A · e^(-t/0.279) · sin(2πt/0.5)` (2 Hz, zeta ~0.27), with the symbol on +A and the word on −A, so the two parts spring away from each other on landing and come to rest together; its endcard reuses the spring at a smaller amplitude.

## Blur

- **Derived for element moves.** It rides the move's own ease and peaks at peak speed. Size the peak to the subject: 10 px on text, 18-20 px on a full-frame surface. HeyGen's 481 blur targets cluster at 8 px (×64) and 20 px (×45); 207 resolve to 0. Blur the wrapper, never its children, and never blur and fade in one tween. CSS blur scales with transform: a raw 2 px reads as ~16 px at ×8.
- **Sharp is also a choice.** Velocity blur shows in only 9 of 29 Skale films and 6 of 18 acclaimed. Poke '7' whips ~20 % of frame height per frame completely crisp; Notion Mail snaps to ×2.4 in 5 frames with no blur.
- **Authored focus is a scene tool.** Arrive defocused and sharpen in 4-8 frames (9 Skale films: the Poke anthology, Taste Labs, Replit Canvas, Adaline, Bevel, Poke '7', Contra Indy, Contra x fal, Conduit), or resolve rows from blur ~0.25 s apart (Linear Agent). The rack-focus cut lives in [[launch-video-cuts]].

## Stamp decisions, ease curves

Glyph flipbooks, typed runs, odometer digits, clicks and highlight hops are per-frame sets; slides, scales and settles are tweens. Never tween a decision; it reads as a smear. `tl.set` is 1,162 of HeyGen's 3,446 calls, a third, and 10 of 18 acclaimed films stamp single-frame decisions: Granola 2.0 swaps pages in one 60 fps frame every ~1.0-1.15 s; Raycast hops its selection one click at a time over one S-curve pan. The sound sits on the stamps ([[sound-from-motion]]).

## Holds

No float, pulse or breathe on a UI object: none of the 18 acclaimed films and no Skale film does it, and motion-doctrine treats a scene that finishes entering early as missing story, not missing wobble. A hold may carry a slow camera push or drift (10 of 29 Skale films, among them T:0, Bud, all three Replit films and Conduit; drift or creep in 10 of 18 acclaimed); HeyGen keeps it on the entry vector. It may also carry status motion only while the system works (Claude Cowork drifts 18-50 px/s on the agent's turn, under 10 px in 2.5 s on the user's), ambient brand light, or a living background plate that never stops (one linear master tween) and makes its big shift ~0.1 s before each scene change (HeyGen's inspector-launch). HyperFrames' product-launch-video would rather hold still with a small jitter; inside a project keep jitter off UI objects and creep only as the entry's continuation ([[hyperframes-reconciliation]]). Test: pause anywhere; something meaningful is mid-flight, or the frame is a deliberate hold.

## Rhythm and causes

A montage runs legible, then accelerating, then a blur zone, and snaps to a hold: timeline-launch's prompt firehose steps 3 prompts at 0.42 s, 6 at 0.17 s and ~20 at 0.07 s while blur ramps 0 → 2 px, then snaps off on the hold. Before a climax, hold 0.3-0.75 s of stillness, the picture half of the pre-reveal subtraction in [[launch-video-sound]]. A cause visibly launches its effect: click, squash, release, flight, impact. Inside a HyperFrames project each effect starts on its causing frame (motion-doctrine's causal motion); outside one, a click may let its press read first ([[launch-video-ui-demo]]). Anticipation, freeze, release is the strongest form; HeyGen's liquid pop builds pressure on `power3.in` (scaleX 1 → 1.1, scaleY 1 → 0.78), freezes everything for 0.4 s, then ruptures on `power4.in` in 0.2 s. Cursor mechanics also live in that UI-demo node; cut cadence belongs to [[launch-video-cuts]], stagger cadence to [[launch-video-type]].

## When to apply

Every shot of a launch film, sting or README film. UI-scale springs stay in [[spring-animations]] and UI easing in [[easing-curves]]; inside a HyperFrames project the seam stamp's eases and exit timings win, and [[hyperframes-reconciliation]] settles overshoot, blur and hold motion.

## Reference

One push-in, specified so it reads as a single move:

```ts
gsap.to(view, { scale: 1.6, ease: 'power2.out' }); gsap.to(view, { x: -180, duration: 0.8 }) // bad: two eases read as two moves
const a = bezier('camera')(t / 1.1)                    // good: one channel, Stageshow `camera` [0.45, 0, 0.1, 1], 1100 ms
const scale = 1 + 0.6 * a, x = -(scale - 1) * FOCUS_X  // derived, pinned on the column the eye tracks; the cursor holds still
```

- Stageshow's camera agrees with this node and adds limits: a push-in needs a reason (the payoff unreadable at the shown size), the wide shot is a good still first, one push-in per story, in and back out, at most 2x with 32 px padding (`Camera` defaults).
- Benji's call differs: moves inside a shot ride a bezier with a long soft tail (`house` `[0.65, 0, 0.1, 1]`, peak near 40 %, 1.4 to 2.7 s), not an exponential settle. Neither overshoots; pick one family per film.
- Gold example: `stageshow/kit/motion/Camera.tsx` and `stageshow/kit/ease.ts`; claude-design-send (above) for the one-channel camera.
- Check: Stageshow's motion-without-hierarchy test: cover each moving element in turn, and cut any the shot reads more clearly without.

## Gotcha

A spring on every arrival reads as a toy, and a breathe loop on a held card reads as the video waiting. The films called lively are lively because the camera creeps, the rhythm accelerates and every cause visibly launches its effect; bounce is not what makes them lively.

# Launch-video registers

Cut rate, stillness, move length and loudness are properties of a launch film's register, not marks of quality. Skale's UI-motion films are 9 % still and cut 4 times a minute. Product-camera films (Linear Agent, Raycast, Claude Cowork) are 49 % still and cut 14 times a minute. Beat-cut sizzles cut a median of 31 times a minute, and three of the four master at -12 to -13 LUFS. Pick the register from the product and the brief, then keep the film's cut rate, still share and move length inside that row. Choose loudness on purpose in [[launch-video-sound]]; the LUFS column is what the films measured, not a target.

Method: every film was measured at its native frame rate, and cuts were counted from the frames by eye. The automatic detector matched that count exactly in only 9 of 29 Skale films and came within ±1 cut in only 5 of 18 acclaimed films. A frame counts as still only when nothing visible changes, so a cursor or a caret makes it moving; compare still share only inside one register ([[launch-video-review]]).

## The registers

Values are medians. Brackets are the quartiles in Skale's UI row (18 films) and the lowest and highest film in every other row; the two-film row gives both films.

Two more rows rest on one film each (n = 1), so read them as single films, not tendencies. The first is a CG teaser (Work Louder, 17 s: 24.2 cuts/min, still 0.046, -13.1 LUFS). The second is character-led (Notion 3.0: 16.7 cuts/min, still 0.395, -18.7 LUFS).

A zero-cut morph chain is a continuity choice, not a register; it turns up inside the UI-motion, founder, keynote and type registers, and [[launch-video-seams]] names the films and how they carry the eye.

## Differences that are not taste

- **In this corpus the studio films mostly morph and the in-house films cut.** The 4 studio films (Claude Opus 4.6's BUCK credit is per the brief) cut at a median of 3.1 a minute. Three of them show almost no visible cuts (the Google Gemini app hides its four inside fills); the exception is Claude Opus 4.6, a stamped collage at 76+ a minute. The 14 in-house or uncredited films cut at 15.6 [0, 60.6]. Two of the four studio films are Google films credited to Ordinary Folk (AI Mode by inference), so treat this as a lead, not a law.
- **Skale moves longer; the acclaimed films move shorter and hold more.** Pooled across registers, still share is 0.116 vs 0.321, the median move run 1.04 s vs 0.416 s, and moves 25.2 vs 50.6 a minute. Register mix does not explain all of it: the acclaimed rows with the most motion (kinetic type 0.171, continuous camera 0.165 and 0.188) are still stiller than Skale's UI row (0.091). Drift does not explain it either, because 15 of 29 Skale films and 10 of 18 acclaimed films creep under their holds. Whether the rest is restraint or capture (60 fps screen recordings, carets) is open.
- **HeyGen's renders land on both sides.** The frame.md launch (4 hard cuts) and the K3 promo hold like the acclaimed films: still 0.337 and 0.364, move runs 0.33 and 0.32 s. The zero-cut Codex replica (10 s) is 0.072 still with 1.57 s runs, in Skale's range, though mostly because a playing video and typing never stop.
- **A studio's reel is not its client work.** Skale's own reel is 0.329 still (about 3 points of it pulldown duplicates), near the acclaimed median, while its 28 client films are 0.116. Check a studio's client films before calibrating on its reel.

## Other signatures

Skale's 29 vs the acclaimed 18: voice-led films 10 of the 28 with sound vs 1 of 18; light-dominant films 19 vs 8 and dark-dominant films 2 vs 6; colourfulness 19.3 vs 13.8. Openings, proof beats, poster frames and endcards differ too ([[launch-video-structure]]), and so does the speed of a typed prompt ([[launch-video-ui-demo]]). The frame shape is shared: 16:9 in 27 of 29 and 17 of 18 (the Poke anthology and Poke '7' are 4:3; Linear Agent is 2:1).

## Picking

- The product of a known brand is the hero: product camera, or keynote cards when the demo needs chapters.
- A feed sizzle of 40 s or less whose every shot is a live component or effect: beat-cut. All four beat-cut films run 38.1 s or less, but length alone does not pick it: Raycast (38.6 s), Granola 2.0 (29.3 s) and Claude Opus 4.6 (39.5 s) are other registers. Three of the four (Material 3 Expressive, Figma glass, Arc on Windows) are among the four loudest acclaimed films, at -12.1 to -13.0 LUFS.
- A founder explains the product or announces a raise: founder hybrid, led by the voice.
- The words are the product, as in a model launch: kinetic type.
- A brief that asks for "lively" UI motion graphics: Skale's UI-motion register. 13 of Skale's 29 films are under 10 % still.
- None of these (a product its audience does not know yet, no founder on camera, no brief): Skale's UI-motion register, the largest measured row (18 of Skale's 29), with the name early or where the problem act ends, not held to ~70 % ([[launch-video-structure]]).

A second register can ride inside the primary one, as an act or as a layer: a material act in Framer 3.0's tagline, a character layer through Notion Mail's cards, a material showcase across all of Figma glass. Take the numbers from the primary row.

## When to apply

This is the first decision on any launch film, sizzle or README film, and it comes before the storyboard. The beats come next, in [[launch-video-structure]]; where each cut lands is in [[launch-video-cuts]], and how things move inside a shot is in [[launch-video-motion]]. HyperFrames' `/hyperframes` front door routes by deliverable; this node picks the editorial register inside that deliverable. Where a HyperFrames default disagrees with the row, such as product-launch-video's injected crossfade or media-use's -14 LUFS socials recipe, [[hyperframes-reconciliation]] settles the motion and [[launch-video-sound]] the loudness.

## Reference

The register sets the numbers; inside it, each demo shot still needs a story shape:

| Brief | Register | Shape of the demo shots | Gold |
|---|---|---|---|
| a dev tool its audience doesn't know, music only | UI motion graphics | how it feels to use: one gesture, the result under the hand | `stageshow/examples/hero-demo/` |
| billing or infrastructure, work done out of sight | UI motion graphics | what the system does: no cursor, the consequence lands elsewhere | `stageshow/examples/subscriptions/` |
| a phone flow of a few screens | UI motion graphics | a flow: one continuous object, payoff on the last screen | `stageshow/examples/phone-touch/` |
| a known brand's product | product camera | no Stageshow shape; one constant world cut by scale | Linear Agent |

- When two shapes fit, Benji picks the calmer, fuller, better-framed one over the one with more story (`stageshow/examples/payout-flow/`). Stageshow covers demo shots and loops; it sets no register, cut rate or loudness.
- Gold example: the Gold column; for the known-brand row, Linear Agent as measured in this node's product-camera row.
- Check: before the storyboard, write one line (`register: UI motion, ~4 cuts/min, ~9 % still; shape: what the system does`), then set the first finished still beside the gold's at the shown size.

## Gotcha

Compare cut rate and still share only within a register, and never average two rows into a target. Averaging Skale's UI row with the product-camera row gives 9 cuts a minute at 29 % still, a film neither of those registers makes. A product-camera film judged against Skale's medians looks too still. Reach is no guide either. Across Skale's films, views track no craft metric (Spearman |ρ| ≤ 0.18; views vs cut rate 0.03), and like rate vs duration is -0.29. The posting account and suspected paid promotion are the likelier drivers.
