--- title: logical-properties-rtl summary: Write anything that mirrors as leading and trailing — margin-inline-start, inset-inline-end, text-align start, float inline-start. Physical left and right are for physical geometry (safe-area insets) with a [dir="rtl"] override; translateX and background-position have no logical form. Visual order matches DOM order, only direction-bearing icons mirror, and mixed-direction values go in . tags: [layout, rtl, i18n, logical-properties, bidi] --- # Logical properties and RTL A layout written in `left` and `right` has to be rewritten for Arabic and Hebrew; one written in *start* and *end* mirrors itself when `dir="rtl"` lands. Write direction-dependent layout as leading and trailing from the first line, because retrofitting is an audit of every rule. ## The mapping | Physical | Logical | |---|---| | `margin-left` / `padding-right` | `margin-inline-start` / `padding-inline-end` | | `left` / `right` (positioned) | `inset-inline-start` / `inset-inline-end` | | `top` / `bottom` margins and padding | `*-block-start` / `*-block-end` | | `text-align: left` | `text-align: start` | | `float: left` | `float: inline-start` | | `border-top-left-radius` | `border-start-start-radius` | | Tailwind `ml-4` / `pl-4` / `left-0` | `ms-4` / `ps-4` / `start-0` | ## Where physical stays - **Safe-area insets are physical.** `env(safe-area-inset-left)` is the left edge of the glass in any language, so a floating button pairs each physical side with its own inset and overrides in RTL: `right: calc(16px + env(safe-area-inset-right))`, then `[dir="rtl"] .fab { right: auto; left: calc(16px + env(safe-area-inset-left)) }`. Mixing `inset-inline-*` with `safe-area-inset-left` is the bug. - **No logical form exists** for `translateX` or `background-position: left`. Both need a `[dir="rtl"]` override — and so does a slide-in drawer's transform ([[transform-mastery]]). ## Order and mirroring - **Visual order is DOM order.** Never move content out of source sequence with `order`, `row-reverse` or grid placement: keyboard and screen-reader order follow the DOM, so the reading order and the focus order diverge. - **Within a row**, identifying content leads and metadata and actions trail — which in RTL means the right edge leads. Logical properties do that for free. - **Mirror only icons whose meaning follows reading direction**: back and forward arrows, a reply arrow, a progress chevron, a list-indent glyph. Never a play triangle, a clock, a checkmark, a logo, or a slash ([[icon-systems]]). ## Text inside the layout Set `lang` so quotes, hyphenation and pronunciation are right, and `dir` on the document and wherever direction changes. A value that may run the other way — a username, a product name, a URL, a number in an RTL sentence — goes in ``, so punctuation stays on the right side; never reorder digits by hand. Wrapping, casing and truncation are [[line-behavior]]'s. ## Reference A list row with trailing metadata, a back button and a brand name inside Arabic copy: - Bad: `.row .meta { margin-left: auto; padding-left: 12px }` with `[dir="rtl"] svg { transform: scaleX(-1) }`, which pins the date to the wrong edge and mirrors the checkmark and the logo too. - Good: `.row .meta { margin-inline-start: auto; padding-inline-start: 12px }` with `[dir="rtl"] .icon-back { transform: scaleX(-1) }`, so only the back arrow turns. - Good: `

Acme Pro متاح الآن.

`, so the full stop stays at the sentence's end and the Latin name stays in one piece. Gold example: the FAB recipe in Jakub Krehel's `skills/better-layout/spacing-and-adaptivity.md`, which this node already cites. Check: screenshot the screen in LTR and RTL at 390 with real Arabic or Hebrew strings and lay the two side by side. The RTL shot is a mirror image except the play triangle, checkmark, clock and logo; then Tab through it, and focus moves right to left in the order the eye reads. ## Gotcha Testing RTL by flipping `dir` in devtools catches layout and misses content: run it with real RTL strings, mixed-direction values and an LTR brand name inside an RTL sentence ([[stress-scenarios]]). A screen that mirrors perfectly with English copy can still put the full stop on the wrong side of every Hebrew sentence. ## Sources - Jakub Krehel, interfaces skills (MIT, github.com/jakubkrehel/skills, HEAD `592aedc`, read 2026-10-25): `skills/better-layout/SKILL.md` (**Logical properties for anything that mirrors**, **Order by importance**, Before-you-finish rows), `grouping-and-alignment.md`, `spacing-and-adaptivity.md` (the FAB recipe); `better-ui/icons.md` (icons in RTL); `better-typography/SKILL.md` (**Language and bidi behavior**). - CSS Logical Properties and Values Level 1. - Related: [[growth-and-overflow]], [[grouping-by-space]], [[interfaces-reconciliation]].

# Marketing surface rules

[[marketing-vs-product-ui]] says *why* marketing tolerates more expression. This node is the build checklist: what a landing page, blog, docs site, or changelog has to do to be fast, readable, and honest. A visitor sees the page once, not a hundred times a day, so the animation budget is larger; it is still small, and restraint is the house style.

## Motion

- **Motion maps to user input.** No scroll-triggered fade-ups, no scroll hijacking, no parallax that isn't 1:1 with scroll, no auto-advancing carousels. If the user didn't cause it, cut it.
- **Intro animations play once per session.** Gate hero reveals and logo sequences with `sessionStorage` so internal navigation skips them but a genuinely new visit sees them. `localStorage` would kill them forever.
- **A product demo is a figure, not page motion.** One looping or play-once demo may lead a viewport: stopped offscreen, a poster under reduced motion, and a visible pause when it moves for more than 5 s ([[stageshow-reconciliation]], [[MOC-faux-ui]]).
- Hover-revealed content still obeys [[touch-and-focus]]: gated, and never the only route.
- **Readable on the first frame.** In taste-skill's capture of 99 Awwwards Sites of the Day (October 2026), 60 opened on a loading screen and a third were still unreadable 4.5 s after load. The model panel's design marks were the same whatever the wait; only usability fell. No preloader; the title readable on first paint; any load sequence over by 1.2 s. Scroll hijacking scored 6.01 on usability against 6.50 for pages that scroll. Only 35 of 99 had any `prefers-reduced-motion` rule, and under it the finished state must show, never a hidden one ([[prefers-reduced-motion]]).

## Performance

- **Pre-render everything.** Blog, docs, changelog — build-time generation with revalidation, never request-time fetching.
- **Kill layout shift at the source.** Preload fonts (`<link rel="preload" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>`) and above-the-fold images; lazy-load the rest. See [[performance-discipline]].

## Structure

- **Content lives in the DOM.** Hover-revealed nav submenus are visually hidden, not mounted on hover — crawlers and assistive tech need the real markup.
- **CTAs know who's looking.** Logged-out: "Get started". Logged-in: "Open app". Never "Sign up" to a signed-in user.
- **First viewport**: brand, one headline, one supporting line, one CTA group, one dominant visual. No card soup, stat strips, or floating promo chips — see [[unslop-pass]].
- **Code-built illustrations** get `role="img"` + `aria-label`, `user-select: none`, and `pointer-events: none` unless interactive.

## Docs, blogs, changelogs

- **Docs are for copying.** A copy button on every snippet; every page exportable as markdown (a "Copy as Markdown" button and `.md` URLs such as `/docs/getting-started.md`) — people and the models reading your docs both want it; a visual example for every concept.
- **Blogs and changelogs are feeds.** RSS at predictable paths (`/blog/rss.xml`, `/changelog/rss.xml`); `text-wrap: balance` on article headings.

## Pre-ship checklist

- [ ] No scroll-triggered animation, hijacking, non-1:1 parallax, or auto-carousel
- [ ] No preloader; the `h1` readable on first paint, under reduced motion too
- [ ] The frame holds at 1440, 768 and 390: equal margins, no holes ([[page-frame]])
- [ ] Intro gated behind `sessionStorage`
- [ ] Fonts and hero image preloaded; no shift on load
- [ ] Content pages statically generated with revalidation
- [ ] Nav submenu content present in the DOM when closed
- [ ] CTAs switch copy and destination on auth state
- [ ] Snippets have copy buttons; pages export as `.md`; concepts have visual examples
- [ ] RSS live; headings balanced
- [ ] Code illustrations labeled, unselectable, inert
- [ ] The [[ai-default-tells]] deletion pass has run

## When to apply

Creating or reviewing any public-facing page, and any time parallax, a carousel, or a scroll animation is tempting.

## Reference

The figure in a first viewport and a feature grid below it, as Benji Taylor's Stageshow sizes them:

| Part | Spec |
|---|---|
| Hero demo beside copy | About 720 × 340 at 1:1; corner bleed, inset 10% top and left, 15 to 35% past right and bottom; no plate behind it on a white page |
| Full-width hero | A 900 to 1100px window at 1:1, inset top, off the bottom |
| Loop | 10 to 16 s, three to five beats; the payoff holds 2 s; `poster` is the payoff frame, which is also what reduced motion shows |
| Phone column | A `compact` second design at 358 wide in a 390 viewport, recomposed rather than scaled |
| Feature grid | One stage per tile; tile copy is page HTML at 17 to 24px outside the picture; one hero tile; window chrome at most once |

Gold example: `stageshow/examples/hero-demo/` for the hero, `stageshow/examples/bento/` for the grid.

Check: film the page at 1440 and 390 with reduced motion on and off. The poster alone tells the story, nothing on the first screen is hidden waiting for a reveal, and one thing moves per viewport. Benji's call differs: a supporting bento tile may play its one small motion once as the grid scrolls in, staggered 80 to 120ms in reading order (`references/bento.md` rule 11); this node still bans scroll-triggered fade-ups of page content.

## Gotcha

"Marketing tolerates more motion" is read by agents as "marketing wants more motion". The permitted extra is one first-run hero moment. A page where every section animates in is the AI-default look, not expression. taste-skill's inspector fails a page where fewer than 8 elements move; this graph does not adopt that floor.

summary: The viewport, keyboard, scroll and browser-chrome fixes that make a web app feel installed — the baseline meta tag, dvh vs svh, safe areas in all four directions, the Android keyboard, scroll lock through a dialog primitive, overscroll none vs contain, per-scheme theme-color, text-size-adjust — each with its reason, verified on a real phone.

# Mobile platform layer

Most "feels like a website on my phone" reports are not design problems. They are a handful of platform defaults — the URL bar, the keyboard, the notch, the rubber band — each fixed by one declaration that matters only where its reason applies. Reach for a media query or meta tag before JavaScript, and gate by capability, never by user agent. [[touch-and-focus]] owns taps, hover and focus; this node owns the frame those live in.

## Baseline, before the first component

```html
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1, viewport-fit=cover, interactive-widget=resizes-content" />
<meta name="theme-color" media="(prefers-color-scheme: light)" content="#ffffff" />
<meta name="theme-color" media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" content="#0a0a0a" />
```

```css
html { -webkit-tap-highlight-color: transparent; -webkit-text-size-adjust: 100%; overscroll-behavior: none; }
```

In Next.js these are the root layout's `viewport` export (`viewportFit`, `interactiveWidget`, `themeColor: [{ media, color }]`). Never `user-scalable=no` or `maximum-scale=1`: fix the sub-16px input that caused the zoom ([[forms-behavior]]).

## The rules and their reasons

- **Height.** `100vh` is the viewport with the chrome *collapsed*, so on load it overflows by the URL bar. App shells and bottom-pinned UI use `100dvh`; heroes use `min-height: 100svh`, because `dvh` re-lays-out mid-scroll. Tailwind's `h-screen` carries the old bug; use `h-dvh` / `min-h-svh`. `lvh` is the old `vh` under a new name and almost never what you want.
- **Safe areas.** `viewport-fit=cover` paints under the notch; `env(safe-area-inset-*)` pads content back. Without the meta tag every inset is `0px`. Headers take top, tab bars and sheets take bottom, sidebars take left/right in landscape. Inside `calc()` give a fallback: `env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)`.
- **Keyboard.** iOS shrinks the visual viewport; Android Chrome overlays the keyboard on the page. `interactive-widget=resizes-content` makes Android resize too, so a composer at the bottom of a `100dvh` column rides above it with no script. A fixed bottom CTA hides the last field: pad the scroller by the CTA height plus the bottom inset. Never autofocus on a coarse pointer.
- **Overscroll.** `none` on the root stops pull-to-refresh and the page rubber band in an app; `contain` on inner scrollers keeps their own bounce without chaining to the page. Drop the root rule on a document where pull-to-refresh is welcome. Never `touchmove` + `preventDefault()`: it blocks scroll and makes the listener non-passive.
- **Scroll lock.** Behind a modal or sheet, lock through a dialog primitive (Base UI, Radix, vaul). `overflow: hidden` on `body` is ignored by iOS touch scrolling.
- **Status bar.** One `theme-color` per scheme, matched to the top of the page (the header), not the brand colour; update the tag on a class-based theme toggle. A PWA's manifest colours are the same decision: an installed iOS PWA also reads `apple-mobile-web-app-status-bar-style`, set together with the manifest's `theme_color` and `background_color`, and `<meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark">` sits beside the two theme-color tags when both schemes ship.
- **Anchors** clear a sticky header with `scroll-margin-top` equal to its height; cap that header, since 80px is a quarter of a landscape phone.

## Prove it on hardware

Emulation reproduces none of this. Serve on `0.0.0.0`, open by LAN IP; Safari → Develop → device on iOS, `chrome://inspect` on Android. Use a phone a few years old, with the keyboard open, once in landscape, and installed as a PWA if that ships — standalone changes the viewport, insets and status bar. The Xcode Simulator beats desktop emulation for viewport and insets, but it still can't show how touch feels.

## Reference

A checkout screen with a pinned Pay button over a form:

- Bad: `main { height: 100vh } .pay { position: fixed; bottom: 0; left: 0; right: 0; height: 56px }`. On load the button sits under the URL bar, rests on the home indicator, and the last field hides behind it.
- Good:

```css
.shell { height: 100dvh; display: grid; grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto; }
.header { padding-top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px); }
.form { overflow-y: auto; overscroll-behavior: contain; }
.pay { margin: 12px 16px calc(12px + env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)); }
```

Gold example: Emil Kowalski's `skills/mobile-native/SKILL.md`, the source this node distils.

Check: open it by LAN IP on a real phone, focus the last field with the keyboard up, then turn to landscape. Pay stays visible above the keyboard and inside the margins, and nothing sits under the notch or the island. Benji Taylor's rule for drawn phones holds for real ones too: nothing under the island, and a sheet or its grabber starts below the status bar.

## Gotcha

`dvh` everywhere is the overcorrection: a hero sized in `dvh` jumps as the URL bar collapses mid-scroll, which is exactly the jank the fix was for. Shells track the chrome; first screens don't.

title: page-frame
summary: The frame readers judge before any detail — one pair of equal margins, no half-empty sections, no holes, a first screen that says what this is, a heading on every section. Each rule is a measurement you can run on a render.
tags: [layout, marketing, margins, whitespace, hierarchy, review, measured]
---

# Page frame

Before a reader sees a typeface or a shadow they judge the frame: "no good margin", "everything is shifted to one side", "big random blank spaces", "no clear title". Each of those complaints is measurable on a rendered page. taste-skill's study of 97 Awwwards Sites of the Day (October 2026) measured them, and the strong pages agree on five things.

## The rules

| Rule | Measure | Fails when |
|---|---|---|
| **One pair of equal margins** | content's distance from the left and right edge at 1440, 768 and 390 | the sides differ (warn from 16 px of drift); the header sits on one inset and the page on another |
| **Text never touches the edge** | nearest text box to the viewport edge | under 16 px on desktop, under 12 px on a phone |
| **Use the width you set up** | a section with 12+ words, its content all on one side | about half the width is plain ground; in the study about 1 text section in 100 does this. The other half gets the section's picture, a second column, a list or a figure |
| **No holes** | the tallest run of the page with nothing in it | over about half a screen holds nothing; one empty block takes ≥ 28 % of the first screen; a gap between sections passes ~40 % of a screen |
| **Say what this is, first** | the first screen's `h1` | it is missing, it is only a name or slogan, or it is not readable on first paint. In the study 15 of 97 first screens never said what the thing was, and they lost usability marks, not design marks |
| **Title every section** | sections of 30+ words with no heading | 82 % of the studied sections open with one: median 57 px, about 3.5× body, the same left edge each time |
| **Few left edges** | the three most-used left edges' share of left-aligned text | under 60 %: text starts on too many lines |

Spacing that keeps the frame: sections 120–240 px apart on desktop and 72–112 px on a phone (the study's median gap is ~230–250 px), the gap between sections clearly larger than any gap inside one, and at least twice the space above a heading as below it ([[type-scale-and-rhythm]]).

## A rest is not a hole

Empty space is placed when something closes it: the picture with type docked at its edge, a headline big enough to span it, or the wordmark and one fact in the corners like a mount around a print. If nothing closes it, it is a hole. Holes come, in order, from section gaps stretched to 250–760 px, text in one half with nothing in the other, content waiting on a reveal, a footer padded to `100vh`, and a pinned scene holding nothing for several screens. One deliberate rest per page; two near-empty screens fail. When a section looks empty, make its main element bigger or cut it; adding a decoration is almost never the fix.

## When to apply

Reviewing any marketing page or landing page in a browser at 1440, 768 and 390, after [[marketing-surface-rules]] and before polish ([[unslop-pass]]). Asymmetry is fine *inside* the frame — an off-centre anchor line at a third or 42 % — never in the margins themselves.

## Reference

A landing hero at 1440 with copy on the left and the product on the right:

- Bad: copy 40px from the left edge, the product window whole and centred in the right half on a `#f6f5f4` plate with 48px of air on all four sides, its right edge 96px from the viewport. Two margins, a box inside a box, and a floating window.
- Good: one gutter (say 64px, 16px at 390) on both sides of the page; the window in a corner bleed, its top-left whole, running 15 to 35% past the right and bottom of its column; no plate, because the page is the ground; every section heading on the copy's left edge.
- One figure language down the page: one ground, one gutter, one hero shadow, one radius set. A second shadow or radius has to mean something, or it is a mistake.

Gold example: `stageshow/examples/hero-demo/` (corner bleed beside copy), with `stageshow/teaching/scenes.tsx` (`story-crop`) for why a deliberate crop beats a whole window shrunk to a thumbnail.

Check: measure at 1440, 768 and 390. The left and right margins agree within 16px, the hero's top-left is in view, and no edge crosses or stops short of the gutter by under 24px (Benji's rule 11 in Stageshow `references/framing.md`). Then shrink the screenshot to a thumbnail: the subject, its support and the empty space make one picture, not a boxed screenshot.

## Gotcha

Reveals cause holes. A section that fades in on scroll is bare ground until it fires, and in the motion study about a third of award sites still showed a loader or nothing readable 4.5 s after load. Content is in place on first paint; an entrance moves what is already there ([[marketing-surface-rules]], [[prefers-reduced-motion]]).

## Sources

- Leonxlnx, taste-skill v2.1.1 (MIT, HEAD a9c73c3): `skills/taste-skill/references/layout.md` §4–5 (the 97-site October 2026 study: margins, the one-in-a-hundred half-empty section, holes and closers, 15 of 97 unsaid first screens, 82 % headed sections) and `scripts/lib/rules.mjs` (`off-centre`, `edge-text`, `lopsided`, `blank-gap`, `hero-void`, `untitled-section`, `ragged-edges`). Usability and design marks there are model-panel judgements of screenshots, not human jurors.

title: scroll-anchoring
summary: When content above the view changes height, keep the row the reader is looking at where it is on screen. Pick an anchor when the user scrolls, keep its screen offset until they scroll again, compare scroll positions by value (never by "a scroll event fired"), and store the scrollTop the browser read back.
tags: [layout, scrolling, virtualization, lists, chat, resize]
---

# Scroll anchoring

Rows above the view grow, an image loads, older messages prepend, the window narrows and every row reflows — and the paragraph the reader was on jumps away. The fix is to anchor the view to a row, not to a pixel offset: the row at the top of the view keeps its position on screen through any change above it. A view that was showing the end of a list, a chat log for example, keeps showing the end after an append.

## The pattern

1. **Read `scrollTop` once** at the start of the frame.
2. **Compare it with the value stored last frame.** If it differs, the user scrolled: pick a new anchor (the first row whose bottom is below `scrollTop`) and record its screen offset, its top minus `scrollTop`. If it matches, data or size changed: keep the old anchor.
3. **Lay out, then restore the offset.** When the anchor row's top moved, `scrollTop = anchorTop − anchorOffset`. If it didn't move, leave the scroll alone.
4. **Write the DOM first, scroll last**, with `behavior: 'instant'`. Write a spacer's new height *before* the new scroll position, or the browser clamps the scroll to the old height.
5. **Read `scrollTop` back and store that**, not the value you asked for. Ask for 10.6 and the browser may hold 10 or 10.5; storing 10.6 makes the next frame think the user scrolled.

## The traps

- **Don't infer user scrolling from scroll events.** Your own `scrollTo` fires one too. React 18 can batch a scroll handler's flag with an unrelated data update into one render, which skips the adjustment exactly when rows shifted. The comparison by value in step 2 has neither problem.
- **Keep the offset from when the anchor was picked.** Adding a per-frame delta to the rounded `scrollTop` drifts: Cheng Lou measured 3–4 px over a 15-step continuous resize in Safari and headless Chrome.
- **One owner.** If you anchor in code, set `overflow-anchor: none` on the scroller so Chrome's built-in anchoring doesn't move the view a second time. CSS `overflow-anchor` alone is the cheaper option for simple pages, with less control.

## When to apply

Feeds, chat logs, virtualized lists, galleries that reflow on resize, any list where rows above the view change height ([[viewport-custom-design]], [[url-as-state]] for restoring position on back).

## Reference

The frame loop for a chat log that prepends older messages and reflows on resize:

```js
const top = scroller.scrollTop
if (top !== lastTop) {                       // the user scrolled: pick a new anchor
  anchor = firstRowWithBottomBelow(top); offset = anchor.offsetTop - top
}
layoutRows()                                 // heights and spacers first
const want = anchor.offsetTop - offset
if (want !== top) scroller.scrollTo({ top: want, behavior: 'instant' })
lastTop = scroller.scrollTop                 // what the browser kept, not `want`
```

Gold example: Cheng Lou's `docs/Scrolling.md` ("Scroll Anchoring"), the source this node already cites. Inside the view the matching rule is Benji Taylor's: a new row carries the rows below it (`stageshow/teaching/relationships.tsx`, `list-reflow`).

Check: film a 15-step continuous resize and a prepend of 20 messages, then step through every frame. The anchor row's top holds the same screen offset on every frame, with no `jump:` or `drift:` frames, which is how Stageshow's film reads geometry (`references/rehearse.md`).

## Gotcha

When the row at the top of the view shrinks by more than its part above the fold, it leaves the view and the next row becomes the anchor. That's correct, and it looks like a jump of one row. Anchoring with fractional row tops jitters by a sub-pixel each frame, because the browser rounds `scrollTop`; whole-pixel layouts don't.

## Sources

- Cheng Lou, chenguini (MIT, HEAD 84fb27d): `docs/Scrolling.md` "Scroll Anchoring", "React 18+ Pitfall", "Less Preferred Alternatives" (the 3–4 px drift).
- Cheng Lou, handwired (MIT, HEAD 257856e): `docs/behavior-choices.md` "Anchor the scroll position to the row at the top of the view" (`overflow-anchor: none`; spacer height before scroll position).
- Benji Taylor, Stageshow 1.1.1 (MIT, github.com/benjitaylor/skills, HEAD `299140f`, read 2026-11-07): `stageshow/teaching/relationships.tsx` (`list-reflow`), `references/motion.md` (a new row carries the rows below it), `references/rehearse.md` (Jumps: `jump:` and `drift:` per animation frame).
- Related: [[sticky-and-scroll-tells]], [[frame-rate-independence]], [[performance-discipline]].

title: share-and-crawl-metadata
summary: A public page is read by people in tabs, by link previews in chat apps, and by crawlers — each needs a real title, description, image and crawl rule. Wire the template; take the words from the page; and walk the one paying flow end to end before launch.
tags: [layout, marketing, seo, metadata, launch]
---

# Share and crawl metadata

Launch day *is* people pasting the link into chat. A page with no title shows its URL in the tab, in search and in every preview; a framework default title is worse; a missing preview image turns the link into a bare URL and a broken one into a grey box. Wiring the metadata is a fix. **The words are content**: take the title from the page's `h1` and the description from existing copy (the hero subhead, a post's excerpt), and flag the gap when there is nothing to take. [[marketing-surface-rules]] owns motion, performance and CTAs on these pages; this node owns what machines read.

## Titles and descriptions — blocker

- One title template in the root layout (`%s · Product`), and per-route metadata on every public route. Dynamic routes generate theirs from the record, not a static string.
- Set the production origin as the metadata base. Without it, relative preview-image URLs resolve to localhost in production.
- The same title on every route is a finding: tabs, history and screen-reader users can't tell pages apart.

## Link previews — should fix, blocker when the launch depends on sharing

Open Graph image at least 1200×630, the large-image card type, and a file that actually exists. Per-page images only when a generator already exists; a site-wide image is fine otherwise. A missing image can't be invented, so it goes on the human list. Device check: paste the production URL into two chat apps and look.

## Crawl rules — should fix

- A leftover staging `Disallow: /` or a site-wide `noindex` de-indexes the whole site: **blocker**.
- The sitemap lists real pages and excludes scaffolding and auth-gated routes ([[leftovers-and-leaks]]).
- A canonical link on any page reachable at more than one URL.

## Icons — should fix

The product's own favicon, an SVG icon, and an `apple-touch-icon` (without it iOS uses a page screenshot for a home-screen shortcut). Check the favicon on a dark tab bar. A web manifest with the framework's default name is a finding.

## The conversion path — blocker

The one flow that pays for the launch: landing, CTA, signup or checkout, first screen. Every link resolves; the price on the pricing page matches the billing config; the plan the button names is the plan checkout opens; the post-signup redirect exists. Hunt test-mode payment links (`/test_` in a checkout URL), placeholder social handles, and newsletter forms that post nowhere. Code can find a price mismatch but not settle it: state both values and ask which is right.

## Analytics — should fix

Loaded once, from the root layout, async or through the framework's script strategy. Whether a consent banner is legally required is the user's decision; note what tracking exists and leave it on the human list. A banner that pushes content down when it mounts is a layout-shift finding ([[empty-loading-states]]).

## Reference

```html
<title>Ledger · Acme</title>
<meta name="description" content="Close the month in an afternoon. Ledger reconciles every account as payments land.">
<meta property="og:image" content="https://acme.com/og/ledger.png"><!-- 1200×630, absolute production URL -->
<meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">
<link rel="canonical" href="https://acme.com/ledger">
```

- Bad: `<title>Create Next App</title>` and `og:image` of `/og.png` resolving to localhost. Good: the page's `h1` through the `%s · Product` template, the hero subhead as the description, an absolute image URL.
- The preview card is the one frame most people ever see, so Benji's poster rule for demos carries over: it tells the story on its own, with the result on screen, never caught mid-change. The favicon is the product's real mark, never a letter in a colored square.
- Gold example: `stageshow/SKILL.md` step 7 (poster) and `stageshow/references/craft.md` (No invented logo); the checklist above for everything machines read.
- Check: paste the production URL into two chat apps on a phone; count real strings in the card (title, description, image text) and confirm each came from the page, none truncated mid-word.

## Gotcha

Deciding the CTA by reading cookies in the marketing layout opts the whole page out of static rendering. Keep the page static and resolve the signed-in state on the client.

## Sources

- Emil Kowalski's design-engineering practice, distilled by AgentsORG.
- Benji Taylor, Stageshow 1.1.1 (MIT, github.com/benjitaylor/skills, HEAD `299140f`, read 2026-11-07): `stageshow/SKILL.md` (step 7, poster), `stageshow/references/craft.md` (No invented logo).
- Related: [[ship-check]], [[content-authenticity]], [[marketing-vs-product-ui]].

title: sticky-and-scroll-tells
summary: Background-blur on sticky sections is an AI tell. Scroll hijacking confuses users. Native scroll usually wins.
tags: [layout, sticky, scroll, anti-pattern]
---

# Sticky and scroll tells

Two of the most overused (and easiest-to-misuse) page-level patterns: blurred sticky nav, and scroll hijacking. Both signal "AI-generated landing page" when applied generically.

## Blurred sticky nav — the AI tell

```css
/* The pattern that gives it away */
.nav {
  position: sticky;
  top: 0;
  background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.7);
  backdrop-filter: blur(12px);
}
```

This pattern is fine *in moderation* and *with context-specific tuning*. But the default-AI-output version is:
- 12px blur (too strong).
- 70% white background (too opaque).
- Universal application (sticks on every page, even pages where it shouldn't).
- No border-bottom for separation (so scrolled content bleeds under the nav awkwardly).

The result: every AI-generated landing page in 2025–2026 has the same blurred nav. It's become a *tell*.

## What to do instead

Pick one of these:

### A. Solid sticky with subtle separation

```css
.nav {
  position: sticky;
  top: 0;
  background: var(--bg-base);
  border-bottom: 1px solid var(--border-default);
}
```

Cleaner, faster (no GPU blur), no AI smell.

### B. Hide on scroll-down, show on scroll-up

```ts
let lastY = 0;
window.addEventListener('scroll', () => {
  const y = window.scrollY;
  document.querySelector('.nav').style.transform =
    y > lastY && y > 100 ? 'translateY(-100%)' : 'translateY(0)';
  lastY = y;
});
```

The nav appears when the user wants it (scrolling up, presumably to navigate) and stays out of the way otherwise.

### C. No sticky at all

For long-form content (articles, docs), the nav can simply scroll off-screen. The user scrolls back to top when they want nav. This is the calmest option.

### D. Blur — but tuned

If you genuinely want the blur effect, tune it:
- `backdrop-filter: blur(6px)` (not 12px).
- `background: rgba(var(--bg-base-rgb), 0.85)` (matches your palette, not pure white).
- Add `border-bottom: 1px solid var(--border-default)` for clean separation.
- Apply *only* on marketing pages, not in-product.

## Scroll hijacking — avoid

"Scroll hijacking" = the page intercepts the user's scroll input and does something other than scroll (snap to sections, trigger animations, change layout). Examples:

- `scroll-snap-type` on a long page where the user wants to scroll freely.
- Parallax that decouples scroll speed from visual movement.
- Section-by-section snap navigation that prevents the user from skimming.
- "Scroll-jacking" entrance animations that lock the scroll until they complete.

These confuse users because the OS scroll feels broken — the same gesture produces different results in different contexts.

## When scroll-snap *is* the right answer

Limited cases:

- **Horizontal carousels** — scroll-snap-x on a single-row carousel is the right answer. The user expects each card to land aligned.
- **Image galleries with explicit slides** — vertical scroll-snap on a presentation-style page with discrete slides.
- **Story-driven onboarding** — first-time experiences where you specifically want each "step" to land precisely.

In all these cases, the *vertical page scroll* should still be free. Snap only the contained scroll, not the page scroll.

## Scroll-driven animations — judiciously

`scroll-driven animations` (the new CSS feature) are powerful and worth knowing. They let you scrub an animation as the user scrolls — e.g., a hero image scales up as the user enters its viewport.

The right uses:
- **Reveal-on-scroll** — content fades/scales in as it enters the viewport. Subtle.
- **Progress indicators** — a top-of-page progress bar fills as the user scrolls.
- **Parallax (gentle)** — backgrounds move at 0.7x scroll speed for depth. NEVER 0.3x or below (causes nausea).

The wrong uses:
- Anything that *changes the scroll behavior* itself.
- Anything that *slows* the user's perceived scroll.
- Anything that animates as the user scrolls *up* differently than down — feels broken.

## When to apply

- Designing any landing page with a top nav.
- Reviewing a PR that adds sticky behavior or scroll-driven animation.
- Auditing for AI-default tells ([[ai-default-tells]]).
- Rows above the view change height and the reading position jumps: [[scroll-anchoring]].

## Reference

- Bad: `position: sticky; background: rgba(255,255,255,.7); backdrop-filter: blur(12px)` on every route. Good: `position: sticky; top: 0; background: var(--bg-base); border-bottom: 1px solid var(--border-default)`.
- A contained list softens its edges only once it has scrolled, so the fade means "more here"; at rest on whole rows it has none (adapted from `stageshow/kit/motion/Scroll.css`):

```css
.list[data-scrolled] {
  mask-image: linear-gradient(to bottom, transparent, #000 18px, #000 calc(100% - 18px), transparent);
}
```

- Benji clears the fade at the end of the scroll and treats a hard clipping edge as the bad half of the pair; a permanent fade on a list that never scrolls is decoration.
- Gold example: `stageshow/teaching/edges.tsx` (the viewport-edge bad/good pair), `stageshow/kit/motion/Scroll.css`.
- Check: film a scroll down and back up at 390 wide and step the contact sheet: the content tracks the finger 1:1, the nav never covers a row without its rule, and the fade appears only on edges hiding rows.

## Gotcha

`backdrop-filter: blur()` is GPU-cheap but interacts weirdly with `position: sticky` and `overflow: hidden` parents in some browsers. Always test on Safari + Firefox before shipping a blurred sticky nav.

Also: `scroll-snap` on iOS Safari can interact poorly with the URL bar collapsing. Test on real iPhone before shipping snap-based layouts.

## Sources

- guidelines.sh — "Background blur on sticky sections is an AI giveaway" + "Avoid scroll hijacking."
- web.dev — scroll-driven animations docs.
- Benji Taylor, Stageshow 1.1.1 (MIT, github.com/benjitaylor/skills, HEAD `299140f`, read 2026-11-07): `stageshow/kit/motion/Scroll.css`, `stageshow/teaching/edges.tsx`, `stageshow/references/motion.md` (Scrolling and the camera).
- Related: [[viewport-custom-design]], [[ai-default-tells]], [[transform-opacity-only]].

title: viewport-custom-design
summary: Each viewport gets its own design, not just a scaled version of desktop. Narrow columns are valid. Break the grid for delight.
tags: [layout, responsive, viewport]
---

# Viewport-custom design

"Responsive" doesn't mean scaling desktop. It means designing each viewport with intent.

## What this means

The default workflow:
1. Designer builds desktop in Figma.
2. Engineer "makes it responsive" by setting flex/grid breakpoints.
3. Mobile looks like a thinner version of desktop.

This produces *technically* responsive UI that feels designed for one viewport and bent to fit others. The fix is designing each major viewport (mobile, tablet, desktop, ultra-wide) with its own layout intent.

For mobile, this often means a *completely different* layout — not a single-column stack of desktop elements. For example:

| Desktop | Mobile |
|---|---|
| Sidebar + main content | Bottom tab bar + full-width content |
| 3-column grid of cards | Horizontal-scroll carousel or vertical stack with different priority |
| Wide hero with image right | Stacked hero with image full-width below |
| Dense table | Card-per-row with key fields prioritized |

- A narrow layout is a second design, not a squeeze: crop closer, drop or stack the secondary piece, keep the action and its result whole (Benji Taylor's `compact` rule).

## Narrow columns are valid

A common mistake: making content full-width because the viewport allows it. A 2400px-wide article is unreadable; 65 characters per line is the sweet spot for prose ([[line-length-tracking]]).

```css
.article {
  max-width: 65ch; /* or 720px */
  margin: 0 auto;
  padding: 0 24px;
}
```

Blog content, documentation, long-form reading — these often benefit from a narrow central column even on a 4K monitor. Don't fill space just because it's there.

## 12-column grids as foundation

The 12-column grid is the most flexible base because 12 divides into 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. You can have a one-third / two-thirds split, a quarter / three-quarters, a six-column gallery, etc.

```css
.grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(12, 1fr);
  gap: 24px;
}
.hero { grid-column: span 12; }
.feature { grid-column: span 4; }
.sidebar { grid-column: span 3; }
.main { grid-column: span 9; }
```

Use this as the foundation. *Then* break it intentionally for delight.

## Break the grid (deliberately)

Small graphical elements that escape the grid signal craft — a quote with a hanging punctuation mark in the left margin, an illustration that overlaps a section divider, a callout that bleeds outside the column.

This is a marketing-page move ([[visual-imperfection]]). In-product, hold the grid.

## Bento layouts (the modern landing-page pattern)

Bento boxes — irregular grid layouts where tiles vary in size and feature their own micro-content — are a 2024–2026 landing-page staple:

```
[ tall feature ] [ wide visual    ]
                 [ wide visual    ]
[ small ] [ small ] [ small      ]
[ wide quote that bridges 3 cols  ]
```

When done well, each tile is self-contained, hierarchy is clear from size alone, and the overall layout reads as composed (not random). When done poorly, it reads as a Bootstrap grid that someone broke. Planning the tiles themselves (which are UI, the one hero, neighbours of different kinds, one Stage per tile) is [[bento-grids]].

## When to apply

- Designing any new screen — start with the viewport-specific layouts, not a single desktop comp.
- Reviewing a "responsive" PR — ask whether mobile was designed or just scaled.
- Landing pages and marketing pages — bento and break-the-grid live here.

## When NOT to apply

- Forms — single-column, top-to-bottom, no exceptions.
- Dashboards with comparable widgets — symmetric grid wins for scannability.
- Content the user reads (long articles, docs) — narrow central column.

## Reference

| Piece | Wide (900–1100px hero) | Phone column (390 viewport) |
|---|---|---|
| Hero demo | Window at 1:1, inset top, running off the bottom | Its own design at 358 wide: `compact={{ below: 560, width: 358, height: 320 }}` |
| Secondary card | Sits on the window's lower edge | Dropped, or stacked under the window |
| List rows | Title, labels column, avatar | Labels column dropped, title shortened (as `examples/linear` does) |
| UI type | 11–15px | Nothing under 10px |

- Bad: the 1000px hero scaled into a 390 column, its 13px row names now about 5px. Good: a 358-wide composition cropped to the focal row, its action and result whole.
- Gold example: `stageshow/examples/linear/` (its compact layout drops the label chips) and `stageshow/references/framing.md` (Small formats and the page).
- Check: screenshot at the shown width and at 390 side by side; if the 390 frame is the wide one shrunk, with nothing cropped, dropped or restacked, it was not designed.

## Gotcha

Don't apply marketing-grade asymmetry to product UI. Asymmetric grids in a settings page look broken; in a hero, they look intentional. See [[marketing-vs-product-ui]].

Also: viewport-custom design isn't an excuse to ship inconsistency. The *components* should be consistent across viewports; the *composition* of components varies. A button looks the same on mobile and desktop; the screen they're on differs.

## Sources

- guidelines.sh — "Design for each viewport" + "Narrow columns are valid" + "12-column grids" + "Break the grid for delight."
- Bento Grids (bentogrids.com) — modern landing-page bento examples.
- Benji Taylor, Stageshow 1.1.1 (MIT, github.com/benjitaylor/skills, HEAD `299140f`, read 2026-11-07): `stageshow/SKILL.md` (step 1), `stageshow/references/framing.md` (Small formats and the page; Wide hero), `stageshow/references/craft.md` (Type), `stageshow/references/verify.md` (390 width, nothing under 10px on the phone), `stageshow/examples/linear/index.tsx`.
- Related: [[sticky-and-scroll-tells]], [[marketing-vs-product-ui]], [[visual-imperfection]].

summary: Install Agentation in localhost dev. Click any element to annotate. Two-session workflow: critique loop in Session 1, fix loop in Session 2.

# Agentation workflow

[Agentation](https://www.agentation.com) (by Benji Taylor, [github.com/benjitaylor/agentation](https://github.com/benjitaylor/agentation)) is the productized version of the [[pointing-beats-describing]] principle. It mounts a toolbar in your dev environment that lets you click on any element on the page, write a short critique, and emit structured annotations the agent can read.

This skill **recommends installing Agentation** alongside Obsidian for any team doing AI-assisted UI work. See the README's "Recommended companions" section.

## Install (Next.js example)

```bash
npm install --save-dev agentation
```

```tsx
// app/layout.tsx (App Router)
import { Agentation } from "agentation";

export default function RootLayout({ children }) {
  return (
    <html>
      <body>
        {children}
        {process.env.NODE_ENV === "development" && <Agentation />}
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}
```

Mount under `NODE_ENV === "development"` so the toolbar never ships to production.

For non-Next setups, install the [`agentation`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/agentation) skill itself — it has framework detection:

```bash
npx skills add benjitaylor/agentation
```

This adds an `agentation` skill to your agent's library that knows how to install the React component in your specific framework (Next.js App Router, Pages Router, Vite, Astro, Remix).

## Add the MCP server (optional but recommended)

The MCP server lets your agent **read annotations directly** instead of having you copy-paste them. Two install paths:

```bash
# Universal — works with Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, 9+ agents
npx add-mcp agentation

# Claude Code only (slightly more features)
npx agentation-mcp init
```

With MCP installed, the agent can call `agentation_watch_annotations` and read every annotation in real time as you create them.

## Manual workflow (no MCP)

1. Run your dev server.
2. The Agentation toolbar appears bottom-right.
3. Click "Annotate" → click any element on the page.
4. Type 2–3 sentences of critique. Be specific and reference principles (visual hierarchy, Gestalt grouping, whitespace). Cite comparable products (Stripe, Linear, Vercel).
5. Submit. Agentation outputs structured markdown — selectors, file paths, computed styles, your critique.
6. Copy the output into Claude Code / Cursor / your agent of choice.

## Two-session workflow (with MCP)

With MCP enabled, you can run two agent sessions in parallel:

```text
┌──────────────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────────────┐
│   Session 1: Critique    │         │    Session 2: Fix        │
│                          │         │                          │
│ - Open localhost in      │         │ - Watches for new        │
│   headed agent-browser   │         │   annotations via MCP    │
│ - Scrolls through pages  │  ───►   │ - Reads each annotation  │
│ - Adds 5–8 annotations   │         │ - Edits code to address  │
│   per page autonomously  │         │ - Commits + pushes       │
│ - Names the principle    │         │ - Loops to next          │
│   in each annotation     │         │                          │
└──────────────────────────┘         └──────────────────────────┘
```

This separates the **critique loop** from the **fix loop**. Each session has a single, focused job. The annotation is the API between them — the same selector + critique that a human would have written.

Use this when you want fully autonomous design review without human-in-the-loop on every annotation. Add human-in-the-loop on PR review of the resulting commits, not on each annotation.

## Critique style

From Agentation's own skill:

- **2–3 sentences max** per annotation. Longer reads as essay; shorter reads as too vague.
- **Specific + actionable**. Bad: "this section needs work." Good: "Use a 3-column card grid with icons — similar to Stripe's guidelines pattern."
- **Name the principle**. Visual hierarchy. Gestalt grouping. Whitespace. F-pattern scanning. These vocabulary words are how the agent looks up the right pattern.
- **Reference comparable products**. "Like Stripe", "like Linear's command bar", "like Vercel's monochrome dashboard."
- **Link the principle node** when applicable. `[[hover-states-subtle]]`, `[[shadows-whisper]]`, `[[color-monochromatic]]`.
- **One instance per annotation.** Feedback addresses an instance; a guideline describes a principle. A note that would fit every page belongs in a node, not on an element (Benji Taylor, benji.org/annotating).

## When to apply

- Any team using an AI coding agent on UI work.
- Solo developers who want structured design-review on their own work.
- Design engineers who want to give precise feedback to PMs / engineers without writing essays.

## When NOT to apply

- Production environments — Agentation is dev-only.
- Pre-launch marketing pages — at low frequency, manual pointing is faster than setting up the toolbar.
- Components without a localhost preview — Agentation needs a running app to click on.

## Reference

One annotation on a pricing card, written badly and then well:

- Bad: `div.card` → "This feels cluttered, make it cleaner and more modern."
- Good: `[data-testid="plan-pro"] .plan-name` → "The plan name sits 16px above its price and 12px below the card above, so it reads as part of the wrong record (Gestalt proximity). Title 4–6px over its metadata, the air in the row's padding, as Gmail's rows do."

The good one points at one instance by a stable selector, names the principle once and gives the number the fix lands on, in three sentences.

Gold example: `stageshow/references/review.md`, where every finding is what you would screenshot, which frame shows it and the fix in one line. An annotation has the same shape.

Check: hand the annotation alone to a fresh session with the page closed. If it cannot find the element from the selector and apply the fix from the sentence, rewrite it before Session 2 picks it up.

## Gotcha

Annotation selectors break when the DOM changes. If you annotate `.product-card > div:nth-child(3)` and someone reorders the divs, the annotation now points at the wrong element. Prefer `data-testid` or stable class names. Audit annotations weekly — old broken ones add noise without signal.

Also: Agentation's license is PolyForm Shield 1.0.0 (non-permissive — restricts use by competing products). Read the license before adopting in a commercial product that might overlap with Agentation's space.

summary: Meta's Astryx design system as a companion — in a project that depends on @astryxdesign/core, its CLI and MCP server pick the template, components and props, and its theme owns the values; this graph keeps the review, the contract precedence and pov. What was distilled (press, hover-intent, reduced-motion, dismissal, mobile type, reorder), which of its records are current versus draft, its on-system rules, and five conflicts settled.
tags: [meta, companion, astryx, design-system, reconciliation]

# Astryx, reconciled

Astryx is the design system that grew inside Meta for eight years and was opened under MIT: 150+ accessible React 19 components styled with StyleX (invisible to consumers), seven themes as CSS custom-property overrides, templates, and a CLI and MCP server built so that a person and an agent build from the same reference (astryx.atmeta.com). Its design and family records are written as numbered requirements (DR, FR, INV), each marked `draft`, `current` or `archived`, and only `current` ones govern. This graph distilled the current ones that were new to it: [[press-and-pending-states]], [[hover-intent-timing]] (from a draft motion record, adopted on its own merits), [[reduced-motion-by-pointer]], [[overlay-dismissal-stack]], [[mobile-type-pin]] and [[reorder-insertion-cue]].

## Who owns what in an Astryx project

A project is an Astryx project when `@astryxdesign/core` is a dependency.

| Job | Owner | This graph keeps |
|---|---|---|
| Which page template, blocks and components to start from | `astryx build "<request>"`, then `astryx template <name> <path>` and `astryx component <Name>`; or the MCP server (`https://astryx.atmeta.com/mcp`, tools `search` and `get`) | [[page-frame]] as the check on the result |
| Props, slots, composition | the component's own docs (`astryx docs`, `{Name}.doc.mjs`). Read them before inventing a prop | [[component-api-design]] for components the app writes itself |
| Colours, spacing, radii, motion values | the active theme's tokens (`--color-*`, `--spacing-*` in rem) | [[skill-router]] precedence: a `.design` contract still outranks both |
| Agent setup | `astryx init` writes the project's agent docs; `npm i -g @astryxdesign/cli` adds one global skill | — |
| Review | its *is my code good* rubric (context first, compare sibling surfaces, an app convention is not a finding) | [[review-format]], [[pov]], [[gotchas]] on top |
| shadcn users | its shadcn registry items (draft) install compositions and CSS imports, never component source | [[shadcn-reconciliation]] |

Its on-system rules, which agree with this graph and are worth enforcing in any Astryx app: start every page from a template (frame first, region budgets before content); dense data in rows (Table, List), not cards ([[dashboard-tells]]); status as a status dot or token, never a decorative badge; semantic tokens only, no hard-coded colour or spacing; no inline `style` on raw elements; navigation through the app's link component, never a bare `<a>`; controlled form inputs.

## Draft records that confirm, not add

Its draft records on spatial hierarchy, shape, elevation and control rhythm restate rules already here: gaps grow from local to group to section and space comes before another card ([[grouping-by-space]]); nested curves stay concentric and an accent edge follows the corner instead of a side stripe colliding with it ([[depth-and-nesting]]); one edge language leads, a border or a soft shadow, not both at full strength, and a focus ring is never elevation ([[shadows-whisper]]); mixed controls in one row share an apparent height and baseline while the hit target may be larger ([[touch-and-focus]]). Its agentic-states record is a list of open questions, not answers; [[agent-trace-states]] uses them as a review checklist.

## Conflicts, settled

| Topic | Astryx | This graph | Settled |
|---|---|---|---|
| Overshoot | a theme's expressive character may overshoot on entrances and moves | bounce only after a drag ([[gesture-phases]]) | Inside an Astryx app the theme wins; elsewhere this graph's rule holds |
| Reduced-motion replacement | ≤ 200 ms cross-fade on touch, immediate otherwise | a ~120 ms opacity fade ([[prefers-reduced-motion]]) | Astryx's split, recorded in [[reduced-motion-by-pointer]] |
| Values passed by the caller | guidance over enforcement: pass a value and the component renders it | review flags off-scale values | The component renders it; the review still flags it as a finding |
| Tooltip first-open delay | owner's choice, may be zero with a reason | 400–700 ms ([[duration-table]]) | 400–700 ms unless the owner wrote down why not |
| Card use | widgets, galleries, settings groups only | [[cards-design]] | Same rule; Astryx's list is the tie-breaker |

## Sources

- Meta, Astryx (MIT, github.com/meta/astryx, HEAD `9f55320`, read 2026-11-09; astryx.atmeta.com): `README.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `docs/design/`, `docs/families/`, `docs/architecture/theme-tokens.md`, `packages/cli/assets/docs/` (`working-with-ai`, `principles.doc.dense`, `is-my-code-good`, `shadcn-compatibility.doc.draft`). title: build-a-tool
summary: When prompting for an artifact keeps landing on "closer, but not quite", stop iterating on the output and build the small tool that produces it — diagnose the gap, pitch the tool, put every judgment on a live control, save writes a file, harvest the config.
tags: [meta, tooling, workflow, process]
---

# Build a tool to build the thing

Prompting for an intricate result is a slot machine: every attempt costs a round trip, lands "close", and gives the user no way to steer except rewriting the prompt. A tool converts that loop into knobs — the process is built once and the taste decisions become adjustments the user makes by eye in seconds. Two halves in strict order: **diagnose, then build.** Skipping the diagnosis produces a generic playground.

## Diagnose the gap

Answer from the conversation; ask only for what you can't infer.

- **What actually ships?** Name the artifact and where it lives. The tool is never it.
- **Why can't you build it directly?** Classify:

```text
Why does prompting keep missing?
├── Judgment only the user's eye can make (density, balance, "when it feels right")
│   → dial-in tool: rebuild the process, bind every taste value to a control
├── Must match something that exists (a design, another app's output, a reference)
│   → matching tool: reproduce the process that made the reference, render beside it at ship size
├── Exists in the wrong form (right pixels, wrong format)
│   → converter: ingest the source, export exactly what the project needs
├── Can only be judged in a state that is slow to reach (a screen, a dataset, a moment)
│   → stage: a route that puts the work in that state instantly
└── No target yet — the user will know it when they see it
    → exploration, not matching: [[vibe-to-generator]]
```

Most real tools combine two branches; name the combination.

- **What knows the process?** An app that produced the reference, a named technique, a spec. Reproduce a process known to work; don't invent one. If an existing app made the reference, its settings panel is your parameter list.
- **What format does the project need?** Decided by what the code must do with the output, never by what is easiest to export.

**When not to.** One or two direct attempts would land it; the result is fully determined with no judgment left; unclear which side you're on → make one honest direct attempt first. **The stop-the-loop rule:** if a round of "closer, but not quite" has happened, the diagnosis is done — say so and propose the tool instead of retrying the prompt in different words.

## Pitch it, then build it

Four lines before code: **the gap** (one sentence), **the tool** (what it renders, which branch), **the controls** (which decisions belong to the user's eye), **the export** (the exact format and how saving works). This is the cheapest moment to be corrected.

Then, in one sitting:

1. **Isolated route** (`/lab/<slug>`); nothing in production imports it.
2. **Rebuild the process, not the output.** A tool that traces the output matches once and can't be adjusted.
3. **The target stays on screen**, beside the output, at ship size. Matching from memory across a tab switch is how "close enough" ships.
4. **Every judgment call is a live control**, with tested bounds — a slider that reaches a broken render teaches distrust. Fixed values are only for the rules of the process.
5. **Instant feedback.** No "apply" step; keep panel rows unconditional.
6. **Save writes a file.** The full configuration as JSON in the project (plus the artifact data if separate), path shown in the UI. Production imports that file, so saving *is* shipping the decision.

Hand off in two lines — the URL and the verbs — and stop. Hovering with suggestions defeats the point of the knobs.

## Tools that review, not make

The same move works for checking. When you keep checking one thing by hand, build a mountable inspector for it. Two examples are a nested-radius inspector, which shows the actual and expected value per corner on hover (inner = outer − inset), has a page-scan button and a "copy report" button that pastes into the agent, and a focus-path overlay that numbers and draws the Tab order. These let you review a preview URL or someone else's work without opening the code. Build one only for a check you repeat; a one-off check stays a checklist row ([[review-checklist]]).

- A reviewing tool ends in a verdict, not only pictures. Stageshow's `film.mjs --gate` ends `rehearsal passed` or prints each fault as a line that is never intentional (Benji Taylor, `references/rehearse.md`).

## Harvest

When the user picks a keeper: read the saved config (never copy values by eye), wire the export and the cleaned-up render logic into the real artifact, and leave the tool in place unless asked — the next asset in the same language goes through it.

## When to apply

"Build me a tool for this", a result the agent keeps missing, two rounds burned on one artifact. Sibling workflows: [[prototype-picker]] compares discrete directions; [[vibe-to-generator]] searches a space with no target.

## Reference

The same gap, re-prompted and then tooled:

- Bad: a third "make the list entrance feel more natural, a bit less robotic".
- Good: `/lab/list-entrance` with a stagger slider bounded 40–80ms (default 60, Benji's reading-order range), a curve menu holding only named curves, Replay, Step 40ms, and Save writing `lab/list-entrance.json` with the path printed under the button.

Every control is a call the user's eye makes. Anything that is a rule of the process stays fixed and never becomes a knob.

Gold example: `stageshow/scripts/film.mjs`, a tool that reviews. It shoots one contact sheet at true size, steps one beat at 50ms with `--at <mark>`, zooms with `--zoom` and gives a verdict with `--gate`. Its making half is `stageshow/playground/` (Pause, Step, Replay pair).

Check: drag every control to both ends and film the output at each bound. A bound that reaches a broken render gets narrowed before handoff.

## Gotcha

A tool whose knob bucket is empty didn't need building — the idea was fully determined. Go build the output.

## Sources

- Emil Kowalski's design-engineering practice on tools as a means to an end, distilled by AgentsORG.
- Related: [[prototype-picker]], [[vibe-to-generator]], [[taste-is-trained]].
- Benji Taylor, Stageshow 1.1.1 (MIT, github.com/benjitaylor/skills, HEAD `299140f`, read 2026-11-07): `stageshow/scripts/film.mjs`, `stageshow/references/rehearse.md` (flags, gate lines, Pause and Step), `stageshow/references/teaching.md` (Replay pair), `stageshow/references/motion.md` (stagger 40–80ms), `stageshow/kit/ease.ts` (named curves).

title: change-scoped-review
summary: Reviewing a diff, not a screen. Resolve the scope (commits ahead of the merge base plus uncommitted work), expand changed files to the surfaces they render in, read the removed side of every hunk for lost signals, and status each finding Introduced, Regression or Pre-existing by cause, not by location. Only the first two block; three pre-existing findings is a courtesy, thirty is another review.
tags: [meta, review, diff, pull-request, regression]
---

# Change-scoped review

The author of a pull request is asking "did I make this worse?". A review that answers "here is everything wrong with this codebase" answers a question nobody asked and buries the two lines that matter. Scope the review to the change, then report in [[review-format]]'s table with one extra column: status.

## 1. Resolve the scope

With no target named: if `HEAD` is ahead of `git merge-base origin/<default> HEAD`, review that range **plus** any uncommitted changes, and say how many commits and how many uncommitted files. Else, if the tree is dirty, review the uncommitted changes. Else there is no change — ask what to review rather than inventing a scope. Read the whole diff before forming an opinion; a skimmed diff produces findings the next hunk already fixed.

## 2. Expand to the blast radius

A changed file is evidence, not the subject. Its **blast radius** is the set of surfaces it renders in — every screen using a changed component, every consumer of a changed token. Review those surfaces, not just the hunk.

## 3. Read the removed side

Regressions are invisible in the after state. Search the `-` lines (`git diff -U0 … | grep '^-'`) for signals that left:

| Removed | Check |
|---|---|
| `aria-*`, `role=`, `alt=`, `<label`, `htmlFor`, `scope=` | Lost name, description, announcement or association ([[screen-reader-announcements]]) |
| `<button>`, `<a>`, `<nav>`, `<main>` turned `div` / `span` | Keyboard and assistive behaviour traded for styling ([[keyboard-patterns]]) |
| `:focus-visible`, `outline`, `tabindex` | The focus indicator or the tab stop is gone |
| `prefers-reduced-motion`, `prefers-contrast` | The user's system preference is now ignored |
| Logical properties swapped for `left` / `right`; `lang=`, `dir=` | Direction handling dropped ([[logical-properties-rtl]]) |
| `text-wrap`, `line-clamp`, `tabular-nums` | Wrapping or figure alignment silently changed ([[line-behavior]]) |
| A token swapped for a literal or a lighter token | The rendered pair may now fail — measure it |
| A user-facing string deleted or shortened | A label, error or empty state lost its information |

A signal is a lead, not a finding. **Equivalent replacements clear it:** `aria-label` → `aria-labelledby` on visible text; a `role` dropped because the element became native; `outline` → a `box-shadow` ring on the same `:focus-visible`; a literal → a token of the same value; physical → logical (that is the fix); a string moved into the catalogue. Read the hunk around each removal before deciding — `-U0` hides the element it came from.

## 4. Status by cause

- **Introduced** — the change created it.
- **Regression** — the change weakened something previously correct.
- **Pre-existing** — present before, not made worse.

Status follows cause, not location. An untouched consumer of a changed token that now fails contrast is **Introduced**; a bug three lines from a hunk that the change did not touch is **Pre-existing**. Only Introduced and Regression findings count toward severity and the verdict, so a change whose only findings are pre-existing is an approve.

## Reporting

`| Severity | Status | Location | Before | After | Why |`, Introduced and Regression only, ranked by severity then reach. Then at most **three** pre-existing findings, plainly marked not this change's responsibility. With nothing caused by the change: "No actionable interface findings in this change." Correctness, tests, security and performance belong to the general code review — name such a concern once and drop it.

- End with **Not checked:** the widths, looks and states you did not look at. A predicted pass is not a pass (Benji Taylor, Stageshow `references/review.md`).

## Reference

One regression row, then the close:

| Severity | Status | Location | Before | After | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| High | Regression | `Toolbar.tsx:42` | `<button onClick={save}>` | `<div className="btn" onClick={save}>` | Tab skips it and Enter does nothing; the after screenshot is identical, only the `-` line shows it |

Below it: "Pre-existing (not this change): `Menu.tsx:88` delete is hover-only." Then "Not checked: dark theme, 390px." A review that says nothing about a width reads as a pass at that width.

Gold example: Jakub's `removed-signals.md` for the `-` side; `stageshow/references/review.md` for the close, which ends every review with what could not be checked and treats a predicted pass as no pass.

Check: reproduce each Introduced or Regression row on the running surface: a before-and-after frame at its shipping widths for a visual finding, a Tab press for a keyboard one. A row with nothing behind it is a prediction, so drop it or go get the evidence.

## Gotcha

The most-missed regression is a `<button>` that became a styled `<div>` in a "refactor to the new design system" PR. The after state looks identical, so only the `-` side shows it.

## Sources

- Jakub Krehel, interfaces skills (MIT, github.com/jakubkrehel/skills, HEAD `592aedc`, read 2026-10-25): `skills/interface-review/SKILL.md`, `scope-resolution.md`, `removed-signals.md`. With the companion installed, route a diff review to `/interface-review` ([[interfaces-reconciliation]]).
- Related: [[review-checklist]], [[ui-reviewer]], [[skill-router]].
- Benji Taylor, Stageshow 1.1.1 (MIT, github.com/benjitaylor/skills, HEAD `299140f`, read 2026-11-07): `stageshow/references/review.md` (say what you could not check; a predicted failure or pass is not a finding).

title: cross-model-testing
summary: Test skill routing and execution against GPT, Claude Opus, Claude Sonnet. Sonnet and GPT behave quite differently.
tags: [meta, testing, evals, models]
---

# Cross-model testing

Perplexity's Agents team: *"Sonnet and GPT behave quite differently when it comes to Skills."* What loads on one model may not load on another. What works on Opus may fail on Haiku. Routing precision is model-dependent.

This is non-obvious. Most skill authors test on one model (the one they happen to use) and assume the routing is universal. It isn't.

## What to test cross-model

For each model family you support:

1. **Loading precision** — Does the agent load the skill when it should? Run 10 positive queries; the skill should load on all 10.
2. **Loading recall** — Does the agent *not* load the skill when it shouldn't? Run 10 adjacent-but-distinct queries; the skill should not load on any.
3. **Progressive read targeting** — When the skill is loaded, does the agent open the right atomic node? Test 5 queries each mapped to a specific node; verify the agent reads that node.
4. **End-to-end output quality** — For a given input (e.g., "review this CSS"), does the agent produce the right output format? Test with the [[review-format]] table requirement.

## Models to cover (as of 2026)

| Family | Models |
|---|---|
| Claude | Opus 4.x, Sonnet 4.x, Haiku 4.x |
| GPT | GPT-5, GPT-5-mini |
| Gemini | Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 2.5 Flash |

You don't need to cover every model. Cover the orchestration models your downstream users will most likely use. For this skill, the priority is Claude Sonnet + Opus (designed for) and GPT-5 (most common alternative).

## How to run cross-model evals

The `evals/` folder in this repo has three eval files:

- `loading.jsonl` — query + should_load (true/false)
- `progressive-reads.jsonl` — query + expected_node
- `end-to-end.md` — sample tasks + expected output structure

To run them:

```bash
# Pseudo — depends on your harness. Common patterns:
agent-eval skills/design-engineering/evals/loading.jsonl --model claude-sonnet-4
agent-eval skills/design-engineering/evals/loading.jsonl --model claude-opus-4
agent-eval skills/design-engineering/evals/loading.jsonl --model gpt-5
```

Compare results across models. Any divergence ≥5% on the same eval set is a routing problem that needs description-tuning.

## Common cross-model failure modes

1. **GPT loads on broader keywords** — GPT tends to route on noun matches ("CSS", "animation") more aggressively than Claude. If your description uses generic nouns, GPT may load on tangentially-related queries.
2. **Claude Sonnet skips on verbose descriptions** — Sonnet sometimes skips skills with descriptions over ~80 words. Tighten the description if Sonnet recall is low.
3. **Haiku doesn't load multi-node skills well** — Haiku can struggle with the MOC → leaf navigation. Often it stops at the SKILL.md and never opens references. If supporting Haiku, consider inlining critical nodes into SKILL.md.
4. **Opus over-reads** — Opus may open multiple atomic nodes "just in case." Token budget concern; not a routing bug.

## When to run

- Before changing the SKILL.md description (the routing-critical line).
- Before any change to atomic node summaries (which the agent uses to decide which to read).
- Before a new release / version bump.
- Quarterly, as model behavior drifts with model updates.

## Reference

Two routing rows worth running on every model, in the file's real shape (`loading.jsonl` uses `should_load`):

```json
{"query": "the toast just pops in, can you fix it", "should_load": true, "reason": "enter/exit motion, phrased as a complaint"}
{"query": "toast the bread for three minutes", "should_load": false, "reason": "noun match only: the broad-keyword failure"}
```

Take positives from real complaints in logs ("pops in", "feels cheap"), never the description's words. A row that repeats the description's nouns only proves the description matches itself.

Gold example: this repo's `skills/design-engineering/evals/loading.jsonl` and `progressive-reads.jsonl`.

Check: on each model, run one end-to-end task with the skill and without it and put the two outputs side by side, the way Benji compares skill against no-skill. If the with-skill output isn't visibly better on a model, routing passed there but the skill did not.

## Gotcha

Don't test on synthetic queries you wrote yourself. Source from real user queries (production logs, user feedback, hero queries). Synthetic queries have a flavor that biases the model toward the answer you expect — they tell you the description matches the queries you wrote, not whether it matches reality.

## Sources

- Perplexity Agents team — *"Designing, Refining, and Maintaining Agent Skills"*.
- Anthropic — eval harness patterns.
- Related: [[gotchas]], [[review-format]], the repo's `.github/CONTRIBUTING.md`.
- Benji Taylor, benji.org/stageshow (read 2026-11-07): skill against no-skill, side by side.

title: design-benchmarks
summary: How design output gets measured — DesignBench's generation / edit / repair tasks with compile, CLIP, and MLLM-judge metrics; Design Arena's anonymous pairwise votes aggregated by Bradley-Terry — and this skill's own eval suite that borrows both shapes.
tags: [meta, evals, benchmarks, testing]
---

# Design benchmarks and this skill's evals

Taste is trained, but it is also measurable, and two public benchmarks define the shapes worth borrowing. Neither measures *craft* directly — one measures whether generated UI matches and compiles, the other measures whether people prefer it — so this skill runs both shapes side by side with its own checklist-derived assertions. [[cross-model-testing]] covers routing evals; this node covers output quality.

## DesignBench (WebPAI, arXiv 2506.06251)

900 webpage samples across 11 topics, four stacks (vanilla HTML/CSS, React, Vue, Angular), three tasks that mirror real work: **generation** (UI image → code), **edit** (change an implementation from an instruction, with image, code, or both as context, across 9 edit types: add/change/delete × text, color, position, size, shape, component-level), and **repair** (fix a broken UI across issue categories such as occlusion, crowding, alignment, color and contrast, overflow). Metrics: compile success, visual similarity via CLIP, code-modification similarity, and MLLM-as-judge scoring; difficulty is graded by element count, interdependencies, and cascading scope. Headline findings: models adopt framework components poorly (about 19% Angular component adoption), detect UI issues badly (average accuracy around 0.27), and edit better from code than from images.

What to borrow: the **task triad**. A design skill that only helps generation is untested on the two-thirds of real work that is editing and repairing.

## Design Arena (by Intelligence)

A crowdsourced arena: a prompt is sent to several models, the first outputs are shown anonymously side by side, a human picks the better one, winners are matched again until a 1–4 ranking exists, and every pairwise choice is a vote. Ratings come from a Bradley-Terry fit (iterated to convergence, normalized, then `400 × log10(strength)`), models below a minimum vote count are dropped, and identities stay hidden to prevent brand bias. Separate leaderboards per category — websites, UI components, mobile apps, slides, games, 3D, SVGs, data visualizations, logos, video, text-to-speech — plus an overall frontend board.

What to borrow: **anonymous pairwise judgment.** "Which of these two is better?" is answerable by a person or a judge model where "is this good?" is not, and it is the only honest way to score an aesthetic change.

## This skill's suite

| Layer | File | Shape | Asserts |
|---|---|---|---|
| Routing | `evals/loading.jsonl`, `evals/progressive-reads.jsonl` | fixtures | The skill loads when it should; the right node opens |
| Contract | the repo's `eve/evals/review-format.eval.ts`, `motion-values.eval.ts`, `sound-values.eval.ts` | eve scored | Review tables, concrete values |
| Craft floor | `eve/evals/design-bench.eval.ts` + `skills/design-engineering/evals/design-bench.jsonl` | generation / edit / repair fixtures | Deterministic checks lifted from [[review-checklist]]: no `transition: all`, no `scale(0)`, reduced-motion present, inputs ≥ 16px, labelled icon buttons, no `z-index: 9999`, no hover-only actions, no sound before a gesture |
| Preference | `design-bench.jsonl` rows tagged `arena` | pairwise | Two candidates per prompt; a human or judge model picks; log the win rate per node change |

The craft floor is DesignBench's *repair* task pointed at our own tells: each fixture is a broken snippet and the row the checklist should catch. The preference layer is Design Arena's protocol at PR scale: when a node changes what the agent produces, generate before-and-after candidates for three fixtures, judge them blind, and record the result in the PR. A node that loses the pairwise more than it wins is reverted, however good it reads.

- Run one round as skill against no-skill on the same prompt, not only before against after. A node can beat its old self and still lose to no skill (Benji Taylor compares Stageshow output this way, benji.org/stageshow).

## When to apply

Before changing the SKILL.md description or any node that alters output (motion values, palette rules, sound defaults); when comparing models for a design task; when someone asks "is this skill actually helping?"

## Reference

One PR's preference record, in the shape to paste into the PR body:

```text
node: motion/stagger-choreography   fixtures: arena-hero-01, edit-dropdown-01, repair-spinner-01
judge: blind, A/B order shuffled per fixture
evidence per candidate: poster still, 390px still, contact sheet of the motion
result: B 2, A 1, tie 0  ->  keep
```

Judge stills and films, never code: the craft floor has already read the code.

Gold example: `stageshow/scripts/film-checks.mjs`, Benji's deterministic floor, with one named detector per fault (`nearTangent` flags edges 0.75–3px apart). Every gate line is at zero before a person judges; Benji's own caveat is that checks catch mistakes, not dull ideas, and passing is necessary, not sufficient, which is why the pairwise layer exists.

Check: every pairwise vote has frames from both candidates at the shown width and at 390. A vote on one wide screenshot misses what breaks at phone width.

## Gotcha

Compile rate and CLIP similarity reward *matching the reference*, including its flaws. A repair that fixes an overflow the reference also had can score lower than a faithful reproduction of the bug. Read the pairwise layer before trusting the similarity layer.

## Sources

- Xiao et al., *DesignBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for MLLM-based Front-end Code Generation* (arXiv 2506.06251), and the WebPAI/DesignBench repository and annotation guideline.
- Design Arena methodology notes (notes.designarena.ai/methodology) — Bradley-Terry aggregation, anonymity, vote thresholds.
