title: stress-scenarios
summary: Render one component under every scenario that can actually reach it — content length and shape, quantity, container width, state — each axis kept only when its cue matches, side by side on a throwaway harness page that is itself the report. Product states (data, account, feature) come from branches the code already has, fed at the data boundary. Viewing modes are named for the user to toggle, never simulated.
tags: [meta, testing, states, harness, robustness]
---

# Stress scenarios

A component looks finished with the mockup's copy, three rows and a 1280px container. Production sends it an empty string, a German label, 400 rows and a 320px sidebar. Render the hostile cases before users do, and keep only the ones the component can actually receive — stress what varies, nothing else. [[states-are-the-work]] says why states matter; this node is how to make them all visible at once.

## Axes and their cues

| Axis | Keep it when… | Scenarios |
|---|---|---|
| Content length | it renders text it doesn't author (user input, CMS, API, translations) | empty · one word · typical · several sentences · one unbreakable string (a long URL, `Donaudampfschiffahrtsgesellschaft`) |
| Content shape | text can come from users or locales the team doesn't write in | emoji alone and mixed · RTL · mixed direction · diacritics and tall scripts · figures that must align |
| Quantity | it repeats over items | zero · one · the realistic count · ten times that |
| Container | always | a 320px container · squeezed by a flex or grid sibling · very wide |
| State | it receives the state as a prop | loading · error · disabled |

Write the kept scenarios down first, one line each, and the dropped axes with a reason in one line, so a wrong inference is cheap to catch. A static icon button with a fixed label gets container and environment, never long text. Add any value the component's own data makes worse — the longest real option, copied into a fixture.

**Every hostile value is realistic or the real limit.** A hyphenated, accented two-part surname, a 60-character corporate email, a two-letter first name, a workspace of 1,284 — or the exact cap from the validation schema, the column type, or the form's `maxLength`. Random strings get dismissed as "never happens" and end the conversation. No limit anywhere is a finding ("unbounded"); so is a 50-character input saving to a 255-character column, because imports and the API will send the longer value. Spread the failures across the first rows the way real data does, rather than stacking them in row 1. Numbers, time, collections, states, content and media have their own breaks in [[worst-case-values]].

## Failure signatures

| What you see | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Avatar or icon squished into an oval | flex child shrinking | `flex-shrink: 0` on fixed-size boxes |
| Text pushes past its box; trailing ••• off-screen | `min-width: auto` on the text column | `min-width: 0` (grid: `minmax(0, 1fr)`); `flex-shrink: 0` on the action |
| Email or URL runs off the edge | no break opportunity | `overflow-wrap: anywhere` ([[line-behavior]]) |
| Badge wraps to two lines | badge allowed to shrink | `white-space: nowrap; flex-shrink: 0`, and decide what yields |
| Avatar adrift beside a three-line name | `align-items: center` on wrapping rows | top-align once text can wrap |
| Diacritics or tall scripts clipped | tight `line-height` + `overflow: hidden` | looser leading, no clip on text boxes |
| Orphaned `—` where an optional field was | placeholder for missing data | omit the line, or reserve its height on purpose |
| "1 members", `1284`, `NaN` | hardcoded plural, raw number | `Intl.PluralRules`, `Intl.NumberFormat`, guard null ([[strings-and-locale]]) |
| Broken-image icon, wrong initials | no `onError`, naive `split(' ')[0][0]` | fallback chain in [[avatar-systems]] |
| 1,000 rows stutter | every row rendered | virtualize or paginate ([[performance-discipline]]) |

## Product states come from the code

For a component you'll keep working on, render its product states one at a time behind a switcher instead of stacked:

| Kind | States |
|---|---|
| Data | loading · empty · error · one item · a typical set · long enough to scroll or paginate · some resolved, some pending · stale while refetching |
| Account | plan tier · role and permission checks · owner vs member |
| Feature | flags · trials · limits reached · locked |

A state the code cannot reach is not a state: never add a branch to render one; list a designed-but-missing state as missing. Feed fixtures at the **data boundary** — the hook, the fetch, the store — never by editing the component.

## The harness

A throwaway route, scenarios side by side, each in a fixed container (a box on the page, not a resized viewport), the breaks marked. The page is the deliverable: build, look once, report what visibly broke, and name the node that owns each fix ([[line-behavior]], [[growth-and-overflow]], [[logical-properties-rtl]], [[empty-loading-states]], [[wcag-thresholds]]). Afterwards, delete the route and toggle in one step and grep for them, but **keep the worst-case fixture** beside the demo data: it is the regression test for the next person who touches the component. The harness rules match [[prototype-picker]]'s: visibly outside the design system, never imported by product code.

**Viewing modes are the user's to toggle** — dark mode, browser zoom, reduced motion, keyboard focus. Name them in the report; re-declaring dark tokens under a class on the page observes a different component. Direction is content, not a viewing mode: wrapping a scenario in `dir="rtl"` is fair. The full run, toggle and report is [[cmd-break]].

## Reference

One row, one hostile fixture, three boxes. The bad harness proves nothing; the good one is the report.

- Bad: `<MemberRow name="Ana Silva" email="ana@acme.com" />` once, in a 1280px page, one screenshot.
- Good: the same row fed `name: "María-José Fernández-Castellanos"`, `email: "procurement.notifications@northwind-logistics.co.uk"`, `role: "Billing admin"`, `seats: 1284`, in fixed boxes of 320, 560 and 1100px side by side, each captioned with its break as one line and one cause: `spills its slot: email past the 320 box`, `tight inset: badge 4px from the row edge`.
- Borrow Benji's harness habit: shoot the page at the shipping width and again at 390 (`references/rehearse.md`), and when Stageshow's scripts sit beside the project, run `node scripts/layout.mjs <harness-url> --select .harness --width 390 --strict`, which checks plain UI outside a Stage. His Liveline chart was stress-tested the same way, with worst-case data.

Gold example: Jakub's `skills/break/scenarios.md` for the scenario list; `stageshow/references/rehearse.md` (Lines that are never intentional) for writing each break as one named line.

Check: every box carries a named break or the word "holds". A break cleared by deleting the hostile value from the fixture, or by clipping it with no decision about what yields, stays open, the way Stageshow's gate counts a line cleared by hiding the thing it points at as a bug.

## Gotcha

Isolation is the point here and the trap in [[prototype-picker]]: stress tests run in a bare harness because the question is whether the component defends itself; design variants run on the real page because the question is how it looks in context. Don't swap them.

# Upstream skills by lifecycle stage

Pick a skill by the stage the work is in first, and by its neighbour second. Emil Kowalski's skills (emilkowalski/skills) split one job into narrow passes, and this graph carries the same values behind its verbs. So every upstream skill has an owner here and a short list of next steps. When the user asks "what do I run after this?", find the row, name the next stage and stop ([[cmd-small]] `which`).

## The map

| Stage | Upstream skill | Owner in this graph | Next |
|---|---|---|---|
| Before building | `animation-vocabulary` | `name` · [[design-vocabulary]] | `animate` to build what you named; `choreograph` if several things move |
| Before building | `pick-ui-library` | `pick` · [[library-picks]] | `ask-sonner` once Sonner is chosen; `prototype` to try a few |
| Before building | `prototype` | `options` · [[prototype-picker]] | the generalist for each version's bar; `review-animations` on the winner |
| Building | `emil-design-eng` | the router's polish phase · [[ui-polish-pass]] | `animate` for one motion; `review-animations`; `apple-design` for springs |
| Building | `animate` | [[cmd-motion]] build sequence | `choreograph`; `animation-vocabulary` first if unnamed; `review-animations` |
| Building | `choreograph` | [[motion-choreography]] | `animate` per element; `remove-animations` to ask if the group must move |
| Building | `gestures` | [[gesture-phases]] | `apple-design` for momentum; `animation-performance` so the drag stays smooth |
| Building | `mobile-native` | `mobile` · [[cmd-mobile]] | `apple-design` for native gestures; `break-ui` for narrow screens |
| Building | `apple-design` | companion; digest in [[apple-design-principles]] | the generalist for the rest; `animation-performance` for drags |
| Refining | `animation-performance` | [[performance-discipline]] | `apple-design` for smooth gestures; `review-animations` before ship |
| Refining | `break-ui` | `break` · [[cmd-break]] | `mobile-native` for phones; `review-animations` for the motion half |
| Refining | `review-animations` | [[cmd-motion]] review, closed Block or Approve | `animate` to rebuild what it flags; `improve-animations` for the whole codebase |
| Whole app | `remove-animations` | `motion remove` · [[animation-removal-hazards]] | `improve-animations` for what stays; `find-animation-opportunities` |
| Whole app | `improve-animations` | `motion audit` (plans only) | `find-animation-opportunities`; `review-animations` on the plans |
| Whole app | `find-animation-opportunities` | `motion opportunities` · [[delight-impact-curve]] | `animate` to build a pick; `remove-animations` the other way |
| Other | `animate-expo` | companion; digest in [[react-native-motion]], [[expo-tool-ladder]] | `apple-design` for the reasoning |
| Other | `ask-sonner` | companion; [[sonner-usage]], [[sonner-api-surface]] | `pick-ui-library` for the rest of the stack |
| Other | `write-swift` | companion only; Swift language is not design | none here |

The whole-app row order is the point: remove, then improve what stays, then add the few missing moments. Retuning a motion you are about to delete wastes the pass, and an addition is only judged fairly once the noise is gone ([[stacking-chains]]).

## Precedence

1. **A slash command the user typed wins.** `/animate` or `/break-ui` with the repo installed: name the command and stop, as with any user-invoked companion ([[skill-router]] §4).
2. **A plain request stays in the graph.** The verbs carry the same values, with the contract and [[pov]] applied on top.
3. **A focused skill beats the generalist** inside its topic: `animate` over `emil-design-eng` for one dialog's motion.
4. `pick-ui-library`, `prototype` and `review-animations` are user-invoked only upstream; never start them unasked. Suggest them by name, or run the graph's own verb.

## Gotcha

Almost every row ends at a review. A lifecycle that stops at "built" skips the stage that catches `ease-in` and `scale(0)`. If a user asks what comes after building one motion, the answer is the review ([[review-format]], Block or Approve), not another build skill.

- Emil Kowalski, skills (MIT, github.com/emilkowalski/skills, HEAD `715c180`, read 2026-11-09): `README.md` and each `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` (invocation flags, scope).

summary: How the agent discovers, reads, follows, updates, and verifies a project's .design contract — and why it outranks this skill's defaults.

# Using a `.design` contract

A `.design` file (schema `design.v1`, spec mirrored at [`docs/spec/design-file-spec.md`](../../../../docs/spec/design-file-spec.md)) is a machine-readable visual contract: tokens, components, copy voice, executable policy, and a committed aesthetic intent. When a project has one, it is the source of truth and **this skill drops to advisory**.

## Where this skill sits

The format defines a precedence chain, and it is worth internalizing because it decides who wins every disagreement:

1. Explicit user prompt (this task only)
2. The nearest `.design`
3. The `design` skill procedure
4. **Generic taste skills — this one**
5. Model defaults

So: if `.design` sets `tokens.motion.duration.base: 400ms`, you use 400ms even though [[duration-table]] says most UI lands under 300ms. Raise the tension once, in prose, then comply. The skill supplies craft **where the contract is silent** — that gap is large, and it is where the whole motion and surface canon still applies.

## Detection

Walk up from the file you're editing. Match the extension case-insensitively: the usual form is a named `<name>.DESIGN` (e.g. `campusbinge.DESIGN`). Prefer a literal `.design`; otherwise exactly one `*.DESIGN` in that directory. Several candidates → ask which system. Resolve `extends` depth-first, child overriding parent. In a monorepo, a package's nearer contract beats the repo root.

If UI work is requested and no contract exists, **offer to bootstrap — don't invent an untracked system.** Scan adjacent signals first: design notes in `AGENTS.md`, an existing `DESIGN.md` (see [[using-design-md]]), global CSS, Tailwind config, `components.json`. Extract the whole visual vocabulary — density, elevation language, motion character, copy tone — not just hex values.

## Reading

Load `agent.instructions` first — it is required and self-contained, so the file works even where no skill is installed. Then `intent` → `constraints` → `policy` / `decisions` → `tokens` → `voice` → `components`. Pull `rationale.*` on demand for the task at hand.

`intent` is the field with no `DESIGN.md` equivalent, and it is the one that resolves taste arguments: `direction` (the committed aesthetic), `signature` (where boldness is allowed to concentrate), `treatment` (`utilitarian` vs `editorial` register). Calibrate per surface — `patterns.<name>.treatment` overrides `intent.treatment`. A dashboard gets restrained product craft; only editorial surfaces run the distinctive-identity register. Everything outside `signature` stays quiet, which is the same instinct as [[delight-impact-curve]] with a budget written down.

## Following

Bind every property a component lists — `backgroundColor`, `textColor`, `typography`, `rounded`, `padding`, `size`, `height`, `width`. Never write a raw hex, spacing, or radius when a token exists. Obey `when` / `when_not` and walk `decisions` first-match-wins. When a component isn't catalogued, `policy.if_missing` decides: `ask`, `nearest`, or `invent_with_note`.

Apply `voice.*` to UI copy with the same force as tokens — `register`, `casing`, the `terminology` map, `action_naming` continuity, and the `errors` style rule. This is [[copy-voice]] with the vocabulary pinned.

## Updating and verifying

Edit the YAML in place and bump `version`; git is the audit trail. Never add `proposed_changes` or an in-file changelog. Ask before touching any dot-path in `locked`.

A drift check compares `tokens` against the real CSS/Tailwind theme and `components` against real imports, then reports per token group as **added / removed / modified** with a **regression** flag — closer to [[review-format]]'s discipline than to a lint pass. Report before fixing; update the contract only when asked.

## shadcn

When `integrations.shadcn.enabled`, prefer installed shadcn primitives over parallel ones, and write `css_vars` into the declared CSS file. **Tokens outrank stale `css_vars` literals** — refresh the CSS after token edits rather than trusting what's already in `:root`. Emit the full variable set including charts and sidebar. See [`spec/design-file-spec.md`](../../../../docs/spec/design-file-spec.md) for the Tailwind v4 mechanics.

## Sound, video, and companions

Contract 1.3 adds `tokens.sound` (default toggle state, one material, levels, durations, sync tolerance), `assets.sounds`, `decisions.sound`, `targets[]` video entries, and `exports.frame_md`. When they exist they outrank [[sound-spec]] and [[sound-decision-framework]]; when the group is absent, the contract is saying *silent* and this graph must not add a sound. A `video` target flips the default — see [[launch-video-sound]] — and `exports.frame_md` is how a HyperFrames project inherits the brand's motion and material. The `design` skill also names the companions it routes to; [[skill-router]] is this graph's side of the same handshake.

## `.design` vs `DESIGN.md`

Both can exist. `.design` is the machine-readable contract with intent and executable policy; `DESIGN.md` is prose-plus-tokens ([[using-design-md]]). When both are present, `.design` wins and `DESIGN.md` becomes rationale — offer to converge them rather than maintaining two sources.

## Reference

Bind by role, never by a value that looks close. For a component the contract doesn't list, map roles the way Stageshow maps a product's look from its code (`references/looks.md`, From a codebase): primary to the one accent, button or input radius to the middle radius, menu item to the small one, popover or card to the large one, input height to the control size.

- Bad: `.plan-card { background: #5b5bd6; border-radius: 6px; padding: 14px; }`, because 6px "looked like" the button.
- Good: `.plan-card { background: var(--surface); border-radius: var(--radius-lg); padding: var(--space-4); }`, the accent kept for the single primary action `intent.signature` names, plus a one-line note when `policy.if_missing` is `invent_with_note`.
- Drift line, reported before any fix: `tokens.radius  modified  lg 10px -> 12px in app/globals.css  regression: yes`.

Gold example: [`registry/design-engineering.design`](../../../../registry/design-engineering.design), whose `agent.instructions` block holds the whole read, follow, update and verify loop in one place; `stageshow/references/looks.md` for the role mapping.

Check: put a still of the generated screen beside a screenshot of the product's existing screens at the same scale. Accent, gray temperature, radii and type should match at a glance; if one control looks foreign, re-read the contract and its real neighbor's computed styles rather than nudging by eye.

## Gotcha

Don't let the contract's existence stop the craft work. A `.design` that pins colors and radii says nothing about whether a spinner flashes under 800ms, whether the exit is 60% of the entrance, or whether a hover shifts 1px or 4px. Silence is not permission to default — it's where [[review-checklist]] still runs.

# Using design.md

When a user's project contains a `DESIGN.md` file (per [Google Labs Code's design.md spec](https://github.com/google-labs-code/design.md), mirrored at [`docs/spec/design-md-spec.md`](../../../../docs/spec/design-md-spec.md)), the agent has access to a machine-readable description of the design system. Use it.

> **Check for a `.design` contract first.** If the project has one, it outranks DESIGN.md and this skill both — see [[using-design-file]]. When both exist, `.design` is the contract and DESIGN.md becomes rationale.

## Detection

Before generating any UI, look for `DESIGN.md` in:

1. The repo root: `DESIGN.md`.
2. A `design/` subfolder: `design/DESIGN.md`.
3. A `.design/` hidden folder: `.design/DESIGN.md`.

If found, read it before writing any component, styling any element, or proposing any tokens.

## What to do with the frontmatter

The YAML frontmatter is **normative**. Treat the tokens as the source of truth:

- **`colors`** — when picking a color in generated UI, reference a token (`var(--color-primary)`, `{colors.primary}`, or `theme.colors.primary`) — *don't* hardcode a hex.
- **`typography`** — match `fontFamily`, `fontSize`, `fontWeight`, `lineHeight`, `letterSpacing` to a defined typography token. If the body uses `Public Sans 16/1.6`, don't generate `Inter 14/1.5`.
- **`rounded`** — use the scale (`sm`, `md`, `lg`, `full`). Mixing `borderRadius: 6` when the scale defines `4/8/16` is a tell.
- **`spacing`** — same. The scale is the contract.
- **`components`** — if a `button-primary` is defined, use it. Don't invent your own primary button.

## What to do with the markdown body

The body is **context**, not contract. Read it for:

- **Overview** — what the system is *trying to feel like*. Use this to disambiguate ambiguous token choices.
- **Do's and Don'ts** — explicit anti-patterns. Treat these as hard constraints.
- **Components section** — usage notes that token definitions can't capture (e.g., "primary buttons are reserved for the single most important action per screen").

## Reading order

For a typical UI generation task:

1. Read `DESIGN.md` (whole file — it's small).
2. Identify which tokens you'll need (colors, typography, spacing, the specific component variants).
3. Cross-reference with this skill — e.g., if `colors` defines a saturated accent, check [[delight-impact-curve]] before applying it everywhere.
4. Generate the UI using token references, not hardcoded values.

## When to propose updating DESIGN.md

The agent **does not** autonomously rewrite a user's DESIGN.md. It's authored by humans (designers + design engineers), not generated.

The agent *may* propose updates — always with human approval — in these cases:

- **Missing token** — generating a component requires a token that doesn't exist. Propose adding it with rationale.
- **Contrast failure** — the contrast linter (`contrast-ratio` rule) flags a token pair. Propose adjustment.
- **Component variant gap** — `button-primary-hover` exists but `button-primary-active` doesn't, and you need it.

Surface the proposal as a code review or PR comment, not a silent edit.

## Validating

Use the `@google/design.md` CLI to validate any change:

```bash
npx -y @google/design.md lint DESIGN.md
```

Run before committing. The linter catches broken refs, contrast failures, missing sections, and section-order violations.

For programmatic use in CI:

```ts
import { lint } from '@google/design.md/linter';
const { findings } = await lint(contents);
if (findings.some(f => f.severity === 'error')) process.exit(1);
```

## Cross-references

| design.md token category | This skill's relevant nodes |
|---|---|
| `colors` | [[color-monochromatic]], [[dark-mode]], [[contrast-and-color-scheme]] |
| `typography` | [[typography-humanity]], [[line-length-tracking]] |
| `rounded` | [[border-radius]] |
| `spacing` | [[viewport-custom-design]] |
| `components.button-*` | [[responsive-feedback]], [[hover-states-subtle]] |
| `components.modal`, sheet, tray | [[tray-rules]], [[fly-not-teleport]] |
| Overall feel / "Do's and Don'ts" | [[feeling-right]], [[unseen-details-compound]] |

## When to apply

Any task where the user has a project with a `DESIGN.md` file. Read it once at task start; reference tokens throughout.

## Reference

Frontmatter tokens bind; prose picks between them. Given `rounded: { sm: 4px, md: 8px, lg: 16px }` and a body style of Public Sans 16/1.6, a settings card comes out as:

- Bad: `font: 14px/1.5 Inter; border-radius: 6px; color: #6b7280;`, three values the file never defined.
- Good: `font-family: var(--font-body); font-size: var(--text-body-md); border-radius: var(--rounded-lg);`, the field inside at `{rounded.md}` and its menu items at `{rounded.sm}`, color from `{colors.primary}` only on the one primary action.
- A token the file lacks (`button-primary-active`) becomes a proposal comment, never a literal.

Gold example: `stageshow/examples/looks/radix.css`, a public design system's tokens set as one look file. It sets only what that system defines and leaves the rest to the kit's defaults, which is how this skill fills what DESIGN.md leaves out.

Check: grep the generated file for literals (`#[0-9a-fA-F]{3,8}`, `[0-9]+px`) and name the missing token behind every survivor. Then render once per color scheme the file defines; as Stageshow's craft rules put it, a light pass does not prove dark.

## Gotcha

DESIGN.md is currently `version: alpha` — the spec is evolving. If the user's file uses fields you don't recognize, pass them through unchanged rather than flagging as errors. The format will expand.

Also: not every project has a DESIGN.md, and not every team wants to author one. If asked "should we add a DESIGN.md?", weigh it against [[dependency-discipline]] — the file pays its way on multi-developer projects, less so on solo work.

title: vibe-to-generator
summary: When the user has a mood, not a spec, don't prompt for finished outputs. Research the visual language until it has names, compress it into rules, then build a seeded generator — pure render(config), click to regenerate, every taste decision a knob, save writes the winning config.

# From vibe to generator

Creative work has to produce something new, and prompting alone is bad at new: the model falls back on known patterns, the user rejects the result, asks for "a few more", and the loop burns time without converging. The escape has two halves. **Research** turns a vibe into rules the user can point at — most looks people reach for were shaped by a real process, and that process's constraints *are* the style. **A generator** then plays those rules: every variation one click, every taste decision a knob, the keeper reproducible forever.

## Route first

```text
Can the user point at or precisely describe the exact output?
├── Yes → build it; if too intricate to land by prompting → [[build-a-tool]]
└── No
    ├── Product UI with a few nameable directions? → [[prototype-picker]]
    ├── Can they state the idea as rules a stranger could follow? → skip research
    └── Only a vibe — mood words, an era, "I'm stuck"? → research. Never interrogate
        them into a spec first; the research exists because they can't answer yet.
```

**The two-round rule.** About to produce a *second* round of prompted variants of one visual idea? Stop and propose this pipeline. Two rejected rounds means the user is searching a space, not requesting an item.

## Research the visual language

1. Capture the vibe in the user's own words, verbatim. "Warm", "old-timey", "kind of hand-done" are data; rewriting them into your nearest cliché is how the result drifts.
2. Research the tradition behind it, answering three questions: **what process made this look** (printing method, material, tool, era — its quirks are the process's constraints), **what did the process do to color, texture, and composition**, and **what are the recurring patterns called** (a named pattern can be requested precisely and bound to a knob).
3. Spend tokens here without guilt; a cheap research pass produces generic rules and generic rules produce the mush the user came to escape.
4. Compress into **5–10 rules stated as constraints** ("no more than N colors", "X darkens where it crosses Y", "edges are never clean") plus named patterns. Show them and let the user strike or keep lines **before any code exists** — rules are cheap to edit, renders are not.

## Hard rules for the generator

1. **Output is a pure function of the config**, seed included. All randomness from a seeded PRNG (mulberry32) initialized from `config.seed`; never a bare `Math.random()` in the render path. The save button is a lie otherwise.
2. **A new variation is one click**, not one prompt. Clicking the canvas assigns a fresh seed and re-renders.
3. **Every taste decision is a knob** with tested min and max. Fixed values only for the rules that make the idea itself.
4. **Save writes the full config** as JSON — clipboard at minimum, a file in the project when there's a dev server, path shown after saving. Production imports that file.
5. **The tool is scaffolding; the config and render function are the deliverable.** Isolated route, nothing in production imports it; promote the JSON plus the render, or a static SVG/PNG export when the artifact needn't stay live.

## Sort, build, harvest

Sort every rule into **rules** (hardcoded, what makes it this idea), **modes** (discrete sub-directions, tabs with their own knobs), and **knobs** (every continuous value). An empty knob bucket means the idea is determined — build the output. Build in one sitting: one canvas rendered large (thumbnails hide the texture that makes or breaks generative work), mode tabs, knob panel, click-to-regenerate, the seed visible, save plus a rail of saved configs re-applied on click. Hand off in two lines and stop. Harvest by reading the saved JSON, never by eyeballing the panel; keep the lab route for the next asset.

## When to apply

"I'm stuck", "I need inspiration", "something like…", a mood instead of an image, endless variations of one idea, a rejected round of prompted variants. Pairs with [[svg-creation]] when the output is vector art and with [[visual-imperfection]] when the vibe is texture.

## Reference

The keeper is a config that names the seed and every knob:

```json
{ "seed": 48213, "mode": "halftone", "inks": 2, "dotPitch": 6, "misregister": 1.5, "grain": 0.22 }
```

- Bad: the user says "too dirty behind the headline", so the exported PNG gets patched by hand.
- Good: the note becomes a rule ("texture never sits under text"), the `grain` knob's max drops from 0.6 to 0.35, and every saved config re-renders from scratch. Benji runs his own skill this way: each correction becomes a permanent rule and the work is rerun, not hand-fixed.

Gold example: `stageshow/examples/backgrounds/`, one small interface over twenty grounds (tint, fields, light, linework, material, six gradients, six textures including halftone, grain and blueprint). Read it as the sheet a generator's modes should produce: each ground changes direction, value or material, not only hue, and its halftone grows toward one corner so the texture frames the UI instead of sitting under it.

Check: render twelve seeds at full size on one contact sheet. If they read as one picture, the rules are generic; if neighbors differ only in color, the knobs are moving the wrong thing.

## Gotcha

The generator's job is to play the rules, not to be tasteful on its own. If the rules were generic, every seed looks the same and the knobs move nothing worth moving; go back to research.

## Sources

# MOC — Motion

The largest cluster. Read [[animation-decision-framework]] first — it tells you whether to even animate. The rest of the nodes are tactical.

## Decision-first nodes (read before deciding)

- [[animation-decision-framework]] — Should this animate at all? Frequency-based decision tree.
- [[fly-not-teleport]] — When components persist between states, motion clarifies the spatial path. From Benji.

## Tactical nodes (read while implementing)

- [[easing-curves]] — Custom cubic-bezier > built-in CSS easings. Never `ease-in` for UI.
- [[duration-table]] — Specific durations by element type. UI < 300ms. Buttons 100–160ms.
- [[spring-animations]] — When springs beat curves. Apple's spring configuration. Interruptibility.
- [[frame-rate-independence]] — The same gesture ends in the same place at any frame rate: fixed 4 ms steps or closed forms, a capped catch-up, events at their timestamps, store what the user placed, no decisions from last frame's value.
- [[animated-hit-testing]] — A press on something still animating goes to where it's heading; drags grab what's drawn, pin the spring to the pointer, keep the released item on top until it settles; select list rows on release.
- [[transform-opacity-only]] — The only two properties that are cheap to animate. The hardware acceleration rule.
- [[performance-discipline]] — The rest of the discipline: named transition properties, `will-change` as a targeted fix, virtualization past ~50 rows, frames out of React state, reserved space, preload, off-screen pause, muted theme swaps.
- [[transform-mastery]] — translateY percentages, scale() scales children, 3D transforms, transform-origin fundamentals.
- [[clip-path-tricks]] — The most underrated animatable property. 5 patterns: tabs, hold-to-delete, image reveals, comparison sliders, directional swap.
- [[never-scale-from-zero]] — Why `scale(0)` looks like an inflating balloon. Use `scale(0.95)` + opacity, or `@starting-style` for modern CSS.
- [[gesture-momentum]] — Velocity-based dismissal. Damping at boundaries. Pointer capture.
- [[gesture-phases]] — Track 1:1 while the pointer is down, release into a velocity-seeded spring; dismiss on distance or velocity, linked values from the drag, catchable mid-close, the Vaul curve and the floating-drawer override.
- [[motion-choreography]] — Several parts on one event: cast lead, support, decoration, still; relate each pair (together, overlap, sequence, carry); hook secondary motion to a moment of the lead; test mid-flight.
- [[stagger-choreography]] — Cascading reveals (30–80ms delays). When to stagger and when not.
- [[responsive-feedback]] — Button press states, popover origin awareness, tooltip skip-delay. The micro-feedback nodes consolidated.

## Library-design nodes

- [[sonner-principles]] — Ten principles from Sonner: DX is the product, defaults > options, naming, invisible edge cases, transitions over keyframes, docs as deliverable, cohesion, opacity+height trial, sleep-on-it review, asymmetric timing.

## Workflow nodes

- [[debugging-animations]] — Slow-motion playback, frame-by-frame inspection, real-device testing. The three tools.
- [[css-conventions]] — `1turn` over `360deg`, unitless line-height, hex over rgb, native over libraries. Ben DC's CSS dialect choices.

## Benji's catalog (benji.org)

Distinctive techniques from Benji Taylor's body of work — Family, Honk, Liveline, Agentation, Drawesome, Stageshow. His faux-UI practice (Stageshow) is its own cluster, [[MOC-faux-ui]]; Honk's presence patterns are [[presence-signals]]; Drawesome's toolbar is [[drawing-toolbar]].

- [[lerp-breathing]] — Lerp at 8% per frame applied uniformly across multiple visual elements so the UI "breathes" as one organism instead of fragments updating independently; plus Liveline's loading, empty, paused and direction states and its stress tests.
- [[morphing-icons]] — 3-line SVG constraint system. Same-shape icons rotate; different-shape icons interpolate coordinates. Unused lines collapse to invisible center points.
- [[shared-letter-morph]] — Continue→Confirm text-state transitions where the shared letters ("Con") stay anchored as the rest morphs.
- [[text-morph-engine]] — Whole strings and numbers: words aligned first, characters only inside similar words, replaced runs recede as one, digits roll by place value, interruptions keep their speed. From Lochie Axon's torph.
- [[tray-rules]] — Six rules for tray / sheet / bottom-drawer UI: user-initiated, height variation, single focus, title + dismiss, context preservation, transient actions only.

- [[hover-default-imperative]] — From lucide-animated.com. Hover triggers the animation by default; expose a `ref` / `trigger()` API for touch contexts.

## Launch video

Launch films have their own cluster, [[MOC-launch-video]]: register, structure, type, UI demo, film motion, seams and cuts, review. UI timing in this MOC does not transfer to a film.

Catalog of canonical transitions for common UI archetypes. Implementation layer under the principle layer above.

- [[cross-blur-transitions]] — Pair opacity 0↔1 with `filter: blur(2px) ↔ 0` to mask imperfect crossfades.
- [[compose-subtract-asymmetry]] — Enter with 5 properties, exit with 3. Disappearance feels soft.
- [[distance-falloff-propagation]] — Per-element lift via `lift * pow(falloff, distance)` for grouped hover.
- [[multi-segment-shake]] — Form-error shake at 0%, 28.57%, 57.14%, 78.57%, 100% over 280ms.

- See [[ai-default-tells]] in [[MOC-anti-patterns]] for animation tells (crossfading icons, gradient flourishes).
- See [[animations-dev-curriculum]] for the external course pointer; don't duplicate course material here.

tags: [motion, interaction, hit-testing, drag, springs, touch, lists]

# Animated hit testing

An animated element has two positions: where it is **drawn** this frame, and where its spring is **heading**. Hit-test presses against the destination. A stack of toasts sliding up after one is dismissed is the test. With destinations, three presses 80 ms apart on the same spot near the top dismiss three toasts, the way rapid clicks on one spot close Safari's tabs one after another. Against drawn positions only the first lands: the second and third hit the gap a toast is still sliding up to fill.

```js
// a press: test the stable target, not the moving picture
const hit = items.findIndex(item => contains(item.destRect, pointer))
// the start of a drag: test what the user sees under the finger
const grabbed = items.findIndex(item => contains(item.drawnRect, pointer))
```

The pointer and the rectangles must share one coordinate space. Inside a scroll view, convert the pointer first: `pointerYLocal = pointerY + scrollTop`.

## Drag and release

- **Pin the spring during the drag.** Set both position and destination to the pointer each move (`x.pos = x.dest = dragX`), so the element sits under the finger with no springy lag. On release, the layout sets a new destination and the spring takes it there, carrying the release velocity ([[gesture-momentum]]).
- **Three depth bands.** The dragged item sits on top, the just-released item stays above the rest while it animates back, and everything else keeps its stable order underneath. Dropping the released item back into normal order on `pointerup` makes it slide *under* its neighbours on the way home. Clear the "last dragged" mark once its position and scale have settled ([[z-index-strategy]]).
- `user-select: none` on the draggable, so a drag never starts a text selection.
- **Drop targets never travel.** The slot shows in the cell under the pointer and jumps to the next cell, hidden over the card's own cell; a slot that chases the card gives every press a moving target. Keep the grab offset where the hand took hold, never re-centred.

## Select on release in a scroll list

In a list the user scrolls by touch, a press can't select a row: the press that starts a scroll ends in `pointercancel`, and a selection on press would fire on every scroll. Select the row under the **release**, and only when the press also started on the list. A release is never the start of a scroll. Read `scrollTop` at the top of the frame so the row under the release matches what is drawn.

## When to apply

Toasts, tab strips, reorderable lists, stacked cards, anything a user can press twice before its animation ends ([[sonner-principles]], [[responsive-feedback]]). A press that starts a drag still grabs the drawn position.

## Reference

A reorderable row, carried and released, in CSS:

- Bad: the row keeps `transition: transform 0.32s` while carried, so it trails the pointer and the next press hits where it was a frame ago.
- Good: carried, the lifted slot has `transition: none` and sits at `z-index: 2`; only the row inside eases `scale: 1.02` and the lift shadow over `0.25s`. Released, `transform 0.32s cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)` takes it home.
- Interrupted: a second choice 200ms into a 600ms highlight move continues from where the highlight is drawn, never from its start.

Gold example: `stageshow/examples/freeform-drag/` (`drag.css`, the carried vs lifted card) and `stageshow/examples/reorder/`; the interrupt pair in `stageshow/teaching/contrasts.tsx`.

Check: film the drop and step it at 40 to 80ms. On every frame from release to settle the released row is drawn above its neighbours, and a press fired 80ms after release lands on the row's destination, not on the gap it is leaving.

## Gotcha

Two destinations can overlap, for example while items swap places, and then a press can hit both. Pick one deliberately (the topmost destination, or the one whose drawn rectangle also contains the pointer), or the result depends on array order. A press 80 ms after a dismissal can also act on a different element than the one drawn under it. That is the point of the rule, but it surprises anyone testing with screenshots.

# Animation decision framework

The most-skipped step in design engineering is asking "should this animate at all?" The default answer is *no*. Read this before reaching for keyframes.

## The decision tree

1. **How often does the user encounter this?** See [[delight-impact-curve]].

   | Frequency | Decision |
   |---|---|
   | 100+ times a day (shortcuts, command palette, tab switches) | No animation |
   | Tens of times a day (hover, list navigation) | Near-imperceptible, or nothing |
   | Occasional (modals, drawers, toasts) | Standard animation |
   | Rare or first-time (onboarding, success) | The delight budget lives here |

   **Keyboard-triggered actions never animate** — a disqualifier, not a judgment call; Raycast's menu has no open/close motion. **Data the user is reading or acting on** (charts, tables, numbers) doesn't move for style; animate only a real change in value.
2. **What is the purpose?** Name one, or don't build it:
   - **Feedback** — confirm the action happened (press, hold-to-confirm fill).
   - **Spatial consistency** — show where something came from or went (see [[fly-not-teleport]]).
   - **State indication** — make a state change legible.
   - **Preventing a jarring change** — bridge content that would otherwise teleport.
   - **Explanation** — show how something works (marketing and onboarding only).
   - **Delight** — only at the rare tier.

   Invalid purposes:
   - **Decoration** — animation as garnish.
   - **Filling time** — animation to mask slow code (fix the code).
   - **"Because we can"** — Framer Motion is installed and we should use it.

3. **Which tool?** The cheapest that works: CSS transition (state you toggle) → `@starting-style` (entry on mount) → CSS animation (predetermined motion while the page is busy) → WAAPI (JS control, CSS performance) → Motion (springs, layout, exits, gestures). If the job is a whole component (toast, drawer, menu), use a library ([[dependency-discipline]]).
4. **What easing curve?** Custom cubic-bezier almost always beats the built-in CSS easings. See [[easing-curves]].
5. **How long?** UI is sub-300ms. Buttons are 100–160ms. See [[duration-table]].
6. **What property?** Only `transform` and `opacity` are cheap. See [[transform-opacity-only]].

## Quick checks before adding any animation

- Would the UI feel broken without it? If no, delete it.
- Does it survive [[prefers-reduced-motion]]? If not, fix it.
- Will it look right at 25% playback speed? If not, the timing is off.
- Would it still feel right on the 50th encounter? See [[delight-impact-curve]].
- Cover it. Hide each moving element in turn; if the screen reads clearer without one, cut that one.
- Feedback starts on the input and stays as quick as the real product; only explanation (marketing, onboarding) slows down.

## Application heuristics

- **Persistent elements:** if a component is present before and after a state change, animate the change — don't crossfade. See [[fly-not-teleport]].
- **Symmetric vs asymmetric timing:** enter and exit often want different durations. Exits can be faster. See [[duration-table]].
- **Stagger only when grouping helps comprehension.** Random stagger reads as noise.

## Reference

The tree run on three real elements of one screen, every column filled before any code:

| Element | Frequency | Purpose | Tool | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Command palette on Cmd+K | 100+ a day, keyboard | none | none | No motion: opens on the frame the key lands |
| Row hover in a list | tens a day | state | CSS transition | `background-color 120ms ease`, nothing moves |
| "Link copied" toast | occasional | feedback + spatial | CSS transition | Enters and exits; stays mounted until its fade ends |
| Account menu, opened all day | tens a day, pointer | spatial | CSS transition | One ~150ms scale from the trigger; items arrive together, no stagger |

Gold example: `stageshow/teaching/contrasts.tsx`, the press and exit pairs: each changes one thing with the same endpoints, which is how to argue a row.

Check: cover test on a filmed contact sheet. Mask each moving element in turn; any row whose verdict is "animate" must make the frame harder to read when hidden, or it moves to "No motion".

## Gotcha

The bug is almost never "this needs more animation." The bug is almost always "this animation is doing the wrong thing." Adding motion to fix bad UI compounds the problem. Fix the UI first.

# Animation removal hazards

When an interface feels slow or over-animated, the fix is subtraction: every animation must defend itself against [[animation-decision-framework]], and the ones that can't get deleted or reduced. But motion is load-bearing in ways that don't show in the diff. Pull it out carelessly and elements stay invisible, unmounts stall, and layout jumps reappear. Check every removal against the hazards below before you edit.

## Hazards

- **Hidden start states.** `initial={{ opacity: 0 }}`, a keyframe with `fill-mode: forwards` starting from `opacity: 0`, or a reveal class waiting on an `IntersectionObserver`. Delete the animation and keep the start state, and the element never appears. Remove both together.
- **Code that waits.** `onAnimationEnd`, `transitionend`, and `setTimeout` calls sized to a duration keep pausing the UI for motion that no longer exists. Delete the wait with the animation.
- **Exit-delayed unmounts.** `AnimatePresence` holds a component in the DOM until its exit finishes, then fires `onExitComplete`. With no exit, unmount is immediate, so move that callback's work to the moment the component closes.
- **Layout animations masking a jump.** A `layout` prop or FLIP animation may be hiding a layout shift. If removing it exposes the jump, keep it and report the shift as its own finding.
- **Focus moved after motion.** Focus set in an animation callback must move immediately once the animation is gone.
- **Tests.** Selectors or waits keyed to animation classes or durations need the same removal.
- **Reduced motion is the settled frame.** Turning motion off for `prefers-reduced-motion` shows the finished state with nothing transitioning, so no element is ever held mid-fade or at its start state.

## Reduce before delete

| Today | Reduced to |
|---|---|
| Hover with scale, lift or shadow growth | Color or opacity only, ≤150ms, `ease` |
| Slide or scale entrance on a frequent surface | Opacity only, 150ms, ease-out |
| UI animation over 300ms | 200–250ms on the same curve |
| Stagger over 80ms per item or 300ms in total | 30ms per item, or fade the group as one |
| Infinite pulse, shimmer or glow on a persistent element | Play once, keep the static end state |

If the reduced version no longer carries its purpose, delete it instead.

## Cleanup

Delete what the removals orphaned: unreferenced `@keyframes` and animation utilities, `motion.div` back to `div` where no motion props remain, empty `AnimatePresence` wrappers, unused variants and imports, zero-reference entries in the Tailwind config or token files. Grep every removed name afterwards. If the motion library is no longer imported anywhere, propose dropping the dependency; don't uninstall it yourself ([[dependency-discipline]]).

## When to apply

"The app feels slow", "too much animation", "tone down the motion", or `/design-engineering motion remove` ([[cmd-motion]]). Prime targets: keyboard-triggered menus, in-app route and tab transitions, fade-in-on-scroll on every section, hover lift on non-primary cards, charts that redraw from zero on every mount, numbers that count up on load, spinners and shimmer on loads under 300ms ([[empty-loading-states]]). The mirror pass is `motion opportunities`, which looks for places that should move. A survivor that is badly built (ease-in, wrong origin) goes to `motion audit`; never retune it here.

## Reference

A removal report for one settings screen, the shape every restraint pass hands back:

| Animation | Action | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Sections fading in on scroll (`.reveal` + `IntersectionObserver`) | Removed, with the `opacity: 0` start class and the observer | Decoration |
| Card hover `translateY(-2px) scale(1.02)` over 300ms | Reduced to `background-color 150ms ease` | Frequent surface |
| "Saved" toast exit | Kept | Without it the toast vanishes on the first frame |
| Height of an added row | Kept | The line below would jump instead of being carried |
| Arrow-key selection highlight, `translateY` 300ms ease-in-out | Removed, moves on keydown | Keyboard-triggered; at a 120ms key repeat it trails several rows behind |

Gold example: `stageshow/teaching/contrasts.tsx`, the exit pair (removed on the first frame vs fades out before it is removed) and the space pair (a new row carries the next line with it): the two motions this table keeps.

Check: film the screen before and after the pass and step both at 40 to 80ms. After: no element at rest is invisible, no single frame where a toast disappears, no line that jumps; and a grep for every removed class and keyframe name returns nothing.

## Gotcha

Deleting everything is also wrong. A toast that would otherwise teleport in, or a panel that shows where it came from, earns its motion; removing it trades slowness for disorientation. Every removal report lists the animations deliberately kept and the purpose that saved each one — that list is what separates a restraint pass from deleting every `transition` in the repo.

## What the course covers

If the user wants depth on motion, send them there.

- The user wants to learn motion deeply, not just apply rules.

# Debugging animations

An animation that "looks off" is hard to diagnose at 60fps. Three techniques expose what's actually happening.

## 1. Slow-motion playback

The single most useful debugging tool. Slow the animation to 25% or 10% speed and watch each frame:

### In code (one-line)

```css
/* Temporarily multiply all durations */
* { transition-duration: 2000ms !important; animation-duration: 2000ms !important; }
```

Or in Framer Motion / Motion:

```tsx
<MotionConfig transition={{ duration: 2 }}>
  <App />
</MotionConfig>
```

### In Chrome DevTools

DevTools → ⋮ menu → More tools → Animations panel. There's a playback speed slider (10%, 25%, 50%, 100%). Doesn't require code changes.

When animations look "twitchy" or "off," 9 times out of 10 the bug is visible at 25% speed and invisible at 100%. Examples:
- A `scale` and `opacity` transition that don't share a curve, so they desync visibly when slow.
- An element flashing to its end state for one frame before the animation starts.
- A jitter caused by `transform-origin` mismatch.

## 2. Frame-by-frame inspection

Chrome DevTools → Performance → Record → Run the animation → Stop. The flame chart shows every frame. Look for:

- **Long frames (>16ms)** — the animation drops below 60fps. Causes are usually layout, paint, or non-GPU properties.
- **Layout/paint events during the animation** — means you're animating a property that's not `transform` or `opacity` ([[transform-opacity-only]]).
- **Style recalculation cost** — large when CSS custom properties on the root are being updated mid-animation. See gotcha below.
- **A one-frame flash or hop** — a contact sheet sampled every 50ms steps over it. Sample every frame for hand-offs, morphs and the loop seam; keep the sheet for layout.

The Animations panel also lets you scrub the animation timeline like a video editor, with keyframes marked.

## 3. Test on real devices

What looks smooth on a MacBook Pro can be unusable on a 3-year-old Android. Real devices reveal:

- GPU memory pressure (animations skip frames or stutter).
- `will-change` over-application (browser pre-allocates layers, exhausts memory).
- Network-heavy pages where main-thread JS blocks the animation start.

Workflow:
- iPhone: connect via USB → Safari → Develop menu → [device name] → page. Full DevTools attached.
- Android: connect via USB → `chrome://inspect` → Inspect. Full Chrome DevTools attached.
- Use the device's real power profile, not "throttled to 4x slowdown" simulation — they behave differently.

A common shock: an animation that's flawless in desktop dev becomes choppy on a real mid-tier phone. The fix is usually reducing `filter: blur()` radius, removing `box-shadow` animations, or simplifying gradients.

## 4. Record before and after, then diff

A fix to one animation quietly changes three others. Record the same interaction before the change and again after it, then compare the two: duration, easing, end values and which elements moved. Line the recordings up by named moments (the click, the peak, the settle), never by milliseconds, since the two runs never start on the same frame. "One settles and the other never does" is a finding, not noise. Watch both at 25% first.

## When to apply

- Any animation that "feels off" but you can't articulate why.
- Before shipping a new component to production.
- When a user reports "the modal is choppy" but it looks fine locally.
- Reviewing animation PRs — slow them to 25% in your browser before approving.

## Reference

```js
// Live pacing probe: paste in the console, trigger the motion, read the table.
const el = document.querySelector('.panel'), rows = [], t0 = performance.now();
(function tick(now) {
  rows.push({ ms: Math.round(now - t0), transform: getComputedStyle(el).transform });
  if (now - t0 < 1000) requestAnimationFrame(tick); else console.table(rows);
})(t0);
```

- Gold example: Stageshow films one beat frame by frame (`scripts/film.mjs <url> --at drop --every 50 --count 24`, from `stageshow/references/rehearse.md`), and `stageshow/scripts/motion-watch.mjs` names what it finds between frames, such as `appears, then moves`: an entrance already fully visible with over 40% of its travel left.
- Check: in the table, two or more identical `transform` rows followed by a jump is a clock or scheduling bug, not an easing problem; a row that repeats after the motion should have ended means something is still moving that no one asked for.

## Gotcha

`transition-duration: !important` on `*` will affect things you didn't expect (focus rings, scrollbar animations on Safari). Apply it scoped to the component you're debugging, then remove. Don't ship the `!important` hack.

Also: the Performance recording is heavy and changes the page's own behavior slightly (it's adding instrumentation). If you can't reproduce a bug with recording on, try recording for a shorter window (just before/during/after the animation).

## Sources

- Chrome DevTools — Animation inspector docs.

title: distance-falloff-propagation
summary: Per-element lift via `lift * pow(falloff, distance)` for grouped hover. Avatar groups, list rows.

# Distance-falloff hover propagation

When you hover one element in a group (avatar stack, row of icons, list of cards), neighboring elements can subtly react. Done well, this signals "this group is connected" without being theatrical. Done poorly, it's distracting.

Jakub Antalik's transitions.dev catalog uses a clean formula:

```
shift = lift * pow(falloff, distance)
scale = 1 + (max_scale - 1) * pow(falloff, distance)
```

Where:
- `lift` = maximum displacement of the hovered element (e.g. -8px on hover).
- `falloff` = how quickly the effect decays per neighbor (e.g. 0.45).
- `distance` = number of elements between the hovered and the current one.

## Concrete example — avatar stack

```ts
const lift = -8;       // px
const maxScale = 1.08;
const falloff = 0.45;

avatars.forEach((avatar, i) => {
  const distance = Math.abs(i - hoveredIndex);
  const shift = lift * Math.pow(falloff, distance);
  const scale = 1 + (maxScale - 1) * Math.pow(falloff, distance);

  avatar.style.transform = `translateY(${shift}px) scale(${scale})`;
});
```

Result:
- Hovered avatar: full lift (-8px) and full scale (1.08).
- Neighbor at distance 1: -3.6px, scale 1.036.
- Neighbor at distance 2: -1.6px, scale 1.016.
- Neighbor at distance 3: -0.7px, scale 1.007.

By distance 4, the effect is below 1px and visually invisible — which is correct. The propagation should fade to nothing within 3–4 neighbors.

## The two-phase curve trick

Jakub uses a different easing on **lift** vs **return**:

```css
.avatar {
  transition: transform 200ms var(--ease-out-quart);
}
.avatar.returning {
  transition: transform 350ms cubic-bezier(0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1); /* bouncy */
}
```

- **Lift uses ease-out-quart** — feels responsive, settles cleanly.
- **Return uses a spring-shaped bezier** — feels alive, has a tiny bounce on settle.

The asymmetry is what gives the interaction its character. Same curve in both directions feels mechanical.

## When to apply

- Avatar groups (user mentions, collaborator pills).
- Toolbar rows where each item has personality (emoji reactions).
- Image carousels with thumbnail rows.
- List rows where the next/prev rows should subtly respond.

## When NOT to apply

- High-density data tables. Propagation makes the whole row feel like it's moving when the user scans.
- Touch-only UIs. There's no hover; the technique doesn't fire.
- Lists of more than ~20 elements at once. The reflow cost rises.

## Performance

This pattern modifies `transform` on N elements every mouseover. Use:
- `transform` only (GPU-accelerated, see [[transform-opacity-only]]).
- `requestAnimationFrame` to batch updates.
- Don't `setState` per element in React — use refs and direct `style.transform` assignment, or use a single CSS variable trick:

```css
.group { --hover-index: -1; }
.item {
  --my-distance: abs(var(--my-index) - var(--hover-index));
  transform: translateY(calc(-8px * pow(0.45, var(--my-distance))));
}
```

(CSS `pow()` requires modern browsers. Fall back to JS for legacy support.)

## Reference

- Bad: a five-face stack where every face takes the same `translateY(-8px)` on group hover; the row lifts as one slab and nothing says which face the pointer is on.
- Good: the hovered face at -8px and 1.08, neighbours at -3.6px, -1.6px, -0.7px, and each face's overlap cutout moving with the face it makes room for:

```ts
// Face i's cutout tracks face i + 1 (in face i's own space), so a lifted neighbour never shows a crescent of page.
const mask = `radial-gradient(circle at ${size - overlap + r}px calc(50% + ${shift[i + 1] - shift[i]}px),
  transparent ${r + gap}px, #000 ${r + gap + 0.5}px)`;
```

- Gold example: transitions.dev prototype P8 for the motion; for the stack itself, Stageshow's `stageshow/kit/parts/Facepile.tsx`, which cuts each face out where the next overlaps (22px faces, 6px overlap, 2px gap) with a mask rather than a ring, so no translucent edge sits over a neighbour.
- Check: hover the middle face of five at 25% speed and zoom the overlaps to 4x: no page colour shows between faces at the peak, and the end faces, two away, move about 1.6px.

## Gotcha

The falloff coefficient matters more than the lift. A falloff of 0.8 propagates far and feels like the whole group is moving. A falloff of 0.2 dies too fast and looks like only the hovered item is reacting. **0.4–0.5 is the sweet spot.**

## Sources

- Jakub Antalik — transitions.dev, prototype P8 (avatar group).

# Animation durations

There is no universal "feels right" duration. The right duration depends on what's moving and how often.

## Reference table

| Element | Duration | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Button press feedback | 100–160ms | Anything slower feels laggy |
| Hover state change | 120–200ms | Faster on inputs, slower on cards |
| Tooltip appearance | 125–200ms; 0ms for siblings | First tooltip: 400–700ms delay, then ~125ms. While one is open, neighbours skip delay and animation |
| Popover / dropdown | 150–250ms | Should feel instant, not theatrical |
| Modal | 200–300ms | Slightly slower because it's a hierarchy shift |
| Tab content swap | 200–250ms | Crossfade or directional slide |
| Page transition | 250–400ms | The longest "ok" UI duration |
| Skeleton → content | 150ms | Resolve fast; the skeleton already paid the wait |
| Confetti / celebration | 600–1200ms | Rare moment, can be theatrical |
| Onboarding hero motion | 400–800ms | First-run gets a longer budget |

## Asymmetric enter/exit

The exit is usually 60–80% of the enter: the user has already moved on. A panel that takes 250ms to slide in should take ~180ms to slide out. Use transitions, not keyframes, so an open interrupted by a close reverses from where it is.

```css
.panel { transition: transform 180ms var(--ease-out-quart); }            /* exit */
.panel[data-state="open"] { transition-duration: 250ms; }                /* enter */
```

A worked pair, a static dialog given motion by default:

- Before: scale 0→1, `ease-in`, 400ms in and 400ms out. It swells from a point and starts slowest on the frame the user is looking at.
- After: scale 0.95→1 with opacity, the strong ease-out token, 300ms to open and 150ms to close. When the user chose to dismiss it, an exit at about half the enter is fine; 60–80% stays the default for panels.

A second asymmetry applies where the user is deciding: the deliberate phase is slow and the system's answer snaps (hold-to-confirm: 2s linear on press, 200ms ease-out on release; see [[clip-path-tricks]]).

Sonner itself is the counter-example: its toasts run a symmetric ~400ms `ease`, slower than the UI budget on purpose to match the component's calm personality ([[sonner-principles]]). Treat that as a deliberate exception, not a default.

## How to choose

- **Smaller element, shorter duration.** A 12px icon doesn't need 300ms.
- **More frequent, shorter duration.** See [[delight-impact-curve]].
- **More important, slightly longer.** A modal earns more time than a tooltip.
- **If unsure, halve it.** Most "feels slow" animations are too long. Most "feels jumpy" animations are too short.
- **Feedback starts on the input.** A delay before a press responds reads as lag at any duration; only storytelling motion (a demo, a film) earns slower timing.

## Reference

One product's whole set, read from a real kit, so every part stays in proportion:

| Part | In | Out |
|---|---|---|
| Button press | `transform` 180ms `cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1)` to `scale(0.97)` | same |
| Menu row under the pointer | 0ms | `background-color` 150ms `ease` |
| Tooltip | 150ms fade with a 2px rise | 100ms |
| Toggle knob, Segmented thumb, Tabs indicator | 250ms, 300ms, 350ms `cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)` | same |

- Gold example: `stageshow/kit/controls/Button.css`, `stageshow/kit/parts/Menu.css`, `stageshow/kit/parts/Tooltip.css`, `stageshow/kit/controls/Toggle.css`, `Segmented.css` and `Tabs.css`. Benji's call differs on one: Stageshow's Popover fades in over 0.18s and out over 0.24s, because in a filmed demo a very short fade falls between frames (`stageshow/kit/motion/Popover.css`); keep this node's shorter exits for product UI.
- Check: record the press at 60fps; the first frame after `pointerdown` already differs from the last frame before it, and the whole response lands in about 11 frames.

## Gotcha

`prefers-reduced-motion` does not mean "make everything 0ms." It means "no large translations or scale changes." A 120ms opacity fade is fine. See [[prefers-reduced-motion]].

# Easing curves

The default CSS easings (`ease`, `ease-in`, `ease-out`, `ease-in-out`) are blunt instruments. They were good defaults in 2010. They are a tell now.

## The rules

- **Never `ease-in` on UI, exits included.** Its slow start delays the exact frame the user is watching; the same 200ms feels slower with `ease-in` than with `ease-out`. An exit that should feel quiet gets fewer properties and less time ([[compose-subtract-asymmetry]]), not an ease-in.
- **Decision order:** entering or exiting → ease-out; moving or morphing on screen → ease-in-out; hover and color change → `ease`; constant motion (marquee, progress, a hold-to-confirm fill) → `linear`; unsure → ease-out.
- **Custom `cubic-bezier()` beats the built-ins** for anything deliberate. A small variation on the curve communicates personality without anyone noticing why.
- **Name each curve by its job and write its duration range beside it** in the token file, so nobody reaches for the travel curve on a press.

## House tokens

```css
/* out-quart — sharp start, smooth tail. Default for hover and menus. */
--ease-out-quart: cubic-bezier(0.25, 1, 0.5, 1);

/* out-expo — steeper start, long tail. For taps, presses. */
--ease-out-expo: cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1);

/* In-out — symmetric, for elements that travel between states. */
--ease-in-out: cubic-bezier(0.65, 0, 0.35, 1);

/* Back-out overshoot (y > 1). Playful moments only, never a dialog. */
--ease-spring: cubic-bezier(0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1);
```

## The strong set

Stronger than the house tokens, for motion that should feel decisive:

```css
--ease-out-strong: cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1);    /* quint-strength enter/exit */
--ease-in-out-strong: cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1); /* on-screen travel, clip reveals */
--ease-drawer: cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1);        /* iOS-like sheet and drawer */
--ease-drawer-float: cubic-bezier(0.165, 0.84, 0.44, 1); /* small floating drawer, 200ms */
```

Use the first for dropdowns, popovers, toasts and modals; the second for a tab indicator or anything moving A→B across the screen; the third for drawers and sheets that slide from an edge, the fourth for a small floating drawer and its overlay ([[gesture-phases]]). Need another curve? Take it from easing.dev or easings.co rather than hand-rolling one.

## How to choose

- **Will the element overshoot?** Use `--ease-spring` (has values > 1 in the curve).
- **Is it primarily an entrance?** Use `--ease-out-quart`, `--ease-out-expo` or `--ease-out-strong`.
- **Is it a two-way transition (open/close, expand/collapse)?** Use `--ease-in-out`.
- **Is it a spring physics scenario (drag, dismiss, gesture)?** Don't use curves — use [[spring-animations]] instead.

## When to apply

Every CSS transition you write should pick a curve deliberately. The browser's default `ease` is rarely the right choice. Add `--ease-*` variables to your token set and reference them everywhere.

## Reference

- Bad: `transition: all 300ms ease-out` on the press, the tab indicator and a 600px card trip alike; the hierarchy goes flat.
- Good: a curve per job, each with its own duration:

```css
.button { transition: transform 180ms cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1); }      /* press */
.tabs__indicator { transition: transform 350ms cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1); } /* A to B */
.demo-card { transition: transform 1s cubic-bezier(0.45, 0, 0.1, 1); }        /* story travel */
```

- Gold example: `stageshow/kit/ease.ts`, which names each curve by its job (house, through, settle, enter, trip, camera) with a comment on its use and, for house and settle, its duration range, and exports `startSlope()` to compare how fast each leaves rest. Benji's call differs on exits: Stageshow's Popover shrinks out on `cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 1, 1)`, an ease-in, under an `ease` fade (`stageshow/kit/motion/Popover.css`); this node's no-ease-in rule stands for product UI.
- Apple's call differs too: it mirrors the curve on a reversible path, inverting the control points so the return retraces the trip out. Inverting an ease-out gives an ease-in, so this graph keeps ease-out both ways and lets a transition retarget mid-flight ([[compose-subtract-asymmetry]]). Keep the mirror for a long reversible move between two resting places, never an exit.
- Check: for every token compute `y1 / x1`; a curve under 1 leaves rest slower than linear and must not sit on a press or an entrance.

## Gotcha

A pretty cubic-bezier on the wrong duration looks worse than `ease-out` on the right duration. Curve and duration are coupled. Tune them together, never separately. See [[duration-table]].

summary: Screen-to-screen motion in Expo Router comes from native stack options, never a JS rebuild. Push for depth, modal for an abandonable task, formSheet with detents for a short interruption, no motion between tabs, fade under reduced motion, and animationMatchesGesture with any custom animation.
tags: [motion, react-native, expo, navigation, sheets]
---

# Expo navigation motion

Screen transitions in an Expo app are configured on the native stack, not built. The OS animates it off the JS thread, the interactive back swipe comes with it, and it looks like the rest of the system. Navigation is the one place to match the platform's own timing (an iOS push runs about 350ms); every other UI motion stays under 300ms and beats it ([[duration-table]]). The thread and spring rules are in [[react-native-motion]].

## Pick the option

| The user is | Option |
|---|---|
| Going deeper into a hierarchy | `animation: 'default'`, the platform push, untouched |
| Starting a self-contained task they may abandon | `presentation: 'modal'` |
| Briefly interrupted (picker, filter, share) | `presentation: 'formSheet'` with `sheetAllowedDetents` |
| Switching tabs | `animation: 'none'` |
| Asking for reduced motion | `animation: 'fade'` on the stack's `screenOptions` ([[prefers-reduced-motion]]) |

## The back swipe must match

Whenever a screen gets a custom `animation` (say `slide_from_right`), also set `animationMatchesGesture: true`. The iOS back swipe then plays your transition in reverse under the finger. Without it, pushing forward and dragging back look like two different apps.

```jsx
<Stack screenOptions={{ animation: reduced ? 'fade' : 'default' }}>
  <Stack.Screen name="settings" options={{ animation: 'slide_from_right', animationMatchesGesture: true }} />
  <Stack.Screen name="filter" options={{ presentation: 'formSheet', sheetAllowedDetents: 'fitToContents' }} />
</Stack>
```

## formSheet is native on both, not the same on both

- **Three detents on Android.** A longer `sheetAllowedDetents` list works on iOS and is cut short on Android without a warning. Design for three.
- **The grabber is iOS-only.** `sheetGrabberVisible` draws nothing on Android.
- **No native header or nested stack inside an Android sheet.** Keep the sheet to one screen; if it needs its own navigation, it is a `modal`.
- **`fitToContents` needs sized content.** A root that only says `flex: 1` gives the sheet nothing to measure, so the detent comes out wrong; set a real size on the content.

A formSheet's drag and settle come from the platform for free; hand-build a sheet only when it isn't a screen, using the spring rows in [[react-native-motion]] and [[gesture-phases]].

## Gotcha

A grabber as the sheet's only "you can drag this" cue looks right on an iPhone and is simply absent on Android, so the swipe-down goes undiscovered there. Give the sheet a visible close or done control as well, and check both platforms on hardware, not one simulator.

## Sources

# Expo tool ladder

In an Expo app, pick the cheapest tool that does the job and stop there. Each step down costs more code, more runtime work or a heavier dependency. A worklet behind an on/off switch is overbuilt in the same way a motion package added for a single fade is. [[react-native-motion]] covers how each tool must be used once picked.

## The ladder

| Need | Tool |
|---|---|
| A state change with no gesture (press, toggle, colour) | Reanimated CSS transition |
| A loop, several stages, or a play-on-mount | Reanimated CSS animation (keyframes) |
| Mount, unmount or a list reflowing | Layout animations (`entering`, `exiting`, `itemLayoutAnimation`) |
| A finger drives it, or scroll does | Shared value + `Gesture` + `useAnimatedStyle` |
| Screen to screen | Native stack options ([[expo-navigation-motion]]) |
| A sheet that is its own screen | `presentation: 'formSheet'` |
| Tab bar | `NativeTabs` |
| Context menu, press-and-hold peek (iOS) | `Link.Menu` / `Link.Preview` |
| Header collapsing into a large title (iOS) | `headerLargeTitleEnabled` |
| Pull to refresh | `RefreshControl`, unless the pull is a signature interaction |
| UI that follows the keyboard | `react-native-keyboard-controller` |
| Illustration, celebration, empty state | Lottie, never for UI state |
| A huge scene or freeform drawing | Skia, only when the view tree itself is the bottleneck |

Climb to a shared value only for a number that changes continuously or has to be caught mid-flight: a drag qualifies, a press scale does not.

## Small rules

- **Press.** Set `pressRetentionOffset` so a press survives the small finger movement that happens while holding it. Use the same scale on both platforms; an Android ripple belongs only in a Material-styled app.
- **Builders live outside JSX.** Declare layout-animation builders at module scope; wrap per-index delays in `useMemo`. An inline chain is rebuilt on every render.
- **An RN toast** enters with `FadeInDown` over 300ms and leaves with `FadeOutDown` over 250ms, by the same edge, at `insets.bottom + 16`. A bare `bottom: 16` sits under the home indicator. On the web, use Sonner ([[sonner-usage]]).
- **Tab pill.** Trigger the selection haptic at the moment of the tap; tied to the pill's arrival it feels late ([[haptic-feedback]]).

## Setup that silently kills motion

- Install with `npx expo install`, which resolves the versions that match the SDK; plain `npm install` does not.
- Expo's Babel preset adds the worklets plugin for you. A bare RN project adds it by hand, last in the list; a missing or misplaced plugin throws `Failed to create a worklet`.
- `GestureHandlerRootView` wraps the root `_layout` once. Without it gestures do nothing and nothing errors.
- Keyboard-controller hooks need `KeyboardProvider` at the root, or the height stays at 0.
- Reanimated 4 needs the New Architecture.

## Gotcha

The commonest overbuild is a large-title header rebuilt as a scroll worklet with an animated height. The native stack already does it with `headerLargeTitleEnabled`, on the platform side and without a dropped frame. The counter-case: the option is iOS-only, so a collapsing header on Android (or any custom one) is a translate inside a fixed, clipped container, as [[react-native-motion]] describes, never a height animation.

- Related: [[animation-decision-framework]], [[dependency-discipline]], [[performance-discipline]].

Crossfading reads as two separate elements. The right answer is to *move* the element from its A position to its B position, so the user can see it's the same thing. ## The principle > If a component occupies a space and will persist in the next phase, it should remain consistent. Three corollaries: 1. **Persistent elements travel, they don't restart.** No re-animation of an element that was already on screen. 2. **Identity is communicated by motion.** A label that morphs from "Continue" to "Confirm" (sharing the letters "Con") tells the user it's still the same button. A button that crossfades is two buttons. 3. **Direction carries meaning.** A modal opening from the bottom should close to the bottom. title: frame-rate-independence
summary: Animation state should depend on time and events, never on which frames happened to run. Step springs on a fixed clock or sample a closed form, cap the catch-up after a stall, apply events at their timestamps, store what the user placed and derive what fits, and never let last frame's value make a decision.
tags: [motion, springs, performance, state, animation-engineering, measured]
---

# Frame-rate independence

The same gesture should end in the same place at 30, 60 and 120 fps, and after the tab stalls. It usually doesn't. Code written as "per frame" (`velocity *= 0.99`, a spring stepped once per `requestAnimationFrame`, a value stored every frame) ties state to the frame rate. `0.99` per frame decays to 0.55 over a second at 60 fps and to 0.74 at 30. Cheng Lou measured the worst case in handwired: with the usual render order, the same input differed by up to 359 px between 10 fps and 120 fps at shared timestamps.

## The rules

1. **Step on a fixed clock, or don't step.** Run springs in fixed 4 ms steps (4 per frame at 60 fps, 2 at 120). An 8 ms step can miss a 120 Hz frame entirely. Or sample a **closed form**: an exponential decay `x0 · e^(−kt)`, or an analytic spring, gives the exact value at any timestamp with no loop and no drift. Closed forms stop working once moving elements push on each other; then you are stepping again.
2. **Cap the catch-up.** After a stall, `steps = floor(elapsed / 4 ms)` can reach thousands, and running them all makes the next frame late too: a spiral. Cap it at about 300 steps (1.2 s of simulation). Then pick a named fallback: *carry* the rest into later frames, or *snap* every object onto its destination. Either is fine, as long as you chose it.
3. **Apply events at their timestamps.** Step springs up to the event's time, then apply the event. The new target starts pulling within one step of the press at any frame rate, instead of from the previous frame's time. Recorded input then replays to the identical screen, which is what makes screenshot tests stable.
4. **Store what the user placed; derive what fits.** Keep a window's or panel's rectangle as the user left it, and compute the clamped-to-viewport version every frame without storing it. Store the clamp instead, and a phone turned sideways and back leaves every window squashed into the smallest viewport it ever saw.
5. **Last frame's value is for display, never for decisions.** Reading a value one frame late can smooth a chain of dependencies, but a grid that picks its column count from last frame's width jumped a thumbnail by up to 533 px while a drawer sprang open. The lag is harmless on a position and wrong on a choice.

## When to apply

Any spring or decay you write by hand, drag-and-throw physics, window managers, resizable panels, anything with a screenshot test. Library springs (Motion, react-spring) handle rule 1 for you; rules 3–5 are yours.

## Reference

```ts
// Bad: x += (target - x) * 0.08 on every rAF; tuned at 60fps, it runs twice as fast at 120.
// Good: the same 60fps feel from elapsed time, with a stall capped.
let last = performance.now();
function tick(now: number) {
  const dt = Math.min(100, now - last); last = now;
  x += (target - x) * (1 - Math.pow(1 - 0.08, dt / (1000 / 60)));
  requestAnimationFrame(tick);
}
```

- Gold example: `stageshow/kit/motion/Follow.tsx`, a spring that keeps its 60Hz trajectory at any refresh rate: it accumulates elapsed time (capped at 100ms a frame), steps in fixed 1000/60 ms steps, interpolates the partial step, and retargets from the rendered position and velocity. Benji's call differs on the numbers: 16.7ms steps plus interpolation instead of 4ms steps, and a settle band of 0.05 instead of 0.01.
- Check: log rAF timestamps against the transform on a 60Hz and a 120Hz screen; poses match at shared timestamps, and repeated poses followed by a jump mean a clock bug.

## Gotcha

"Settled" is never exact: a spring oscillates forever inside a small band. End it when both the distance to the target and the velocity are under ~0.01, then set position to destination and velocity to 0. An "exactly at rest" check never fires, and a snap from a band that is too wide is a visible jump ([[spring-animations]]).

A high frame rate alone is not smoothness either. An element that jumps far between frames strobes at 120 fps. For a very fast UI move (a flung card, a long snap), add a slight directional blur or stretch at peak speed and drop it at rest, as [[launch-video-cuts]] does in film.
