title: gesture-phases
summary: Every gesture has two phases. While the pointer is down the element is the finger (1:1, no easing); once it lifts, a spring seeded with the release velocity finishes the move. Dismiss on distance or velocity, link the overlay to the drag, keep it catchable.
tags: [motion, gesture, drag, sheet, mobile]
---

# Gesture phases

A gesture is direct manipulation, and it splits in two. **Track:** while the pointer is down, the element's position is the pointer's, 1:1, with no easing, duration or spring. **Release:** once the pointer lifts, physics finishes the move, as a spring that starts at the speed the finger had. Most gestures that feel wrong mix the two up, most often a spring running during the track.

For a drawer or bottom sheet, use Vaul before you write one. Momentum, an overlay tied to drag progress, velocity-aware dismissal, focus trapping and Escape are weeks of edge cases. Hand-roll a gesture only when no library covers it (swipe cards, bespoke drags).

## Before the track: recognising the gesture

- **A tap lights up on press and commits on release.** Allow about 10px of slop past its edge; sliding off cancels it, sliding back restores it.
- **A drag picks its axis only after about 10px of travel**, then tracks 1:1 (the web form of RN's `activeOffsetX`, [[react-native-motion]]).
- **Start every recognizer that could apply on the first `pointermove`** and cancel the losers once intent is clear. Result-only events (`swipeleft` and the like) throw away the tracking that feedback needs.
- **Listening for a double tap delays every single tap.** Pay that only where a double tap does something.

## Track

- **Drive position from a motion value or a direct `transform` write.** A spring or a transition here makes the element trail the finger, as if dragged through syrup.
- **Write `transform` on the dragged element itself**, never a CSS variable on a parent ([[performance-discipline]] has the Vaul case). No React state per `pointermove`: a render each move drops frames.
- **Resist past the edge instead of stopping.** In Motion, `dragElastic` (~0.2) moves the element a fixed share of the overshoot. When you hand-roll, the Apple curve in [[gesture-momentum]] levels off and is what iOS ships; a linear share never levels off, so cap the travel on a long overscroll.
- **`touch-action` on the surface leaves only the other axis to the browser:** a vertical drag gets `pan-x`, a horizontal one `pan-y`. Use `none` only on a surface that owns both axes ([[touch-and-focus]]).

## Release

- **A spring seeded with the release velocity**, never a fixed-duration ease: with a fixed ease every fling lands the same way, and that reads as fake. Measure velocity over a window, as [[gesture-momentum]] describes.
- **Dismiss on distance *or* velocity.** Past about 40–50% of the travel dismisses, and so does a fast flick over a short distance. In Motion, `onDragEnd` gives both (`info.offset`, `info.velocity`). With a distance-only threshold, flicks are ignored. Mind the units: Motion's `info.velocity` is px/s, and a sheet dismisses on `info.offset.y > threshold || info.velocity.y > 500`. The 0.11 px/ms in [[gesture-momentum]] is 110 px/s, the line between letting go and throwing; a sheet asks for a firmer flick. Convert before comparing: px/ms × 1000 = px/s.
- **A snap-back is fast.** A slow return reads as the UI disagreeing in slow motion.
- **Bounce only after a drag.** A drag applies force, so a small overshoot on release is physical. The same sheet closed by a button gets none. Small elements need a little more bounce to read the same as large ones ([[spring-animations]]).
- **Lean toward the outcome.** In-between frames show where the gesture is going: a module that expands grows toward the finger that opened it, not evenly from its centre.

## Keep it catchable

The user must be able to catch a closing sheet and drag it back. A retargeted spring keeps its current velocity, so the change of direction is seamless. A `@keyframes` animation restarts from zero, so nothing a gesture can touch gets one ([[sonner-principles]]).

**Derive linked values from the drag; don't animate them separately.** The overlay's opacity and the page's scale behind the sheet come from the same motion value (`useTransform(y, [0, height], [1, 0])`). Two animations drift apart the first time a gesture reverses mid-way.

## Sheets, holds and direction

- **Vaul's CSS curve** is `cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1)` over 500ms. It is steep at the start, so it still feels quick ([[easing-curves]] `--ease-drawer`). That timing suits a full-width sheet attached to the screen edge. A small floating drawer wants about 200ms: override `[vaul-drawer]` to `transform 0.2s cubic-bezier(0.165, 0.84, 0.44, 1)` and give `[vaul-overlay]` opacity the same 0.2s curve, so the scrim moves with the drawer. Its height change and content crossfade use the same timing family, or the component stops reading as one thing. Mark buttons inside it `data-vaul-no-drag`.
- **`dragMomentum`** is on by default in Motion. That suits a flung card. Turn it off when the element should stop where the finger stops.
- **Dismiss along the axis it entered on.** A toast that rises from the bottom swipes down to dismiss. A gesture that reverses the entrance needs no teaching.
- **Holds are asymmetric:** `linear` while held, because the fill shows time passing, then a fast ease-out snap back if the user lets go early ([[duration-table]], [[clip-path-tricks]]).

## Reduced motion

Tracking stays: the user makes that motion. Under `prefers-reduced-motion`, the momentum fling, the bounce and any decoration around the gesture go. Settle with a short position or opacity change ([[prefers-reduced-motion]]).

Check: record the drag on a real phone at 120fps (use the dev server's LAN IP; trackpads and 60Hz monitors hide this). While the pointer is down, the element sits under the finger on every frame. On release, the first frame's speed matches the last tracked frame's.

## Gotcha

A gesture that feels "weird" after release is usually under-damped. Raise `damping` before you touch stiffness. A gesture that stutters while tracking is a performance problem, not an easing problem: go through the track rules above, then the diagnosis order in [[performance-discipline]], then scrub a recording frame by frame ([[debugging-animations]]).

## Sources

- Emil Kowalski, skills (MIT, github.com/emilkowalski/skills, HEAD `715c180`, read 2026-11-09; unchanged in substance since `5206a95`, as `7cdf994` only removed links to skills that do not exist): `skills/gestures/SKILL.md` (the two phases, distance-or-velocity dismissal, linked values, Motion drag props, the Vaul curve and the floating-drawer override, spatial consistency, hold asymmetry, the touch checklist, the px/s velocity sample, the floating-drawer overlay curve). Paraphrased; the `touch-action` axis rule and the `dragElastic` cap are settled against this graph.

title: hover-intent-timing
summary: Anything a hover reveals waits a short entry delay and leaves through a short exit guard, so a brushing pointer neither flashes it in nor flickers it out. Moving between open triggers in one group hands off at once; keyboard focus reveals immediately; touch is never delayed by the gate. Callers get delay and hideDelay props and change them only for a stated reason. From Meta's Astryx.
tags: [motion, hover, tooltip, menu, timing, astryx]
---

# Hover-intent timing

A hover is weak evidence of intent. A pointer crossing a toolbar on its way somewhere else touches five triggers; if each one renders on contact, the screen strobes and the app does five renders' worth of work. Astryx makes every **hover-to-display** surface (tooltip, hover card, hover-opened menu or flyout, a container that reveals on hover, a preview) follow one timing contract. [[duration-table]] has the numbers for tooltips; this node is the contract that makes them behave.

## The contract

| Part | Rule |
|---|---|
| **Entry delay** | Wait a short delay before rendering or updating. The surface's owner picks the default (tooltips 400–700 ms per [[duration-table]]); zero only with a written reason |
| **Exit guard** | Leaving the trigger does not remove the content at once: it stays until a short exit delay, or for a container reveal until its fade ends, so out-and-back-in reads as one hover |
| **Group hand-off** | While one trigger in a group is open, moving to the next shows it immediately. The entry delay applies to the first open only |
| **Keyboard** | Focus reveals at once, no dwell |
| **Touch / coarse pointer** | The hover gate never delays touch. Whether a tap opens the surface is the component's decision, not the gate's |
| **API** | Timer-driven surfaces expose `delay` and `hideDelay` in ms; callers shorten or remove them only for a stated use case |

Under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` a container reveal's fade is instant, so its content leaves at once ([[reduced-motion-by-pointer]]).

## Where hand-built menus fail

Astryx's audit of its own components found the gaps a hand-built nav usually has: a submenu with the delay hard-coded and no prop, and a nav-heading menu whose **first** open had no entry delay at all. Check both when reviewing a mega-menu or sidebar flyout: the missing first-open delay is the one that makes a page feel twitchy.

## Gotcha

An exit guard without a hover bridge still loses the pointer on its way across the gap between trigger and panel. Keep the guard long enough to cross the gap, or make the gap part of the hit area ([[animated-hit-testing]]).

## Sources

- Meta, Astryx (MIT, github.com/meta/astryx, HEAD `9f55320`, read 2026-11-09): `docs/design/motion.md` "Hover-to-display delay" and its inventory (draft record), `docs/architecture/interaction-modality.md` INV4, INV11 (current). Paraphrased.

title: momentum-projection
summary: On release, project where the flick would come to rest (current + (v/1000)·d/(1−d), d ≈ 0.998), snap to the target nearest that point, hand the release velocity to the spring, decide by velocity sign, run X and Y on separate springs, and always start from the on-screen value.
tags: [motion, gesture, spring, velocity, interruptibility]
---

# Momentum projection

A flick is a small input that asks for a big output. Snapping to the target nearest the *release point* ignores what the finger was doing; project the resting point from the release velocity, the way scroll deceleration does, choose the target nearest that projection, and let the spring carry on at the finger's speed so there is no seam between drag and animation. [[gesture-momentum]] covers capture, sampling and boundaries; this node is what happens after the finger lifts.

## Project, then pick

```js
// d ≈ 0.998 feels like normal scroll; 0.99 stops sooner
const project = (v /* px/s */, d = 0.998) => (v / 1000) * d / (1 - d);

const resting = current + project(releaseVelocity);
const target = nearestSnapPoint(resting);
animateSpring(target, { velocity: releaseVelocity });
```

This is exponential decay, not the textbook `v²/(2a)`. At 0.998 a 1000 px/s release projects about 500px ahead; a gentle 200 px/s release projects about 100px and usually stays on its current snap.

## Hand the velocity over

- Pass the release velocity as the spring's initial velocity. Motion takes absolute px/s; an API that wants *relative* velocity needs `v / (target − current)`: 50 px/s with 100px left to go is `0.5`.
- **Commit or reverse by the velocity's sign**, not by which half of the track the element sits in. A sheet dragged 70% open and flicked down closes.
- Measure velocity over the last ~100 ms of samples ([[gesture-momentum]]), never from two events.

## Interruptible from the screen

- A new animation starts from the **presentation value**: read the live transform, never the logical target. Starting from the target jumps.
- Never lock input during a transition. A closing sheet the user grabs again follows the finger at once.
- On a reversal, re-target a spring that keeps its current velocity. Cancelling one animation and starting another at zero hits a velocity wall.
- **2D motion gets one spring per axis.** One spring on the combined distance desyncs when X and Y velocities differ (a thrown picture-in-picture window).
- Keep the grab offset: the element stays where the finger took it, never recentred under the pointer.

## When to apply

Sheets, drawers, carousels, snap-point lists, swipe-to-dismiss, draggable windows — any release that chooses between resting places.

## Reference

A 600px sheet is 180px from open when the finger lifts moving down at 900 px/s.

- Bad: it is past halfway open, so it snaps open from rest and the flick is ignored.
- Good: `180 + 0.9 * 0.998 / 0.002` rests near 629px, the nearest snap is closed (600), and the spring starts at 900 px/s.

The same rule in 2D: a picture-in-picture window is flicked up and to the right from the bottom-left corner.

- Bad: take the corner nearest the release point. That is still bottom-left, so the throw is lost.
- Good: `px = x + project(vx)`, `py = y + project(vy)`; pick the corner nearest (px, py); start an x spring at vx and a y spring at vy, on Apple's move pair (damping 1.0, response 0.4; [[spring-animations]]).
- Check: a gentle flick stays put; a hard diagonal flick crosses to the opposite corner without bending its path.

With no spring to hand the speed to (a CSS throw), give the curve a first slope equal to the finger's speed. Adapted from `stageshow/examples/swipe/index.tsx`, with `v` in px/ms from the last four drag samples:

```ts
const ms = 300, x1 = 0.25;
const y1 = Math.min(0.95, (x1 * v * ms) / remaining); // remaining px to travel
row.style.transition = `transform ${ms}ms cubic-bezier(${x1}, ${y1.toFixed(3)}, 0.35, 1)`;
```

- **Gold example:** `stageshow/examples/swipe/` (the row stays 1:1 under the finger, then carries on at the speed it left, with no step at the hand-over) and the interrupt pair in `stageshow/teaching/contrasts.tsx` (a second choice continues from the highlight's current position instead of restarting).
- **Check:** film the release at 40 to 80ms a frame: the row travels as far in the first frame after lift as in the last frame before it. Then grab it again mid-settle: it follows the finger from where it is, never from the target.

## Gotcha

Projection without velocity hand-off still looks wrong: the element picks the right target and then starts from rest, which reads as a stall right after release. Both halves, or neither.

title: morphing-icons
summary: Constraint-driven icon system — every icon = N SVG lines, unused lines collapse to invisible center points, same-shape icons rotate.
tags: [motion, icons, svg, benji]
---

# Morphing icons — the constraint-driven approach

Benji Taylor's icon system for the Claude app: every icon in the set is constructed from exactly **three SVG lines**. Icons with fewer visible elements collapse their unused lines to invisible center points. Icons sharing geometry differ only by rotation. The result: every icon can morph smoothly into any other icon in the set, because they all share the same data shape.

## The 3-line constraint

```ts
type IconLine = { x1: number; y1: number; x2: number; y2: number; opacity?: number };
type Icon = [IconLine, IconLine, IconLine]; // always 3 lines

const arrowUp: Icon = [
  { x1: 7, y1: 12, x2: 7, y2: 2 },   // vertical shaft
  { x1: 2, y1: 7,  x2: 7, y2: 2 },   // left wing
  { x1: 12, y1: 7, x2: 7, y2: 2 },   // right wing
];

const dotIcon: Icon = [
  { x1: 7, y1: 7, x2: 7, y2: 7, opacity: 0 }, // collapsed
  { x1: 7, y1: 7, x2: 7, y2: 7, opacity: 0 }, // collapsed
  { x1: 7, y1: 7, x2: 7, y2: 7, opacity: 1 }, // visible single point
];
```

A collapsed line is `{ x1: 7, y1: 7, x2: 7, y2: 7 }` with `opacity: 0`. Visually it's a point at center; arithmetically it's still a "line" the morph can tween between.

## Two morph strategies

### 1. Coordinate interpolation (different shapes)

When morphing between two icons with *different* geometries, let Motion (or your animation library) interpolate each coordinate independently:

```tsx
<motion.line
  x1={current[0].x1} y1={current[0].y1}
  x2={current[0].x2} y2={current[0].y2}
  animate={{ x1: target[0].x1, y1: target[0].y1, x2: target[0].x2, y2: target[0].y2 }}
/>
```

Motion handles the tweening. The animation is smooth because the *count* of lines is constant (3 → 3); only the coordinates change.

### 2. Rotation morph (shared geometry)

When two icons share the same line *shape* (e.g., all four directional arrows), rotate the whole icon instead of tweening coordinates:

```tsx
<motion.svg
  animate={{ rotate: rotationFor(currentDirection) }}
  transition={{ type: 'spring', stiffness: 380, damping: 30 }}
>
  {/* same SVG content for all four arrow directions */}
</motion.svg>
```

Rotation is cheaper, faster, and reads as more obviously "the same object turning" instead of "two different objects swapping."

Use rotation when the geometric difference is purely angular (arrows by 90°, plus → cross by 45°). Use coordinate interpolation when the geometry actually changes (arrow → checkmark).

## When to apply

- Toggle states: play/pause, expand/collapse, mute/unmute, follow/unfollow.
- Directional icons: chevron up/down/left/right.
- Status indicators that shift meaning: dot → ring → check.
- Toolbar icons that change mode.

## When NOT to apply

- Marketing/decorative icons where personality and detail matter more than morphability. Use a real icon pack like Phosphor or Hugeicons ([[icon-systems]]).
- Icons that need filled shapes (the constraint here is stroke-only).
- Icon sets larger than ~20 icons. The 3-line constraint gets restrictive past that.

Constraints are the engine: forcing every icon into one 3-line schema is what makes every icon morph-compatible with every other.

## When the icons can't share a schema: the contextual swap

For a stock icon pair (copy → check, like → liked), swap them with a deep scale, not a plain fade: `scale 0.3 → 1`, opacity `0 → 1`, `blur(3px) → 0`, spring `{ type: "spring", duration: 0.35, bounce: 0 }`, inside `AnimatePresence mode="popLayout" initial={false}`. A timid 0.8–0.9 scale reads as a glitch. Without Motion, render both icons stacked and cross-fade classes over ~300ms with `cubic-bezier(0.25, 0.1, 0, 1)`. Keep it for state toggles and contextual toolbars, never always-on navigation icons.

## Reference

- Bad: plus and close are two icons in an `AnimatePresence` crossfade; mid-swap four strokes show and nothing reads as turning.
- Good: one plus, `<path d="M5 12H19M12 5V19" />`, rotates 45 degrees into the close with `transition: transform 0.45s cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)`, the same two strokes in every frame.

That is the rotation group at its smallest: when the difference is purely angular, rotate, because tweening an arrow's points to another direction bends its lines on the way. Benji's call differs from the contextual swap above: he rejected a crossfade for his set because it loses the sense of transformation, so keep that scale-and-blur swap for stock pairs that cannot share a schema, never inside a morphing set.

- **Gold example:** the identity pair in `stageshow/teaching/contrasts.tsx` (its rotation is in `teaching/contrasts.css`), and the three-line set itself at benji.org/morphing-icons-with-claude.
- **Check:** film each morph at 40 to 80ms a frame: no frame shows more strokes than one icon has, no line bends on an arrow turn, and the poster or screenshot is never caught mid-morph (`stageshow/references/motion.md`, Story).

## Gotcha

3 lines is right for the Claude app icon vocabulary. Your product may need 4 (more complex icons) or 2 (simpler set). Pick the smallest N that covers your icon space. Larger N means more "collapsed" lines per icon, which is fine, but eventually you've defeated the purpose — pick judiciously.

Also: opacity-collapsed lines still render in the SVG. If you have hundreds of icons on a page, the DOM weight adds up. Use this pattern for ~5–20 icons in active use, not for an icon library.

## Sources

- Benji Taylor — *Morphing Icons with Claude*, [benji.org/morphing-icons-with-claude](https://benji.org/morphing-icons-with-claude) (read 2026-11-07).

- Benji Taylor, Stageshow 1.1.1 (MIT, github.com/benjitaylor/skills, HEAD `299140f`, read 2026-11-07): `stageshow/teaching/contrasts.tsx` and `stageshow/teaching/contrasts.css` (identity pair), `stageshow/references/motion.md` (Story, the poster).

title: motion-choreography
summary: When several things move on one event, cast each a role (lead, support, decoration, still), relate each pair (together, overlap, sequence, carry), hook secondary motion to a moment of the lead, and test the group mid-flight. Most groups get smaller, not slower.
tags: [motion, choreography, sequence, orchestration, stagger]
---

# Motion choreography

One animation is a curve and a duration ([[easing-curves]], [[duration-table]]). Two or more on the same event are a relationship, and that is where generated UI goes wrong: each part is smooth, the sum is a queue the user waits through. The fix is almost always fewer moving parts running at the same time, with a sequence only where order means something.

## 1. Cast before timing

List everything that moves on the event, then give each one role:

| Role | What | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| Lead | the one thing to notice: the new view, the title, the acted-on item | starts first, travels furthest |
| Support | the rest of the content | shorter, smaller moves after the lead |
| Decoration | badges, pills, dividers, accents | fades in place, or nothing |
| Still | containers whose content moves, everything else | does not animate |

Two candidates for lead is a hierarchy problem; motion will not settle it. A drawer with eight items is one move: the drawer slides and the items are simply inside it.

Before casting, run each element past [[animation-decision-framework]]; still is the right role for most of them. If nothing is left to sequence, the job is done.

## 2. Relate each pair

- **Together** when both belong to one object or one moment (a drawer's height and its content; a chip leaving and its siblings closing the gap). Also when order would carry no meaning: order without meaning is delay.
- **Overlap** (a stagger) when order means something and both can be visible: [[stagger-choreography]] has the gaps.
- **Sequence** only when overlap would look broken: two dense views morphing in a container that changes both width and height, one element passing through another, a box drawing before its check. Start the second just before the first ends, so it reads as one gesture.
  - Worked case: a compact pill grows into a full card. Before, one 320ms crossfade spans the whole resize, so both layouts are readable at once. After, the old view is gone in about 90ms, the new one starts just before that, and the shape keeps growing under both. The resize carries the time; the old content's exit stays short.
  - If you still want a crossfade between dense views, mount the view twice. One copy plays only the enter. An absolutely positioned twin stays at opacity 0 and shows only on the way out, fading from full. Scale that twin toward the container's next size (up as it grows; down, with scaleX pulling to the centre, as it narrows). With a few states, tune each pair by hand and pass the values through `custom`.
- **Carry** when a child's motion can't be controlled (shared-layout children): move the parent and let the children ride.

## 3. Rules that hold across the group

- One entrance per container. A panel that slides in does not also stagger its children.
- No stagger on surfaces opened many times a day or from the keyboard: menus, palettes, tab panels, list rows ([[animation-decision-framework]]).
- No uniform stagger. Equal delay, distance and curve on every item reads like `linear` on one element; vary by role.
- Nothing waits for choreography. Every visible control takes input at once.
- A leaving element gives up its space the moment it leaves, so siblings close the gap while it fades (`AnimatePresence mode="popLayout"`, or `position: absolute` at its current box). A same-container view swap is a crossfade, not out-then-in.
- One timing family per component: sub-animations share the container's duration and easing family; an inner fade may be lighter, never a different family. Set it once (`MotionConfig`, or one custom property).

## 4. Hook secondary motion to a moment

Each support move is pinned to the lead's start, impact or settle, not to a delay that looked right. Pulse on the click, not the hover before it. Accents around an icon land in the last fifth of its move, most important first. A repeat action skips the build-up and plays early with the same internal proportions.

## 5. Scale timing to the change

A resize that jumps far gets the full fade; a tiny jump with the same fade flickers, so derive duration from the distance and clamp it: about |Δheight| / 500 seconds, held within 0.15–0.27s. Small elements take more bounce than large ones. With a handful of known states, hand-tune each transition rather than fitting a formula.

## 6. Direction and exits

Forward moves content left and Back moves it right. Pass the direction to exits explicitly (`custom` on both `AnimatePresence` and the child), because an exit reads its props when it starts. Exits are simultaneous, shorter and simpler than entries, leave the way they came, and are never reverse-staggered in product UI. A wide step view slides about 110% of its width; in a small box, or between two views that look alike, use a quick fade with an 8px nudge and a little blur instead.

## Interruption, idling, reduced motion

Re-trigger mid-flight (hover out halfway, Next twice fast, switch menus mid-open): in-flight animations stop before new ones start, a resumed idle loop waits for every reset to finish, and rapid swaps never leave two children mounted (stable `key`s). Gate "only after the build-up" on a ref, not state. An idle hint first plays after about 2.5s, then about every 6s, and stops while the user interacts. Reach for imperative orchestration (`useAnimate`) only when parts coordinate across hover, click and idle and you must wait for them to finish; a plain stagger stays declarative. When the running animations differ in length, await all of them, and stop the in-flight set before starting the next. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` the group appears together with opacity only; if the sequence is the explanation, step between its frames ([[prefers-reduced-motion]]).

## Check

Write the timeline before code: one row per element with role, start, duration, motion and relationship, plus 2–5 elements deliberately left still and why. Then film the interaction and step it frame by frame ([[debugging-animations]]): a wave and a queue look alike at full speed. Imagine the fiftieth use of the day; if you would skip it, cut it.

## Sources

- Emil Kowalski, skills (MIT, github.com/emilkowalski/skills, HEAD `c8a7962`, read 2026-11-07): `skills/choreograph/SKILL.md` and `RECIPES.md` (casting, the four relationships and carry, the hard rules, moment sync, distance-scaled timing, direction, interruption, attention loops, the timeline format). Paraphrased; unchanged through `715c180`.

--- title: multi-segment-shake summary: Form-error shake at 0%, 28.57%, 57.14%, 78.57%, 100% over 280ms with 4px overshoot. tags: [motion, error, form] --- # Multi-segment shake When a form field fails validation, the shake animation is one of the highest-leverage micro-interactions. Done right, it's unmistakable. Done wrong, it's a nervous twitch. ## The Jakub Antalik formula Total duration: **280ms** total. Five keyframe stops (not four, not six — five). Translation peaks at **4px** overshoot. ```css @keyframes shake { 0% { transform: translateX(0); } 28.57%{ transform: translateX(-4px); } 57.14%{ transform: translateX(4px); } 78.57%{ transform: translateX(-2px); } 100% { transform: translateX(0); } } .input--error { animation: shake 280ms cubic-bezier(0.36, 0.07, 0.19, 0.97); } ``` Why these specific percentages? - **0%** — start position. - **28.57%** — first peak, full overshoot in one direction. - **57.14%** — second peak, full overshoot in opposite direction (the "bounce"). - **78.57%** — third peak, half-amplitude in opposite direction (damping). - **100%** — settle. The decreasing amplitude (4px → 4px → 2px → 0) is what makes it feel physical. A uniform-amplitude shake feels mechanical. ## Hold the error state After the shake completes, the field should remain visually marked as errored: ```css .input--error { border-color: var(--danger); background-color: var(--danger-bg); animation: shake 280ms cubic-bezier(0.36, 0.07, 0.19, 0.97); } ``` The shake itself is just the attention-getter. The persistent error styling is what tells the user what went wrong. Pair with an error message that appears just below the field: ```css .error-message { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(-4px); transition: all 200ms 100ms; /* 100ms delay so it appears as shake settles */ } .field--errored .error-message { opacity: 1; transform: translateY(0); } ``` ## Curve choice The cubic-bezier `(0.36, 0.07, 0.19, 0.97)` is a "snappy" curve — it accelerates fast and decelerates fast. A standard `ease-in-out` makes the shake look slow and tentative. The snappy curve is essential. ## When to apply - Form validation errors. - "This field is required" moments after submit. - Password-mismatch animations. - Wrong PIN entry on auth flows. ## When NOT to apply - Soft validation that doesn't block submission ("looks like an unusual format"). Use border color only, no shake. - High-frequency revalidation while typing. Shake should fire on a discrete event (submit, blur), not every keystroke. - More than once in quick succession. Debounce so users don't see two shakes overlapping. ## Reference The five stops land on round times of the 280ms clock, which is how to read a filmed shake frame by frame: | Time | Wrapper `x` | Field | Message lane | |---|---|---|---| | 0ms | 0 | danger ring on | hint out over 0.15s, error in over 0.25s after 0.07s | | 80ms | -4px | | | | 160ms | +4px | | | | 220ms | -2px | | | | 280ms | 0 | ring holds | error fully in by 320ms, held until the value is fixed | Benji's call differs: his form gold does not shake at all. It says the error with the ring and one line, in a lane that exists from first paint so the hint and the error swap in place and the form never grows. Keep the shake for a blocking submit, and give the message that lane rather than inserting it under the field. - **Gold example:** `stageshow/examples/form-error/` (error `Add the domain, like name@company.com`, cleared the moment the ending is typed); the swap timings are `stageshow/kit/motion/States.css`. - **Check:** film the submit at 40ms a frame: the shake starts on the submit frame, the 80, 160 and 220ms frames sit at -4, +4 and -2px, and the button below is at the same y in every frame. ## Gotcha Apply the shake to the field's *wrapper*, not the `` itself. Shaking the input causes the text cursor to jump, which is disorienting and can break IME composition for non-Latin scripts. ```html

# Performance discipline

Most jank is self-inflicted: DOM nodes nobody can see, properties the browser has to watch that never change, animation the GPU can't composite, content fetched at request time that could have been built, layout that moves after the user started reading. The fix is usually deleting or deferring work, not adding cleverness. [[transform-opacity-only]] states the property rule; this node is the rest of the discipline.

## The budget and the tiers

60fps leaves 16.7ms per frame; a 120Hz screen leaves 8ms — design against 8. One layout pass on a complex page can exceed 100ms, a dozen dropped frames at once.

| Tier | Properties | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Composite | `transform`, `opacity` (and, in current Chrome/Firefox, `filter`, `clip-path`, `background-color`) | Cheapest |
| Paint | `box-shadow`, `border-radius`, `color` | A redraw every frame |
| Layout | `width`, `height`, `padding`, `margin`, `top`/`left`, `border-width` | Re-measures, and moves the neighbours |

Swap down a tier: size → `scale()`, position → `translate()`, `display`/`visibility` → `opacity`, `box-shadow` → `filter: drop-shadow()`. Acceleration is something the browser may grant; property choice is what you control, so keep `translateY(100%)` for unknown-size elements even where a browser declines to accelerate percentages. Looking fine on your machine doesn't exempt a layout property: an absolutely positioned box with few children may get away with `padding`, but `scale()` draws the same thing and can't regress on a slower phone. When two properties look the same, take the cheaper tier.

Worked case, a sidebar: `margin-left: -92px → 0` reflows the dashboard beside it on every frame, through all three tiers. Overlay the panel and slide it with `transform: translateX(-100%) → none` (in Motion, the string `transform` form) so only compositing runs. If the content must make room, move it once at the end, never per frame.

## Transitions and compositing

- **Name the properties.** `transition: all` makes every style change a candidate animation and forfeits the engine's optimizations. Tailwind's bare `transition` class compiles to `transition-property: all` — the same bug in disguise; use `transition-transform` or `transition-[opacity,scale]`.
- **Composite-only.** `transform`, `opacity`, `filter`, `clip-path`. Never `height`, `width`, `padding`, `margin`, `top`/`left`. Keep animated `blur()` under 20px (Safari suffers most).
- **`will-change` is a targeted fix.** Browsers promote layers just in time, and that occasionally eats the opening frame — a 1px hitch as motion starts. Apply `will-change: transform` (or `transform, opacity`) to the *animating element* after you observe the hitch. It does nothing for layout or paint properties, `will-change: all` defeats the hint, and every promoted layer holds GPU memory. The one up-front use is an element whose paint is costly, such as a big blurred or filtered panel: promote that element, not its wrapper, and keep the layer as small as the effect allows, since a viewport-sized layer can cost more to composite than it saves.
- **Never animate a CSS variable on a shared parent** — every descendant recalculates style. Set the property on the moving element. Vaul's drag, written as a `--swipe-amount` variable read by `translateY()`, turned laggy once a drawer held ~20 items. Suspect this whenever a `transform` animation degrades as content grows.

## Rendering work

- **Virtualize any list that can pass ~50 items** or grow unbounded (TanStack Virtual or equivalent). Render only what is visible.
- **Frames never go through React state.** A per-frame `setState` is a re-render storm. Write transforms through refs, WAAPI, or the library's own loop. In Motion the string form `animate={{ transform: "translateX(100px)" }}` is hardware-accelerated in every version, and from `motion` 14.2 so is the `x: 100` shorthand; layout animations, `onUpdate` and motion-value-driven values stay on the main thread.
- **CSS/WAAPI for predetermined motion** (stays smooth under load); a JS loop only for dynamic, gesture-driven, or spring values. Vercel's dashboard tab indicator, a Motion shared-layout animation, dropped frames because the next page was loading at that moment; a CSS animation fixed it.

## Diagnosis order

Name the cause before changing code. In order of likelihood: (1) a non-composite property animates (layout first, then `box-shadow`, `border-radius`); (2) the jank coincides with navigation, fetching or hydration; (3) React re-renders per frame; (4) it worsens as content grows; (5) a CSS variable animates, directly or through Motion shorthands before `motion` 14.2; (6) animated `blur()` above 20px; (7) only then `will-change`. Confirm with a Performance recording on a mid-range phone over remote debugging; desktop CPU throttling doesn't model a weak GPU or a small memory budget.
- **Pause off-screen work**: looping animations, video, timers — `IntersectionObserver` or `animation-play-state`, plus `visibilitychange` for hidden tabs.

## Loading and layout

- **Reserve space for everything asynchronous.** Images and video declare dimensions or `aspect-ratio`; skeletons match the loaded box; empty states are sized to the filled state; changing numbers use `tabular-nums`; hover never changes font weight.
- **Preload fonts and above-the-fold images**; lazy-load below the fold. A font without preload is a visible reflow on every cold load.
- **Pre-render content surfaces** (blog, docs, changelog) at build time with revalidation. Never fetch them at request time.
- **Mute transitions during a theme switch**: add a `no-transitions` class, swap the theme, remove the class after a double `requestAnimationFrame`. Otherwise every color on the page tweens independently in a ragged cascade.

## Expanding panels

Animating `height` triggers layout every frame. Use `grid-template-rows: 0fr → 1fr`, a clip, or measure once and animate `transform` — see [[clip-path-tricks]].

## When to apply

"It's slow", "it stutters", "it jumps", any list over ~50 rows, any diff that adds a transition, a font, a hero image, or a theme toggle. Slowness is measured, not judged: if the complaint is "feels wrong" rather than "drops frames", route to [[easing-curves]] and [[duration-table]] instead.

## Reference

A rAF loop for something that has settled is work nobody sees. Run it only while something moves, write through a ref, and let a new target wake it. The shape of `stageshow/kit/motion/Follow.tsx`:

```ts
function step() {
  integrate(cur, vel, target); // fixed 60Hz steps, interpolated on faster screens
  if (Math.abs(target - cur) < 0.05 && Math.abs(vel) < 0.05) { cur = target; vel = 0; }
  el.style.transform = `translateX(${cur}px)`; // a ref write, never setState
  running = cur !== target || vel !== 0;
  if (running) id = requestAnimationFrame(step);
}
const wake = () => { if (!running) { running = true; id = requestAnimationFrame(step); } };
```

- **Gold example:** `stageshow/kit/motion/Follow.tsx`, and `stageshow/kit/motion/Collapse.css` for `will-change` used the way this node asks: one lasting layer on the gliding content, with its reason written beside it (text moved by layout steps whole pixels, and text that ends a transform without a layer of its own hops as it lands).
- **Check:** once the motion settles, a Performance recording shows no more rAF callbacks; scroll it offscreen or hide the tab and its work stops, and on return it resumes without skipping a beat (`stageshow/references/rehearse.md`, Live pacing).

## Gotcha

`will-change` sprinkled on every card "for performance" is the most common cargo cult in generated CSS. It costs a compositor layer per card and fixes stutters the cards never had. Remove it and add it back only where a first-frame hitch is reproducible.

# React Native motion

Mobile changes three things: there is no hover, there are two runtimes, and the user's finger is on the element. React renders on the JS runtime; Reanimated worklets run every frame on the UI runtime. Motion that touches the JS side stutters the moment the app does anything else, so the craft is keeping it on the UI runtime and leaving navigation to the platform. The web rules in [[animation-decision-framework]] and [[transform-opacity-only]] still apply.

## Threads

- **Reanimated, not core `Animated`.** Core `Animated` can't follow a gesture without crossing to JS. Gestures come from `Gesture.Pan()`, never `PanResponder`.
- **Never `setState` in a gesture or scroll handler.** Shared value → `useAnimatedStyle`; React never re-renders.
- **`scheduleOnRN` (which replaces `runOnJS`) only in `onEnd`**, or in a `useAnimatedReaction` that fires when a value crosses a threshold. In `onUpdate` it runs 60–120 times a second.
- **Read and write shared values with `.get()` / `.set()`**, only in worklets, handlers and effects — never during render. Helpers called from a worklet need the `'worklet'` directive.
- **Build a gesture once (`useMemo`) and copy the current value into a start shared value in `onStart`.** A rebuilt gesture can drop a drag in flight; a pan that starts from 0 makes a mid-spring grab jump. On Gesture Handler v3 the gesture is a hook (`onActivate` / `onDeactivate`, `event.canceled` replaces `success`) and needs no memo.

## Tools and properties

- Walk [[expo-tool-ladder]] and stop at the first tool that fits. A two-state press or toggle is a Reanimated CSS transition; a shared value is for continuous or interruptible values only. Rows that reveal action buttons use `ReanimatedSwipeable`; hand-build only a commit that needs momentum projection.
- Use the native stack for screen transitions, `presentation: 'formSheet'` for a sheet that is its own screen, `NativeTabs` for the tab bar ([[expo-navigation-motion]]). **Tabs never slide**: `animation: 'none'`.
- Anything that follows the keyboard is translated by `react-native-keyboard-controller`'s height shared value. `Keyboard.addListener` plus `withTiming` always drifts: the event reaches JS after the keyboard has started, and the system curve is private.
- Layout properties re-run layout for the node and its siblings. The exception is an absolutely positioned element with no children (a tab pill, a progress fill), where `width` keeps the corner radius that `scaleX` would smear.
- `transform` is an ordered array: put translate first, or the scale multiplies it. A `'100%'` translate is the element's own size, so a sheet moves by its own height whatever it holds.
- Collapse a header by translating content inside a fixed-height, clipped container, never by animating `height`. Never animate to a hardcoded height either: at 200% font scale it is wrong. Measure with `onLayout`.
- Never animate Android `elevation` or `BlurView` intensity; crossfade a static pre-rendered layer.
- Never put `entering` on rows of a virtualized list: recycled rows re-fire it while scrolling. Use `itemLayoutAnimation` for reflow.

## Springs

If a finger was involved, use a spring and pass it the release velocity ([[gesture-momentum]]). Pass `reduceMotion: ReduceMotion.System`; reduced means fewer and gentler, keeping opacity and colour ([[prefers-reduced-motion]]).

| Interaction | Config |
|---|---|
| Settle, no overshoot | `{ duration: 400, dampingRatio: 1 }` |
| Snap back after a drag | `{ duration: 400, dampingRatio: 0.8, velocity }` |
| Sheet or drawer | `{ duration: 300, dampingRatio: 0.8, velocity }` |
| Dismiss past a hard edge | add `overshootClamping: true` |

Press feedback is `scale: 0.97` in 100–150ms on press-in; commit on press-out. Targets are 44pt (48dp on Android); grow `hitSlop`, not the visual. Declare the pan axis with `activeOffsetX: [-10, 10]` or it steals vertical scrolls. Clamp every scroll `interpolate` with `Extrapolation.CLAMP`.

## Haptics

`selectionAsync` for a detent tick, `impactAsync(Light)` when something snaps home, `notificationAsync` for success or error. Fire on the causal frame, once per user action, never per frame or on an entrance the user didn't cause, and never as the only feedback.
The same families on the mobile web, with the Android and iOS Safari routes: [[haptic-feedback]].

## Reference

Swipe to archive: the row 1:1 under the finger, thrown off at the speed it left ([[momentum-projection]]), the list told only once it has gone:

```tsx
const start = useSharedValue(0);
const pan = useMemo(() => Gesture.Pan()
  .activeOffsetX([-10, 10])
  .onStart(() => start.set(x.get()))
  .onUpdate((e) => x.set(start.get() + e.translationX))
  .onEnd((e) => {
    const resting = x.get() + (e.velocityX / 1000) * 0.998 / 0.002;
    const to = resting < -width / 2 ? -width : 0;
    const cfg = { duration: 300, dampingRatio: 0.8, velocity: e.velocityX, overshootClamping: to !== 0 };
    x.set(withSpring(to, cfg, (done) => { if (done && to !== 0) scheduleOnRN(archive, id); }));
  }), [width, id]);
```

- **Card-stack flick.** Before: a `PanResponder` on JS, so the card trails the finger, leaves only past half its width (a quick short flick fails) and eases back over 300ms. After: `Gesture.Pan()` 1:1 on the UI runtime, commit when the projected rest point clears the threshold, exit with `withTiming` 200ms, one `impactAsync(Light)` on the commit frame, the cards below reflow through `itemLayoutAnimation`.
- **Gold example:** `stageshow/examples/swipe/` for the anatomy native Mail has: Archive is the row's own back, same height and edge to edge, its mark riding the row's trailing edge, and the gap closes in one ease with the color solid, never through gray. For an in-app response no finger drives, Benji's timing is UIKit-quick, 0.5s on `cubic-bezier(0.3, 0.75, 0.1, 1)`, which is `withTiming(v, { duration: 500, easing: Easing.bezier(0.3, 0.75, 0.1, 1) })` (`stageshow/references/motion.md`, Phones in motion).
- **Check:** on a release build on a device, screenshot the frame at the furthest point of the swipe at full size, the one people share: row text is cut only by the list's edge and the action fills the row's height. Width emulation doesn't change touch, so judge the throw on hardware.

## Gotcha

Expo Go and the simulator hide exactly the problems that matter. Judge feel on a release build on the slowest device you support. On ProMotion iPhones third-party animation is capped at 60fps unless `CADisableMinimumFrameDurationOnPhone` is set in the Info.plist; once it is set, the frame budget is 8ms.

# Reduced motion, by pointer

[[prefers-reduced-motion]] says what to strip. Astryx answers the next question, *what replaces it*, with one rule split by input, which removes the guesswork that leaves most reduced-motion modes either jarring or still moving.

## The rule

While `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` matches, an entrance, exit, presentation switch or state change **must not move, scale, resize or spring** its content. Then:

| Context | Replacement |
|---|---|
| Coarse primary pointer (`pointer: coarse`), or the transition was started by a touch release | **Opacity-only cross-fade, ≤ 200 ms.** The entering element appears in its final place and fades in; the leaving one fades out where it is (iOS *Reduce Motion* with *Prefer Cross-Fade*) |
| Any other pointer (mouse, trackpad, keyboard) | **Immediate.** No animated property at all |
| An in-place value (a progress fill's length, a meter, a counter) | Applies at once on every pointer; no cross-fade, no added element |
| A hover or selection colour, and the onset of a press colour | At once on every pointer. A touch press's release keeps its ≤ 200 ms fade |
| A colour that changes *with* a part that cross-fades (a switch track with its thumb) | Follows that cross-fade |

## What is not a transition

- **Direct manipulation.** Content following a finger or pointer during a drag keeps following it ([[gesture-phases]]).
- **Momentum.** The coast after a throw, and its settle at an edge, keeps decelerating, as native scrolling does under iOS Reduce Motion. A move the component *starts* on release (snap to a detent, dismiss, page to a target) still cross-fades.
- **Native scrolling** belongs to the browser.

## Overrides only tighten

A theme may force the reduced path for everyone (Astryx: `reducedMotion: 'always'`); nothing may loosen it. No component prop or theme value keeps travel, springs or a longer animation under reduced motion.

## Gotcha

A blanket 120 ms opacity fade under reduced motion is right on a phone and wrong on a desktop, where the same fade on every hover-revealed panel reads as lag. Branch on `pointer: coarse`.

# Shared-letter text morphs

Benji Taylor's button transition pattern from Family: when two states of the same button share letters (e.g., **Continue** → **Confirm**), animate the shared letters in place and crossfade only the differing ones. The eye reads it as the same button *changing its mind* rather than two different buttons swapping.

## The principle

> If a component occupies a space and will persist in the next phase, it should remain consistent.

For text labels, "consistent" means the letters the user already sees should stay where they are. Only the letters that change should animate.

## How it works

**Continue → Confirm** shares `Con`. The transition:

1. The "Con" stays in place, unanimated.
2. The trailing "tinue" exits (fade + slight up-translate).
3. The new trailing "firm" enters (fade + slight up-translate, staggered slightly).

```tsx
function MorphingText({ text }: { text: string }) {
  const chars = text.split('');
  return (
    <AnimatePresence mode="popLayout">
      {chars.map((char, i) => (
        <motion.span
          key={`${i}-${char}`}
          initial={{ opacity: 0, y: 8 }}
          animate={{ opacity: 1, y: 0 }}
          exit={{ opacity: 0, y: -8 }}
          transition={{ duration: 0.18 }}
        >
          {char}
        </motion.span>
      ))}
    </AnimatePresence>
  );
}
```

Motion's `AnimatePresence` with `mode="popLayout"` and a key composed of `index + char` automatically does the right thing: characters that exist in both states (same index, same character) stay; characters that change get enter/exit animations.

## Why it works

The brain identifies the button by its persistent letters. As long as the "Con" stays, the user perceives this as the same button entering a new state ("I am acknowledging your continue tap, and now requiring confirmation"). If both states fade entirely, the user perceives two separate buttons appearing one after another — which feels like a UI reset.

## When to apply

- Two-step confirmation buttons (Continue → Confirm, Save → Saved, Submit → Submitted).
- State labels with shared prefixes (Loading → Loaded, Connecting → Connected).
- Counter increments where digits change (`12` → `13` — share the "1").
- Any text-state transition where the words share characters at the same indices.

## When NOT to apply

- States with no shared characters (Cancel → Done). Use a single fade-crossfade ([[cross-blur-transitions]]) instead — there's nothing to preserve.
- Long sentences. The technique works best for short labels (1–3 words). Longer text reads as a sentence, not a label, and per-character morph looks weird.
- Localized text. "Continue" → "Confirm" works in English; the Spanish equivalent ("Continuar" → "Confirmar") shares a different prefix. Don't hard-code shared-letter assumptions.

## Reference

Diff the two labels by shared head and tail, not by index, so "Add file" → "Remove file" keeps " file" still too:

```ts
function splitChange(prev: string, next: string) {
  let h = 0, t = 0
  while (h < prev.length && h < next.length && prev[h] === next[h]) h++
  while (t < prev.length - h && t < next.length - h && prev.at(-1 - t) === next.at(-1 - t)) t++
  return { head: next.slice(0, h), out: prev.slice(h, prev.length - t), in: next.slice(h, next.length - t), tail: next.slice(next.length - t) }
}
// "Continue" -> "Confirm": head "Con", out "tinue", in "firm", tail ""
```

Gold example: `stageshow/kit/motion/Roll.tsx` with `Roll.css`. Head and tail hold still and only the middle moves; on a button (`variant="fade"`) the old part leaves in 0.16s, the new fades in over 0.35s after 0.12s, and the slot eases to its new width over 0.4s so a neighbor travels with it.
Benji's call differs: Stageshow's `Roll` splits numbers by character ("$0.01" → "$0.0098" keeps "$0.0") but moves words whole and never splits a word, so its button would crossfade "Continue" → "Confirm" as one word while the width eases.
Check: step the change at 40ms. The head's pixels match in every frame, and the button beside it moves with the width instead of jumping (`stageshow/teaching/relationships.tsx`, adjacent action).

Past two short labels (a status line, a price, a sentence), use the engine rules in [[text-morph-engine]]: words aligned first, characters only inside similar words, numbers by place value.

## Gotcha

The morph fails if you re-render the parent on state change with no AnimatePresence — React unmounts the old span and mounts a new one with no animation. Wrap the morphing text in `AnimatePresence` and use stable keys (index + char, not random uuid).

Also: a single character changing at the *start* of a word (Submit → Sub*j*ect-like cases) is harder to design well — the shift of the surrounding letters reads as more disruptive than a stable prefix. Where possible, design label pairs that share the *start*.

# Sonner principles

[Sonner](https://sonner.emilkowal.ski/) is Emil Kowalski's toast library. It's one of the most copied production components on the modern web. The principles behind it are transferable to any small, opinionated library or component.

## 1. Developer experience is the product

The API a developer types is the user surface. A library used 1000 times a year by 1000 developers compounds. One unnecessary required prop = millions of keystrokes wasted. Default everything you can.

```ts
// Good
toast("Saved")

// Bad
toast({ message: "Saved", type: "info", duration: 4000 })
```

## 2. Good defaults beat configuration options

Every config option is a tax: docs surface area, decision fatigue, bug surface. Pick the *right* default; let users override only when they need to. Most users will never override; design for them first.

> "What happens if I don't pass anything?" should always produce a good outcome.

- Ship optional features off. Benji Taylor's Liveline chart starts with its features off by default: a line that moves when a number changes is already a complete component.

## 3. Naming creates identity

`toast("Saved")` is recognizable. `notify({ kind: "success" })` is forgettable. Pick a verb that reads like a sentence; don't make users learn vocabulary. Sonner is named so people would *want* to say its name.

## 4. Handle edge cases invisibly

Multiple toasts: stack them. Identical toasts: dedupe. Rapid open/close: throttle. The library handles these without an API. The developer shouldn't think about them.

This is the opposite of "give the user knobs for everything." The library has opinions and enforces them.

## 5. Use transitions, not keyframes — for interruptible UI

CSS transitions interpolate from the *current* state, even mid-animation. CSS keyframes restart from frame 0. For UI that the user can interrupt (rapid clicks, drag-to-dismiss), transitions feel right; keyframes look broken.

```css
/* Good — interruptible */
.toast { transform: translateY(0); transition: transform 200ms; }
.toast.dismissing { transform: translateY(100%); }

/* Bad — restarts if interrupted */
.toast.dismissing { animation: slideOut 200ms; }
```

This is the technical foundation behind Sonner feeling responsive even when you spam-dismiss.

## 6. Build great documentation

The docs site for a library *is* the marketing. If the demo at the top doesn't immediately work and look right, no one installs. Sonner's docs site is itself a polished product (live demo, copy-paste examples, dark/light themes). Same for Vaul, Cmdk, Radix.

Treat docs as a first-class deliverable, not an afterthought.

## 7. Cohesion matters — match motion to component personality

A "spring-bouncy" component and a "crisp-fast" component shouldn't share an easing curve. Once you've picked a personality, every animation in the library should feel like it came from the same hand.

Sonner is *quiet*: its toasts use a slightly slow ~400ms `ease` transition rather than the generic ease-out budget. Vaul is *physical*. Cmdk is *snappy*. Each is consistent within itself.

## 8. Opacity + height is trial-and-error

There's no formula for the perfect collapse animation of a height-changing element. It's: try, watch, tune, repeat. Some combos:

- Animate `opacity` alone, height shifts instantly (often good enough).
- Animate `max-height` from large to 0 (works for known-height content).
- Use `grid-template-rows: 0fr → 1fr` (modern collapse pattern, works without knowing height).
- WAAPI with measured height (most flexible, most code).

Pick by trial. There's no single right answer.

## 9. Review work the next day

Build the animation today. Sleep. Look again. If you still like it, ship. If you don't, you've saved yourself from shipping something the first day's enthusiasm masked.

This is the cheapest QA step in design engineering. Builds in a 24-hour cooling period that catches 80% of "what was I thinking" mistakes.

## 10. Asymmetric enter/exit timing

Covered in [[duration-table]] and [[compose-subtract-asymmetry]]. Exit along the same path it entered — a toast in from the bottom leaves through the bottom, which is what makes swipe-to-dismiss obvious — but with fewer properties and at ~60–80% of the enter duration.

## When to apply

When building any reusable component, especially:
- Toasts, snackbars, alerts.
- Drawers, sheets, dialogs.
- Command palettes (cmdk-style).
- Date pickers, comboboxes.
- Any small library you intend others to install.

## Reference

| Toast | What good looks like |
| --- | --- |
| Copy | "Link copied", "Snoozed until 8:00 AM": one line, the result, no "Success!" |
| Action | one quiet word after the message ("Undo"), never a second button row |
| Enter | rises about 10px while it fades in; never pops in whole |
| Exit | leaves the way it came, faster, and stays mounted until the exit ends |
| Look | dark pill on a light theme, raised surface on dark; `role="status"` |

Gold example: `stageshow/examples/gmail/index.tsx` with `stageshow/kit/parts/Toast.tsx`. Archive raises the toast, and its Undo brings the row back, so the reset has a cause the viewer saw.
Benji's call differs: Stageshow's `Toast` rises over 0.6s `cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)` with a 0.35s fade, a demo kit's pace; Sonner's ~400ms `ease` stays the product default.
Check: fire five toasts 50ms apart and dismiss the third mid-enter, stepped at 40ms. None restarts from its first frame, none appears or vanishes in one frame, and each message fits one line at 390px wide.

## Gotcha

These principles are for components you ship to others. For one-off internal UI, several rules relax (defaults matter less, naming matters less, docs aren't needed). Don't apply them with equal force in both contexts.

## Sources

title: spring-animations
summary: When springs beat curves — interactive/draggable elements. Apple's critically damped default (bounce 0, ~0.35s), the 380/30 drawer spring, bounce only after momentum. Interruptibility.
tags: [motion, spring, physics]

# Spring animations

Curves animate to a fixed duration. Springs animate to a target value with physics. The difference matters when the user is *driving* the animation.

## Use springs when

- The animation is **interruptible** mid-flight (drag, gesture, scroll).
- The animation responds to **velocity** from a real input.
- The target value can change while the animation is running.
- The element should feel **physical** rather than mechanical.

## Use curves when

- The animation is triggered by a discrete event (button click, route change).
- You want **exact timing** (e.g., choreograph multiple animations to land together).
- The element is small and the difference is invisible.

## Apple's default: critically damped

```ts
// Motion — duration + bounce is the form to reason in
const settle = { type: "spring", duration: 0.35, bounce: 0 }
```

Bounce 0, a perceived duration of about 0.3–0.4s, no overshoot. Bounce (0.1–0.3, never more) is earned only when the gesture carried momentum — a flicked card, a drag-to-dismiss release. Overshoot on a menu that simply opened feels wrong.

Apple tunes a spring with two numbers: a damping ratio (1.0 settles with no overshoot; lower overshoots more) and a response, roughly the seconds it takes to reach the target. Settle time falls out of both, so response is not a duration. Shipped pairs: move or reposition (PiP) 1.0/0.4, rotation 0.8/0.4, sheet or drawer 0.8/0.3. In Motion a move is `bounce: 0, duration: 0.4`; the drawer pair's overshoot belongs only after a flick ([[gesture-phases]]), and the RN forms are in [[react-native-motion]].

## The drawer / momentum spring

```ts
const momentum = { type: "spring", stiffness: 380, damping: 30, mass: 1 }
```

- **Stiffness:** how hard it pulls toward the target. Higher = snappier.
- **Damping:** friction. ~30 keeps a released drawer or sheet from oscillating. Lower = bouncy.
- **Mass:** rarely change from 1.

Use it for drawers, sheets and anything settling after a drag, with the release velocity passed in ([[gesture-momentum]]).

## Interruptibility — the real reason to use springs

When a gesture reverses mid-flight, a spring carries its current velocity into the new target; a keyframe restarts from zero and looks broken. A two-state press doesn't need that: a CSS transition already retargets from the current value.

```tsx
// Press: a transition is enough
<motion.button
  whileTap={{ scale: 0.97 }}
  transition={{ duration: 0.16, ease: [0.23, 1, 0.32, 1] }}
/>

// Curve (good for one-shot reveal)
<motion.div
  initial={{ opacity: 0, y: 8 }}
  animate={{ opacity: 1, y: 0 }}
  transition={{ duration: 0.2, ease: [0.16, 1, 0.3, 1] }}
/>
```

## When to apply

Pretty much anywhere the user's input drives motion: drag handles, dismissible cards, sliders, pinch-zoom, scroll-snap. For *triggered* motion (modals, toasts, page transitions), curves are simpler and usually better.

## Reference

A hand-written follow spring, adapted from `stageshow/kit/motion/Follow.tsx` (stepped at a fixed 60Hz):

```ts
const k = 0.25                        // stiffness: a quick, settled follow
const damp = 2 * Math.sqrt(k) * 0.95  // damping ratio 0.95, just under critical
function step(c: Rect, v: Rect, t: Rect) {
  for (const key of ['x', 'y', 'width', 'height'] as const) {
    v[key] += (t[key] - c[key]) * k - v[key] * damp
    c[key] += v[key]
  }
} // a new target keeps c and v; never reset v to 0
```

Gold example: `stageshow/kit/motion/Follow.tsx`, for selection rings, drop targets and hover highlights; a CSS transition restarts from rest on every change and stutters cell by cell on a drag. The interrupt pair is in `stageshow/teaching/contrasts.tsx` (interrupt).
Benji's call differs on bounce: the Stageshow cursor morph springs between outlines underdamped (damping ratio 0.62, angular frequency 15) with no gesture behind it, clamping color and stroke so only the geometry overshoots (`stageshow/examples/cursor-morph/README.md`).
Check: pick Month, then Week before the highlight lands, stepped at 40ms. The second move starts where the highlight is, at its current speed, and the same input lands in the same place at 60Hz and 120Hz.

## Gotcha

Springs left on library defaults produce slow, floaty motion. Always set `duration` + `bounce`, or both `stiffness` and `damping`. And don't reach for a spring because something is "polished": Sonner, the usual example, animates with CSS transitions, not a spring.

## Hand-written springs

Step them on a fixed 4 ms clock or sample a closed form, cap the catch-up after a stall, and apply events at their timestamps, or the same gesture lands in different places at different frame rates ([[frame-rate-independence]]). A press on a spring still in flight goes to its destination ([[animated-hit-testing]]).

title: stagger-choreography
summary: Cascading reveals (30–80ms delays, under ~300ms in total). When stagger helps comprehension and when it just reads as noise; the wider choreography of several moving parts is motion-choreography.
tags: [motion, stagger, choreography]

# Stagger choreography

A stagger is a sequence of similar animations offset by a small delay. Done well, it directs attention and reveals structure. Done badly, it looks like the app is loading slowly. It is one of four ways two moving parts can relate; cast the parts and pick the relationship first in [[motion-choreography]].

## When to stagger

- Multiple sibling elements appearing for the first time (list items, dashboard cards, search results).
- A grouped set of items whose order matters (top-down, left-to-right, by importance).
- A choreographed reveal that pairs with a single trigger event (page enter, modal open).
- Dependent responses to one change: the setting leads, and its dependents start before the previous ones finish, with offsets that keep the order legible while the frame around them holds still (Benji Taylor, Stageshow `references/choreography.md`).

## When NOT to stagger

- The user is in a power-use loop (search-as-you-type, repeated filter changes). The first stagger was fine; the tenth is friction.
- The list has more than ~12 items. Past that, the last items feel sluggish.
- The items are visually identical and the order is arbitrary. Stagger implies hierarchy; arbitrary order misleads.
- The container already enters. One entrance per container: a panel that slides in carries its items, it does not also stagger them.
- The surface is opened many times a day or from the keyboard (menus, command palettes, tab panels, list rows).

## The delay range

```ts
// good
const delay = (i) => i * 0.05; // 50ms per item

// too slow — feels like loading
const delay = (i) => i * 0.15;

// too fast — looks like all at once with extra steps
const delay = (i) => i * 0.02;
```

Sweet spot is **30–80ms** between items. Adjust for item count and physical size on screen. Keep the steps uneven: the lead moves furthest, support less, decoration only fades, and gaps that shrink down the group read as a wave where equal gaps read as a metronome (Motion's `stagger()` takes `from` and `ease` for this).

In plain CSS, give each item `--i` and set `animation-delay: calc(var(--step) * var(--i))` with `animation-fill-mode: both`. Without the backwards half, a delayed item sits at rest through its delay and then jumps to the first frame. A keyframe with only `from` ends on the element's own styles, so there is no end state to keep in sync. Things that land as one beat (a title and its first paragraph) share an index.

## The "stop at 12" pattern

For product UI the cap is about six: items past the sixth share its delay, so a 50–60ms step stays inside the ~300ms budget. Twelve is the ceiling for an occasional, first-run list.

```ts
const STAGGER_CAP = 6; // 12 only for a first-run list
const delay = (i) => Math.min(i, STAGGER_CAP) * 0.05;
```

Items past the cap appear together with the last staggered item. This avoids the "still loading row 47" feel. Whatever the cap, keep the whole cascade under ~300ms; past that, drop to 30ms per item or fade the group as one ([[animation-removal-hazards]]).

## Section entrances: split, then stagger

For a page or hero entrance, don't move one wrapper. Split it into heading, copy and call to action, offset each by ~90–100ms (per word in a hero headline, ~80ms), and enter each with opacity, `translateY(8px)` → 0 and `blur(2px)` → 0. Section pieces are fewer and larger than list items, which is why the gap is wider than 30–80ms. A moment seen once per visit (a hero, a personal site) may widen the step to 100–150ms on 0.5–0.6s entrances; product UI keeps 30–80ms.

## First paint is not an entrance

Anything already at rest when the page paints plays nothing; motion is for changes the user causes afterward. In Motion, `initial={false}` on `AnimatePresence` covers toggles, tabs and icon swaps — but not a deliberate first-run hero, where it would wipe the entrance. Hard-refresh to check. In an exiting group, `mode="popLayout"` lets siblings close the gap while the exit plays.

## Exits go at once

In product UI an exit is simultaneous, shorter and simpler than the entry: the user already chose to leave, so don't reverse-stagger it out. A film or demo loop that resets around an anchor is the exception (Reference below).

## Direction matters

- **Top-to-bottom:** default for vertical lists.
- **Center-out:** for celebratory moments (confetti, success screens).
- **Left-to-right:** for narrative content (onboarding steps).
- **Per-item motion direction matters too:** if items slide up to enter, the stagger should feel like a wave from bottom to top.

## When to apply

First-render of any list of 3+ items. Modal open with multiple internal sections. Search results page on initial query (not on refinement).

## Reference

| Job | Gap |
| --- | --- |
| Rows in reading order | 60ms (40–80), `act.stagger`'s default in `stageshow/kit/act.ts` |
| Tiles of a grid or bento | 80–120ms; one object enters whole |
| Dependents of one change | 0, 100, 220, 420ms on one 900ms curve |
| Exit or reset around an anchor | reverse order, about 70ms apart, done within 0.5s |

Gold example: `stageshow/examples/choreography/` (`choreography.css`, the `transition-delay` lines): a checkout changes market, the currency leads and the pay label, method and address follow, while the comparison beside it starts everything at once so timing is the only variable.
Benji's call differs: when several status words change at once, as a loop resets, Stageshow cascades them about 60ms apart, because a column changing in unison reads as flicker; this node's no-restagger rule still holds for sort and filter.
Check: export a contact sheet at 40ms. Each item's first moving frame falls in reading order, then cover one moving item at a time; if the order reads as well without it, cut its motion.

## Gotcha

Stagger on every state change is exhausting. Only stagger on **first appearance**. Subsequent updates (sorting, filtering) should crossfade in place or use a layout animation. Re-staggering on filter-change makes the UI feel slower than it is.

## Sources

- Emil Kowalski — stagger guidance (30–80ms, decorative, never blocks interaction). The cap at 12 is house guidance; the product cap of six is upstream's.
- Emil Kowalski, skills (MIT, github.com/emilkowalski/skills, HEAD `c8a7962`, read 2026-11-07): skills/remove-animations/SKILL.md (300ms total cap); unchanged through `715c180`.
- Emil Kowalski, skills (MIT, github.com/emilkowalski/skills, HEAD `c8a7962`, read 2026-11-07): skills/choreograph/SKILL.md (one entrance per container, no stagger on high-frequency UI, no uniform stagger, simultaneous exits); unchanged through `715c180`.
- Emil Kowalski, skills (MIT, github.com/emilkowalski/skills, HEAD `715c180`, read 2026-11-09): skills/choreograph/SKILL.md and RECIPES.md (the CSS index stagger with fill mode `both`, the six-item product cap, 100–150ms steps for first-run moments).

summary: Morphing whole strings and numbers, not just two button labels. Diff by word first and by character only inside similar words; a run of six or more replaced characters recedes as one shape; numbers morph by place value, digits sliding in from above; an interrupted morph keeps its speed; the value stays readable to screen readers. # Text and number morphs, engine rules

[[shared-letter-morph]] covers the two-label case: Continue → Confirm keeps "Con". A status line, a price, a counter or a sentence that changes needs more than a shared head and tail. Torph is a dependency-free engine for that, built on the method Benji Taylor described in *Family Values*, and its rules are the ones worth copying whether or not you use it.

## Matching

1. **Split with `Intl.Segmenter`** in the content's locale, so emoji, combining marks and scripts without spaces segment correctly. Never `split('')`.
2. **Align words first** (longest common subsequence over the word list). A word present in both strings moves as a unit to its new place, even when the words around it changed.
3. **Morph characters only inside a word that is similar enough**: at least 40% of its characters shared. Below that, the old word leaves and the new one arrives; per-character morphing between unrelated words looks like noise.
4. **Every segment has one stable id**, and that id is the only identity used for the FLIP measurement and the DOM. Two segments sharing an id lose a character on screen.

## Motion, as shares of the duration

The defaults are 400ms on `cubic-bezier(0.19, 1, 0.22, 1)`, a strong ease-out, or a spring whose duration is computed from its physics.

| Segment | Transform | Opacity |
|---|---|---|
| Persisting | FLIP from its old position to its new one | stays at 1 |
| Leaving | travels with its nearest surviving neighbour, scales to 0.95 | out over the first 25% |
| Arriving | from its nearest neighbour's old offset, scale 0.95 → 1 | in over 50%, starting at 25% |
| A run of 6+ adjacent characters all replaced | the run shrinks to 0.8 around its own centre, as one shape | out in 45%; the new run grows from 0.8, in over 35% |

Fades are fractions of the duration, never fixed milliseconds, so a long morph doesn't leave a character opaque and motionless for most of its run. The group rule exists because past about six characters nothing nearby survived to move relative to, and character-by-character the run smears.

## Numbers by place value

A value that contains a number morphs by place, on by default: `1,204 → 1,318` rolls the hundreds and tens and leaves the thousands alone. Each digit sits in a slot clipped on the block axis only (`clip-path: inset(0 -100vw)`, so glyph overhang isn't shaved; `overflow: hidden` would move an inline-block's baseline). The slot takes the FLIP move; the glyph inside takes a slide of one line height and the fade. **Digits arrive from above, separators and symbols from below**, so each reads as its own event, and the outgoing fade (45%) is longer than the incoming (25%) because a digit already gone is a hole in the number.

Detection is strict: a token counts as a quantity only when it starts and ends with a digit inside optional currency, sign or percent affixes. "COVID-19" and "2024-01-01" are not numbers and morph as text. For a field someone is typing in, pass the caret position: typing `1` before `20` should insert a digit, not renumber every place.

## Interruption, size and access

- **An interrupted morph keeps its momentum.** The container's width and height animate with the box's current velocity added to the new curve's start (bounded to avoid overshoot), and a morph whose target didn't change resumes where it was instead of restarting. Without this, a value updating faster than the morph only ever plays each curve's slow opening and the box crawls behind the text.
- **The container eases to its new width** over the same duration, so a neighbour beside it travels instead of jumping.
- **Screen readers get the plain value** in a visually hidden node; the animated fragments are `aria-hidden`. That node is `user-select: none`, or a copy pastes the value twice.
- **Reduced motion is read live**, not once at mount: with it set, the text swaps without animating.

## Gotcha

Don't rebuild this with a key of `index + char` on a long string: inserting one word at the start re-keys every character after it, and the whole line animates. Identity has to come from the alignment, not the position. And happy-dom has no layout, so test that a transform was applied or an animation cancelled, never a measured distance.

Keying digit spans by their index from the left breaks the moment the length changes: $996 → $1,008 re-keys every glyph, separator included, the width snaps and a trailing unit like /mo jumps. Key by place value from the right and animate the width, or install NumberFlow ([[library-picks]]) when the counter is the whole job.
