title: sound-palette
summary: One material, a handful of sounds. Size maps to pitch and length, direction maps to meaning, consonance to success and dissonance to error. Stock packs are tells.
tags: [sound, palette, earcon, audio, design-system]
---

# Sound palette

A product's sounds are a type family, not a clip-art folder. Pick **one material** — a struck wooden bar, a soft plastic tap, a breath of filtered noise, a muted glockenspiel — and derive every sound from it, the way a palette derives every tint from one hue in [[color-monochromatic]]. Five sounds that share a material feel like a product. Five sounds from five packs feel like a browser toolbar from 2003.

## The grammar

Earcons (Blattner, Sumikawa & Greenberg, 1989) are learned, not mimetic: meaning comes from *contour* and *interval*, and users learn it in a handful of exposures.

| Dimension | Rule | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Size → pitch and length** | Small elements tick high and short (2–6 kHz centroid, 40–120 ms). Big elements land low and long (0.8–1.5 kHz, 300–800 ms). | Physics. A card is lighter than a wordmark; the ear knows. |
| **Direction → meaning** | Rising figure = success, open, join. Falling = dismiss, leave, error. | Discord's join/leave pair; every OS you have used. |
| **Interval → valence** | Major third or perfect fifth for confirmation. Minor second or tritone for error. | Consonance reads as safe; dissonance as tense (IWC study on earcon dissonance and perceived hazard). |
| **Complexity → priority** | Simple, single-hit for frequent actions. Multi-note only for rare or urgent moments. | Frequent complex sounds fatigue in a day (Toptal). |
| **Repeat → variation** | A run that *counts* (pops, stacking blocks, dings) steps pitch up (`playbackRate` +5–10% per hit, about +1 st). A run that *repeats* (keys, steps) cycles 4+ recorded takes, never the same twice in a row, ±1–2 dB, at most ±3 % (½ st) of pitch. The click is the exception: one voice, one level, every time. | Identical repeats read as a machine; Josh Comeau's "glug" pattern. Random pitch on typing is its own tell: real keys vary in take, not pitch ([[designed-sfx-anatomy]]). |

## A minimal family

Most products need **four to six** sounds, not forty:

| Name | Role | Shape |
|---|---|---|
| `tick` | Toggle, select, snap | Single transient, ≤ 80 ms, high |
| `tap` | Primary press in tactile products only | Dull transient with a short body, ≤ 120 ms |
| `send` | Send / save / complete | One or two notes rising, ≤ 250 ms |
| `receive` | Incoming message / notification | Two notes, lower than `send`, ≤ 400 ms |
| `error` | Rejected submit, invalid drop | Low, falling, ≤ 200 ms — paired with [[multi-segment-shake]] |
| `success` | Rare milestone | Three-note figure in the family's key, ≤ 800 ms |

Write the family down as a manifest before generating anything — `scripts/sound-family.mjs` next to `SKILL.md` takes exactly this shape and produces the files via [[sound-generation-elevenlabs]] or the built-in synth from [[sound-generation-open-source]].

## Material, not genre

Apple's sound team records real instruments — glockenspiel, kalimba, marimba — and even struck a hollow Apple Watch case with mallets to find its resonance. "Organic over futuristic" is the stated reason: familiar materials make new technology comfortable. The AI-default failure is the opposite — a glossy sci-fi "digital UI blip" that belongs to no product. Describe a *thing* (soft felt mallet on a wooden bar; a fingernail on glass; a breath through a paper cone), never a *style*.

## When to apply

Before generating or downloading a single file. Decide the material, list the family, then produce. Reviewing a product with sounds: ask whether they share a material; if not, that is the finding.

## Reference

Bad: `tick` a glassy blip from one pack, `send` a synth whoosh from another, `error` a buzzer from a third. Good: one material line, every sound derived from it:

```json
{ "material": "felt mallet on a small wooden block, dry, no reverb, no tail",
  "sounds": {
    "tick":    { "synth": { "type": "tick",  "freq": 3200, "seconds": 0.07 } },
    "send":    { "synth": { "type": "chime", "notes": [523.25, 659.25] } },
    "receive": { "synth": { "type": "chime", "notes": [493.88, 392.0] } },
    "error":   { "synth": { "type": "thud",  "from": 220, "to": 140, "seconds": 0.16 } } } }
```

`send` rises a major third (C5 to E5); `receive` falls a major third (B4 to G4) and sits lower; `error` falls and is the lowest; `tick` is the smallest, so the highest and shortest.

Gold example: `scripts/sound-family.example.json`, the full six-sound manifest this is cut from; run it through `scripts/sound-family.mjs --provider synth`.

Check: play the family back to back, in mono, on a laptop speaker, and name the material in two words. If one sound belongs to a different object, or two sounds can be swapped without changing meaning, the family is not done.

## Gotcha

Do not tune the family in isolation with headphones at midnight. Laptop speakers have nothing below ~200 Hz, so a warm low thud disappears and a bright tick becomes a needle. Design in mono, check on the worst speaker in the office, then set levels per [[sound-spec]].

## Sources

- Blattner, Sumikawa & Greenberg (1989), *Earcons and icons* — structured families of tones whose contour carries meaning.
- *Perceived Hazard of Earcons in IT Exception Messages* (Interacting with Computers, 2013) — consonance/dissonance and pitch drive perceived urgency.
- Twenty Thousand Hertz, *The Sound of Apple* (Hugo Verweij) — real instruments, organic over sci-fi, the Watch case experiment.
- Toptal, *A Quick Guide to Designing UX Sounds* — simple for frequent, complex for high-priority; mid-range frequencies.
- Josh Comeau, *use-sound* — rising `playbackRate` on repeats.
- Leon Lin, earshot (MIT): `skills/real-sound/references/sound-design.md` §6 — take pools cycled, ±1–2 dB, ±0.3–0.5 st at most, the one-voice click.
- Related: [[color-monochromatic]], [[typography-humanity]], [[ai-default-tells]].

title: sound-spec

# Sound spec

A UI sound is a tiny file with strict numbers. Most "this sound feels wrong" complaints are a spec miss — too long for its animation, too loud next to speech, or ten milliseconds of silence before the hit — not a taste miss. Fix the spec first.

## Duration

| Category | Duration | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| Tick / toggle / snap | 40–80 ms | Finishes before the eye has registered the state change |
| Tap / press | 80–150 ms | Only in tactile products — see [[sound-decision-framework]] |
| Hover | 0 ms | Hover is silent. If a design insists, 120–200 ms and off by default |
| Send / save / confirm | 150–250 ms | One or two notes |
| Notification / receive | 200–600 ms | Longer because attention is being *requested* |
| Error | 100–200 ms | Short and low; the shake carries the rest |
| Transition (video / marketing) | 300–1000 ms | Product UI never gets these |
| Brand stinger | 1–3 s | Launch video, onboarding hero, once |

The Toptal rule ties duration to motion: **a sound should not last more than ~300 ms longer than the animation it accompanies.** A 120 ms press with an 800 ms tail is a bell, not feedback. Match the [[duration-table]].

## Loudness

| Sound | Integrated loudness | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Taps, ticks, toggles | −18 to −14 LUFS | Below speech, above silence |
| Notifications | ≈ −12 LUFS | The one class allowed to be louder |
| Launch-video master | −1 dBTP true peak; integrated loudness stated for the register (medians ≈ −18 LUFS; beat-cut sizzles median ≈ −13, 3 of 4 at −12 to −13; the three quietest films, Linear Agent, Cursor 2.0 and Claude Cowork, sit at −33 to −36) | Loudness-normalizing players (YouTube-style) turn loud masters down and do not raise quiet ones — [[launch-video-sound]] |

Peak every file at **−3 dBFS** (−1 dBTP for delivered video). Set the *design* level in the file and the *user* level in the mixer — never bake "a bit quieter" into the asset. Interface sounds stay subordinate to speech and media; convey urgency with timbre and rhythm, not volume.

Integrated LUFS is unstable on files under ~400 ms — for ticks and taps, match by ear against a reference tick at −16 LUFS and check the peak, rather than trusting the meter.

## Format

- **Mono.** Phones, laptops, and Bluetooth speakers sum to mono anyway; stereo UI sounds phase-smear and double the bytes.
- **44.1 kHz, 16-bit WAV** as the source of truth. Ship **MP3 (128 kbps)** for universal playback or **Opus/OGG** for smaller web bundles; keep WAV for native and for video timelines.
- **Zero leading silence.** Trim to the first sample above −60 dBFS. Five milliseconds of pre-roll is a visible sync error — see [[sound-motion-sync]].
- **Short tail, then cut.** Fade the last 10 ms to avoid a click; do not let reverb ride 500 ms past the event.
- **Sprite when there are many.** One decoded buffer, offsets per sound; `use-sound` and Howler support `sprite` maps.

## Frequency shaping

- High-pass at 150–200 Hz. Nothing in that band survives a laptop speaker; it only eats headroom.
- Tame 3–6 kHz by a few dB if the sound is "needly" — that is where small speakers resonate.
- Keep the body in the mid-range (500 Hz–4 kHz), where every device is honest and where the voice lives.

## When to apply

Post-processing every generated or downloaded file, and reviewing any PR that adds an audio asset. `scripts/sound-family.mjs` applies the trim and peak steps automatically; the LUFS check is yours.

## Reference

| `tick` | Bad | Good |
|---|---|---|
| Length | 640 ms, reverb tail | 70 ms, last 10 ms faded |
| Channels, rate | stereo, 48 kHz | mono, 44.1 kHz, 16-bit WAV source |
| Lead-in | 12 ms before the hit | 0 ms above −60 dBFS |
| Peak | −0.2 dBFS | −3 dBFS |
| Low end | full range | high-passed at 180 Hz |
| Shipped as | the WAV | `tick.mp3` at 128 kbps, or Opus |

Gold example: the files `scripts/sound-family.mjs` writes (leading silence trimmed below −60 dBFS, tail cut, 10 ms fade, peaked to −3 dBFS); compare yours against them.

Check: `ffprobe` each file for channels, sample rate and duration against its category band, and `ffmpeg -i tick.wav -af astats -f null -` for the peak. Then play each tick beside a −16 LUFS reference tick, by ear, on a laptop speaker.

## Gotcha

Loudness normalization tools (`loudnorm`, streaming platforms) measure *integrated* loudness across the whole file. A sound that is 60 ms of hit and 600 ms of quiet tail will be normalized *up* until the hit clips. Trim the tail first, normalize second.

## Sources

- Envato, *UI sound design with AI* — LUFS targets by class, duration bands, mono, the 0–5 ms trim.
- Toptal, *A Quick Guide to Designing UX Sounds* — the 300 ms-over-animation rule; mid-range guidance.
- uisfx.com, *UI Sound Design* — subordinate to speech, urgency by timbre not volume, one-shots vs loops.
- EBU R 128 (−23 LUFS, −1 dBTP max) and streaming practice (≈ −14 LUFS): platform reference levels, not what launch films ship at (medians −18.1 LUFS for 28 Skale client films and −18.4 for 18 acclaimed films, measured by AgentsORG 2026-09-28, `docs/research/launch-films/`).
- Related: [[duration-table]], [[sound-palette]].

# web-haptics, reconciled

Lochie Axon's web-haptics package ships a `SKILL.md` of its own (installed as `web-haptics`). When it is installed, it owns the mechanics: `npm i web-haptics`, the React / Vue / Svelte / vanilla entry points (`useWebHaptics`, `createWebHaptics`, `new WebHaptics()`), `trigger(preset)`, `cancel()`, `destroy()`, and the preset values in [[haptic-feedback]]. Its own instruction to ask the user which elements to target, and whether at the shared component or the call site, stands: ask once, prefer the shared component.

This graph owns the decision and the craft around it: [[sound-decision-framework]] (does this moment earn feedback), [[sound-motion-sync]] (which frame), [[pov]] (restraint), and [[ship-check]] (what needs a device).

## Conflicts, settled

| Its rule | This graph | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Primary button tap = medium, secondary = light | A plain press gets no haptic; one that **commits** something (pay, send, delete after confirm) gets one, on the result | Its own anti-pattern list warns against a haptic on every tap; iOS system buttons don't tap back either |
| Modal appear = medium | No haptic for a modal, sheet or menu opening, unless a long press opened it (then heavy, on the open frame) | An appearing surface is not a collision; the visual already says it |
| `buzz` preset, 1000ms at full strength | Never in product UI; demos and games only | Its own rules call long continuous vibration an anti-pattern: web haptics are brief transient pulses |
| No feature detection needed: it no-ops where unsupported | True for code paths, but the design still needs the visual and, where used, the sound to carry the moment alone | Most devices that load the page can't vibrate |
| No user setting | One "Sounds and haptics" toggle in settings, persisted, beside the sound mute ([[sound-playback-web]]); its `showSwitch` is a debug control, not that toggle | The web can't read the phone's own haptics setting |
| Fire on the async result | Agreed, and check the delayed tick on a real iPhone: the switch fallback only promises the tick that fires inside the gesture | A result that arrives after an `await` is outside it |

Where a sound fires too, the haptic and the sound start on the same frame and describe the same event: a heavy impact under a soft pop reads as two things happening ([[sound-palette]]).

## Without the companion

Use `navigator.vibrate` with the patterns in [[haptic-feedback]] for Android only, and say that iOS Safari needs the switch technique the library implements. Write no more than that by hand: it is a few hundred lines of measured fallback, the [[dependency-discipline]] case for a library.

## Sources

# MOC — Surface

The decisions that look invisible but determine whether the UI feels considered or generated. Monochromatic with restraint usually beats colorful.

## Nodes

- [[color-monochromatic]] — Monochromatic with one or two accents beats a five-color palette. Why bright/purple gradients scream AI.
- [[dark-mode]] — Never pure `#000`. Use `#18181b` or `#1a1a1a` with 90–93% opacity white text. Why pure-black breaks.
- [[shadows-whisper]] — Shadows should whisper, not announce. The default `0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,0.1)` is a tell. Concrete spec.
- [[border-radius]] — Uniform radius everywhere is lazy. Capsule buttons need full package. Nested-radius rules.
- [[visual-imperfection]] — Asymmetry in marketing only. Optical over mathematical alignment. Subtle texture/noise. Imperfect shapes — perfect geometry feels cold.
- [[contrast-and-color-scheme]] — APCA over WCAG 2 for contrast math. `<meta name="theme-color">` + `color-scheme: dark`. Interactions raise contrast. Avoid gradient banding.
- [[color-scales-oklch]] — Author in OKLCH: one hue per ramp, L anchored and evenly spaced, chroma as a clamped curve, siblings at the same fraction of their own ceiling, dark mode by remapping steps, contrast repaired by moving L only.
- [[depth-and-nesting]] — Inner radius = outer − padding; shadows elevate, borders separate; dark mode collapses shadows to a ring; 0.5px hairlines, pure black/white image outlines, mask fades, themes flip variables.
- [[z-index-strategy]] — DOM order first, then one global file of sequential layers, local values inside `isolation: isolate`; no magic numbers; what creates a stacking context or escapes a clip.
- [[overlay-dismissal-stack]] — One stack for every dismissible layer: Escape and back reach only the top one, content claims first, IME is not dismissal, backdrop press starts and ends on it, focus returns without scrolling. From Astryx.
- [[color-token-tiers]] — Primitives by hue and step, semantics by role (the only tier components use), a full role inventory, one word per concept, `accent` for the brand so `primary` stays free.

# Border radius

Border radius is a personality dial. A uniform radius across an entire UI is lazy; an intentional scale signals craft.

## The scale

```css
--radius-sm: 4px;   /* badges, micro-elements */
--radius-md: 8px;   /* inputs, small buttons */
--radius-lg: 12px;  /* cards, larger buttons */
--radius-xl: 16px;  /* modals, large surfaces */
--radius-2xl: 24px; /* hero cards, marketing */
--radius-full: 9999px; /* pills, avatars */
```

Pick one as your **default body radius** (usually `lg` for product UI) and use the others deliberately.

## The capsule-button rule

If you use `--radius-full` on a button (pill button), the **inset elements must also be pill-radius**, not square. Common mistake:

```css
/* Wrong — pill button with rectangular inset icon */
.button { border-radius: 9999px; }
.button-icon { border-radius: 0; }

/* Right — pill commits to capsule everywhere */
.button { border-radius: 9999px; padding: 8px 16px; }
.button-icon { border-radius: 9999px; }
```

## The nested-radius rule

When a rounded element contains another rounded element, the inner radius should be **smaller** than the outer radius, ideally by the gap between them:

```
outer_radius - gap = inner_radius
```

```css
.card {
  border-radius: 16px;
  padding: 8px;
}
.card-content {
  border-radius: 8px; /* 16 - 8 = 8 */
}
```

Visually, this makes the two radii feel parallel. Equal radii (both 16px) looks subtly wrong; the inner radius reads as overlapping the outer one.

## Mixing radii

Mixing `sm` and `xl` in the same screen is fine — even encouraged for hierarchy. But mixing `sm` (4px) and `md` (8px) on adjacent elements looks like a mistake. Use either same or noticeably different.

- **One radius set per page.** Every window, card and field on a page draws from the same set, as one ground, one gutter and one window shadow do (Benji Taylor, Stageshow `references/craft.md`, A page of demos: "One figure language").

## When to apply

- Building a tokens file: define the scale up front.
- Reviewing a button or card design: check the nested-radius math.
- Reviewing a pill-button design: check the inset icons.

## Reference

Bad: one `12px` on the menu row, the field, the popover and the window, so nothing reads as nested inside anything.
Good: a radius per role, the set Stageshow's kit ships: menu row `6px`, field `8px`, popover `10px`, window `12px`, chip `999px`; the card derives its inner radius and never lets it hit zero:

```css
.card { --pad: 16px; --radius: calc(var(--radius-md) + 4px);   /* 8 + 4 = 12 */
  --inner: max(4px, calc(var(--radius) - var(--pad)));          /* 12 - 16 clamps to 4, never square */
  padding: var(--pad); border-radius: var(--radius); }
.card > .well { border-radius: var(--inner); }
```

Gold example: `stageshow/kit/parts/Card.css` (the derivation above) and `stageshow/examples/looks/radix.css`, which maps a real system's 4 / 6 / 8 / 12 / full scale onto those five roles.
Check: put a still beside a screenshot of the real product at the same scale; the radii should match at a glance. If a control looks foreign, read its computed `border-radius` again instead of nudging by eye.

## Gotcha

`border-radius` larger than half the element's smaller dimension behaves the same as `border-radius: 50%`. So `border-radius: 9999px` on a small button is functionally a capsule. Useful, but be intentional about it.

## Sources

- guidelines.sh — uniform radius is lazy, nested-radius rules.
- Linear, Vercel — capsule-button discipline.
- Tailwind — radius scale conventions.
- Benji Taylor, Stageshow 1.1.1 (MIT, github.com/benjitaylor/skills, HEAD `299140f`, read 2026-11-07): `stageshow/kit/stage.css` (shape tokens), `stageshow/kit/parts/Card.css`, `stageshow/references/looks.md` (The tokens, Check it), `stageshow/references/craft.md` (Spacing and alignment, A page of demos), `stageshow/examples/looks/radix.css`.

# Monochromatic palettes

A monochromatic palette — one hue across a wide range of lightness values, plus one or two true accent colors — almost always looks more considered than a five-color palette assembled from "what feels good."

## What to do

1. Pick **one neutral hue** as your base. Pure gray is fine. A subtle warm gray (slight yellow undertone) or cool gray (slight blue undertone) is better.
2. Generate **8–12 steps** of that hue from near-white to near-black. Tailwind's `slate`, `zinc`, `stone`, `gray`, and `neutral` are good starting points. Linear, Vercel, Notion all use this approach.
3. Pick **one true accent** for primary actions. Saturated, intentional. Don't dilute it across the UI — earn its use.
4. Optionally pick **one second accent** for warnings or success states. These should be subdued, not loud. If the brand accent is green, success takes a different hue, or users can't tell "primary action" from "it worked".

Three derivation rules keep the set coherent: neutrals share the brand's temperature (a blue brand wants cool greys; warm greys fight it, and an untinted `#808080` reads as placeholder); light tints come from lowering chroma in OKLCH, not lowering opacity, which greys them out; and disabled gets its own muted token rather than `opacity`, which passes contrast on one background and fails on the next ([[color-token-tiers]]).

That's it. The whole palette is ~14 tokens. Most "design systems" with 60 color tokens are overcomplicating.

## What to avoid

- **Bright purple gradients** (any of the `purple → indigo → fuchsia` variants). Universal AI tell.
- **Five-color brand palettes** with no hierarchy. Every color competes for attention; the eye finds nothing to land on.
- **Adjacent hues without intent.** Red + orange + yellow with no narrative reason is muddy.
- **High saturation everywhere.** Monochrome at 5–10% saturation reads as restrained and confident.

## When to apply

- Designing a new product UI from scratch.
- Refactoring a tokens file that has accumulated 60+ colors.
- Reviewing a landing page or PR where the team has added a new accent for "emphasis."

## Why this works

The eye can only track 2–3 colors at once. A monochrome palette gives the user a single tonal language to read; the one accent stands out by *being* the deviation. A multi-color palette dilutes attention — there's nothing to deviate *from*.

## Reference

Bad: a `linear-gradient(135deg, #7c3aed, #db2777 60%, #f59e0b)` ground, a gradient-clipped title, a lilac-tinted card and `#a78bfa` metadata: it says "generated" before a word is read.
Good: one warm neutral family and one accent, spent once. The whole set Stageshow's kit starts from:

| Role | Light | Dark |
|---|---|---|
| canvas / surface / well | `#f6f5f4` / `#fff` / `#efeeec` | `#111113` / `#1a1a1d` / `#0a0a0b` |
| text strong / text / faint | `#262628` / `#7a7a7d` / `#9a9a9d` | `#ececee` / `#9d9da1` / `#6c6c70` |
| accent (the live thing only) | `#3b82f6` | `#3b82f6` |

Gold example: `stageshow/teaching/style.tsx` (`style-purple`, with its values in `style.css`) for the pair, and `stageshow/examples/dark-bento/` for a grayscale still whose one marked row carries the story.
Check: switch the stage to grayscale (Stageshow's `palette="mono"` sends the accent and every status to `#1a1a1a`, `#f2f2f2` on dark). If the thing acted on vanishes, hue was carrying the hierarchy alone: mark it with a solid step in surface and weight, never a translucent wash.

## Gotcha

"Monochromatic" doesn't mean "boring." A monochrome palette with rich texture, considered typography (see [[typography-humanity]]), and tight motion (see [[duration-table]]) feels luxurious. A multi-color palette with bad type and bad motion feels cluttered.

See also [[dark-mode]] for the dark-mode variant of these tokens, [[ai-default-tells]] for what to remove.

## Sources

- guidelines.sh — "Monochromatic with subtle accents; avoid bright/purple gradients."
- Linear, Vercel, Notion — examples of monochrome-with-one-accent in production.
- Emil Kowalski's design-engineering practice, distilled by AgentsORG — status hue, neutral temperature, tints and disabled tokens.

title: color-scales-oklch
summary: Author in OKLCH. One hue per ramp, L anchored 0.97→0.22 and spaced evenly, chroma as a curve clamped per step, siblings at the same fraction of their own ceiling, dark mode by remapping steps, contrast repaired by moving L only.
tags: [surface, color, oklch, palette, contrast, dark-mode]

# Color scales in OKLCH

An `oklch()` value is a measurement, not a recipe: L is how bright the color actually looks, C how vivid, H where it sits. Because the numbers track perception, palette math, contrast repair, and dark mode become arithmetic. Everything new is authored in OKLCH; hex survives only where a third-party consumer parses hex. This node builds the ramps that [[color-monochromatic]] asks for and feeds the checks in [[contrast-and-color-scheme]].

## Reading a value

`oklch(0.586 0.222 17.6)` — L 0–1, C from 0 (gray) to ~0.4 at the extreme, H 0–360 (≈20 red, 90 yellow, 145 green, 195 cyan, 260 blue, 330 pink). Alpha goes after a slash, never as a fourth comma argument. Three decimals is plenty.

## Building a ramp

1. **Anchor L and space evenly.** Step 50 ≈ L 0.97, step 950 ≈ L 0.22, linear between. Even L spacing is the point: every adjacent pair looks equally far apart. Never run to L 0 or 1; chroma collapses there and the ends stop reading as the hue.
2. **Shape chroma as a curve.** Express each step's C as a fraction of that step's sRGB ceiling: ~30% at the extremes rising to ~85% around 400–500. Tints stay airy, shades stay rich, nothing leaves the gamut.
3. **Clamp per step.** The ceiling `maxC(L, H)` moves with lightness, so a saturated base necessarily loses absolute chroma toward both ends. That is the gamut's geometry, not a defect.
4. **Hue is fixed for all eleven steps.** Converting an inherited scale and finding more than ~10° of hue spread end to end means it drifts visibly; rebuild it on the mid-tone hue.

```css
--berry-50:  oklch(0.97 0.007 330);
--berry-400: oklch(0.67 0.251 330);   /* chroma peaks where this hue's gamut is widest */
--berry-950: oklch(0.22 0.03 330);
```

## Families of hues

Brand + success + warning feel like one system when each `-500` sits at the **same L** and each hue takes the **same fraction of its own ceiling**, never the same absolute C. Cyan is cramped at every lightness; violet is roomy. One copied C value over-saturates the roomy hues and flattens the tight ones.

## Dark mode is a remap

Keep one scale and swap which steps the roles point at: `--surface` 50 ↔ 950, `--ink` 950 ↔ 50, 200 ↔ 800, 300 ↔ 700. Perceptually linear L keeps the pairs as distinct after the flip as before. Never hand-pick a second palette. Desaturate brand accents 20–30% if they vibrate on dark, and keep the top canvas the lightest dark surface — see [[dark-mode]].

## Contrast lives in the L gap

Chroma and hue barely move contrast. To repair a failing pair, push the foreground's L away from the background's L and leave C and H alone; raising saturation "to make it pop" does nothing. Fast triage: a surface with L > 0.6 wants dark text; near-white grounds (L ≥ 0.85) want foreground L ≤ 0.45; near-black grounds (L ≤ 0.25) want L ≥ 0.75. Then run the real check: APCA |Lc| ≥ 75 for body (90 preferred), ≥ 60 other content text, ≥ 45 large, ≥ 30 non-text and disabled; WCAG 2 4.5:1 body, 3:1 large, when compliance language names it. The thresholds live in [[contrast-and-color-scheme]].

## Gamut and P3

Syntactically valid values can exceed what sRGB shows. Clamp C holding L and H, and layer wide-gamut chroma behind `@media (color-gamut: p3)` on top of the sRGB-safe base; ceilings, fallbacks and migration steps are in [[oklch-gamut-and-migration]]. Tailwind v4 is authored in OKLCH; custom `@theme` scales should be too, and `/50` opacity suffixes compose out of the box.

## When to apply

Any new palette, any hex → OKLCH migration (swap values only; keep keywords, gradient shape, and hex-expecting config), any "is this readable" question, any dark theme.

## Reference

Bad: `--blue-100: hsl(220 90% 95%)` to `--blue-900: hsl(220 90% 15%)`, spaced on HSL lightness: the mid steps bunch, the tints drift violet.
Good: one hue, L stepped by exactly 0.075 from 0.97 to 0.22, C as a share of each step's ceiling:

| Step | 50 | 100 | 200 | 300 | 400 | 500 | 600 | 700 | 800 | 900 | 950 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| L | .970 | .895 | .820 | .745 | .670 | .595 | .520 | .445 | .370 | .295 | .220 |

Read it as triage before the real APCA check: on a step-50 ground the first text candidate is 700 (L ≤ 0.45), and on step 950 it is 200 (L ≥ 0.75).
Gold example: the `--berry-*` ramp above, then Tailwind v4's `theme.css` (`--color-blue-50: oklch(97% 0.014 254.604)`) as a real OKLCH palette to measure yours against.
Check: print L and H per step. Adjacent L deltas should match to about 0.01 and H should spread under 10° end to end; Tailwind's own blue runs from H 254.6 at 50 to 267.9 at 950, so even a shipped scale needs the check.
Benji's call differs: Liveline derives every variant of its one line colour via HSL (benji.org/liveline), and Stageshow darkens accent text with `color-mix(in srgb, var(--ss-accent) 82%, #000)`. Both are fine for a few variants of one known colour; neither is a way to build an eleven-step ramp.

## Gotcha

HSL's lightness is decorative — `hsl(55 100% 50%)` is nearly white-bright and `hsl(255 100% 50%)` is dark. A ramp spaced on HSL's L inherits that lie and its tints slide toward violet. Never generate scales in HSL.

# Colour token tiers

Naming is what makes a palette usable by someone who didn't build it, and the tier split is what makes it themeable. A codebase that applies `--blue-600` in components has no seam: adding dark mode later means auditing every usage to learn which meant "the accent" and which just wanted blue. [[color-scales-oklch]] makes the values; this node names them.

## Two tiers

**Primitives** name a value — the ramp, by hue and step: `--blue-600`, `--neutral-200`. A primitive says what the colour *is*, so it never changes meaning between themes and is never applied in a component.

**Semantics** name a job and point at a primitive: `--color-text-secondary: var(--neutral-700)`. Components reference only this tier. Dark mode, a white-label theme and an increased-contrast variant all repoint semantics and leave primitives and components untouched ([[dark-mode]]).

A third, component tier (`--color-button-danger-bg`) is for a component that deliberately diverges. One is a documented exception; twenty means the semantic tier is missing roles.

## Build against the role inventory

The system is complete when every role has a token. Build against this list, not as components ask, or the palette ends up shaped like whichever screen came first.

| Group | Roles |
|---|---|
| Surfaces | page, surface, raised (menus, popovers), sunken (inputs, wells), overlay scrim |
| Text | primary, secondary, disabled, inverse, on-accent |
| Borders | subtle, default, strong, focus ring, separator |
| Accent | subtle background, border, solid, solid hover, text |
| Status | per status the product shows: subtle background, border, solid, text |

**Separator and border are two roles** even when they share a value today: a separator divides content, a border encloses a control. They diverge the first time someone restyles inputs.

**Use a token only in its role.** A border token borrowed as caption text works until borders get lighter, and the caption goes with them. A role with no token gets a token.

## One grammar, one word per concept

Neutral roles lead with the property: `--color-{bg|text|border}-{variant}-{state}`. Accent and status lead with the role: `--color-{accent|danger}-{subtle|border|solid|text}-{state}`. Pick `text`, `bg`, `border`, `accent` and never mix in `fg`, `foreground`, `stroke`, `brand`. A reader who has seen `--color-text-primary` must be able to guess `--color-text-disabled`.

**Reserve `primary` for one meaning.** `--color-primary` (the brand) beside `--color-text-primary` (body text) is the most common collision there is. Call the brand `accent`.

| Name | Problem | Instead |
|---|---|---|
| `--color-blue-button` | appearance at the semantic tier | `--color-accent-solid` |
| `--color-sidebar-gray` | named for its first use | `--color-bg-surface` |
| `--color-light-gray` | the dark one in dark mode | a primitive, `--neutral-200` |
| `--color-text-2` | numbers carry no meaning | `--color-text-secondary` |

## In Tailwind v4

Names in `@theme` become the API: declare both tiers there and you get `bg-accent-solid` beside `bg-blue-600`. The doubling in `text-text-secondary` is the price — accept it or follow the project's existing convention. Repoint semantics for dark in a `.dark` block outside `@theme`, without `inline`, so utilities read the variable at render time. A raw `bg-blue-600` in a component is the thing to flag.

## Reference

Bad: an icon coloured with `--neutral-alpha-3` (a primitive at 8% black): it paints darker wherever two strokes cross, and the component has to change for dark mode.
Good: a semantic role per job, repointed per theme, with the derived ones computed from the primitive so a rebrand fixes them for free (adapted from Stageshow `kit/stage.css`):

```css
:root { --color-icon: #707074; --color-accent-solid: var(--blue-500);       /* icon opaque: strokes never stack */
  --color-accent-text: color-mix(in srgb, var(--color-accent-solid) 82%, #000); }  /* darkened to read on white */
.dark { --color-icon: #9a9aa0;
  --color-accent-text: color-mix(in srgb, var(--color-accent-solid) 70%, #fff); }  /* lightened for near-black */
```

Gold example: `stageshow/examples/looks/radix.css`, where each role carries its source step in a comment (`--ss-text: #60646c; /* slate 11 */`): primitives on one side, semantics on the other, nothing applied raw.
Check: switch every theme the product ships (Stageshow's stage ships light, dark, blueprint and glass themes off one role set) without touching a component, then grep the components for a hex or a primitive name: the count is zero.

## Gotcha

`bg-accent-solid/50` is fine for a wash and wrong under text: a colour with alpha renders differently on every background, so no single contrast measurement describes it. Anything carrying text sits on a solid token ([[contrast-and-color-scheme]]).

# Contrast and color-scheme

The contrast and theme-integration choices that decide whether dark mode actually works and whether browser chrome blends in.

Distinct from [[color-monochromatic]] (which defines the *palette*) and [[dark-mode]] (which defines *specific colors*) — this node is about contrast math and browser integration.

## APCA over WCAG 2

The WCAG 2 contrast formula (the 4.5:1 / 3:1 ratios) is a 1980s model and badly approximates real perception. **APCA** (Accessible Perceptual Contrast Algorithm, the WCAG 3 candidate) is the modern alternative.

### APCA thresholds

| Use | Lc (lightness contrast) |
|---|---|
| Body text (fluent reading) | 75+ (90 preferred) |
| Other content text, UI labels | 60+ |
| Large or heavy text (headlines) | 45+ |
| Non-text essentials (icons, borders, focus rings), placeholder, disabled | 30+ (floor, not target) |

APCA is signed (positive for dark-on-light, negative for light-on-dark) and the threshold magnitudes are the same in both directions. Tools: [APCA Contrast Calculator](https://www.myndex.com/APCA/), `apca-w3` npm package.

WCAG 2 still gets you legal compliance in most jurisdictions: 4.5:1 body, 3:1 for large text (~24px, or bold from ~18.5px) and UI components. APCA gets you UI that actually reads. Run both; pass both. Repair a failing pair by moving L only ([[color-scales-oklch]]).

## Interactions raise contrast, not lower

A hover state should make the element *more* contrasty, not less. A pressed state should be *more* contrasty than hover. Disabled is the only state that lowers contrast.

```css
.button {
  background: var(--bg-elevated);     /* baseline */
  border-color: var(--border-default);
}
.button:hover {
  background: var(--bg-elevated-hover);  /* slightly more contrast */
  border-color: var(--border-strong);
}
.button:active {
  background: var(--bg-elevated-active); /* even more */
}
.button:disabled {
  background: var(--bg-disabled);        /* drops contrast — expected */
  color: var(--text-disabled);           /* a token, never opacity */
}
```

Disabled takes dedicated tokens, not `opacity`: opacity lets whatever sits behind show through, so the same button passes on one surface and fails on the next ([[color-token-tiers]]).

- **A filled button's hover is one step of its own color**, `color-mix(in srgb, var(--accent), #000 10%)`, never a swap to gray: the white label gains contrast instead of losing the button's meaning (Benji Taylor, Stageshow `kit/controls/Button.css`).

## Browser chrome integration

### `<meta name="theme-color">`

Sets the address-bar / browser-chrome color on mobile (iOS Safari, Android Chrome). Without it, the chrome stays its default white/grey and your app's background ends abruptly at the bezel.

```html
<meta name="theme-color" content="#18181b" media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)">
<meta name="theme-color" content="#ffffff" media="(prefers-color-scheme: light)">
```

### `color-scheme` CSS property

Tells the browser whether scrollbars, form controls, and `<input>` defaults should render in their light or dark variant.

```css
:root {
  color-scheme: light dark;  /* respect user preference */
}
.dark {
  color-scheme: dark;  /* force dark */
}
```

Without `color-scheme`, dark-mode pages get *light* scrollbars and *light* native `<select>` dropdowns — instantly disorienting. Declare only the schemes you actually designed: a light-only app that writes `light dark` hands dark-OS users dark native controls on a white page. Light-only declares `color-scheme: light`.

## Gradient banding

A gradient between two close colors (e.g. `#1a1a1a → #1c1c1c`) shows visible "banding" — concentric rings instead of smooth gradient. The fix: add a `background-image` of subtle noise.

```css
.surface {
  background:
    linear-gradient(to bottom, #1a1a1a, #1c1c1c),
    url("data:image/svg+xml,...noise.svg");
  background-blend-mode: overlay;
}
```

Or use a `<svg>` filter with `<feTurbulence>` for procedural noise.

## When to apply

- Setting up a new design tokens file: include APCA contrast checks in your design-system docs.
- Implementing dark mode: add `<meta name="theme-color">` and the matching `color-scheme` the day the dark theme exists, not before.
- Reviewing a hover state: confirm it *increases* contrast, doesn't decrease it.
- Designing a hero gradient: test on macOS with night-shift on — banding shows up.

## Reference

Quiet is not faint. The same sharing panel on a `#e9edef` tinted ground, from Stageshow's `surface-contrast` pair:

| | Panel | Heading / body | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bad | `#e6eaec`, one step off the ground | `#a4adb3` / `#aeb7bd` | `#eef1f3` on `#c6cfd5` |
| Good | `#fff` with a `#d9dfe2` edge | `#444` / `#777` | `#fff` on `#333` |

The bad side is calm and unreadable at once; the good side is just as quiet and every word reads.
Gold example: `stageshow/teaching/composition.tsx` (`surface-contrast`; values in `composition.css`).
Check: measure each label against the surface it actually sits on, not the page background, then view the still at its shown size and at 390px wide without zooming. Any word you have to lean in for fails, whatever the ratio said.

## Gotcha

`color-scheme: dark` is *per element*, not per page. If you set it on `.dark` and a child element doesn't inherit, native form controls inside that child render light. Set on `:root` if you want global effect.

- Emil Kowalski's design-engineering practice, distilled by AgentsORG — disabled tokens, declared schemes.

summary: Never pure #000. Near-black surfaces that get lighter as they rise, remapped from the light scale rather than inverted. Accents desaturated 20–30%. Dividers solid, white rings only for elevation. Opacity text only on one known surface. A half-finished dark mode is a blocker.

# Dark mode

Dark mode is its own designed theme, derived from the same scale as light mode by remapping which steps each role uses. The most common mistake is pure black (`#000000`) under pure white (`#ffffff`): the contrast is harsh, the surfaces feel cheap, and OLED screens smear scrolling text.

## Background

Use a near-black with a slight hue bias.

```css
--bg-base: #18181b;        /* Zinc 950 — most products */
--bg-elevated: #1f1f23;    /* +1: cards */
--bg-overlay: #2a2a2f;     /* +2: menus, modals */
--bg-floating: #35353a;    /* +3, rarely needed */
```

In light mode elevation is shadow; in dark mode it is a **lighter surface**, and the topmost layer is the lightest. Pure `#000` is for photo backdrops, video chrome, and OLED themes that opt in.

## Remap, don't invert

Keep one scale and point the roles at mirrored steps (50 ↔ 950, 200 ↔ 800), as [[color-scales-oklch]] describes. That is not the same as inverting colors: re-check every pair, because warm yellows turn muddy and brand accents vibrate. **Desaturate accents 20–30%** on dark surfaces.

## Text

White at 90–93% reads softer than full white:

```css
--text-primary: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.92);
--text-secondary: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.62);
```

Opacity text is safe only on a **single known surface**. Over an elevated card, an image or a tinted panel, the alpha mixes with whatever sits beneath and the contrast changes. Everywhere else, use specific solid tokens (`--text-secondary-on-elevated`) and check them against their real surface.

## Borders and rings

- **Dividers are solid** dark greys (around `#2a2a2a` on `#18181b`): table rules, list separators, input edges. An alpha white line glows.
- **White rings are for elevation only.** Shadows vanish on dark, so a raised card swaps its shadow stack for one ring, `0 0 0 1px rgb(255 255 255 / .09)` ([[depth-and-nesting]]). Images take a white 10% inset outline.
- **A light document over a dark workspace stays a light document**, with its own dark ink and its own edge; inheriting the workspace's light text flattens both materials (Benji Taylor, Stageshow `references/craft.md`; `teaching/scenes.tsx`, `material-contrast`).

## Assets

SVG icons and logos with a hardcoded `fill="#fff"` or `#000` break in one of the two themes. Use `fill="currentColor"` (or a CSS variable) so they follow the text color; keep a separate asset only for full-colour marks.

## When to apply

Any product with a theme toggle or `prefers-color-scheme` support. Pair with the browser-chrome rules in [[contrast-and-color-scheme]].

## Reference

Bad: a `#000` page, a `#000` window with a violet glow around it, and every status pill lit green.
Good: each layer one step lighter than the one under it, a hairline on top instead of a glow, one colour lit once (Stageshow `kit/stage.css` dark tokens):

```css
--canvas: #111113; --surface: #1a1a1d; --chrome: #1d1d20; --raised: #26262a;  /* satellites go on raised */
--text-strong: #ececee; --text: #9d9da1; --text-faint: #6c6c70;            /* opaque, safe on any layer */
--shadow-hero: 0 0 0 1px rgba(255,255,255,.08), 0 30px 60px -12px rgba(0,0,0,.6);
```

Benji's call differs: his dark text tokens are opaque grays rather than white at 92% and 62%, which sidesteps the one-known-surface limit above, and his hero keeps a deep black drop under the white hairline instead of the ring alone.
Gold example: `stageshow/examples/dark-hero/` (a `#09090b` page, the window a step lighter, its chrome a step lighter again, one success green on the new row) and `stageshow/examples/linear/` for satellites on the raised surface.
Check: screenshot the dark theme on its own; a light pass does not prove dark. Then desaturate the shot: the stacking order should still read from the surface steps alone.

## Gotcha

A half-finished dark mode that users can reach is a blocker, not a nit: one white modal, a light native `<select>`, or a black-on-dark logo makes the whole product look broken. If the theme isn't done, don't expose the toggle and don't declare `color-scheme: dark`.

- Material Design 3 — dark theme elevation by surface tint.

summary: Inner radius = outer − padding. Shadows elevate, borders separate. Dark mode collapses shadows to a ring. Hairlines at 0.5px on retina, image outlines pure black or white at 10%, fades by mask, themes by flipping variables.

# Depth and nesting

Depth comes from how surfaces meet: the radius where they nest, the shadow or border that separates them, the gradient that fades them out. Most interfaces that feel "off" fail here, and every fix is cheap. This node is the mechanical layer under [[shadows-whisper]] (the *weight* of shadows) and [[border-radius]] (the *scale* of radii).

## Derive nested radii

A rounded child inside a rounded parent gets its radius by subtraction: **inner = outer − padding**. Copying the parent's radius pinches the corner gap, and it is the most frequent single giveaway of an unpolished UI. Past a ~24px gap the surfaces read as independent and each radius is picked on its own.

```css
.dialog { border-radius: 16px; padding: 6px; }
.dialog-body { border-radius: 10px; }   /* 16 − 6 */
```

## Shadows elevate, borders separate

Pick by the job the line is doing:

- **Raised** (cards, menus, popovers, dialogs, hover lift, anything crossing mixed backgrounds) → a stacked translucent shadow. Transparency composites with whatever is underneath, so one token works everywhere; a solid border color was tuned for exactly one background.
- **Separated** (row dividers, table gridlines, form-field edges, dense hairline rules) → keep the border. A visible input edge is an accessibility feature; converting it to a shadow costs users and gains nothing.

```css
:root {
  --elevation-raised: 0 0 0 1px rgb(0 0 0 / .05), 0 1px 3px rgb(0 0 0 / .05), 0 4px 10px -4px rgb(0 0 0 / .05);
}
.dark { --elevation-raised: 0 0 0 1px rgb(255 255 255 / .09); }   /* shadows vanish on dark; a ring does the job */
.panel { box-shadow: var(--elevation-raised); transition: box-shadow 150ms ease-out; }
```

Three ingredients: a 1px spread standing in for the border, a tight crisp layer, a wide soft ambient layer. On hover transition `box-shadow` only. In dark mode every stack collapses to one low-opacity white ring, because there is nothing dark enough for a shadow to fall on.

## Hairlines, outlines, fades

- **Hairlines at 0.5px on ≥2× displays** via a media-query variable, 1px fallback. Retina dividers at 1px read heavy.
- **Every image gets a 1px inset outline** — `outline: 1px solid rgb(0 0 0 / .1); outline-offset: -1px`, white at 10% in dark. Never a tinted neutral or the accent: a tinted line picks up the surface behind it and reads as grime.
- **Eased gradients**, never two-stop linear ones between solids (they band). **Fades by `mask-image`**, not a gradient overlay: a mask composites with any background. Never fade scrollable content; it hides what the user is scrolling toward.
- **One depth cue per surface.** Border *and* shadow *and* ring *and* gradient on one card is hedging.
- **The shadow goes on the outlined shape, never a wrapper**, and a ring drawn as `inset 0 0 0 1px` never adds to the padding (Benji Taylor, Stageshow `references/framing.md` rule 8; `kit/parts/Card.css`).

## Themes flip variables, not classes

Define a numbered scale as CSS variables and swap the values under the dark selector. Per-component `dark:` overrides scatter the theme across the codebase and rot on the first palette change.

## When to apply

Styling any card, container, dialog, dropdown, or image; any nested rounded surface; any dark-mode pass. Review symptom → fix: pinched corners → derive the radius; card looks stamped on → shadow token; cards vanish in dark → ring; stripes in a gradient → eased stops; dirty image edges → pure black or white outline; `dark:` everywhere → flip variables.

## Reference

A shadow per relationship, not one shadow for everything (Stageshow `kit/stage.css`, light theme):

| Layer | Shadow | Why this one |
|---|---|---|
| Hero window on the page | `0 0 0 1px rgba(0,0,0,.06), 0 30px 60px -12px rgba(50,50,93,.25), 0 18px 36px -18px rgba(0,0,0,.3)` | the ring keeps the top edge visible on a light ground |
| Satellite over the hero | `0 0 0 1px rgba(0,0,0,.04), 0 14px 32px -8px rgba(50,50,93,.24), 0 4px 10px -4px rgba(0,0,0,.1)` | tight on purpose: a wide blur smears on a white window |
| Lone small window on open ground | `0 0 0 1px rgba(50,50,93,.06), 0 24px 48px -24px rgba(50,50,93,.18)` | the satellite's dark contact reads harsh here |
| Card at rest | `inset 0 0 0 1px var(--line), 0 1px 2px rgba(0,0,0,.04)` | ring inside, so the padding stays even |

Benji's call differs on dark: Stageshow keeps the white hairline plus a deep black drop (`0 14px 32px -8px rgba(0,0,0,.7)` on a satellite) and moves satellites onto a lighter `#26262a` surface, rather than collapsing to the ring alone.
Gold example: `stageshow/examples/overlap/` (a checkout card in front of its dashboard, stopping inside the sidebar so it covers filler, never the table) and `stageshow/examples/cards/` (a sunken group whose radius is taken from its card's).
Check: count the distinct `box-shadow` values on the page; each must map to one row above. Then look at the satellite over the white window at 100%: a gray halo around it means the wide token went on the wrong layer.

## Gotcha

The shadow-over-border rule is about *elevation*, not every line. Agents that read it as "delete all borders" strip the edges off inputs and table cells, which is a regression, not polish.

- Benji Taylor, Stageshow 1.1.1 (MIT, github.com/benjitaylor/skills, HEAD `299140f`, read 2026-11-07): `stageshow/kit/stage.css` (shadow tokens, light and dark), `stageshow/kit/parts/Card.css`, `stageshow/references/framing.md` (rule 8, Recipes), `stageshow/references/craft.md` (A page of demos), `stageshow/examples/overlap/`, `stageshow/examples/cards/`.

# Gradient interpolation

The same two stops make three different gradients depending on the space they are mixed in, and the difference lives in the middle. Choosing the space is a look decision, so it is never a review finding by itself — a gradient that goes grey, bands, or puts text on an unmeasured region is.

## Three spaces

```css
background: linear-gradient(#3b82f6, #ec4899);          /* sRGB: the default — midpoint darkens and mutes */
background: linear-gradient(in oklab, #3b82f6, #ec4899); /* even brightness across: the best default */
background: linear-gradient(in oklch, #3b82f6, #ec4899); /* round the hue wheel: vivid throughout */
```

sRGB and OKLab are **rectangular**: they mix along a straight line through the colour space. OKLCH is **polar**: it interpolates the hue angle, so it arcs through every hue between the stops — which is why it stays saturated and why it can produce a hue nobody asked for. Blue to pink in OKLCH routes through purple; that is either the look or a surprise.

## The grey dead zone

Two hues on opposite sides of the wheel sit either side of the neutral axis. A straight line between them passes near grey and the middle goes lifeless. Two fixes: switch to a polar space, which routes round the axis, or add a third stop between them and keep the space. In a polar space you also choose the direction: `in oklch shorter hue` (usually right) or `longer hue` (sweeps most of the spectrum).

## Banding and text

- **Banding** shows on large areas with little contrast between stops on 8-bit displays: a hero-wide gradient steps visibly. Widen the stops' contrast, shrink the area, or add a faint noise layer ([[contrast-and-color-scheme]]; a rendered film bands too — see [[gotchas]]).
- **Text on a gradient** has a different contrast at every pixel, so one number describes nothing. Measure the worst region, not the average, or put a scrim behind the text ([[wcag-thresholds]]).
- **Strong colour stays behind an opaque surface.** A vivid ground does not also need vivid controls, a coloured shadow and a glow; give a banded ground a hierarchy of a dominant field, a supporting colour and an optional narrow highlight (Benji Taylor, Stageshow `references/backgrounds.md`).

## When to apply

Any `linear-`, `radial-` or `conic-gradient`, a mesh-style hero, a chart fill, a hex → OKLCH migration of a gradient (keep its shape and stops; only add a space if the look should change).

## Reference

```css
/* Bad: opposite hues mixed in sRGB, the headline set straight on the muddy middle */
.hero { background: linear-gradient(90deg, #3b82f6, #f59e0b); }
/* Good: one family, a chosen 122deg direction, dominant / supporting / highlight bands (Stageshow bg-ground--bands) */
.hero { background: linear-gradient(122deg, #1c315f 0% 47%, #3d74bd 47% 82%, #cbdfee 82% 100%); }
/* Good, smooth: the same family blended, the space named, the middle stop placed by hand */
.hero { background: linear-gradient(122deg in oklab, #1c315f, #3d74bd 60%, #cbdfee); }
```

Hard stops leave no midpoint to interpolate, so the space question disappears; explicit middle stops shrink it to a few short spans.
Gold example: `stageshow/examples/backgrounds/` (six vivid gradients that change direction, value and material instead of recolouring one glow), with `stageshow/teaching/style.tsx` (`style-purple`) as the fault to compare against.
Check: render at the hero's real size and sample the midpoint: if its chroma sits well below both stops, it is the grey dead zone. Then count effects on the frame: the ground, and nothing else glowing.

## Gotcha

A violet-to-blue gradient across a hero is still the generated-page tell however well it interpolates ([[ai-default-tells]]). The space decides how a gradient mixes, not whether the page should have one.

## Sources

title: oklch-gamut-and-migration
summary: Chroma ceilings swing with hue and lightness — clamp C holding L and H, layer P3 behind a media query over an sRGB base, add a hex floor only for pre-2023 browsers, and migrate hex/rgb/hsl to OKLCH value-for-value, reporting every change.
tags: [surface, color, oklch, gamut, p3, migration]
---

# OKLCH gamut and migration

OKLCH can name colors no screen shows. Whether a value renders faithfully depends on its lightness, its hue and the display's gamut, so high chroma is checked, clamped and progressively enhanced rather than trusted. Migration to OKLCH is a value-for-value substitution that changes nothing else in the file. [[color-scales-oklch]] builds ramps on top of this.

## Ceilings move

Approximate sRGB chroma ceilings:

| L | Roomiest | Tightest |
|---|---|---|
| 0.5 | violet H 285 ≈ 0.29; red H 25 ≈ 0.20 | cyan H 195 ≈ 0.09 |
| 0.7 | pink H 330 ≈ 0.31 | cyan, still cramped |
| 0.9 | spring green H 130 ≈ 0.24 | — |

A threefold spread at one lightness is why two hues never share an absolute C. Plan for muted teals in sRGB.

## Clamp, don't let the browser map

An out-of-gamut value gets mapped by the browser in a way you didn't pick. Keep L and H, lower C to the boundary: `oklch(0.6 0.31 20)` becomes `oklch(0.6 0.241 20)`.

## P3 as enhancement

Display P3 is a superset of sRGB, roughly a quarter larger, mostly in greens, reds and pinks. Ship the safe value, then override:

```css
.cta { background: oklch(0.66 0.2 330); }
@media (color-gamut: p3) { .cta { background: oklch(0.66 0.32 330); } }
```

At L 0.66, H 330 sRGB tops out near 0.30 and P3 near 0.33. Only for browsers older than 2023, put a hex value first and wrap both layers in `@supports (color: oklch(1 0 0))`.

## Migrating a file

1. Hex first (easy to spot), then `rgb()`/`rgba()`, then `hsl()`/`hsla()`.
2. Alpha moves behind a slash: `rgba(255,255,255,.12)` → `oklch(1 0 0 / 0.12)`. Opaque values carry no `/ 1`.
3. Never convert keywords (`currentColor`, `transparent`, `inherit`), gradient interpolation hints (`in oklab`), or config a third-party library parses as hex.
4. Keep comments, order and indentation; the diff shows only color values.
5. Re-run contrast on any pair that mattered ([[contrast-and-color-scheme]]): the conversion is exact, but colors picked by eye in hex often measure slightly off.

In Tailwind v4, re-express every `@theme` color, then hunt the `theme()` calls and hardcoded hex that duplicated them.

## Reporting

Group changes by file; list each declaration's old value beside its new one with a short clause naming the rule (out of gamut, hue drift, too little L gap). Every touched line, not a highlight reel.

## Reference

One migration hunk, written the way the report lists it:

```css
--accent: oklch(0.623 0.188 259.8);    /* was #3b82f6: exact conversion */
--ink: oklch(0 0 0 / 0.06);            /* was rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.06): alpha behind the slash */
--hover: color-mix(in srgb, var(--accent) 90%, oklch(0 0 0)); /* `in srgb` kept: a new space changes the mix */
--cta: oklch(0.6 0.241 20);            /* was oklch(0.6 0.31 20): out of gamut, C clamped, L and H held */
```

- Bad: swapping `#3b82f6` for a punchier `oklch(0.623 0.214 259.8)` "while you're there". Good: `oklch(0.623 0.188 259.8)`. Same L and H, but C 0.214 pushes blue past sRGB at that L and H: a recolor, not a conversion.
- Gold example: CSS Color Level 4, `oklch()`, and the `color-gamut` media feature. Re-read them before you trust a table of ceilings.
- Check: screenshot the page before and after on an sRGB screen and diff the two. No channel should move by more than 1/255, and `git diff --word-diff` should show color values only. Only the P3 block may look different, and only on a P3 screen.

## Gotcha

Raising the base token's chroma to get "more punch" breaks on sRGB screens. The punch belongs in the P3 layer; the base stays inside sRGB.

## Sources

- Emil Kowalski's design-engineering practice, distilled by AgentsORG.
- CSS Color Level 4 (`oklch()`, `color-gamut`).
- Related: [[color-scales-oklch]], [[contrast-and-color-scheme]], [[gradient-interpolation]], [[color-token-tiers]].

title: overlay-dismissal-stack
summary: Every dismissible layer — dialog, drawer, sheet, popover, menu, combobox list, tooltip — joins one stack. Escape and platform close requests reach only the topmost layer, content can claim Escape first, an IME composition is never a dismissal, a backdrop closes only when the press starts and ends on it, the top layer consumes its own outside press, and focus returns to the opener without scrolling. From Meta's Astryx.
tags: [surface, overlays, dialog, popover, escape, focus, astryx]
---

# The overlay dismissal stack

Nested overlays fail in one of three ways: one Escape closes the menu **and** the dialog under it; a text selection dragged past a dialog's edge closes the dialog; or closing returns focus to the top of the page and scrolls it. Astryx prevents all three with a single dismissal stack that every layered surface registers with. [[z-index-strategy]] decides what paints on top; this decides what *closes*.

## Rules

1. **Every dismissible layer participates.** Dialogs, drawers, bottom sheets, popovers, menus, combobox lists, date calendars, pinned tooltips and context menus all register. One that doesn't is the one that steals Escape.
2. **One request, one layer.** An unclaimed Escape goes to exactly one layer, the topmost present one. It either closes or refuses; it never falls through to the layer behind.
3. **Platform close requests use the same rule** (Android back, the `CloseWatcher` close request): topmost only.
4. **Nesting beats placement.** When a layer knows its parent (a menu opened from inside a dialog), that outranks DOM or portal order.
5. **Content claims first.** The shared Escape listener runs in the bubble phase and stands down when the content already handled the key: a combobox clearing its query, an editor cancelling a selection.
6. **Composition is not dismissal.** Escape that cancels an IME composition (CJK input, accents) is consumed without closing anything, and close requests are declined while composing.
7. **A backdrop press starts and ends on the backdrop.** A press that crosses the edge either way (a text selection, a slider dragged past the edge) does not dismiss. A cancelled pointer ends the press.
8. **The top layer consumes its outside press.** The press that light-dismisses a popover inside a dialog does not also close the dialog.
9. **Focus returns to the opener, without scrolling** the page or any scroller, with the focus ring the last input calls for ([[touch-and-focus]]). It works in the document the layer rendered in, including a Picture-in-Picture window.
10. **Registration is not ownership.** The stack calls the layer's own dismiss callback; open state stays with the component's owner.

## Gotcha

`onPointerDown` on the backdrop is the common bug: it fires before the user has finished a drag that started inside the panel. Track the press from down to up and dismiss only when both landed on the backdrop.

## Sources

- Meta, Astryx (MIT, github.com/meta/astryx, HEAD `9f55320`, read 2026-11-09): `docs/families/overlay-dismissal.md` FR1–FR11 (current). Paraphrased.
- Related: [[keyboard-patterns]], [[destructive-actions]], [[astryx-reconciliation]].

title: palette-step-roles
summary: A system is one neutral ramp, one accent ramp and only the status ramps the product renders. Every step exists because a role consumes it (Tailwind 50–950 by lightness, Radix 1–12 by role), solid fills sit on 600 because white on 500 fails, status hues stay 15° from the accent, one filled action per view, and an existing palette is inventoried before it is restructured.
tags: [surface, color, palette, ramps, status, audit]
---

# Palette step roles

A ramp is not a gradient to pick from by eye. Each step exists because a role needs it — page background, hover, border, solid fill, body text — and a step no role consumes is maintenance for zero pixels. [[color-scales-oklch]] computes the steps; [[color-token-tiers]] names them; this node decides which exist.

## What a system needs

| Ramp | How many | Carries |
|---|---|---|
| Neutral | 1 | 80–90% of the interface: backgrounds, borders, body text. Needs the most steps — never fewer than the accent |
| Accent | 1 | The brand: interactive and selected states. A second accent only when two things must be told apart at a glance |
| Status | 0–4 | `danger`, `warning`, `success`, `info` — only the ones the product shows. Most need four roles, not a full ramp |

## Every step has a job

| Role | Tailwind | Radix |
|---|---|---|
| Page / subtle background | 50 | 1–2 |
| Component background | 100 | 3 |
| Hover · active, selected | 200 | 4 · 5 |
| Subtle border, separator | 200 | 6 |
| Border, focus ring | 300 | 7 |
| Hovered border | 400 | 8 |
| Solid fill · its hover | 600 · 700 | 9 · 10 |
| Low · high-contrast text | 700 · 900 | 11 · 12 |

Radix defines steps **by role** — step 9 is the solid fill in every ramp and in dark, so component CSS never changes. Tailwind defines them **by lightness**, so the mapping inverts in dark and the swap belongs in the semantic tier. Match the project; for a new system prefer the role model. The solid fill is `600`, not `500`, because white text on most `500` hues fails 4.5:1 ([[wcag-thresholds]]).

## Rules that hold across hues

- **One colour, one meaning.** Hues within 15° of OKLCH hue read as one colour, so a link blue and a decorative heading blue are one meaning used twice. The rule runs both ways: if the accent means interactive, an interactive element rendered neutral misleads too.
- **Status sits ≥ 15° from the accent.** A red brand cannot also have a red danger; give destruction a distinct treatment ([[destructive-actions]]). Check gain/loss colours per locale — Chinese financial UIs show gains in red.
- **One filled action per view.** The fill goes on the background, not the label: a filled button reads as primary across the room, accent text on a neutral button reads as a link. Selected state may use the accent on glyph and label — that is state, not emphasis.
- **Neutrals: pure grey is a fine default.** Tinting toward the accent (OKLCH C 0.005–0.02 at the accent hue) is an option, not a correction ([[color-monochromatic]]). Warm or cool, hold it across the ramp: a warm grey border on a cool grey surface shows.
- **Increased contrast per appearance.** `prefers-contrast: more` gets a value per light and dark; one shared block darkens the dark theme's colour too and *lowers* contrast there. Widen the L gap by ≥ 0.15 and remeasure.
- **Keep an opaque twin of any translucent step that can overlap.** A translucent ink paints darker where two shapes stack, so piled avatars or chips take the ink already flattened onto the surface (Stageshow's `--ss-fill` is ink-3 on white, `#ebebeb`).

## Auditing an existing palette

1. Collect every literal — hex, `rgb(`, `hsl(`, `oklch(`, utility prefixes, SVG `fill`/`stroke`, chart configs, email templates.
2. Sort by lightness within each hue family; duplicates surface as neighbours.
3. Collapse near-duplicates (ΔE in OKLab under 0.02): keep the most-used, retire the rest. Never average them.
4. Give each survivor a role from the table. One that matches none is a missing token or a mistake — say which.
5. Count the ramps. More than the first table lists means the palette outgrew its structure.

Report the inventory before changing anything: consolidation changes screens nobody asked you to touch.

## Reference

Benji Taylor's starting set for a product surface: every token has a consumer, and none is there for decoration.

| Role | Light value | Consumed by |
|---|---|---|
| canvas · surface · well | `#f6f5f4` · `#fff` · `#efeeec` | page, cards, the stage behind a framed shot |
| ink-1 to ink-5 | `rgba(0,0,0,.04/.06/.08/.1/.15)` | placeholder bars and fills, ghost and tertiary hovers |
| text-strong · text · text-faint | `#262628` · `#7a7a7d` · `#9a9a9d` | title, body, metadata |
| accent · soft · text | `#3b82f6` · 12% tint · mixed 82% with black | the thing being acted on, its wash, a link on white |
| success · danger · warning | each with `-soft` and `-text` | only where status is the subject |

- Bad: a primary button whose hover swaps to `#e5e7eb`. Good: `color-mix(in srgb, var(--accent), #000 10%)`, which is one step of its own color.
- Gold example: `stageshow/kit/stage.css` (the token block) and `stageshow/kit/controls/Button.css` (hover variants).
- Check: grep for color literals outside the token file and expect zero. Then hover every filled button in one contact sheet. The hue holds, only the step darkens, and no status color appears anywhere that isn't status.

## Gotcha

Dark tokens that are the light ramp in reverse step order look right in a swatch and wrong on screen: dark needs lower accent chroma and a wider dark end. Remap, then remeasure every pair ([[dark-mode]]).

title: shadows-whisper
summary: Shadows should whisper, not announce. The default 0 2px 8px is a tell. Concrete spec.
tags: [shadow, surface]

# Shadows whisper

The Bootstrap-default shadow (`0 2px 8px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.1)`) is the most overused shadow on the web. It is a tell.

## The principle

A good shadow is barely visible. Its purpose is to suggest elevation and depth, not to draw attention to the elevated element. If you can clearly *see* the shadow as a soft gray blur, it is too strong.

## The spec

For light mode, layered shadows that whisper:

```css
/* +1 elevation: cards, buttons */
--shadow-sm:
  0 1px 1px rgba(17, 17, 17, 0.04),
  0 2px 4px rgba(17, 17, 17, 0.04);

/* +2 elevation: dropdowns, popovers */
--shadow-md:
  0 1px 2px rgba(17, 17, 17, 0.05),
  0 4px 8px rgba(17, 17, 17, 0.05),
  0 8px 24px rgba(17, 17, 17, 0.04);

/* +3 elevation: modals */
--shadow-lg:
  0 2px 4px rgba(17, 17, 17, 0.06),
  0 8px 16px rgba(17, 17, 17, 0.06),
  0 16px 48px rgba(17, 17, 17, 0.06);
```

Key moves:
- **Layer multiple shadows** at different blur radii. A single shadow with 16px blur looks flat. Three shadows at 2px, 8px, 24px blur read as physical depth.
- **Use a dark base color** (`#111`, not pure black). Slightly warmer if your palette is warm.
- **Opacity at 4–6%, not 10%.** This is the part most people get wrong.
- **No `y-offset` larger than blur radius.** A 2px y-offset with 8px blur is fine; 8px y-offset with 8px blur is not.
- **Lead with a 1px ring** (`0 0 0 1px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.06)`). The drop falls downward, so without it the top edge, or a light sidebar on a light ground, has no line.
- **One shadow per role on a page.** A second hero shadow either means something or is a mistake.

## Dark mode shadows

In dark mode, shadows alone often disappear. Pair with the surface-tint elevation pattern from [[dark-mode]] — use a lighter surface color *and* a much subtler shadow:

```css
.dark {
  --shadow-md:
    0 4px 12px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.4),
    0 0 0 1px rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.06); /* hairline border for definition */
}
```

The 1px hairline border at low white opacity does most of the elevation work in dark mode.

## Inner shadows for surfaces

```css
/* Subtle inner shadow on top edge for a card */
box-shadow: inset 0 1px 0 rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.06);
```

Used by Apple, Stripe, Linear. Adds a hairline highlight to suggest the surface is reflecting light from above.

## When to apply

- Any time you write a `box-shadow`. Reach for the layered token, not a single-shadow blur.
- Reviewing a design system that has one "shadow" value — push for at least three layered tokens.

## Reference

Benji Taylor gives each shadow a job, named by what the surface sits on:

| Role | `box-shadow` |
|---|---|
| card at rest | `0 1px 2px rgba(0,0,0,.04)` |
| satellite over a white window | `0 0 0 1px rgba(0,0,0,.04), 0 14px 32px -8px rgba(50,50,93,.24), 0 4px 10px -4px rgba(0,0,0,.1)` |
| small window alone on the ground | `0 0 0 1px rgba(50,50,93,.06), 0 24px 48px -24px rgba(50,50,93,.18)` |

- Bad: `0 0 24px #6366f166, 0 0 60px #22d3ee44`, a colored glow on the card, the button and the dot. Good: one neutral shadow under the card. Shadows sit; they don't glow.
- Benji's call differs: on a marketing stage his hero window gets `0 30px 60px -12px rgba(50,50,93,.25)`, which is far above 4–6%. Keep the whisper scale for in-product surfaces.
- Gold example: `stageshow/teaching/style.tsx` (the `style-glow` pair), `stageshow/examples/overlap/`.
- Check: screenshot at 1x and look at a 25% thumbnail. You should find the edge, not a gray halo. If a wide blur smears over a white window, switch to the tighter satellite token.

## Gotcha

Don't add `box-shadow` to text. Use `text-shadow` for that — and almost never. Text shadows are an effect from 2008 and they still look like 2008.

## Sources

- guidelines.sh — "Shadows whisper (2px blur, 1px Y, 5% opacity #111)."
- Tailwind v3 shadow scale + improvements from Linear and Vercel.
- Apple HIG — material/elevation tokens.
- Benji Taylor, Stageshow 1.1.1 (MIT, github.com/benjitaylor/skills, HEAD `299140f`, read 2026-11-07): `stageshow/kit/stage.css` (card, satellite, ground and hero shadow tokens and their comments), `stageshow/references/framing.md` rule 8, `stageshow/references/craft.md` (one figure language), `stageshow/teaching/style.tsx` and `style.css` (`style-glow`).

title: translucent-materials
summary: Translucency is a floating functional layer, not decoration. Material weight encodes hierarchy, never stack light glass on light glass, bigger surfaces read thicker, scrim for modal and none for parallel, vibrant text, scroll-edge masks over dividers, materialize with blur + scale, and solid fallbacks for reduced transparency and more contrast.
tags: [surface, glass, backdrop-filter, depth, accessibility]
---

# Translucent materials

A translucent bar lets content scroll under the chrome instead of losing a fixed strip of screen to it, and it keeps the user oriented about what is behind. That only works when the material says *where it sits* in the hierarchy and text on it stays legible over anything. Glass chosen for looks fails both. [[depth-and-nesting]] owns opaque elevation; this node is the see-through layer.

## Weight is hierarchy

- **Heavier, more opaque material for structure** (sidebars, tab bars); **lighter material to draw attention** to interactive pieces.
- **Never put a light translucent layer on another one.** Two blurs compound and text legibility collapses. Make one of them solid.
- **Bigger reads thicker**: a sheet gets more blur and a deeper shadow than a chip. Shadow under glass can be heavier over busy content and lighter over a plain page.
- **Give glass something to take.** Put a color field or crisp bands behind it. Over a plain page it reads as a gray tint, and band edges are what show the blur.

```css
.toolbar {
  background: rgb(255 255 255 / 0.6);
  backdrop-filter: blur(20px) saturate(180%);
  border-top: 1px solid rgb(255 255 255 / 0.4); /* lit top edge */
}
```

## Focus and flow

- A **modal task** pairs the surface with a dimming scrim and pushes the page back. A **parallel, non-blocking panel** stays translucent and offset with no scrim, so the flow isn't broken. Stacked sheets dim and recede each parent a step.
- Where floating chrome overlaps scrolling content, fade a small blur or gradient mask at that edge instead of drawing a 1px divider, and only where they actually overlap ([[sticky-and-scroll-tells]]).
- **Materialize, don't fade**: animate blur radius and a slight scale together on enter and exit, so it arrives as a material rather than a ghost.

## Text on glass

Flat mid-grey text dies over a changing backdrop. Raise contrast, step the weight up one, add a hair of tracking (~0.01em). Put brand colour on a solid layer, never on the translucent foreground. Measure contrast over the worst backdrop the bar can sit on ([[contrast-and-color-scheme]]).

## Preferences

```css
@media (prefers-reduced-transparency: reduce) {
  .toolbar { background: var(--surface); backdrop-filter: none; }
}
@media (prefers-contrast: more) {
  .toolbar { background: var(--surface); border-color: var(--border-strong); }
}
```

## When to apply

Sticky headers, tab bars, toolbars, sheets, popovers over media, and any `backdrop-filter` in a review.

## Reference

Benji Taylor's frosted frame: the frame is glass, the page inside it is opaque.

```css
.frame { background: rgba(248, 250, 253, 0.45); backdrop-filter: blur(12px);
  border-radius: 12px; box-shadow: 0 0 0 1px rgba(229, 237, 245, 0.5), 0 15px 35px rgba(23, 23, 23, 0.08); }
.frame > .page { margin: 0 6px 6px; background: #fff; border-radius: 6px; } /* 12 = 6 + 6 inset */
```

- Bad: a 0.6-alpha card on a white page, with gray text set on the glass. Good: a frame over color bands, words on the white page, and the step from frost to white drawing the card.
- Benji's call differs: his glass theme does frost a popover over a frosted window. He separates them by density (raised 0.74 against surface 0.62) and a brighter 1px rim.
- Gold example: `stageshow/examples/glass/`, `stageshow/examples/finder-glass/`.
- Check: swap the ground for a flat fill. If the glass now looks the same, it was decoration. Over bands, edges blur through the frame and the text stays sharp.

## Gotcha

`backdrop-filter` samples only what is painted behind the element in its own stacking context. A parent with `overflow: hidden`, a `transform`, or `isolation` can leave the blur sampling nothing, and the glass renders as a flat tint. Check it in Safari and Firefox ([[z-index-strategy]]).

## Sources

- Benji Taylor, Stageshow 1.1.1 (MIT, github.com/benjitaylor/skills, HEAD `299140f`, read 2026-11-07): `stageshow/kit/window.css` (`data-chrome="glass"` frame and white page, adapted above), `stageshow/kit/stage.css` (glass theme tokens, orb ground), `stageshow/references/backgrounds.md` (crisp bands show what glass blurs), `stageshow/examples/glass/`, `stageshow/examples/finder-glass/`.
