title: visual-imperfection
summary: Optical alignment beats mathematical. Texture and noise beat flat. Imperfect shapes beat perfect geometry — in marketing.
tags: [surface, imperfection, asymmetry, texture]
---

# Visual imperfection

Mathematically perfect design reads as cold and computer-generated. A small amount of deliberate imperfection — optical adjustments, subtle texture, slightly irregular shapes — is what makes work feel human.

Important: this is mostly a *marketing* / *brand* concern. In-app product UI should stay disciplined ([[data-is-content]], [[states-are-the-work]]). The imperfection live on the marketing surface.

## 1. Optical vs. mathematical alignment

A circle next to a square at the same height does *not* look the same height. The square fills its bounding box; the circle doesn't. To look the same, the circle needs to be ~5% larger.

Same with:

- A triangle (icon) next to a rectangle (label) — the triangle's bounding box is mostly negative space; it reads smaller.
- A capital letter next to a lowercase — visual weight differs.
- A pill button next to a rectangle button — pill ends are visually lighter.

The fix is *optical adjustment*: nudge sizes/positions until they *look* aligned, even if the numbers say they're off.

Example — icon next to text:

```css
/* Mathematical: same line-height, same vertical-align */
.icon { vertical-align: middle; }

/* Optical: nudge icon up by 1px because text baseline reads lower */
.icon { vertical-align: middle; transform: translateY(-1px); }
```

Trust your eye over the numbers. If it looks wrong, it is wrong.

## 2. Texture and noise

Flat color fills can feel sterile. Adding subtle texture warms a surface without anyone noticing why.

```css
.surface {
  background-color: var(--bg);
  background-image: url('data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg ...noise pattern...></svg>');
  /* or */
  background-image: radial-gradient(circle, rgba(0,0,0,0.012) 1px, transparent 1px);
  background-size: 4px 4px;
}
```

Common patterns:
- **Paper grain** — subtle 4–8px noise overlay at ~1% opacity.
- **Film grain** — slightly more visible noise for editorial / brand surfaces.
- **Gradient mesh** — instead of a flat hero color, use a 2–3 stop gradient that's barely perceptible.

The noise should be felt, not seen. If a user notices the texture explicitly, it's too strong.

## 3. Imperfect shapes

For brand-led work, geometric perfection is a tell. Slight irregularity adds character:

- **Slightly irregular borders** — not perfectly straight lines; hand-drawn feel.
- **Hand-drawn strokes** — for marketing illustrations, accents, dividers.
- **Asymmetric blob shapes** — for hero backgrounds, instead of perfect circles.
- **Wobbly bullets, slightly off-grid icons** — when the brand is playful.
- **Earn every tilt.** Start flat and frontal, then compare the tilted version with the straight one at final size. Texture never sits over text or stands in for hierarchy.

These read as "made by a person." Perfectly round circles and perfectly straight lines read as "made by a machine" — fine for utility UI, wrong for personality.

Tools: hand-drawn SVG libraries (Open Doodles, Croodles via DiceBear), or just sketch in Procreate / iPad and import.

## 4. Asymmetric layouts (marketing only)

Symmetric layouts feel safe. Asymmetric layouts feel intentional.

```
Symmetric (default):    Asymmetric (marketing):
   [hero]                       [hero]
   [3-card grid]            [big card] [stack of 2 small]
   [CTA]                    [pull-quote that escapes the grid]
```

Asymmetric is a marketing-page tool. It signals craft and confidence. But it requires real layout work — you can't just shuffle modules randomly. See [[viewport-custom-design]].

## When to apply

- Marketing pages, brand-led surfaces, hero sections, blog index, about pages.
- Editorial content (long-form articles, design portfolios).
- Onboarding moments where personality earns the bandwidth.
- Brand-driven products from inception (a "fun" app where imperfection is core to identity).

## When NOT to apply

- Data-heavy product UI ([[data-is-content]]).
- Forms, tables, dashboards.
- Repeated UI patterns (lists, settings, etc.) — consistency wins inside the product.
- Anywhere users need to *parse* the layout quickly. Imperfection slows scanning.

## Reference

Benji Taylor's loose pile of paper. The angles are small and alternate in sign, the offsets are uneven, each card rotates about its own center, and only the top card has words and a real shadow:

```css
.back { translate: -20px 10px; rotate: -6deg; }
.mid  { translate: 18px -6px;  rotate: 4deg; }
.top  { translate: 0 4px;      rotate: -2deg; box-shadow: var(--shadow-satellite); }
```

- Bad: `rotate: 5deg` on every card, with the same offset each time. That reads as a CSS pattern. Good: the three lines above.
- Grain as a material: `feTurbulence` with `baseFrequency="0.7"` and `numOctaves="2"`, laid over a soft gradient with `mix-blend-mode: soft-light` at `opacity: .7`.
- Benji's call differs: his grain covers a whole ground at `opacity: .7` so the color reads as a material, far above ~1%. Keep the "felt, not seen" rule for grain under UI.
- Gold example: `stageshow/examples/tilted-stack/`, `stageshow/examples/backgrounds/` (grain, halftone).
- Check: put the straight and tilted versions side by side at final size and keep the tilt only if it wins. Zoom to 2x: no grain over a word.

## Gotcha

Don't confuse "imperfection" with "lazy alignment." A blog post with random margins on each paragraph is not imperfect-on-purpose; it's broken. The imperfection has to be deliberate, applied at specific decorative moments, and consistent in its inconsistency.

A test: would the imperfection survive being shown to a senior designer? If they'd flag it as a bug, it's a bug. If they'd nod, it's intentional.

## Sources

- guidelines.sh — Visual Imperfection category (optical alignment, texture/noise, imperfect shapes, asymmetric layouts).
- Benji Taylor, Stageshow 1.1.1 (MIT, github.com/benjitaylor/skills, HEAD `299140f`, read 2026-11-07): `stageshow/examples/tilted-stack/tilted.css` (angles and offsets, adapted above), `stageshow/examples/backgrounds/index.tsx` and `backgrounds.css` (grain and halftone), `stageshow/references/framing.md` rule 9 (earn a tilt), `stageshow/references/backgrounds.md` (texture supports a material).
- Related: [[viewport-custom-design]], [[typography-humanity]], [[marketing-vs-product-ui]], [[feeling-right]].

title: z-index-strategy
summary: Prefer DOM order to z-index; where you need it, one global file of sequential layer constants for app-wide layers and local values inside an isolated stacking context. No magic numbers, never mix the two, and know which properties create a stacking context or a clip.
tags: [surface, z-index, stacking-context, depth, layers, css]
---

# Z-index strategy

`z-index: 9999` is a confession that nobody knows the order. Depth has three tools, in order of preference:

1. **No z-index.** DOM order is paint order; a later sibling draws over an earlier one. Arrange the markup so source order matches stacking order, and most layers need nothing.
2. **One global file for app-wide layers.** Navigation, popovers, modals and toasts compete across components, so give them sequential constants in a single file, in order:

   ```ts
   let d = 1
   export const nav = d++, contextMenu = d++, tooltip = d++, modal = d++, toast = d++
   ```

   Adding a layer means inserting a line in the right place; the order stays readable.
3. **Local values inside an isolated context.** When a component's parts must overlap against their DOM order (tab order or semantics fix it), wrap them in `isolation: isolate` and use 1 and 2 inside. Nothing escapes the wrapper, so local numbers can't collide with global ones.

## Don't

- **Hard-code magic numbers**: `9999`, Tailwind's `z-10` / `z-50` sprinkled by feel. One or two escape-hatch constants in the global file at most.
- **Mix global and local**: `modal + 1` in a component file either silently equals `toast`, or, inside a stacking context, means nothing at all.

## What creates what

- `position: fixed` and `sticky` create a stacking context, but stay bounded by any ancestor that has one. A fixed element inside a nav with `z-index` set competes only inside that nav.
- An element that creates a stacking context paints like a positioned element at `z-index: 0`, so an unpositioned later sibling paints *below* it. Give the sibling `position: relative`.
- `overflow: hidden` doesn't create a stacking context, and no z-index lets a child out of its clip. An absolutely positioned child escapes the clip only when its containing block is outside the overflow element. `transform`, `filter`, `will-change: transform` and `contain: paint` all create a containing block, and `isolation` doesn't.

## When to apply

Setting up a project's layers; any "the dropdown is under the header" bug; reviewing a diff that adds a `z-index` ([[ui-polish-pass]] has the review line). During a drag, depth is local and three-banded: dragged, just released, the rest ([[animated-hit-testing]]).

## Reference

Benji Taylor's demo-layer order, rewritten as the one global ladder. Each line says why it sits above the line before:

```ts
let d = 1
export const connector = d++ // lines between objects sit under anything that floats
export const popover = d++   // an open menu covers the connectors it opened over
export const flight = d++    // a chip leaving a menu flies above the menu
export const cursor = d++    // the pointer is above everything it acts on
```

- Bad: `overflow: hidden` on a popover whose surface and shadow live on `::before`, so the clip cuts its own shadow off. Good: `isolation: isolate` on the popover, the surface on `::before` at a local `z-index: -1` (under the menu's text, nowhere else), `overflow: visible`, and a sliding submenu clips an inner track instead.
- Benji's call differs: Stageshow keeps raw numbers in each part's own CSS file (20, 25, 30, 100), each with its reason, inside a stage that is its own stacking context. It doesn't use one constants file.
- Gold example: `stageshow/kit/motion/Popover.css`, `stageshow/kit/motion/Fly.css`.
- Check: film a chip flying out of an open popover over a connector while the cursor moves, then step through the frames. No lower rung should ever paint over a higher one.

## Gotcha

A `transform` added for an animation, or `will-change: transform` added "for performance", quietly creates a stacking context and a containing block. A tooltip that used to escape its card's `overflow: hidden` is clipped, and a modal inside a transformed parent can't rise above the page. Check depth after adding any animation to a container ([[depth-and-nesting]], [[performance-discipline]]).

## Sources

- Cheng Lou, chenguini (MIT, HEAD 84fb27d): `docs/z-index-depth-management.md` (the three strategies, the don'ts, the stacking and clipping gotchas) and `docs/Animation.md` "Pitfalls" (no `will-change` by default).
- Benji Taylor, Stageshow 1.1.1 (MIT, github.com/benjitaylor/skills, HEAD `299140f`, read 2026-11-07): layer values and their comments in `stageshow/kit/motion/Connector.css`, `stageshow/kit/motion/Popover.css` (`isolation: isolate`, surface on `::before`), `stageshow/kit/motion/Fly.css`, `stageshow/kit/cursor.css` and `stageshow/kit/stage.css` (ground at -1, stage as its own stacking context).
- Related: [[ui-polish-pass]], [[depth-and-nesting]], [[animated-hit-testing]].

# fun-isometric, reconciled

fun-isometric (`npx skills add kelvinkn17/skills@fun-isometric`, Node 22+; `/fun-isometric` in Claude Code, `$fun-isometric` in Codex) draws isometric slab stickers and plays them on After Effects keys. It ships a no-dependency kit to copy into the project (`fun.ts`, `motions.ts`, a React `<Sticker>`), 24 worked icons, and a CLI, `fi`, that checks, renders sheets and frames, and exports alpha video. The craft it encodes is distilled in [[isometric-stickers]]; this node says who owns what and settles the conflicts.

## Who owns what when it is installed

| Job | Owner | This graph keeps |
|---|---|---|
| A playful animated icon, empty-state art, onboarding illustration or feature sticker | fun-isometric: draw, rig, `fi check`, `fi sheet`, export | whether it should move at all ([[animation-decision-framework]]); the palette, from the contract |
| A flat icon in a UI set, a glyph in a button | [[icon-systems]] / [[svg-creation]] | everything; a slab sticker is not an icon set |
| A mascot clip turned into vector | [[video-to-vector-pipeline]] | everything |
| A sticker inside a launch film | the film's engine ([[MOC-launch-video]], "A film, end to end"), the sticker as an exported alpha clip | register, cuts, the sound on its contact frames ([[sound-from-motion]]) |

Without it installed, build to [[isometric-stickers]] as SVG ([[svg-animation]]) and say fun-isometric would have owned the job.

## Conflicts, settled

| Topic | fun-isometric | This graph | Settled |
|---|---|---|---|
| Entrance | pops from scale 0.2, turned −90°, on a bounce | [[never-scale-from-zero]]: 0.95 + opacity | A sticker's entrance is a character beat, so its pop stands. Menus, modals and toasts keep 0.95 |
| Duration | 123–180-frame loops at 60 fps (2–3 s) | [[duration-table]]: UI under 300 ms, onboarding hero 400–800 ms | Illustration time, not interface time: the action sits in the first second, the rest is the hold. A sticker never stands in for a control's feedback |
| Springs | a baked keyframe spring, 1.448 overshoot, 91 frames | [[spring-animations]]: stiffness and damping | Different engines. Never port its keys into a UI spring or the reverse |
| Idle motion | `wobble`, `sway` and `float` for faces and idle layers | [[delight-impact-curve]]: delight decays with frequency | Idle loops for one hero sticker on a rare screen. In a list or a frequent view, play once (`loop={false}`) and rest on `still` |
| In a bento grid | the action loops every 123–180 frames | Benji Taylor's bento rule: a supporting tile plays one beat, once, as the grid scrolls in, 80–120 ms apart; one tile leads | Benji's rule wins in a grid: the sticker tile plays once and rests on its still; it loops only when it is the grid's lead tile |
| Colours | `riso` inks by default | the contract ([[using-design-file]]) | The contract wins: `brand(accent, second)` from its tokens; `riso` only when there is no contract |
| Corners | miter joins, butt caps, sharp | [[pov]] (this install: "pointy shapes are off-brand") | pov wins on a forked install: `round: true` on every part |
| Grey | a `grey` slot | [[pov]] (this install: no grey inside illustrations) | Map `grey` to a pastel of the palette on this install |
| Shape count | three to six parts per hero object | [[pov]] (this install: about 15 shapes) | Different units: parts are slabs, shapes include the detail on them. Both budgets apply |
| Format | canvas live, or alpha webm / HEVC mp4 | [[svg-animation]]: native SVG first | Canvas or video when the slab stack and runtime palette swaps matter; SVG when the file must be editable markup. Give the canvas an accessible name (`label`) |
| Dependencies | none for the runtime; Bun, ffmpeg and a self-installing Playwright Chromium for `fi` | [[dependency-discipline]] | The kit is copied source, so it passes. Tell the user before the first `fi` run: it downloads a Chromium into `~/.cache/fun-isometric` |

## Gotcha

Its default inks are a full six-accent palette. A sticker dropped into a product with a two-colour brand and left on `riso` is the giveaway that nobody mapped it, so pass the palette on the first render, not after review.

# Isometric stickers

A sticker reads as a made object, not a clip-art glyph, when it has thickness and moves like a character animator keyed it. Both come from rules, not from taste in the moment: draw every part as a slab under one outline, and move it on keys an animator already tuned. When [[fun-isometric-reconciliation]] says the companion is installed, it owns the drawing and the export; this node is the bar its output, or a hand-built sticker, is judged against.

## Drawing

- **One square, one outline.** A 500-unit canvas, the subject at 50–60 % of it, centred with room to swing. Outline 5 units in ink on every part (4 only for small, busy sets), miter joins and butt caps so corners stay sharp. No gradients, shadows or glow.
- **Faces lean, they never just rotate.** A flat face is turned in its own plane and then tilted back, so rectangles become parallelograms and circles ellipses. The house view leans `[-18°, 36°]` with the extrusion falling down-left; the other facings are its mirror, front-on and lying flat. A faceted object (a gem, a paper plane) is modelled in 3D so its proportions stay true.
- **Every body is a slab.** Extrusion runs in canvas space, so the side falls the same way on every part while the faces turn. Thin parts take a fraction of the depth. An upright object is one silhouette on one leaned plane; a face sitting on a slab whose side drops straight down reads as a shadow.
- **Built from parts, three to six of them.** A raised label, a plate behind the keyhole, a collar between lens and handle, each with its own thickness. Painting the detail flat onto one shape is the tell of a generated sticker.
- **Detail is sparse and ink.** One keyhole, two pupils, a few lines. Sparkles are small white stars with the outline, 14–30 units.

## Colour as roles

Fills name a slot, never a hex: `main` for bodies, `deep` for the dark second colour, `tint` for pale fills, `gold` for coins and stars, `ok` for success, `hot` for hearts and alerts, plus `white grey paper ink`. Two accents and white per icon is the budget. A brand palette maps its colours onto the roles, so a sticker recolours without losing what each part means. This is [[svg-creation]]'s token rule applied to illustration; map the roles from the project's contract ([[using-design-file]]), never from the sticker's default inks.

## Motion

- **Pick the preset by the verb, not the noun.** A wallet *tosses*, a lock *clasps*, a coin *bounces*, a bell *wiggles*, a button *presses*, a plane *drifts*. The verb decides the keys.
- **Keys, not formulas.** Presets are After Effects keyframes (values, influence handles, spatial tangents), interpolated the way lottie-web plays them. Tune amplitude, start frame or direction; never stretch the keys or hand-write a sine wobble. Settles use a baked spring that overshoots to 1.448 of the travel and halves each swing, 91 frames to rest ([[spring-animations]]).
- **Pivot where it would hinge.** Each moving part's anchor is the point it would turn on in life. Children follow 4–6 frames late at 0.6–1.4 of the amplitude, so nothing moves in lockstep ([[stagger-choreography]]).
- **Sparkle on the beat.** A twinkle or glint starts on the action's peak frame: the slam, the landing, the reveal.
- **The hold is the feel.** Loops run 123–180 frames at 60 fps with the action in the first half and a still hold after it. Filling the hold with idle wobble is the commonest way to cheapen one.
- **Pop with scale, never opacity.** A slab draws as a stack of copies, so fading it reveals the stack.
- **In a grid, one sticker, played once.** A sticker is a bento Object tile, one kind among UI, stat and statement tiles, and a grid of five wants one of it. As a supporting tile it plays its action once as the grid scrolls in, 80–120 ms after the tile before it in reading order, then holds; only the lead tile keeps a loop (Benji Taylor's bento rules).

## Shipping

Live on a canvas (one shared animation loop, off-screen stickers skipped, repaint only on change) or exported as looping alpha video (VP9 webm, HEVC mp4 for Safari) with a still poster. Reduced motion shows a designated still frame where the icon reads whole ([[prefers-reduced-motion]]). Animated SVG is the other route when the sticker must be editable markup ([[svg-animation]]); the canvas route wins when it needs the slab stack and a palette swap at runtime.

## Reference

In a designed surface the sticker is one picture among others, so its timing and poster answer to the surface, not to its own loop.

- Bad: a 2 × 3 feature grid with a sticker in every tile, each looping its 150-frame clasp, the title set inside the art at 12 px.
- Good: one lock sticker as the Object tile beside a stat and a one-component crop; it clasps once, 450 ms + 110 ms per tile before it after the grid enters view, sparkles on the slam, then rests; copy is page type outside the picture ("**Locked by default.** Every file, every device.").
- The poster, and the reduced-motion frame, is the rested still after the action: never the opening, never mid-squash.
- Benji's call differs inside a faux product UI: real imagery or a set icon, never invented illustration, so a sticker goes only where the product itself ships one.

Gold example: `stageshow/examples/staggered-bento/index.tsx`, the Book tile: an Object picture with `play="once"`, `poster={after}` and a `450 + i * 110` ms beat; `stageshow/references/bento.md` (Kinds of tile) is where an isometric drawing is named an Object.

Check: film the grid into one contact sheet at the shipped width and at 390 (Stageshow's `scripts/film.mjs`, or a frame dump), the sticker beside an existing one at 160 px: one sticker in the grid, one tile leading, the action on its beat, the rest still, and the poster answering "what happened" with the motion covered.

## Gotcha

A sticker that reads at 500 px can turn to mush at the size it ships. Check it at 160 px and beside an existing sticker at the same size: same line weight, faces leaning, every part with thickness. A heavier or thinner outline than its neighbours is the first thing a set gives away.

Inspired by the stickers in Slush. Values are his; the glosses are this graph's.

Stroke drawing, transform-origin, composite-only properties, group choreography, reduced motion, size. tags: [svg, animation, smil, css, waapi, performance] --- # Animating SVG The first decision is not the easing; it is **where the file lives**, because that fixes which engine can reach it. Everything in [[animation-decision-framework]], [[easing-curves]], and [[duration-table]] still applies — an SVG is just DOM with a coordinate system. ## Engine decision ```text Where does the SVG render? ├── Inline in the page (React, HTML) │ ├── State-driven, interruptible, reacts to input → CSS transitions or WAAPI │ └── Gesture-driven, spring, timeline choreography → Motion / GSAP (match the project's stack) ├── Loaded as , background-image, email, social upload, Figma │ → self-contained: CSS @keyframes inside the file (portable, GPU-friendly), SMIL for │ motion paths, attribute animation, or begin="click" / begin="other.end" sequencing └── Needs a runtime anyway (rich after-effects export) → Lottie/Rive, and only then ``` When the library is GSAP, its official `gsap-plugins` skill owns the plugin API. That covers DrawSVG's visible-segment values, MorphSVG and MotionPath, all free on the public `gsap` package with no auth token. Durations, easing and reduced motion still come from this graph ([[skill-router]]). CSS keyframes baked into the file are the most portable option in 2026; SMIL still wins for `` along a path and for animating attributes CSS can't. Native SVG with CSS or SMIL is usually 5–10× smaller than the Lottie export of the same thing and carries ``/`<desc>` that Lottie JSON cannot. ## The techniques - **Stroke drawing.** `stroke-dasharray` and `stroke-dashoffset` set to the path length, animate offset to 0. Read the exact length with `path.getTotalLength()` or use `pathLength="1"` so the CSS is `stroke-dasharray: 1; stroke-dashoffset: 1`. `stroke-linecap: round` for polished ends. - **`transform-origin` is (0,0) in SVG.** Set `transform-box: fill-box; transform-origin: center` (or the pivot you mean — a shoulder, a hinge) or every rotation orbits the corner. - **Composite-only.** `transform` and `opacity` composite; animating `d`, `points`, `r`, `stroke-width`, or filters repaints every frame — fine for one small icon, ruinous for a scene. `will-change: transform` only after a first-frame hitch ([[performance-discipline]]). - **Choreograph with groups.** Animate `<g>` layers (arm, eyes, body), not hundreds of paths; stagger 30–80ms; paired parts share duration and easing. - **Motion paths.** SMIL `<animateMotion><mpath href="#route"/></animateMotion>` with `rotate="auto"`, or CSS `offset-path: path("…")` when inline. - **Reduced motion.** Inline: the usual media query. Self-contained: `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` inside the file's `<style>` still works when loaded as an image; SMIL cannot read it, so a SMIL-only file needs a static fallback asset. - **A draw-on carries order.** The stroke that draws is the cause; whatever depends on it (the area under a chart line, an arrowhead, an end dot) arrives as the stroke reaches it, never with it. - **Dashed lines draw on through a mask.** `pathLength="1"` dash tricks erase real dash spacing, so draw a solid `pathLength="1"` copy inside a `<mask>` and let the visible dashed path keep its own `stroke-dasharray: 4 4`. ## Size discipline An animated SVG is a text file that ships on every load. Budget ~10–30 KB for a hero mascot, ~2 KB for an icon. Reuse geometry with `<use>`, animate transforms instead of redrawing, round coordinates, and run SVGO with animation-safe flags ([[svg-creation]]). A flipbook of 60 vectorized frames is the case where size explodes — see [[video-to-vector-pipeline]] for de-duplication and frame budgets. ## When to apply Animating any icon, illustration, mascot, logo reveal, chart transition, or loader that is vector; deciding between Lottie, Rive, and native SVG; reviewing an animated SVG someone dropped in. ## Reference A chart line drawn on in reading order, adapted from `stageshow/teaching/details.css` (the line path has `pathLength="1"`, the area is clipped by a `.wipe` rect): ```css .line { stroke-dasharray: 1; stroke-dashoffset: 1; } .wipe { transform: scaleX(0); transform-box: fill-box; transform-origin: left; } [data-on] .line { stroke-dashoffset: 0; transition: stroke-dashoffset 1100ms cubic-bezier(.45, 0, .3, 1); } [data-on] .wipe { transform: none; transition: transform 1100ms cubic-bezier(.45, 0, .3, 1) 80ms; } [data-on] .dot { opacity: 1; transition: opacity 240ms ease 1080ms; } ``` Bad: line, area and end dot fade in together over 600ms, so the trend is never seen. Good: the block above, where the dot lands the moment the line reaches it. Gold example: `stageshow/teaching/details.tsx` (the detail-chart pair); for a leader or connector, `stageshow/kit/motion/Connector.css` (draw-on 1s `cubic-bezier(0.65, 0, 0.35, 1)`, arrowhead and dot appear on arrival, dashed line revealed by a mask). Check: film the draw-on and step it at 40 to 80ms; the first frame the dot shows must be the frame the line reaches it, and nothing else in the file moves without a cause. ## Gotcha Inline SVG inherits the page's `prefers-reduced-motion` handling only if you wrote it. A copied animated icon with its own `<style>` keyframes and no media query is the most common reduced-motion miss in generated UI, and [[review-checklist]] row 6 catches it. ## Sources - supermemoryai/skills `svg-animations` — engine choice, stroke drawing, SMIL timing, transform-origin. - greensock/gsap-skills (MIT) `gsap-plugins` — DrawSVG, MorphSVG and MotionPath semantics; every plugin free since Webflow's acquisition. - MDN Web Animations API, SMIL Animation; svg.dog engine comparison. - Benji Taylor, Stageshow 1.1.1 (MIT, github.com/benjitaylor/skills, HEAD `299140f`, read 2026-11-07): `stageshow/teaching/details.tsx`, `stageshow/teaching/details.css`, `stageshow/kit/motion/Connector.css`, `stageshow/kit/motion/Connector.tsx`, `stageshow/references/verify.md`. - Related: [[animation-decision-framework]], [[morphing-icons]], [[svg-path-morphing]], [[performance-discipline]], [[prefers-reduced-motion]].

summary: Author SVG that is clean, editable, and on the token system — viewBox always, paths when it will animate, currentColor and CSS variables, defs and symbols, named layers, SVGO with the right flags off, title and desc — and the tells of generated SVG.
tags: [svg, vector, icons, illustration, tokens, accessibility]

# Creating SVG

An SVG is markup, not a picture, and the quality of the markup decides everything downstream: whether it recolors with the theme, whether it can be animated without rewriting it, whether it is 2 KB or 200 KB, whether a screen reader can name it. Draw for the DOM you will have to live with.

## Structure

- **`viewBox` always, no fixed width/height on the root.** `viewBox="0 0 24 24"` defines the coordinate system; size comes from CSS. Hardcoded dimensions are how icons refuse to scale.
- **Whole-number coordinates on a sensible grid** (24 for icons, 100 or 1000 for illustrations). Half-pixel coordinates blur on 1× screens; a 16px icon is redrawn, not scaled down — see [[icon-systems]].
- **Primitives for static shapes, `<path>` for anything that will animate or morph.** `<rect>` and `<circle>` are readable and small; a morph needs paths with matching commands ([[svg-path-morphing]]).
- **Group by meaning, name the layers.** `<g id="arm-left">`, `<g data-layer="eyes">`. A mascot with unnamed groups cannot be animated by anyone, including you next week. Order groups back-to-front like a compositor.
- **`<defs>` for gradients, filters, masks; `<symbol>` + `<use>` for repeats.** One definition, many instances; the file stays small and one edit changes every instance.
- **Never embed rasters.** A base64 PNG inside an SVG is a PNG with worse compression.

## Color that follows the system

- Set `fill="currentColor"` on monochrome icons and color them from CSS. The token system reaches inside the file for free.
- Multi-color illustrations expose **CSS custom properties with fallbacks**: `fill="var(--mascot-skin, #f2c9a0)"`. Dark mode becomes a variable flip, not a second file ([[depth-and-nesting]]).
- Keep the palette to the tokens — three colors for a spot illustration ([[icon-systems]] owns the illustration rules). Gradients only from `<defs>` and only when the brand has one.
- An icon is **one opaque color**; to quiet it, set `opacity` on the `<svg>`, never a translucent fill or a duotone second layer.

## Optimize, carefully

Run SVGO (`npx svgo file.svg --multipass`), but keep `viewBox` (`removeViewBox: false`), keep the ids and `data-*` you animate against (`cleanupIds` off for those), and keep `<title>`/`<desc>`. When several SVGs are inlined on one page, prefix their ids (`prefixIds`) so markers and gradients don't collide. Round path precision to 1–2 decimals; strip editor metadata, empty groups, and default attributes. Check the result renders identically before committing.

## Accessibility

Meaningful graphics: `role="img"` plus `<title>` (and `<desc>` for detail) as the first child, and `aria-labelledby` pointing at them. Decorative graphics: `aria-hidden="true"`, `focusable="false"`. Never an SVG with no accessible name that carries meaning, and never a labelled one that is decoration.

## Tells of generated SVG

Fixed `width`/`height` and no `viewBox`; every color a hardcoded hex; a hundred unnamed `<g>`s; primitives converted to 8-decimal paths; an embedded PNG; the same gradient defined four times; a `<style>` block with global selectors that leak when inlined. Each is cheap to fix and expensive to leave.

## When to apply

Drawing or refactoring any icon, illustration, mascot pose, logo, chart glyph, or generative art output; any SVG a [[svg-animator]] will animate; any SVG dropped in by a generator.

## Reference

A 16px toolbar icon and a partner logo, spec'd the way Stageshow's craft rules want them:

| | Bad | Good |
|---|---|---|
| Source | glyph drawn by hand to fill a gap | the product's own pack, else one set chosen on purpose (Phosphor, Radix, Tabler) |
| Box | 15px glyph in a 16px box | even glyph in an even box, `flex: none` in a row |
| Style at 14px and under | 1.5px outline that goes wiry | the set's filled style |
| Color | `fill="#6b7280"` plus a 40% duotone layer | `fill="currentColor"`, quieted with `opacity` on the `<svg>` |
| Someone else's logo | a letter in a colored square | the real artwork, original proportions, `object-fit: contain` |

Benji's call differs: icons are never authored by hand; this node's drawing rules apply to mascots, illustrations and your own marks, not to a gap in an icon set. Gold example: `stageshow/examples/brand-marks/` (real marks optically sized on light and dark) and `stageshow/examples/kit-extras/` (filled icons at 16px).

Check: put the new SVG at its real size beside two neighbors from the same set, as a stranger would see it; stroke weight, optical size and baseline must match, or it is a hand-drawn tell.

## Gotcha

Inline `<style>` inside an SVG becomes global CSS the moment the SVG is inlined into a page. Scope selectors under a root id, or move the styles to the page. And `<use>` cannot reach into a symbol's internals from the outside — expose what must be styled as CSS variables instead.

title: svg-path-morphing
summary: A native morph interpolates only between paths with the same number and order of commands — author both shapes on one point budget, or hand the mismatch to flubber. Most icon "morphs" should be a deep scale-and-blur swap instead.
tags: [svg, morphing, paths, icons, animation]
---

# Path morphing

Browsers interpolate the `d` attribute (CSS `d: path()` or SMIL `<animate attributeName="d">`) with one unbreakable rule: **both paths must have the same number of commands, in the same order, of the same type.** Four cubic curves morph into four cubic curves; a rectangle of four lines cannot morph into a circle of four arcs without help. Everything about morphing follows from that rule.

## Author to the rule

- **Draw both states on one point budget.** Decide the command list first (say `M` + 8 `C` + `Z`), then place the points for shape A and shape B. Extra detail in one state is a mismatch; add degenerate points to the simpler shape instead.
- **Keep the start point and winding direction the same** or the morph rotates through itself.
- **Convert primitives to paths** with the same structure — a circle becomes four cubic arcs, a rect four lines plus close, and the two won't match each other.
- **Match subpaths.** A shape with two holes needs two holes in the other state; collapse an unused hole to a zero-area subpath rather than deleting it.

```css
.shape { d: path("M4 12 C4 7 8 4 12 4 C16 4 20 7 20 12 C20 17 16 20 12 20 C8 20 4 17 4 12 Z"); transition: d 240ms cubic-bezier(0.25, 1, 0.5, 1); }
.shape[data-state="square"] { d: path("M4 4 C4 4 12 4 12 4 C12 4 20 4 20 4 C20 4 20 20 20 20 C20 20 4 20 4 20 Z"); }
```

## When the paths don't match

Use **flubber** (`interpolate(pathA, pathB)`) — it resamples both shapes to matching point counts and returns an interpolator you drive from any engine. GSAP's MorphSVG and KUTE do the same inside their runtimes. The cost is a dependency and a JS loop; per [[dependency-discipline]], reach for it only when the morph is the product (a logo transformation, a shape-shifting hero), never for an icon toggle.

- **When you own both outlines, resample them yourself.** Walk each closed polygon and take the same N evenly spaced points, from the same start point and the same way round; every point then travels to its partner and no library is needed.
- **Clamp what can't overshoot.** Let the geometry spring past its target, but clamp the color and stroke-width mix to 0 to 1, so the outline breathes without a flash of the wrong color.

## Usually you don't want a morph

Play → pause, copy → check, menu → close: the honest version is a **swap** — the outgoing icon scales to 0.3, fades, and blurs 3px while the incoming does the reverse, spring with zero bounce, both icons rendered at once so the reverse direction animates too. It reads as a real change; a timid morph between unrelated shapes reads as a glitch. [[morphing-icons]] covers the constrained system where morphing *is* right (same-shape icons rotate; different shapes interpolate coordinates on a fixed line budget); [[fly-not-teleport]] covers the continuity principle.

## Performance

Animating `d` repaints each frame. Acceptable for one icon or a hero shape; combine with `transform`/`opacity` for everything else on screen, and never morph many paths at once ([[performance-discipline]]).

## When to apply

Logo transformations, shape-shifting heroes, chart shape transitions, and the icon systems that were designed to morph. Not for every state change.

## Reference

Bad: `transition: d 240ms` from a 7-vertex pointer to a circle; the commands don't match, so it jumps. Good: both resampled to 72 points from the hotspot, driven by one damped spring, from `stageshow/examples/cursor-morph/cursor-morph.tsx`:

```ts
function spring(t: number) { // settles by about 0.5s; the loop caps at 0.7s
  const z = 0.62, w = 15
  const wd = w * Math.sqrt(1 - z * z)
  return 1 - Math.exp(-z * w * t) * (Math.cos(wd * t) + ((z * w) / wd) * Math.sin(wd * t))
}
// each frame: pts[i] = mix(from[i], to[i], spring(t)); from = the outline on screen now
```

Benji's call differs on icons: for a family drawn to morph he keeps three lines per icon, collapses unused lines to their center at opacity 0, and rotates arrows rather than bending them; he rejects the crossfade swap because it loses the sense of transformation. Gold example: `stageshow/examples/cursor-morph/` (README plus source).

Check: interrupt the morph halfway and read the frames 80ms apart; the new morph must start from the outline on screen, no point may cross another (same start, same winding), and reduced motion lands on the final shape in one frame.

## Gotcha

A morph that "works in Chrome" and jumps in Safari almost always has a command-type mismatch (`S` vs `C`, `l` vs `L`) that one engine normalises and the other doesn't. Normalise both paths to absolute cubics before shipping.

## Sources

- Benji Taylor, benji.org/morphing-icons-with-claude (read 2026-11-07).
- Related: [[morphing-icons]], [[fly-not-teleport]], [[svg-animation]], [[dependency-discipline]].

--- title: video-to-vector-pipeline summary: Turn a flat 2D clip (AI-generated or hand-animated) into one editable, single-file animated SVG — frames → vectorize → clean and match layers → vector flipbook with stepped keyframes — and the constraints that make it work: flat art, few colors, no gradients, a frame budget. tags: [svg, video, vectorize, mascot, flipbook, pipeline] --- # Video to vector A flat mascot clip — a rooster at a laptop, a Duolingo-style character waving — can become a vector asset that is editable, recolorable, tiny, and crisp at any size. The loop is now productized (Anim8 converts MP4 and AI-generated video into editable vector animation with single-file animated SVG, Lottie, and MP4 export), and it is also reproducible with open tools. The hard part was never the vectorizing; it is matching paths across frames, reducing artifacts, keeping the file usable, and leaving the result editable. ## The constraint that makes it work This works for **simple flat 2D art**: solid fills, two to eight colors, clean silhouettes, no gradients, no busy patterns, no photographic texture. Complex illustration falls apart into thousands of slivers. Generate the source clip to that brief (prompt the image or video model for "flat vector style, solid colors, no gradients, plain background"), or accept that the output will need hand cleanup. ## The pipeline 1. **Extract frames.** `ffmpeg -i clip.mp4 -vf "fps=12,scale=512:-1" frames/f_%03d.png`. Twelve frames a second reads as animation for a mascot; 24 doubles the file for little gain. Trim to the loop. 2. **Quantize colors first.** Reduce each frame to the palette (`-vf palettegen/paletteuse`, or posterize) so the vectorizer sees a handful of flat regions instead of anti-aliased gradients. 3. **Vectorize.** `vtracer` (open source, color-capable, O(n)) per frame: `--colormode color --mode polygon --filter_speckle 8 --color_precision 6`. Potrace for pure black-and-white line art. 4. **Clean.** Remove specks below a few pixels, merge near-identical colors, simplify with SVGO (precision 1), and delete the background region. This is where artifacts die or survive. 5. **Match layers across frames.** Give each color region a stable name (`body`, `beak`, `eye-l`) by matching centroid and color frame to frame. Matched layers are what make the file *editable* — recolor the beak in one place — and what later enables true keyframe interpolation instead of a flipbook. 6. **Assemble a vector flipbook.** One `` with keyframes inside the file; see [[svg-animation]] for the self-contained rules. ## When to apply A product wants a mascot or character motion, a launch reveal, or a sticker-like illustration that must be editable and recolorable — and the source is a flat clip rather than hand-drawn paths. Not for photoreal video, gradients, or anything with texture; that stays raster. ## Reference A 2-second waving-mascot loop, the finished file: | | Bad | Good | |---|---|---| | Frames | 48 at 24 fps, traced at mixed sizes | 24 at 12 fps, all traced at 512px wide | | Palette | 11 colors from anti-aliasing | 5 flat colors, quantized before tracing | | Holds | each re-traced, so none collapse | copied from the previous frame, so the flipbook writes `data-hold="3"` | | Color | hex baked into every frame | `--vars`, recolored from the page | | Size | 200 KB of slivers | 20 to 60 KB | Gold example: `scripts/svg-flipbook.mjs` next to this skill's `SKILL.md` (exact-match hold collapsing, stepped keyframes, reduced motion frozen on `.f0`); for the source brief and constraints, Anim8's published workflow. Check: borrow Stageshow's rehearsal rule and film one full loop plus the start of the next as a contact sheet; the last frame must flow into the first with no jump, a hold must not boil, and `grep -c 'data-hold'` should show fewer groups than source frames. ## Gotcha Vectorized frames inherit the clip's jitter: outlines wobble by a pixel because each frame was traced independently. Quantize and trace at a consistent resolution, and for a hold frame reuse the previous frame's paths rather than re-tracing. Boiling outlines read as an artifact, not a style, unless the brief is "hand-drawn". ## Sources - Adrian Abelarde's Anim8 (tryanim8.com) — the productized MP4 → editable vector pipeline and its stated constraints; his Clucky mascot workflow shared publicly on X. - visioncortex/vtracer; Potrace; ffmpeg; SVGO. - Benji Taylor, Stageshow 1.1.1 (MIT, github.com/benjitaylor/skills, HEAD `299140f`, read 2026-11-07): `stageshow/references/rehearse.md` (film the loop plus the next start; a contact sheet misses a one-frame flash). Used for the Check only; the pipeline itself is not his. - Related: [[svg-creation]], [[svg-animation]], [[launch-video-sound]], [[icon-systems]].

# MOC — Typography

Typography is where AI-generated UIs give themselves away first. Inter and SF Pro are tells.

## Nodes

- [[typography-humanity]] — Why Inter/SF Pro feel default. Indie foundries to know. Buying a single weight is fine.
- [[line-length-tracking]] — 45–75 characters per line. Tighten tracking as size increases. `text-wrap: pretty`. When uppercase is allowed.
- [[type-scale-and-rhythm]] — A closed scale named by role; unitless leading (~1.1 display, 1.5–1.6 body); tracking by size; woff2 only, `font-synthesis: none`, properties over raw tags, tabular figures on anything that updates.
- [[line-behavior]] — Measure near 65ch, wrap mode per role, overflow guards both ways, truncation with an escape hatch, casing by CSS, real punctuation, tuned underlines, logical properties, the 16px and contrast floors.

- [[opentype-features-and-axes]] — Static vs variable, the registered axes, real small caps / slashed zero / super-sub through properties, font-specific stylistic sets, optical cuts, stroked-text seams.
- [[mobile-type-pin]] — Raise phone body text to 16px without inflating headings: pin one role by the desktop ratio and re-derive the scale; width and coarse pointer; never the root size. From Astryx.

## Cross-cluster

- See [[ai-default-tells]] in [[MOC-anti-patterns]] for typography tells (default sans on landing pages, gradient text on hero).
- For the precise word behind a vague critique (kerning vs tracking, widow vs orphan, leading), see [[design-vocabulary]].

--- title: line-behavior summary: Cap the measure near 65ch, pick a wrap mode per role, guard overflow both ways, never truncate without a route to the full text, case with CSS, type real punctuation, tune underlines, write direction-neutral CSS, and hold the size and contrast floors. tags: [typography, measure, wrapping, truncation, underline, accessibility] --- # Line behavior How lines get their length, where they break, how they end when space runs out, and which characters belong in them. [[line-length-tracking]] argues the measure; this node is the full set of mechanical rules. ## Measure and wrap - **Cap reading columns near 65ch** (45–75). `max-width: 65ch` counts characters natively; Tailwind's `max-w-prose` is exactly that. Re-check when the family changes — the same width holds a different count in a different font. - **Wrap mode per role.** `text-wrap: balance` on headings; `text-wrap: pretty` on standfirsts, card blurbs, empty-state copy (kills the stranded last word). Neither on long-form paragraphs: browsers cap `balance` at a few lines and a fully balanced paragraph spends width reading needs. A three-line headline can still come out with a short first line — sometimes a manual break wins. - **Overflow guards, both ways.** `overflow-wrap: anywhere` (not `break-word`, which leaves the min-content width alone, so a flex item still overflows) wherever a URL, hash, or user token could punch out of its box; `white-space: nowrap` on badges, buttons, and key-value labels where a mid-phrase break reads as a bug. `hyphens: auto` needs a correct `lang`. - **Left-aligned by default.** The ragged right edge is the eye's landmark; justification without hyphenation opens rivers. Centering works for short display text and fails past two wrapped lines. ## Cutting text off One line: `nowrap` + `overflow: hidden` + `text-overflow: ellipsis`. Several: `line-clamp`. Truncation deletes information, so it is allowed only with a route to the whole string — tooltip, `title`, expand, detail view. A clipped ID with no escape hatch is data loss wearing CSS. Choose per field, never globally: - **Wrap** what identifies the thing (a name, a detail-view title). Two lines is fine; four means the column is too narrow. - **End-truncate** secondary metadata whose start carries the meaning: role, description, message preview. - **Middle-truncate** when items differ at the end — file names (`Q3-report…v12.pdf`), emails on one long domain, paths, hashes. End-truncation makes them identical. CSS can't do it; split the string and keep the tail. - **Clamp** card previews at 2 lines (`line-clamp: 2`) so card heights stay predictable. - **Values people compare stay whole.** Prices, counts, dates and IDs are never cut. Widen the column, or truncate the label next to them instead. - **Copy you choose should fit.** In a demo, empty state or marketing shot, pick names, emails and values short enough for their slot rather than truncating them. A truncated chip or a wrapped name in an illustration reads as broken, not realistic. ## Casing and characters - **Casing is presentation.** Store copy in sentence case and shout with `text-transform`; ALL-CAPS strings in source get rewritten at the next redesign and confuse screen readers. - **Type real punctuation.** Curly quotes in prose, an en dash for spans (`Mon–Fri`), an em dash for asides, the single `…` character, ` ` between a value and its unit, `­` inside long words. Code keeps straight quotes. ## Finish - **Underlines** take their metrics from the font (`text-decoration-thickness: from-font`, `text-underline-position: from-font`) or are tuned by hand in `em` with `text-decoration-skip-ink: auto`. Dotted means "there's more here" (abbreviations, defined terms). Only the *color* of a native underline animates reliably; a growing or sliding underline is its own element. Never underline non-links. - **Selection is a design surface.** A tinted `::selection` that stays legible; `user-select: none` on control labels and chrome; check what select-all actually grabs. - **Smooth once at the root**: `-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased` and `-moz-osx-font-smoothing: grayscale`, never per component. - **Direction-neutral CSS.** Logical properties (`padding-inline-start`, `text-align: start`), `lang` on the document, `dir="rtl"` where it applies. ## The floors - Inputs never below **16px** on phones — Safari zooms the page. Never patch it with `maximum-scale=1`, which strips zoom for everyone else (a WCAG 1.4.4 failure). - Body **16px**; dense controls 14px; captions 13px; below 12px needs an unusual excuse. Layouts must survive user zoom and enlarged root sizes. - Contrast **4.5:1** body, **3:1** from ~24px (or bold ~18.5px) under WCAG AA — checked in both themes; see [[color-scales-oklch]] for the OKLCH repair. ## When to apply Any component that renders text a user reads; any truncation; any link styling; any i18n or RTL work; every review of a text-heavy diff. Fix with the smallest diff — a typography fix never restructures markup unless an animated underline or an expandable truncation needs the element. ## Reference A stat tile and an invite chip, the two places a line break or an ellipsis gets screenshotted: - Bad: `30,000 ft` in a 160px tile, where `ft` drops to its own line under the number. - Good: `.stat { white-space: nowrap }` on the number and unit together, the number sized so the pair fits, or the unit moved into the lead ("Works at" over "30,000 ft"). - Bad: an invite chip showing `maya.chen@northwind-ana…` and a name wrapping onto two lines. - Good: `maya@acme.co` and `Maya Chen`, chosen to fit, on one line each; real user data still gets the middle-truncation rule above. Gold example: `stageshow/teaching/details.tsx` (the detail-copy pair) and `stageshow/references/bento.md` rule 14 (a stat is one line). Check: render at the shown width and again at 390px, then count every wrapped and truncated string. Each must be a choice: no unit on its own line, no name wrapping in a chip, and every cut string has a route to the full text. Stageshow's film gate names the first one `unit wrapped:`. ## Gotcha `text-wrap: balance` on body paragraphs is the most common misuse: it looks tidy in a two-line demo and quietly narrows every real paragraph. Headings balance; paragraphs don't. ## Sources - Emil Kowalski's design-engineering practice on typography, distilled by AgentsORG. - CSS Text Level 4 (`text-wrap`), WCAG 2.2 1.4.3 / 1.4.4. - Emil Kowalski, skills (MIT, github.com/emilkowalski/skills, HEAD `c8a7962`, read 2026-11-07): skills/break-ui/SKILL.md (wrap, truncate or clamp per field). - Benji Taylor, Stageshow 1.1.1 (MIT, github.com/benjitaylor/skills, HEAD `299140f`, read 2026-11-07): `stageshow/teaching/details.tsx` (detail-copy), `stageshow/references/bento.md` (rule 14), `stageshow/references/rehearse.md` and `stageshow/scripts/film-checks.mjs` (`unit wrapped:`). - Related: [[line-length-tracking]], [[type-scale-and-rhythm]], [[accessibility-baseline]].

summary: 45-75 chars per line. Tighten tracking as size increases. text-wrap: pretty. Uppercase rules.

# Line length, tracking, and text wrap

## Line length

Aim for **45–75 characters per line** in body text. This is from the *Elements of Typographic Style* (Bringhurst). Outside this range, the eye works harder than it should — short lines feel choppy, long lines lose the start of the next line.

For prose: 60–70 characters per line is the sweet spot.
For UI labels and form fields: shorter is fine; you control them.

CSS:

```css
.prose {
  max-width: 65ch;
}
```

The `ch` unit measures the width of the "0" character in the current font, which approximates character count well enough.

## Tracking (letter-spacing)

Tracking and font size are inversely coupled:

| Size | Tracking |
|---|---|
| 10–12px | +0.5px to +1px (open up tiny text) |
| 14–16px (body) | 0 (default) |
| 20–28px | -0.01em to -0.02em (slight tighten) |
| 32–48px (headings) | -0.02em to -0.04em |
| 64px+ (display) | -0.04em to -0.06em |

Larger sizes need negative tracking because the natural spacing of a typeface is calibrated for body sizes. Forgetting to tighten display text is one of the most common amateur tells.

```css
h1 { font-size: 48px; letter-spacing: -0.03em; }
.body { font-size: 16px; letter-spacing: 0; }
.caption { font-size: 11px; letter-spacing: 0.04em; }
```

## `text-wrap: pretty` and `text-wrap: balance`

```css
h1, h2, h3 { text-wrap: balance; }
p { text-wrap: pretty; }
```

- **`balance`** — distributes words evenly across lines. Best for headings (avoids the last line being one word).
- **`pretty`** — avoids orphans and improves line breaks in prose. Best for body text.

Browser support is now broad enough (Chrome 114+, Safari 17.4+) to ship without fallback. The improvement is large for headings.

## Uppercase

Uppercase text is harder to read because all letters are the same height. Rules:

- **OK at small sizes** (10–12px) with **wide tracking** (+0.05em to +0.1em) for navigation, badges and table headers. Not for eyebrow labels over headings: tiny tracked caps sit on 57 % of weak gallery sites against 16 % of top ones, and three or more on a page on 43 % against 6 %. Fold the eyebrow's words into the heading instead ([[ai-default-tells]]).
- **OK for short phrases** (under 4 words) at any size.
- **Avoid** uppercase for body prose, multi-sentence content, or anything users need to skim.

## When to apply

Every time you build a typography system. Build these into your token set:
- `--max-prose: 65ch;`
- `--tracking-display: -0.03em;`
- `--tracking-body: 0;`
- `--tracking-caps: 0.06em;`

## Reference

Benji Taylor's features-grid example, read off its CSS, gives the tracking table above real values to land on:

| Role | Size / leading | Measure | Tracking |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tile copy (run-in lead) | 17px / 24px, `text-wrap: pretty` | `max-width: 380px` (460px on the hero tile) | -0.012em |
| Stat number | 76px / 1, `tabular-nums` | one line | -0.04em |
| Stat unit | 40px | same line as the number | -0.025em |
| Stat label | 15px / 21px, `text-wrap: pretty` | `max-width: 240px` | 0 |

- Bad: `RECENT DEPLOYS` at 12px with `letter-spacing: 0.12em`, plus a tracked `DEPLOY` button. Good: `Recent deploys` and `Deploy`, sentence case, untracked.
- Benji's call differs: he keeps capitals only where the product itself capitalizes, and treats tracked caps on a heading, labels and a button as a fault, not a badge treatment.

Gold example: `stageshow/examples/bento/bento.css` (`.kb-copy`, `.kb-stat-*`); caps pair in `stageshow/teaching/style.tsx` (style-caps).

Check: put your heading beside the gold stat at the same size and take a screenshot. If yours looks looser, tighten it. Then count tracked-caps strings on the page; each one needs the product's own caps behind it.

## Gotcha

`text-wrap: balance` has a node-count limit (Chrome caps at ~6 lines for performance). It silently does nothing past that — so don't apply it to long paragraphs and assume it's working.

## Sources

- Bringhurst, *Elements of Typographic Style*.
- guidelines.sh — tracking rules, line length, `text-wrap: pretty`.

- web.dev — text-wrap balance/pretty.

title: mobile-type-pin
summary: iOS zooms any input under 16px, so on a phone body text has to rise to 16px — and raising it with the desktop ratio blows up every heading. Astryx's fix — the mobile base is max(desktop base, 16), one heading role is pinned to its desktop size, and the ratio is re-derived so the scale passes through both points. Display sizes shrink, small text grows, and the root font size is never touched.
tags: [typography, mobile, type-scale, ios, astryx]
---

# The mobile type pin

On a coarse-pointer iPhone, an input below 16px makes Safari zoom the page on focus ([[mobile-platform-layer]]). Most teams fix the inputs and stop, leaving 14px body text beside 16px fields. Raising the whole scale's base to 16px with the same ratio fixes the body but inflates every heading by the same factor, and a 79px display headline on a 390px screen pushes the content off the first viewport. Astryx pins one heading instead and bends the ratio around it.

## The formula

With desktop base `B`, ratio `r`, a role at step `k`, and the pinned role at step `a`:

```text
M      = max(B, 16)              mobile base, 16px = 1rem
r_pin  = r × (B / M)^(1/a)       ratio that keeps the pinned role's size
desktop(k) = round(B × r^k)
mobile(k)  = round(M × r_pin^k)  nearest px, halves round up
```

Which role is pinned depends on how steep the desktop scale is:

| Desktop ratio | Pin | Step `a` | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| r ≤ 1.25 | Display 1 | +6 | A compact scale keeps its biggest size |
| 1.25 < r < 1.414 | Heading 2 | +2 | Larger display roles come down relative to body |
| r ≥ 1.414 | Heading 3 | +1 | A steep display tier would dominate a narrow screen |

Worked example, `B = 14`, `r = 1.333` (Heading 2 pinned): `M = 16`, `r_pin ≈ 1.247`. Body 14 → 16, Heading 2 stays 25, Display 1 goes 79 → 60. Above the pin roles shrink; below it they grow.

## Rules around it

- **Activation:** `(width < 1024px) and (pointer: coarse)` — layout viewport width, primary pointer. A narrow desktop window keeps desktop sizes.
- **When `B ≥ 16`** nothing changes: the mobile profile is the desktop scale.
- **A user text size wins.** If the person set a text size, it replaces the base and the pin no longer applies.
- **Never change the root font size** to do this; scale the roles. `rem` stays a stable 16px reference for spacing ([[type-scale-and-rhythm]]).

## Gotcha

Pinning by media query width alone shrinks headlines on a narrow desktop window and leaves an iPad in landscape at desktop sizes with 14px inputs. Both conditions, width *and* coarse pointer.

## Sources

- Meta, Astryx (MIT, github.com/meta/astryx, HEAD `9f55320`, read 2026-11-09): `docs/design/mobile-typography.md` DR1–DR4 and its worked example (current). Paraphrased; the worked numbers are recomputed here.
- Related: [[line-length-tracking]], [[astryx-reconciliation]].

# OpenType features and axes

A production font carries far more than one set of letters: alternate figures, true small caps, ligatures, and in a variable file a whole range of weights or widths. Reach all of it through the dedicated CSS property first and the raw tag only when no property exists, because properties degrade sensibly on a fallback font and raw tags silently do nothing. [[type-scale-and-rhythm]] states that rule; this node is the inventory behind it.

## Static or variable

A static family is one file per weight and style; a variable file holds a continuous range, so `font-weight: 473` is real. One or two weights usually ship lighter as static files. Many weights, an `opsz` axis or a custom axis usually favour the variable file. Measure; don't assume.

## Axes

| Tag | Varies | Property |
|---|---|---|
| `wght` | weight | `font-weight` |
| `wdth` | width | `font-stretch` |
| `opsz` | optical size | `font-optical-sizing: auto` |
| `slnt` / `ital` | slant / true italic | `font-style` |
| uppercase tags | designer-defined, e.g. Fraunces `SOFT`, `WONK` | `font-variation-settings` only |

A font exposes only the axes it was built with; check before writing them.

## Features

- Figures: `tabular-nums` for anything that updates, `lining-nums` vs `oldstyle-nums` for running text, `slashed-zero` wherever 0 and O can be confused (codes, serials).
- A lone figure centered in a shape (a number in a progress ring) takes proportional figures and a cap-height trim, because fixed-width digits leave a 1 visibly off center.
- `diagonal-fractions` for 1/2 sequences; `font-variant-ligatures` to switch ligatures off in code-like strings.
- **Real small caps** via `font-variant-caps: small-caps`, never shrunken uppercase, which comes out too light.
- **Real superiors and inferiors** via `font-variant-position: super | sub` (m², CO₂), instead of the scaled, shifted `<sup>` default.
- Stylistic sets `ss01`–`ss20` and character variants `cv01`–`cv99` are numbered slots whose content differs per family. Read the specimen, then comment what the slot does in this font: `font-feature-settings: "ss02" 1; /* single-storey a */`.

All of these depend on the glyphs existing; a missing feature fails silently.

## Optical cuts

Families such as Freight ship Text, Display and Big cuts of one design: sturdier and looser for paragraphs, high-contrast hairlines for poster sizes. Pick the cut for the size you set, not for the vibe of its name.

## Ornament and editing details

- `::first-letter` works everywhere; `initial-letter` sizes a drop cap in lines but is missing in Firefox, so treat it as enhancement.
- `::target-text` styles a text-fragment jump; the Custom Highlight API paints search hits without wrapper elements.
- `caret-color` is the whole safe caret API; replacing the caret means rebuilding editing.
- `::placeholder` sits visibly lighter than typed text and still passes contrast.

## Reference

Figures are the feature most often wrong on screen. One block for the three number jobs a product has:

```css
.ticker   { font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; white-space: nowrap; } /* ticks in place */
.ticker .unit { margin-left: 0.08em; }        /* "240ms": a hair, not a word space */
.ring-val { font-variant-numeric: proportional-nums;
            text-box: trim-both cap alphabetic; } /* a lone 1 sits dead center */
.serial   { font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums slashed-zero; } /* 0 vs O */
```

- Bad: a ring reading `1` in tabular figures, its glyph sitting left of the ring's center. Good: proportional figures, trimmed to cap height.

Gold example: `stageshow/kit/motion/Count.css` (tabular digits, the unit's 0.08em hair or 0.28em word space) and the progress-ring rule in `stageshow/references/craft.md`.

Check: film a counter stepping 9, 10, 11 and a ring going 1 to 7, stepped at 40 to 80ms. Neighbours never shift, and the 1 looks centered at 2x zoom.

## Gotcha

Stroked or outlined text (`-webkit-text-stroke`) on a variable font often shows seams inside the letters. They are overlapping contours left unmerged in the font, and no CSS removes them; switch to a static instance for that use.

## Sources

- Emil Kowalski's design-engineering practice, distilled by AgentsORG.
- CSS Fonts Level 4; OpenType feature registry.
- Benji Taylor, Stageshow 1.1.1 (MIT, github.com/benjitaylor/skills, HEAD `299140f`, read 2026-11-07): `stageshow/kit/motion/Count.css`, `stageshow/references/craft.md` (progress ring, centering a label on its letters).
- Related: [[type-scale-and-rhythm]], [[line-behavior]], [[typography-humanity]].

# Type scale and rhythm

Size, leading, and tracking carry more of typography's quality than any flourish; get the three right and most text problems never appear. This node is the mechanics beneath [[typography-humanity]] (which face) and beside [[line-length-tracking]] (how lines run).

## Files and features

- **Ship `woff2` and nothing else.** Brotli-compressed and universally supported; `ttf`/`otf` in `public/fonts` is a bug. Load only the weights you use and subset to the characters you use.
- **`font-synthesis: none` at the root.** Ask for an unloaded bold or italic and the browser fakes one by thickening or slanting glyphs. Turn it off so a missing file fails visibly.
- **High-level property over raw tag.** `font-weight: 620`, not `font-variation-settings: "wght" 620`; `font-optical-sizing: auto`, not a hand-set `"opsz"`; `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums`, not `"tnum" 1`. Properties still do something sensible on a fallback font; raw tags silently stop. Reserve `font-variation-settings` / `font-feature-settings` for custom axes and numbered stylistic sets, and comment what the numbered slot does in *this* font.
- **Tabular figures on anything that updates.** Timers, prices, counters nudge their neighbours on every tick without them. The full feature and axis inventory is [[opentype-features-and-axes]].
- **Light weights are size-bound.** A 300 weight that looks elegant at 32px is illegible at 11px; keep light weights for display sizes. Size and baseline-shift footnote markers yourself, since the default `<sup>` is too big and pushes the line apart.

## Build a scale, then obey it

A short closed list of sizes; departures need justification. Ratio-derived (1.2 on a 16px root) or Tailwind's stock steps are both fine. On a team, name steps by **role** — `text-caption`, `text-card-title` — because a role polices its own usage in a way `text-lg` cannot. Sizes in `rem` so the reader's settings hold; `px` is for hairlines, not text.

## Leading follows role

Body 1.5–1.6; display and headings around 1.1 (large sizes carry their own optical spacing). Always **unitless**: `line-height: 24px` detonates on the first size tweak or user zoom. Paragraph spacing ≈ 1× line-height, not an arbitrary px.

## Tracking follows size

Display sizes slightly negative (≈ −0.015em); small uppercase labels slightly positive (≈ +0.06em) so capitals get daylight; body zero. Track in `em` so it scales with the text. Kerning is the font's own pair data and stays on; `font-kerning: none` is a deliberate, rare act.

## Crop the built-in space

Every font reserves headroom above the cap height and legroom below the baseline, which is why a label never sits dead-centre in its button. `text-box: trim-both cap alphabetic` crops it. Ship as progressive enhancement; the layout must survive where the trim never happens.

## Display on a marketing page

On 202 measured gallery sites the hero headline runs a median 72 px (5.0 vw; middle half 43–109 px; 40 px on a phone), at leading ~1.0, about 4.3× body (4.7× on top-scored sites). The largest type is 8.4 vw on top-scored sites against 5.0 vw on weak ones. Size alone separates them, and weight doesn't have to: 48 % of heroes are regular weight. Budget the words before the size. Characters per line ≈ line width ÷ (size × k), with k ≈ 0.40 condensed, 0.50 most faces, 0.58 wide or caps, so a two-line headline at 44 px on a 390 px phone holds about 32 characters (four to six words). Over that, cut words before shrinking type. Product UI never gets this scale ([[dashboard-tells]]).

## Pairing and count

Two faces cover most products; three is the ceiling. Pair across categories (serif display over sans text), never within. Two lookalike grotesques read as a version-control accident. Weights and sizes obey the same economy: each exists to mark hierarchy, and stacking too many erases the distinctions they were meant to draw. Two families at the same `font-size` rarely look the same size — x-height decides — so re-tune sizes when swapping faces and match the fallback stack's x-height to avoid a jolt on load.

## When to apply

Setting up a project's type; any "text feels cramped here, airy there" complaint (one-off sizes are the cause); any live number; any font-loading diff.

## Reference

A closed product-UI scale taken from Stageshow's list row, with the page scale beside it:

| Role | Desktop | iOS list row | Leading |
|---|---|---|---|
| Row title | 12px, 600 | 17px | 16px (22px on iOS) |
| Subtitle | 11.5px | 15px | 16px (20px on iOS); 2px gap under the title (0 on iOS) |
| Metadata | 11px | 15px | 16px (22px on iOS) |
| Tile copy (page type, outside the picture) | 17 to 24px | same | 24px at 17px |
| Stat | 48 to 72px, unit on the same line | same | 1 |

- Bad: 10px names, 8.5px timestamps and an 18px button to fit more rows. Good: 14px names, 12px metadata, fewer rows.
- Benji's call differs on units inside a product shot: faux-app text and its leading are set in px at the product's real size and the stage scales it. Keep `rem` and unitless leading for the page.

Gold example: `stageshow/kit/parts/Row.css` (the scale tokens) and the style-tiny pair in `stageshow/teaching/style.tsx`.

Check: count the distinct font sizes on screen; each one should map to a role in the table. Then film at 390px. Nothing is under 10px, and no window text sits at 16px just because nothing sized it (the gate's `unsized text:` line).

## Gotcha

Never change font weight on hover or selection. The text reflows by a pixel and the layout shifts. Hold weight constant and signal state with color; if emphasis must move, use a variable axis at the same advance width.

# Typography humanity

Inter and SF Pro are the AI defaults. They are well-designed, neutral, and so widely used that they have become invisible. That's not a virtue — it's a tell.

## What "default" looks like

If a landing page uses Inter Variable from Google Fonts at the standard weights with the standard tracking, the page is competing with every other AI-generated page that did the same thing. Even if the layout is otherwise good, the typeface signals "default."

## Better choices

- **PangramPangram** — Object Sans, Pangram Sans, Pangram Sans Rounded. Free for personal use.
- **Displaay** — Grato, Migra, Neulis. Editorial energy.
- **Grilli Type** — GT Walsheim, GT America, GT Maru. Swiss, considered.
- **Søren Sprogø** — open-runde (free). Geometric with personality.
- **Vercel Geist** — Geist Sans, Geist Mono. Now widely used, but still better than Inter.
- **GitHub Mona** — well-tuned, less common.

## The single-weight rule

For a project's first iteration, buy or download **one weight** of a paid font (the variable family if you need ranges). Use it for headings, body, everything. Pair with the system default for fallback.

This is faster, cheaper, and produces better hierarchy through size and spacing alone. Add weights only when a real need arises.

- **Monospace is not personality.** Keep it for code, identifiers and aligned numbers; a technical product's labels set in mono read as costume.

## When to apply

Anytime you reach for Inter, SF Pro, Roboto, or "system-ui" on a marketing page — stop and pick something else. For in-app product UI, Inter / SF Pro are *fine* (they're optimized for screen UI), but if you do use them, you've used your one default. Don't also use the default colors and the default Lucide icons.

## Reference

The chosen face belongs to the page. A picture of a product uses that product's own faces:

| Surface | Face |
|---|---|
| Page: hero, tile copy | one chosen face, one weight, per the rule above |
| Inside a Notion shot | `ui-sans-serif, -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", Helvetica, sans-serif` |
| Inside a Wikipedia shot | `'Linux Libertine', 'Georgia', 'Times', serif` for the title, a sans stack for the interface |
| Code, IDs, aligned figures | `"SF Mono", "SFMono-Regular", ui-monospace, Consolas, monospace` |

- Bad: a faux Notion window set in GT Walsheim to look designed. Good: Notion's stack, with the humanity coming from the page type around it.
- Benji's call differs inside product shots: there the default system stack is correct, because the product uses it.

Gold example: `stageshow/examples/wikipedia/wiki.css` (the product's real serif and sans together) and `stageshow/examples/notion/notion.css`.

Check: hide the logo and the name. If the page type could belong to any product in its category, the face is still a default.

## Gotcha

Custom typography on tiny UI text (10–12px) often loses legibility. Geometric sans like Walsheim or Pangram look great at 14px+ but mush at 10px. Test at every size you actually use. Inter exists because it's hyper-legible at 12px — sometimes that wins.

See also [[line-length-tracking]] for the rules around how to *use* whichever font you pick.

## Sources

- guidelines.sh — "Inter/SF Pro are AI defaults; explore PangramPangram, Displaay, Grillitype."
- Emil Kowalski / Vercel Geist — single-weight workflows.
- Benji Taylor, Stageshow 1.1.1 (MIT, github.com/benjitaylor/skills, HEAD `299140f`, read 2026-11-07): `stageshow/references/craft.md` (Type: one family, monospace only for code, identifiers and aligned numbers), `stageshow/kit/stage.css` (`--ss-font`, `--ss-mono`), `stageshow/examples/wikipedia/wiki.css`, `stageshow/examples/notion/notion.css`, `stageshow/references/review.md` (could it be any product in its category).
